🏠 Septic systems with no power, and greywater Find out now which kind of septic system you have (🖼️ tank cross-section, Compendium p. 68; Drain field). - Gravity (pipes slope down to the tank and drainfield) keeps working with no power (Texas AgriLife, p. 2). Flush with a bucket of used wash water (rule of thumb). - Pump tanks, sand filters, aerobic units, pressure or drip lines stop. The reserve may be only 80 gallons for a 3-bedroom house. Use water only to flush and wash hands, stop if drains slow, and stop all use in a long outage (Texas AgriLife, p. 3); switch to a bucket toilet. Many Josephine County homes on clay or serpentine have these (rule of thumb). With no pump trucks: a tank needs pumping when scum is within 6 in of the outlet or sludge within 12 in, normally every 3–5 years. Additives do nothing. Never pour grease, oil, solvents or paint down a drain (EPA SepticSmart, pp. 3, 4, 7); keep food scraps and wipes out too (rule of thumb). After a flood: don't use it until water has left every part, and don't pump a tank empty while the ground is soaked: it can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3–4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2
septic-systems-with-no-power-and-greywater

can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3–4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2 in under soil or mulch, 4 ft above groundwater, 100 ft from wells, and never onto edible parts of crops or root vegetables (🖼️ a simple system, DEQ p. 15). - A soak pit (🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 130) is 5–13 ft deep, filled with rocks, 6½ ft above the highest groundwater. Clay won't take it (Compendium, p. 150). On valley clay in winter, carry greywater to higher ground or use it to flush (rule of thumb). - Kitchen water: a barrel grease trap (gravel, then ashes or sand, burlap on top), cleaned every 2 days (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164; 🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 131; Grease trap). 📚 Go deeper: Texas AgriLife Septic Systems in Outages and Floods — which systems stop; EPA Homeowner's Guide to Septic Systems; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater.

🧼 Handwashing and water for hygiene Build a tippy tap (USAID, pp. 1–2): 1. Take a 1½-gallon (5 L) plastic jug with a handle. Warm the base of the handle over a candle, pinch it shut with pliers, and let it cool watertight. 2. With a candle-heated nail, make a small hole in the handle just above the seal, and two bigger holes in the back, halfway up, for the hanging string. 3. Hang it from a stick so the full jug tilts at 45°. Hang soap on a string under an upside-down tin can. Pull a string tied to the cap to tip water onto your hands. 4. Scrub the outside daily; clean the inside weekly. Put one within 16 ft (5 m) of every toilet and wherever food is made. No water? Rub hands with ash or alcohol hand rub (Compendium, p. 40). Sanitizer needs 60%+ alcohol and fails on visibly dirty hands (OSU, p. 4). See hand washing (🖼️ the steps, WHO/WEDC p. 40; 🖼️ WHO handwashing steps, MCPC pp. 51–53; 🖼️ field handwashing devices, FM 21-10 p. 139) and hand sanitizer. Wash hands before cooking, eating or feeding anyone, and after the toilet, caring for someone with diarrhea, cleaning a child's bottom, cleaning up feces or vomit, or touching a body (MSF Cholera, p. 46). How much water (WHO/WEDC, pp. 36–37): | Use | Per person
handwashing-and-water-for-hygiene

with diarrhea, cleaning a child's bottom, cleaning up feces or vomit, or touching a body (MSF Cholera, p. 46). How much water (WHO/WEDC, pp. 36–37): | Use | Per person per day | | Drinking | 2.5–3 L (about ¾ gal) | | Hygiene | 2–6 L | | Cooking | 3–6 L | | Bare survival, total | 7.5–15 L (2–4 gal) | | Minimum for real hygiene | 20 L (5 gal) | | A cholera patient | 60 L, plus 15 L for the carer | Enough water matters as much as safe water (Hesperian Ch 5, p. 3). 📚 Go deeper: Tippy-Tap — the picture guide; WHO/WEDC, p. 36 — water quantities; Army FM 21-10 — field hygiene for a group.

🧺 Dishes, laundry and periods Dishes: scrape scraps into a bucket for the chickens. Wash in hot soapy water (120–140 °F) and rinse. Then dip in boiling water for 10 seconds, or in 1 Tbsp unscented bleach per gallon, and air-dry (FM 21-10, p. 114; OSU EM9273, p. 3). Laundry: soap and cold water don't get rid of lice. Wash clothes and bedding above 140 °F (60 °C), then iron or dry in full sun (Rozendaal, p. 274). No hot water? Seal them in a plastic bag for 72 hours for scabies, or 2 weeks for head-lice items (MSF Clinical Guidelines, pp. 133, 136). Never wash a sick person's clothes in a creek or any drinking source (MSF Cholera, p. 46). Periods: a year's supply per woman is 6 reusable pads (or 4 m² of absorbent cotton), 6 pairs of underwear, and an extra 250 g (½ lb) of soap a month (Sphere, p. 129). Change cloth pads (🖼️ pattern, WASHplus) several times a day, wash with soap and dry in the sun. Change a tampon at least 3 times a day, or it can cause serious infection (WWHND ch. 5, p. 4). Plan a private place to wash and dry pads by the latrine (Compendium, p. 44). 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus pad pattern — sew your own; FM 21-10, p. 114 — dishwashing setup; Make-Do guide — laundry soap

dry pads by the latrine (Compendium, p. 44). 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus pad pattern — sew your own; FM 21-10, p. 114 — dishwashing setup; Make-Do guide — laundry soap and hand washing.

🦠 How germs spread, and stopping an outbreak The "F-diagram" (fecal–oral route): germs from feces reach the mouth by fingers, flies, fields, fluids (water) and food. Every barrier counts: latrines, handwashing, safe water, covered food, animals kept out of the house (Hesperian Ch 5, p. 6; WTND ch. 12, p. 3; 🖼️ the barriers drawn, WHO/WEDC p. 39; 🖼️ SEI p. 12). An outbreak is starting when you see bloody diarrhea, watery diarrhea in anyone over 5, suspected cholera, or yellow eyes or skin in several people. Start isolation and hygiene measures neighborhood-wide (WHO, p. 115). "Enteric isolation" (cholera, shigella dysentery, typhoid, E. coli, hepatitis A) means handwashing, the sick person's own dishes, and safe disposal of their feces and soiled things (WHO, p. 133). - Typhoid: a separate room; stools buried deep. People who recover can carry it for a long time and must not cook for others (WTND ch. 14, p. 12). - Hepatitis A and E: antibiotics don't help, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) further damages the liver (WTND ch. 13, p. 22). Isolate kindly (WHO, p. 132): let one family member care for each sick person, with gloves and an apron and a lesson in using them. Explain isolation to everyone. Shame and fear make people hide sick relatives, and hidden cases spread the outbreak. Rehydration drink (WTND ch. 13, p. 2; oral rehydration; 🖼️ drawn, Hesperian Ch
how-germs-spread-and-stopping-an-outbreak

isolation to everyone. Shame and fear make people hide sick relatives, and hidden cases spread the outbreak. Rehydration drink (WTND ch. 13, p. 2; oral rehydration; 🖼️ drawn, Hesperian Ch 5, p. 10): 1 litre (about 1 quart) of clean water and ½ level teaspoon salt. Taste it: it must be less salty than tears. Then add 8 level teaspoons sugar. Keep giving food and breast milk. Cholera or bloody diarrhea in the house (MSF Cholera, pp. 46–48): 1. Wipe up vomit or feces first, put it in the latrine or bury it, then wash the spot with soap. 2. Wash the sick person's clothes and bedding with soap and dry them in the sun. Sun the mattress too: the cholera germ dies when dried. 3. Don't spray whole houses with chlorine. No study shows it helps, and it makes families hide cases. A kit of bucket, soap, detergent and cloths does more. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Communicable Disease Control in Emergencies — isolation and disease pages; MSF Management of a Cholera Epidemic — household rules.

🧪 Chlorine strengths from household bleach These are for cleaning — never for drinking. Even the weakest (0.05%) is far too strong to drink. To make drinking water safe, use 8 drops of 6% bleach (6 drops of 8.25%) per gallon and wait 30 minutes (Water Purification guide; EPA, p. 2). | Strength | Use it for (Compendium, p. 174) | From 6% bleach | From 8.25% bleach | | 0.05% | Skin and hands (if no soap), laundry, latrines, kitchen | About 2 Tbsp per gallon | About 1½ Tbsp per gallon | | 0.2% | Floors, beds, clothes, objects | About ½ cup per gallon | About 6 Tbsp per gallon | | 2% | Feces, vomit, washing bodies | 1 part bleach + 2 parts water | 1 part bleach + 3 parts water | The rule is parts of water = (bleach % ÷ % wanted) − 1 (MSF Cholera, p. 226); the amounts above are that arithmetic. - Read the strength on the label; use plain, unscented bleach. - Mix fresh every day, and clean first: bleach doesn't work through dirt. - Never pour it into a urine bucket or mix it with ammonia or vinegar. - Drinking water needs a far weaker dose: see the Water Purification guide. 📚 Go deeper: MSF Cholera, p. 226 — dilution tables; Compendium, p. 174 — cholera disinfection.

🪰 Flies, mosquitoes, lice and scabies Flies (housefly) go from egg to adult in 6–42 days, faster in heat (Rozendaal, p. 314; 🖼️ the fly and its life cycle, p. 315). In hot weather empty and bury garbage at least twice a week: maggots leave closed bins after 3–4 days. Cover a garbage pit with fresh soil at least weekly; fit latrines with tight lids or screened vents (p. 321; 🖼️ tight-lidded bins, p. 321; 🖼️ a fly- and mosquito-proof latrine lid, p. 160). June–September is peak fly season here (rule of thumb). Mosquitoes take about 7–13 days from egg to adult, so empty and scrub small water containers weekly, and cover barrels with tight lids or netting (Rozendaal, pp. 23, 156; 🖼️ mosquito life cycle, p. 22; 🖼️ lids and netting, p. 156; Mosquito). Ditches, stock tanks, old tires and open rain barrels breed them here, and West Nile virus has been found in southern Oregon (rule of thumb) (West Nile virus; Culex tarsalis). Body lice (body louse) live and lay eggs in clothing seams, and spread typhus, relapsing fever and trench fever. Hot washing and ironing fix it; in an outbreak, dust 0.5% permethrin powder inside clothes (Rozendaal, p. 274; 🖼️ how to dust clothing, p. 275; MSF Clinical, p. 136). Head lice (🖼️ the three kinds of lice, Rozendaal p. 266; 🖼️ checking hair and combing, pp.
flies-mosquitoes-lice-and-scabies

p. 274; 🖼️ how to dust clothing, p. 275; MSF Clinical, p. 136). Head lice (🖼️ the three kinds of lice, Rozendaal p. 266; 🖼️ checking hair and combing, pp. 268–271): dimeticone (from age 6 months) or 1% permethrin (from 2 months) lotion, repeated after 7 days; treat only contacts with live lice or nits (same page). Scabies (🖼️ the mite and an infested wrist, Rozendaal pp. 291–292; Sarcoptes scabiei): itching worse at night, with fine wavy burrows between the fingers and on the wrists. Treat everyone in close contact at the same time, even if they don't itch: permethrin 5% cream (age 2 months and up) left on 8 hours, repeated after 7 days. Wash bedding hot or bag it 72 hours (MSF Clinical, pp. 133–134). A first-time rash can take 4–6 weeks to show, so one case means others are probably infested already (Rozendaal, p. 292). Stock permethrin and dimeticone now (rule of thumb). Ticks (western black-legged tick) are in the Make-Do guide. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Vector Control (Rozendaal) — flies, mosquitoes, lice, fleas and mites; MSF Clinical Guidelines, p. 133 — scabies and lice treatment.

🐭 Mice, hantavirus, fleas and plague Hantavirus: in the West the deer mouse carries it, and people usually catch it by breathing dust from droppings. Illness starts 1–8 weeks later with fever, aches and vomiting; 4–10 days after that comes shortness of breath. There is no specific treatment (NPS, p. 1). Woodsheds, cabins, root cellars and barns here all hold deer mice (rule of thumb). Keep them out: seal every gap wider than ¼ in (🖼️ gaps around pipes, USDA p. 18), keep food and trash sealed, and keep plants 18 in from walls (NPS, p. 1). Use snap traps (Mousetrap) or cats, not poison, which kills pets and children (WTND ch. 14, p. 12). Cleaning up droppings (NPS, p. 2): 1. Open the windows and leave for 30 minutes. Never sweep or vacuum. 2. With gloves on, soak droppings, nests and dead mice with 1:10 bleach (about 1½ cups per gallon of water), mixed fresh that day. Spray 2 ft around, and wait at least 10 minutes. 3. Wipe up with paper towels. Pick up dead mice with a bag turned inside out over your gloved hand. Double-bag everything. 4. Spray the gloves before taking them off, then wash your hands with soap. Fleas and plague): flea cocoons can wait up to a year in an empty house and hatch all at once when people move in (Rozendaal, p.
mice-hantavirus-fleas-and-plague

your hands with soap. Fleas and plague): flea cocoons can wait up to a year in an empty house and hatch all at once when people move in (Rozendaal, p. 256; 🖼️ rat, human and cat fleas, p. 255; Oriental rat flea). Don't handle dead rats or squirrels: their fleas jump to people. Drown dead rats, then burn them (WTND ch. 14, p. 12), or bury them deep in fire season. Plague lives in wild ground squirrels (California ground squirrel), chipmunks and their fleas in parts of Oregon. Keep cats from hunting, and treat a cat with a swollen neck or fever as dangerous (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Hantavirus Fact Sheet — cleanup steps; USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 27 — keeping rodents out.

🗑️ Garbage when no truck comes Open trash piles breed rats, flies and mosquitoes, and their chemicals seep into soil and water (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 5); heaps catch fire, and rain washes them into water supplies (WHO/WEDC, p. 27). So make less, and sort it in the kitchen into two or three bins (🖼️ Hesperian Ch 18, p. 13). A household garbage pit or trench - Where: 100 ft (30 m) from wells, springs and creeks, downhill of them, the bottom 5 ft above groundwater (Sphere, p. 140), 100 ft from the kitchen (FM 21-10, p. 129), and on higher ground, dug in the dry season, as for latrines. - A pit is 4 ft square and 4 ft deep, filled to 1 ft below ground and mounded over with earth (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164; 🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 129). Cover each layer with 4 in of soil or ash, and a full pit with 20 in (WHO/WEDC, p. 29). - A trench lasts longer: 2 ft wide, 3–4 ft deep, filled to within 1 ft of the top and dug onward, the new dirt covering the last load (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164). - In the wet months, dig a small new hole each week or month and roof it against rain (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 29). Fence it, and keep it deep enough that animals can't dig in (WWHND ch. 10, p. 4).
a-household-garbage-pit-or-trench

A shared neighborhood dump Country garbage usually goes into family or shared neighborhood pits (WHO/WEDC, p. 28). A shared one needs: 1. A site 820 ft (250 m) from streams and ponds and 1,640 ft (500 m) from homes and wells, out of any flood zone, its bottom 6½ ft (2 m) above the highest groundwater (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 27). 2. A fence with a locking gate, sand or soil kept there for fires (🖼️ p. 28), and no open flames (WHO/WEDC, p. 28). 3. Each load pressed down and covered with soil, or soil, ash and sand, under a roof (Hesperian p. 29). 4. One person or team in charge, with gloves, boots, masks, overalls and tetanus shots (WHO/WEDC p. 28). 5. When full, a cap of 3 ft (90 cm) of soil, planted with grass, never food plants, and no grazing until it's grown over (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 29). Circles of dead grass mean landfill gas: keep 33 ft (10 m) away (p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: Hesperian Ch 18 Solid Waste — reducing, sorting, reusing, landfills; WHO/WEDC Technical Note 7, p. 27 — solid waste in emergencies.

🌱 Composting food, yard waste and manure A hot pile reaches 130–150 °F, which kills most weed seeds and germs; a slow pile kills far fewer (WSU EB1784E, p. 2, written for the Northwest; Compost). Building a hot pile (WSU, pp. 3–6): 1. Collect at least 1 cubic yard at once: a heap 5 ft wide and 3 ft high, or a bin 3 × 3 × 3 ft of pallets, lumber, wire mesh or blocks (pp. 4–5). Small piles stay cold. 2. Mix 1 part "greens" to 2 parts "browns" by volume (p. 3). Greens are wet and rich in nitrogen (p. 2): food scraps, fresh manure (Hesperian Ch 18, pp. 17–18). Browns are dry: straw, brown leaves, husks, shredded paper (p. 18), wood chips (WSU p. 3). 3. Squeeze a handful: barely a drop should come out. Too dry, add water; too wet, add browns (p. 5). 4. Turn it weekly for 4–6 weeks, and cover it in rainy weather, or in a wet winter it may never heat (pp. 4–5). 5. After several hot weeks it cures 2–3 months. It's ready when turning no longer heats it and it looks dark and crumbly (p. 6). Rotting instead of heating? Add browns. Smells? Turn it for air. Flies? Cover it better with soil (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Slow pile: heap yard waste for a year, tucking scraps
composting-food-yard-waste-and-manure

of heating? Add browns. Smells? Turn it for air. Flies? Cover it better with soil (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Slow pile: heap yard waste for a year, tucking scraps into the middle, then turn it and leave it a second year (WSU, pp. 4–5; 🖼️ two-pile system, p. 5). It won't kill weed seeds or germs, so pull weeds before they seed (p. 5). Worm bin (vermicompost): 1 cubic foot of bin, no more than 1 ft deep, per pound of scraps a week (a 14-gallon tote suits 2–3 people); outdoors, on the north side of a building, safe from rats and raccoons (OSU EM 9034, pp. 2–3; 🖼️ p. 4). Keep out: meat, bones, fish, grease and dairy, which draw pests and bears (WSU, p. 6; ODFW, p. 2). Bury fruit and vegetable scraps fully inside the pile, or use a pest-proof bin (🖼️ WSU, p. 5). Also keep out dog and cat feces (WSU p. 7), plastic, metal, glass and poisonous plants (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Human waste: see "Composting toilets, humanure and urine". Manure can carry Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7: give manure compost a year or more before it goes on root crops, lettuce or strawberries. Bought hay or straw may carry clopyralid or aminopyralid weed killers that pass into manure and harm tomatoes, potatoes and beans: ask the grower (WSU, p. 7). Cover

or strawberries. Bought hay or straw may carry clopyralid or aminopyralid weed killers that pass into manure and harm tomatoes, potatoes and beans: ask the grower (WSU, p. 7). Cover dung heaps with plastic so the heat kills fly maggots (🖼️ Rozendaal, p. 320). 🐻 Garbage, bears and pests Oregon has 25,000–30,000 black bears; one that gets human food or garbage loses its fear of people and often has to be killed (ODFW Living with Black Bears, p. 1; American black bear). "Do not bury garbage or fish refuse; bears will dig it up" (p. 2). A homestead still needs a pit, so keep every food smell out of it, cover each layer, and fence it, with electric wire whenever bears are about (rule of thumb). Around the house (ODFW, p. 2): keep garbage cans in a shed or behind chain-link or electric fence, scrubbed with bleach. ODFW also suggests mothballs: don't, they poison children and pets (rule of thumb). Electric-fence compost, gardens, orchards, berries and hives; pick up fallen fruit; feed pets indoors; lock up livestock feed, since plastic tubs won't stop a bear (BearWise, p. 1); and ask the neighbors to do the same. Electric fence for bears (BearWise, p. 2; Electric fence): - At least 3 wires (5 or 6 is better), 8–10 in apart: lowest 7–9 in up (a little lower stops skunks and raccoons too), top 36–42 in. - An energizer of at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joules; plants kept off the wires; voltage tested often. - Step-by-step photos: "Honey, wax, bears and stings" in the Goats, Dairy & Bees guide (🖼️ UF, pp. 3–5). Cougars: leave no
garbage-bears-and-pests

plants kept off the wires; voltage tested often. - Step-by-step photos: "Honey, wax, bears and stings" in the Goats, Dairy & Bees guide (🖼️ UF, pp. 3–5). Cougars: leave no food or garbage outside; anything that draws other wildlife can draw a cougar, and so can animal kills (ODFW, p. 2). Raccoons that learn the garbage cans go after the poultry next (Kentucky ID-245, p. 2). Rats: "Neatness is of prime importance": covered cans, a deep covered pit for tin cans, lumber on racks 18 in high, woodpiles and manure piles away from food (USDA Rat Proofing, p. 6). Deer mice: see "Mice, hantavirus, fleas and plague". Flies breed mostly in garbage, then rotting grass clippings and compost (Rozendaal, pp. 316–317), and spread dysentery, typhoid and cholera (p. 319). Empty and clean bins twice a week in hot weather, weekly in cool, scraping out the bottom (p. 321); more in "Flies, mosquitoes, lice and scabies". 📚 Go deeper: ODFW Living with Black Bears, p. 2 — the homeowner's checklist; BearWise, p. 2 — electric fence facts.

🔥 Burning trash and brush, and ash Oregon bans burning these in the open, anywhere, any time, and a burn barrel counts as open burning (DEQ Southern Oregon Outdoor Burning Guide, p. 1): plastic, rubber, tires (even to start a fire), wet garbage and food waste, dead animals, oil and anything petroleum-treated, asphalt, auto parts, asbestos, and anything making dense smoke or foul odors. Plastic smoke carries dioxins, furans and PCBs (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 24). Never burn treated wood, even in a stove: its smoke and ash carry poisons (Wood Handbook, p. 329) such as arsenic (ATSDR, p. 1); nor old paint (lead: Shelter guide), batteries, bulbs or chemicals (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 25). Every 3 bags burned still leave about 1 bag of toxic ash (Hesperian Ch 19, p. 6). When: DEQ allows open burning in the Rogue Valley only outside fire season, on burn days; Josephine County's burn-day line is 541-476-9663, and fire districts can still say no (DEQ, pp. 1–2). With nobody to ask: no open burning June–October (rule of thumb), and otherwise only on wet, calm days, in daylight (OSU EC 1574, p. 4). A burn barrel, for dry paper, cardboard and clean wood only: 1. Cut both ends out of a 55-gallon drum, punch many holes near the bottom, fit a grate a few inches above them, and raise it on stones or bricks

1. Cut both ends out of a 55-gallon drum, punch many holes near the bottom, fit a grate a few inches above them, and raise it on stones or bricks so air gets under (🖼️ Special Forces Handbook, p. 165). 2. Top it with a lid or screen with holes no bigger than ¾ in, clear 10 ft of ground around it, and keep a hose or extinguisher ready (FEMA, p. 126). 3. Cover one when 80% built so it stays dry for a winter burn, and pull the plastic off before lighting: OSU says a polyethylene cover may burn

💉 Sickroom and birth waste From Hesperian Ch 19, pp. 21–22: - Needles and blades go in a hard, sealed container (🖼️ Hesperian Ch 19, p. 17; Sharps waste). - Dig a waste pit 165 ft (50 m) from water and buildings, downhill from wells, its bottom 5 ft above the water table. - After each load, cover with 4 in of soil, or soil mixed with lime. - When it's 20 in from the top, cover with 20 in of soil and seal with 4–12 in (10–30 cm) of concrete (🖼️ the finished pit, p. 22). - A placenta can go into the latrine or a deep burial (p. 12). 📚 Go deeper: Hesperian Ch 19 Health Care Waste — building the waste pit.

🐄 Dead animals and gut piles Move a dead animal at once: carcasses draw predators (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6), and botulism poison builds up in maggots on dead birds, which chickens eat (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 70). Oregon law, while enforced: a carcass within ½ mile of a home or ¼ mile of a running stream must be dealt with within 15 hours of death or discovery, and may not be burned in the open (ODA Livestock Mortality, pp. 1, 3). Could it be anthrax? If an animal died suddenly with dark blood from the nose, mouth or anus, don't cut it open: the spores foul the soil for good (Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 215). People catch it too. Keep dogs and scavengers off, and bury it unopened, where it lies, deep, under quicklime (Zoonoses, pp. 69–70; Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 108). Zoonoses would rather burn it in a pit, with old tires for heat (p. 69): never burn tires, and Oregon bans burning carcasses (DEQ, p. 1). Burying a carcass (Oregon's recommendations, ODA, pp. 1–2): - A dry hole bottom: never soggy, flooded or floodplain ground, and groundwater 25 ft below it. Valley clay is wet 2–3 ft down in winter (Soil Survey, p. 33), so bury on higher ground. - 500 ft from creeks, ponds and wells where you can, never under 100 ft; 300

2–3 ft down in winter (Soil Survey, p. 33), so bury on higher ground. - 500 ft from creeks, ponds and wells where you can, never under 100 ft; 300 ft from a neighbor's house and 50 ft from a property line, on nearly flat ground. - Lime under the carcass and dusted on top (it cuts smell and seepage), sod and manure around it, and 3–4 ft of soil over it, mounded for settling and topped up as it sinks. More than 3 ft (1 m) keeps dogs from digging it up (WTNAD, p. 229). Lime is for animals; for people, see "Caring for the dead". - No more than 1,000 lb per hole, except one bigger animal; over 4,200 lb needs an ODA plan or DEQ permit. Put down by a vet, or shot with lead: the usual euthanasia drug, pentobarbital, poisons eagles, hawks, ravens, bears, coyotes, cougars and dogs that eat the remains, and lead harms scavengers too (AVMA, p. 17). Bury these deep at once (if the ground is frozen, cover them securely until you can), and never leave one out for scavengers (ODA, p. 2), nor gut piles from lead-shot game (rule of thumb). ⚰️ Caring for the dead Bodies don't cause epidemics when people died of injury, fire, cold or hunger. The exceptions are deaths from cholera, Ebola-type fevers and similar infections (PAHO, p. 17). Handlers need waterproof gloves, an apron and boots, and must wash with soap before eating; masks aren't essential (p. 18; 🖼️ photo of the gear, p. 18). Burial (PAHO, p. 38; WHO/WEDC, p. 33): - An individual, marked grave 5–10 ft (1.5–3 m) deep, no lime or chemicals on the body (🖼️ wrapping a body for burial, WHO/WEDC p. 32). - At least 100 ft (30 m) from springs or streams and 650 ft (200 m) from any well. - At least 4 ft between the grave bottom and the water table (5 ft in sand). With our valley clay wet 2–3 ft down in winter, choose higher, well-drained ground, and choose it now (rule of thumb). - Record who is buried where, on a map and with a durable marker. After a cholera death (MSF Cholera, pp. 47–48): bury within 24 hours, near the place of death, more than 165 ft (50 m) from water, under at least 3 ft of soil. Wash hands after touching the body. Funeral meals cooked by people who handled the body spread cholera. Let families keep their customs with these hygiene rules; banning funerals makes people hide deaths (p. 48). While

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - The "burn-out latrine", burned daily with 1 qt gasoline to 5 qt diesel (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162). It wastes fuel and risks burns and wildfire; the same page admits burning and lime don't stop flies or smell. Use a lidded pit, VIP or bucket toilet, with ash. - Spraying latrine pits with insecticide twice a week (same page). Use tight lids, screened vents and ash. - DDT and lindane for lice, scabies and spraying (Rozendaal, pp. 274, 293). Obsolete and toxic. Use permethrin or dimeticone. - Tossing each day's waste bag outside (Kearny, p. 108). Fine for two weeks in a fallout shelter; for long-term living, bury or compost the bags. - Boiling laundry "with soap and kerosene" (Household Discoveries, p. 191). Fire and fume hazard. Use hot soapy water and sun. - Concrete "at least 90 centimeters thick" over a waste pit (A Book for Midwives, p. 22). Almost certainly a misprint: Hesperian says 10–30 cm (Ch 19, p. 22). - Lime on dead bodies. PAHO says don't (p. 38). Lime does help dry and disinfect waste in compost toilets and sickroom-waste pits. - Latrines only 65 ft (20 m) from water (WTND ch. 12, p. 9; Hesperian Ch 7, p. 18). Sphere, the Army and Oregon use 100 ft. Use 100. - Burning "cleaned plastic containers" (Rozendaal, p.

m) from water (WTND ch. 12, p. 9; Hesperian Ch 7, p. 18). Sphere, the Army and Oregon use 100 ft. 🚰 Water Purification — With What You Have How to make creek, spring, rain or well water safe to drink when there's no store and no power: settling and straining, homemade sand, biosand and clay-pot filters, charcoal (what it does and doesn't do), boiling, bleach and pool shock, sunlight, solar stills, simple tests, and safe storage. The manuals are in Water-Purification\ (Filters-Sand-Charcoal-Ceramic, Disinfection, Settling-Coagulation, Overviews-Testing), Water\ and Homestead-Skills\Sanitation-Water. Getting the water out of the ground is in the Wells & Pumps guide. ### The four rules of safe water 1. Clear it, then kill the germs. Settle or filter muddy water first; then boil or disinfect. 2. Charcoal and sand filters alone do NOT make water safe. They clear water and improve taste; charcoal beds even grow bacteria and shield them from chlorine. Charcoal goes last, after disinfection (WHO, pp. 51–52; Wilderness Medical Society, p. 6). 3. Boiling kills germs but removes no chemicals — not fuel, metals, salt or fire-retardant runoff. 4. Keep treated water clean: covered container with a spout, never dip a cup into it.

🫙 Step 1 — Clear the water - Let it settle. Three-pot method: fill pot 1 from the source; each day pour pot 1 gently into pot 2, and pot 2 into pot 3 (your drinking pot) — water sits at least 2 days and much of the dirt and some germs settle out. Still disinfect it (CAWST, p. 4). - Strain through cloth: old, soft cotton folded 7–8 times catches particles bigger than about 20 microns — silt, worms, the plankton cholera rides on — but not bacteria or viruses. Wash the cloth after each use (CAWST, pp. 14–15; 🖼️ photo of a folded-cloth filter, p. 14). - Make the mud drop (coagulants): - Alum (pickling alum): about ⅛ tsp per gallon; stir fast 1 minute, slowly 5 minutes, settle at least 30 minutes, pour off through cloth (WMS, p. 7; how the mud clumps). - Wood ash, lime, crushed beans also work as rough coagulants (same source). - Moringa seed: about 1 crushed kernel per liter of muddy water — shake the paste in a cup of water, strain it in, stir 1 minute fast and 5–10 minutes slow, settle 1–2 hours (ECHO note; WEDC, p. 3). Moringa won't grow here (frost) — stockpile seed if you want it. - Coagulants clear water; they don't make it safe. Always disinfect afterward. - Is it clear enough? Look down

Look down through a clear 2-liter bottle of the water at large print — if you can read it, it's under about 50 NTU, clear enough for filters. Biosand filter (best household filter you can build) A concrete or plastic box of sand with a living layer on top (the "schmutzdecke") that eats germs (CAWST Biosand Construction Manual; 🖼️ labeled cut-away, p. 17): - Layers, bottom to top: 2 in of drainage gravel (¼–½ in), 2 in of small gravel, then fine washed sand (0.7 mm or finer) filled with water already in the box so no air gets trapped (pp. 59, 92; 🖼️ filling it, step by step, p. 92). - About 2 in of water must stand above the sand when it stops flowing — more starves the living layer of air; letting it dry out kills it. A diffuser plate keeps poured water from digging up the top (pp. 18–19; 🖼️ the standing-water level drawn, p. 24). - Use it every day, one bucket (12–18 L) at a time, 6–12 hours apart. The living layer takes up to 30 days to grow — disinfect the output until then and always for babies and the sick. When flow gets slow, stir the top inch and scoop off the dirty water ("swirl and dump") (CAWST Fact Sheets, pp. 18–19; 🖼️ swirl-and-dump drawings). - Results once mature: bacteria about 88–98% removed in the field, Giardia-type parasites over 99.9%, viruses less reliable (p. 19). - Cold winter water slows the living layer — filter slower and disinfect (EPA slow

about 88–98% removed in the field, Giardia-type parasites over 99.9%, viruses less reliable (p. 19). - Cold winter water slows the living layer — filter slower and disinfect (EPA slow sand, p. 9).

Slow sand filter (for a group or homestead) The same idea, bigger: water trickles down through about 3 ft of fine sand at 0.1–0.2 m per hour; build two beds so one can be cleaned (scrape off the top inch). A mature filter removes 95–100% of fecal bacteria and nearly all viruses and cysts. Takes about 3 weeks to "ripen" when new (IRC Slow Sand Filtration, pp. 38, 48; 🖼️ parts of a slow sand filter, p. 32).
slow-sand-filter-for-a-group-or-homestead

The bucket "layer filter" — gravel, sand, charcoal A bucket of gravel, sand and charcoal clears and improves water but is not a germ barrier. The right way to use charcoal is the three-stage system: gravel roughing filter → slow sand biofilter (germs) → crushed charcoal (chemicals and taste) → covered storage; replace the charcoal yearly (Aqueous Solutions Biochar Water Filter, pp. 2–9; 🖼️ the three-drum layout, p. 2; 🖼️ what goes in each drum, p. 9).
the-bucket-layer-filter--gravel-sand-charcoal

Clay pot (ceramic) filter Clay mixed with sawdust or rice husk (about 50:50 by volume to start) is pressed into a pot and fired to about 900 °C (1,650 °F) — the sawdust burns out and leaves tiny pores (CMWG Ceramic Pot Filters, p. 62; RDIC handbook). It sits in a covered bucket with a tap (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ Potters for Peace filter) and gives 1–3 liters an hour. Test local clay first (clay testing); flow-test each pot (at least 1 liter in the first hour, not too fast — too fast means cracks) (CMWG, p. 114). They work best with a colloidal silver coating, which you can't make from raw materials — without it, still disinfect. Replace every 1–2 years or when cracked. Kiln plans: Mani kiln (🖼️ cut-away drawing, p. 3). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Biosand Filter Construction Manual; IRC Slow Sand Filtration; CMWG ceramic filter manual; Wikipedia: biosand filter · slow sand filter · ceramic water filter.
clay-pot-ceramic-filter

⚫ Charcoal: making it and using it right - What it does: soaks up taste, odor and many organic chemicals (pesticides, some fuel residues). What it doesn't: reliably remove germs — WHO doesn't recommend it for germs, and bacteria grow in the bed (WHO, pp. 51–52). - Plain vs. activated: ordinary charcoal has its pores clogged with tar, so it adsorbs poorly. Factories "activate" it by heating to about 800 °C in steam, which opens the pores (FAO Industrial Charcoal Making, p. 28). - Homemade water-treatment charcoal (Aqueous Solutions Char Drum Oven): 1. Pack dry wood pieces (1–2 in thick) tightly in a steel drum, set a chimney drum on top, and light it from the top (🖼️ the stacked drums). It burns about 2 hours down to faint blue flames (🖼️ flame colors). 2. Quench with plenty of water (🖼️ photo) — the steam partly opens the pores (crude activation, not true activated carbon). 3. Crush and sieve to 1–5 mm pieces; wash out the dust. - Use it as the LAST step after the water is filtered and disinfected, or in a column after a sand filter; replace it yearly. Hardwood (oak, madrone) makes good charcoal. Chemical activation (acids, zinc chloride) isn't a safe home method (rule of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief (🖼️ a portable metal kiln, p. 3) and the Peace Corps charcoal
charcoal-making-it-and-using-it-right

(acids, zinc chloride) isn't a safe home method (rule of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief (🖼️ a portable metal kiln, p. 3) and the Peace Corps charcoal manual. 📚 Go deeper: FAO — what activated charcoal is, p. 28; Aqueous Solutions — charcoal oven; Wikipedia: activated carbon.
charcoal-making-it-and-using-it-right

🔥 Step 3 — Kill the germs Boiling — the surest method. A rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft — we're far below that) kills bacteria, viruses and parasites even in cloudy water. Let it cool covered; don't add ice (WHO Boil Water, p. 1; OSU, p. 5). Fuel cost: about 0.2 kg (½ lb) of wood per liter — a family's 4 gallons a day is about 7 lb of wood a day (WHO Bulletin, p. 4) — see the Firewood guide. Bleach (plain unscented, 6–8.25% sodium hypochlorite) — EPA, p. 1: | Water | 6% bleach | 8.25% bleach | | 1 quart, clear | 2 drops | 2 drops | | 1 gallon, clear | 8 drops | 6 drops | | 1 gallon, cloudy or very cold | 16 drops | 12 drops | Stir, wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine; if not, dose again and wait 15 more minutes. Cold water needs longer: 1 hour at 50–65 °F, 2+ hours below 50 °F — winter creek water (CAWST, p. 59). Bleach loses strength — use it within a year. Chlorine is weak against Cryptosporidium: settle or filter first. Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) — stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock
step-3-kill-the-germs

Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) — stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock to 100 parts water (1 pint per 12½ gallons), wait 30 minutes (EPA, p. 2). Use plain granules (no algaecide or stabilizer), mix outdoors with eye protection, and make stock in small batches — it lasts about a month in heat, longer cool and dark (CDC Safe Water Systems, p. 62). Iodine: 5 drops of 2% tincture per quart (10 if cloudy), wait 30 minutes (EPA, p. 2) — fine short-term (a month at most), never for pregnant women or anyone with thyroid disease or an iodine allergy (WMS, p. 14). Sunlight (SODIS): clear plastic (PET) bottles of clear water, lying flat in full sun 6 hours (2 days if more than half cloudy). Works well here March–September, poorly in the winter rains (EAWAG SODIS manual, p. 23; 🖼️ how-to drawings, p. 26; 🖼️ the home poster, p. 76). Solar pasteurizing: water held at 65 °C (150 °F) is pasteurized — a solar box cooker can do several gallons on a summer day (Ciochetti & Metcalf). A lump of beeswax in a sealed tube melts at about 62 °C — just under the target, so melted wax means "nearly there": keep it hot a while longer, or boil it, to
step-3-kill-the-germs

in a sealed tube melts at about 62 °C — just under the target, so melted wax means "nearly there": keep it hot a while longer, or boil it, to be sure (CAWST, p. 75). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water; CDC Safe Water Systems handbook — making and storing chlorine; Wilderness Medical Society guidelines; Wikipedia: SODIS.
step-3-kill-the-germs

☀️ Salty or chemical water: the solar still A shallow black basin under sloped glass or clear plastic: the sun evaporates the water, it condenses on the cover and runs into a gutter (🖼️ photos of stills, CAWST p. 71) — leaving salt, metals and germs behind. Expect about 1 gallon a day per 10–12 sq ft of glass (CAWST, p. 71; Aprovecho, p. 43). Some fuel-type chemicals can carry over (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST — solar distillation; Wikipedia: solar still.
salty-or-chemical-water-the-solar-still

🔬 Simple tests - Turbidity tube: a clear tube with a black-and-white disk at the bottom — pour water in until the disk disappears; the depth tells cloudiness (disk gone at 18 cm ≈ 50 NTU; at 85 cm ≈ 5 NTU) (Myre & Shaw, pp. 11–16; 🖼️ the parts, p. 7; 🖼️ finished tubes, p. 10; Secchi disk — the same idea in a lake). - H₂S bacteria test: a paper strip with a special medium in a bottle of water turns black in 1–2 days if fecal bacteria are present — keep it warm (above 77 °F). Agreed with lab tests about 90% of the time; sulfur well water can give false alarms (WHO, pp. 16, 33; 🖼️ a test vial, CAWST; coliform bacteria). The test bottles must be bought ahead. - Chlorine check: a faint chlorine smell 30 minutes after dosing means enough was added (🖼️ checking it with a color comparator). - Sanitary check: look at the source — animals, outhouses, runoff upstream? Fix the source first (CAWST Testing; 🖼️ how springs and wells get polluted). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Introduction to Drinking Water Quality Testing; Turbidity tube.
simple-tests

🪣 Storing water safely - Covered container with a tap or narrow spout, opaque, easy to clean; never put untreated water in it; clean it with soap or chlorine; keep it off the ground in shade; pour, don't dip (CAWST, pp. 83–84; 🖼️ safe storage containers; 🖼️ a tap fitted to a bucket; jerrycan). - Don't reuse milk jugs — they can't be cleaned well (OSU, p. 2). - Chlorinated water keeps best; boiled water can be recontaminated — drink it within a day or two. 📚 Go deeper: CAWST — safe storage and handling, p. 83; CDC Safe Water Systems — choosing a storage vessel, p. 69; CAWST Biosand Manual — cleaning a storage container, p. 106.
storing-water-safely

🔥 After a wildfire Burned slopes send ash, metals, nitrate and organic chemicals into creeks after storms — levels jumped 10 to 10,000 times after a Colorado fire (USGS, p. 1). Boiling, chlorine, sunlight and sand or clay filters do not remove these. Fire-damaged plastic pipes can leach benzene, and boiling doesn't remove it (WQA). After a fire, prefer springs or wells outside the burn, or rainwater; distilling and charcoal are the only partial chemical barriers here. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Wildfire Effects on Source-Water Quality; OWRD — your well after wildfire.
after-a-wildfire

💧 Water Wells, Pumps, Springs & Cisterns How to keep water coming when the power is out for good: understanding your well, running the well pump from a generator or solar, getting water up by hand, moving creek water uphill with no fuel (ram pumps), developing a spring, catching rain in a cistern, and keeping it all clean. The manuals are in Water-Wells-Pumps\ (Wells, Pumps-No-Grid, Hand-Ram-Rope-Pumps, Springs-Cisterns, Water-Quality, Oregon) and Water\. Making water safe to drink is in the Water Purification guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst problems - Never pour outside water into a well and never leave a well open — one bucket of creek water or a drowned animal can contaminate it (OWRD Wells and Drought). - Well pumps run on 240 volts. Shut off the breaker before touching the pressure switch or wiring, and connect a generator only through a transfer switch — never backfeed. - Don't run a flooded pump until it's dry and checked (EPA). - Test the water — clear, cold water can still carry bacteria or arsenic.

🕳️ Know your well Three kinds of wells (USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner, pp. 16–17; 🖼️ all three drawn side by side, p. 15): - Dug wells: wide and shallow, often lined with rock or concrete rings. Easy to contaminate and the first to go dry in drought — but you can lower a bucket into them (🖼️ a lined dug well). - Driven wells (sand points): a pipe with a screened tip driven into shallow sand or gravel. Cheap, shallow, easily contaminated (🖼️ a well point; 🖼️ driving one by hand). - Drilled wells: a steel or plastic casing (usually 6 in) sealed into the ground, often hundreds of feet deep, with an electric submersible pump at the bottom (🖼️ OWRD drawing of a drilled well's parts; borehole). Most valley homes have this kind. About 5 gallons a minute is a normal household supply. Find your well's records. Oregon has driller's reports for most wells drilled since 1955 — Josephine County well IDs start with "JOSE". The report gives the depth, where water was found, the static water level and the tested yield — all things you need to plan a hand pump or generator (OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook, pp. 27, 30; 🖼️ a filled-in sample report, p. 28). Print it and keep it with this drive. Look it up on OWRD's Well Log Query (by
know-your-well

Well Owner's Handbook, pp. 27, 30; 🖼️ a filled-in sample report, p. 28). Print it and keep it with this drive. Look it up on OWRD's Well Log Query (by owner, location or well ID) while the internet works (rule of thumb). What the ground here gives (Grants Pass area, the nearest USGS study; 🖼️ how aquifers hold water; aquifer): river gravels 5–50 gpm but easily polluted when shallow; weathered granite up to 50 gpm, solid granite under 5; serpentine rock — common around the Illinois Valley — gives few if any good wells, and high-magnesium water (USGS HA-480 Plate 1; Plate 2). In summer a household uses several times its winter water. Measure your water level (water table; 🖼️ how pumping draws it down; cone of depression) twice a year (spring and fall), from the same point on the casing, after the pump has rested several hours, and keep a log. A ¾-in slotted PVC measuring tube taped to the pump pipe lets a tape get past the wires (OWRD Handbook, pp. 15–16; 🖼️ measuring-tube diagram). A chalked weighted tape shows the wet line (rule of thumb). Rules worth knowing: household use up to 15,000 gallons a day, livestock water and up to ½ acre of garden need no water right (OWRD Exempt Uses). Wells must be at least 50 ft from septic tanks and 100 ft from drain
know-your-well

water and up to ½ acre of garden need no water right (OWRD Exempt Uses). Wells must be at least 50 ft from septic tanks and 100 ft from drain fields, with the top at least 12 in above ground (OWRD Handbook, pp. 23–24; 🖼️ setback diagram, p. 24). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook — Oregon's complete owner guide; USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner; Wikipedia: water well.
know-your-well

🔌 Running the well pump without the grid From a generator (Franklin Electric AIM Manual, pp. 8–9; generator photos) — a well pump needs far more power to start than to run: | Pump size | Minimum generator — 2-wire pump | 3-wire pump (has a control box) | | ½ hp | 3 kW | 2 kW | | ¾ hp | 4.5 kW | 3 kW | | 1 hp | 6 kW | 4 kW | | 1½ hp | 7.5 kW | 5 kW | - Example: a ½ hp pump runs on about 670 watts but draws over 6 times that for a moment when it starts (AIM, p. 41). The pump's size is on the control box or the well report. - Start the generator first, then the pump; switch the pump off before stopping the generator. Never let the generator run out of fuel with the pump on (AIM, p. 8). - Pump into storage — run the generator an hour or two and fill tanks, instead of running it all day. From solar: a DC solar well pump with its own panels pumps whenever the sun shines (🖼️ NRCS system drawing, p. 9; 🖼️ set up on a well, p. 35; photos). Store water, not electricity — a tank holding about 3 days' water beats batteries for cost and upkeep (NRCS Solar-Powered
running-the-well-pump-without-the-grid

9; 🖼️ set up on a well, p. 35; photos). Store water, not electricity — a tank holding about 3 days' water beats batteries for cost and upkeep (NRCS Solar-Powered Water Pump Systems, pp. 27, 29). Choose a brushless pump; brushed ones need new brushes about every 2 years (Practical Action, p. 4). Pressure tank and switch (UNL G2152, pp. 2–3; 🖼️ well-to-house layout, p. 1; 🖼️ inside a bladder tank, p. 3; pressure switch): the switch starts the pump at a low pressure (often 30 or 40 psi) and stops it at a high one (50 or 60). A bladder tank's air charge should be 2 psi below the start pressure, checked with the tank empty and power off. | Problem | Usual cause (AIM, p. 28) | | Pump starts and stops every few seconds | Waterlogged tank (low air charge), leak, stuck check valve | | Pump runs and won't stop | Water level below the pump, worn pump, clogged screen, broken pipe | | No water, pump silent | Breaker, pressure switch contacts, control box, wiring | | Sputtering, air in the water | Water level dropping to the pump — rest the well, use less | 📚 Go deeper: Franklin Electric AIM Manual — the pump-maker's troubleshooting bible; UNL Pumps and Pressure Tanks; NRCS solar pump design; Engines guide — generators.

✋ Getting water up by hand The suction limit: a pump at the top of a well doesn't "lift" water — air pressure pushes it up. In practice a pitcher pump or any suction pump stops working at about 20–22 ft of lift, a little less at our elevation (USDA FB 1448, p. 27; Peace Corps Wells Construction, p. 262; 🖼️ how a piston pump works). Deeper than that, the pumping part must be down in the water — there's no limit on pushing water up from below. | Water level | Options | | Under ~20 ft | Pitcher pump (🖼️ drawing); rope pump; bucket and windlass on a dug well (🖼️ drawing) | | 20–150 ft | Rope pump (to about 115 ft); deep-well lift handpumps (Afridev, India Mark II up to about 160 ft) | | Deeper | Generator or solar on the existing submersible; well bucket (below) | - Rope pump: an endless rope with small pistons every meter runs up a pipe over a hand wheel. About 35 liters a minute at 33 ft, 10 at 115 ft; fits a 3-in borehole; can be built from local materials (Practica Rope Pump Handbook, pp. 8–9; 🖼️ assembly drawing, p. 48; 🖼️ older bucket and chain pumps). - Deep-well handpumps: a cylinder set below the water on rods. Set the cylinder below the lowest water level you've
getting-water-up-by-hand

assembly drawing, p. 48; 🖼️ older bucket and chain pumps). - Deep-well handpumps: a cylinder set below the water on rods. Set the cylinder below the lowest water level you've measured while pumping (Afridev manual, p. 26; India Mark II manual; 🖼️ a deep-well pump on a borehole; 🖼️ suction, force and deep-well pump parts). Commercial deep-well hand pumps can be fitted beside the electric pump in a 6-in casing (rule of thumb). - Well bucket (bailer): a narrow tube about 3 in wide with a flap valve in the bottom fits down a 4–6 in casing beside the pump pipe and brings up 1–2 gallons a trip on a rope and pulley. You must open the well cap and keep everything clean — sanitize the bucket and rope, and close the well between uses (rule of thumb; no manual found). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Human-Powered Handpumps, p. 5 — which pump for which depth; Practica Rope Pump Handbook — building one; Peace Corps Wells Construction — digging and lining a well by hand; Wikipedia: rope pump.
getting-water-up-by-hand

🔁 Ram pumps: creek water uphill with no fuel A hydraulic ram uses the force of falling water in a long pipe (water hammer) to push part of that water much higher — day and night, with no fuel (Practical Action Hydraulic Ram Pumps; 🖼️ how it works, p. 2; 🖼️ step-by-step drawings). - Rule of thumb: water delivered ≈ water going in × fall ÷ lift × about 0.5, with both measured from the ram. Example: 10 gallons a minute falling 20 ft into the ram can push about 0.8 gpm — roughly 1,200 gallons a day — to a tank 100 ft above the source (120 ft above the ram) (Peace Corps Hydrams, p. 66). Another: 3 gpm with a 12-ft fall lifts about 780 gallons a day to 48 ft (USDA FB 1448, pp. 24–25). - The drive pipe from the source to the ram must be straight, rigid (steel is best) and long — about 3–7 times the fall, and at least 100 times its own width (Practical Action, p. 3; 🖼️ layout of a ram installation). - You need: a reliable flow and a few feet of fall — a creek with a small dam or a spring above the ram. The water that doesn't get pumped flows back out the waste valve. - Tune the waste valve's stroke for the best output; build one
ram-pumps-creek-water-uphill-with-no-fuel

or a spring above the ram. The water that doesn't get pumped flows back out the waste valve. - Tune the waste valve's stroke for the best output; build one from pipe fittings with the Peace Corps manual (🖼️ a homemade ram from plumbing parts). - Oregon water law and fish screens apply to diverting creek water — see the Engines guide creek-power section. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps Hydrams workshop manual — build and repair one; USDA FB 1448 — rams and windmills; Wikipedia: hydraulic ram.

🌬️ Windmills Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed (twice the wind = 8 times the power); a water-pumping windmill (🖼️ photo; photos) pays off where the average wind is above about 7 mph, and needs a storage tank for calm days (Practical Action Wind Pumping, p. 2). Sheltered valley floors here may be too calm — ridges and open ground are better (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Wind Pumping; USDA FB 1448 — windmills; Wikipedia: windpump.
windmills

⛲ Springs A spring box collects spring water before animals and surface runoff can foul it (Virginia Tech Spring Development, p. 5; 🖼️ spring box drawings, p. 5; springs)): - Dig back to where the water comes out of the ground and lay a gravel-packed collection pipe or trench (🖼️ cross-section, p. 3; 🖼️ a seep spring, p. 4). - A concrete box at least 4 ft deep, sticking up 1 ft above ground, with a tight overlapping lid, an outlet pipe, a screened overflow (so animals and insects can't crawl in) and a drain for cleaning. - Dig a ditch upslope to steer surface runoff away, and fence livestock out of the area above the spring; keep outhouses and corrals at least 100 ft away (🖼️ a protected spring, 1933). - Measure flow with a bucket and a watch; test the water and shock-chlorinate a new box (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination). - Spring water runs by gravity to the house or garden — no pump at all if the spring is uphill. 📚 Go deeper: Virginia Tech Spring Development and Protection; EPA Manual of Individual Water Supply Systems — springs, wells and cisterns.
springs

🛢️ Cisterns and rainwater Our winters are wet: every square foot of roof catches about 0.6 gallons per inch of rain (Texas Rainwater Harvesting, p. 34; 🖼️ a whole system, p. 10; rainwater harvesting). A 1,500 sq ft roof in a 10-inch rain month could fill a 9,000-gallon tank (rule of thumb arithmetic). - First-flush diverter: dump the first dirty water off the roof — about 13–49 gallons per 1,000 sq ft (Texas, p. 13; 🖼️ standpipe diverter, p. 14; 🖼️ its parts, OSU). A standpipe of 4-in pipe holds about 1 gallon per 18 in. - Size the tank for summer: almost no rain falls June–September, so store enough to carry you through (🖼️ ferrocement tank; 🖼️ 1933 cistern and filter plans; cistern; rain tanks). - Opaque, covered, screened tanks; clean gutters; treat roof water before drinking (Water Purification guide). Oregon rules for rain tanks: OSU EM 9448 (🖼️ system diagram, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: Texas Manual on Rainwater Harvesting; OSU Harvesting Rainwater for the Garden.
cisterns-and-rainwater

🧪 Keeping well water clean - Test yearly for coliform bacteria and nitrate, and at least once for arsenic (treat at 10 ppb or more) (OWRD Handbook, p. 34). Without a lab, a home H₂S bacteria test helps — see the Water Purification guide. - Shock chlorination after repairs, floods or a bad test: for 5.25% bleach, about 2½ quarts for a 4-in well with 100 ft of water, 4 quarts for a 6-in well with 100 ft, 1½ gallons for 6-in with 200 ft. Run every tap until you smell chlorine, leave it 12–24 hours, flush it away from the septic system, and retest in 1–2 weeks. Today's bleach is often stronger (6–8.25%): the same amounts just make it stronger. Oregon's OHA bulletin uses 1 cup of 8.25% bleach per 100 gallons of water standing in the well, left at least 8 hours (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination, p. 3; OHA bulletin; 🖼️ pouring and circulating the chlorine). - After a flood: wells under 50 ft deep or over 10 years old are probably contaminated (EPA, p. 1; 🖼️ cleaning out a flooded dug well). - After a wildfire: check the wellhead, wiring and pipes, and test before drinking (OWRD after wildfire). - "Dry" well? Often the water only dropped below the pump — lower the pump (not to the very bottom) and fit a pump-saver switch (OWRD Wells and
keeping-well-water-clean

after wildfire). - "Dry" well? Often the water only dropped below the pump — lower the pump (not to the very bottom) and fit a pump-saver switch (OWRD Wells and Drought; 🖼️ how a well "goes dry"). - Protect the wellhead: tight sanitary cap, ground sloping away, no fuel, manure or chemicals nearby (OSU Twelve Simple Things; 🖼️ two wellhead types, p. 4; 🖼️ how wells and springs get polluted; 🖼️ sealing the top of a dug well). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Handbook — testing schedule, p. 34; Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination; OSU Twelve Simple Things to Protect Your Well Water.

🥫 Food When It's Scarce: Storage, Rationing & Nutrition How to keep a household fed for a year or more with no stores: how much food people need, what to store and how to keep it good for decades, how to share it out fairly, how to prevent the hunger diseases, how to refeed someone who is starving, how to keep babies alive, and what wild food the Illinois Valley gives month by month. The books are in Food-Security\ (Storage-Rationing, Nutrition-Deficiency, Foraging). Growing, milling and cooking staples are in Food-From-Scratch\, and cellars and drying in Food-Storage\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Grain alone is not enough. Stored wheat, rice and beans have almost no vitamin C. Store vitamin C tablets and learn to sprout seeds. Under 10 mg a day can cause life-threatening scurvy within months (BYU, p. 1). - Never oxygen-pack or vacuum-seal moist food. It can grow botulism. Dry food under 10% moisture only (USU, p. 97). - Feed a starving person slowly. Big meals all at once can kill them. - Babies: breast milk first. Never give plain animal milk under 6 months (WHO 2004, p. 40). - Never cut the share of children, pregnant or nursing women, or the sick first. - Eat no wild plant you have not identified for certain. Death camas and water hemlock grow right here and kill.

🍽️ How much food people need Daily needs (US official tables; "active" there only means walking over 3 miles a day — wood, water and hand-digging are heavier, so plan from the top of each range) (Dietary Guidelines, pp. 153–154; protein p. 146, p. 148): | Person | Calories a day | Protein a day | | Man, 19+ | 2,200–2,600 inactive; 2,800–3,000 active | 56 g | | Woman, 19+ | 1,600–2,000 inactive; 2,000–2,400 active | 46 g | | Teen boy | up to 3,200 | 52 g | | Child 9–13 | — | 34 g | | Child 2–8 | 1,000–2,000 | 13–19 g | | Pregnant | +340 (2nd trimester), +452 (3rd) | 71 g | | Nursing | +330 (first 6 months), +400 after | 71 g | Plan on 2,100 kcal per person per day, averaged over all ages, with at least 10–12% from protein and 17% from fat (WHO 2002, p. 6; Sphere, p. 228) — at least 53 g protein and 40 g fat (Sphere, p. 260). Adjust it (WHO 2002, pp. 11–13): - Cold: add 100 kcal for every 9 °F (5 °C) the average temperature is below 68 °F. Valley winter days average about 40 °F, so a poorly heated house should plan about +300 kcal per person, November–March (rule of thumb from that formula). - Sick or already
how-much-food-people-need

Valley winter days average about 40 °F, so a poorly heated house should plan about +300 kcal per person, November–March (rule of thumb from that formula). - Sick or already thin: add 100–200 kcal. Heavy work: more. What 2,100 kcal looks like: 400 g cereal (about 2 cups dry), 60 g beans, 25 g oil (2 Tbsp), 50 g fortified flour, 15 g sugar, 5 g iodized salt = 2,113 kcal, 58 g protein (WHO 2002, p. 14). For a year: about 322 lb grain, 48 lb beans, 20 lb oil, 12 lb sugar, 4 lb salt per person (our arithmetic). Handy number: 790 g (1.74 lb) of dry wheat gives 2,600 kcal and 103 g protein — so 1 lb of dry grain ≈ 1,500 kcal (Kearny, p. 90). 📚 Go deeper: Food and Nutrition Needs in Emergencies, p. 11 — adjusting for cold, sickness and work; Dietary Guidelines, p. 153 — calories by age and activity.

📦 Storing it for years Heat is the main enemy. Keep food at 40–70 °F. In BYU research, wheat stayed good 25 years in a cool basement but only 5 in a hot garage or attic. Keep containers off bare concrete (USU, p. 31). Our summers pass 100 °F and sheds get hotter — use the coolest inside room or a cellar (Root Cellar guide). Keep grain dry. Above 12% moisture it starts to break down, above 15% it molds, at 20% bacteria grow. Freezing does not harm it (USU, p. 66). Seal it in the dry season (July–September), not in wet winter air (rule of thumb). Packing with oxygen absorbers (USU, p. 98): 1. Use oxygen-tight containers only: #10 cans or Mylar/foil bags. Plastic buckets slowly let oxygen in — put a Mylar bag inside the bucket; the bucket keeps rats out. 2. Absorber size: 100 cc per quart jar, 300 cc per gallon bag or #10 can, 2,000 cc per 5-gallon bucket. (Some charts say 500 cc, but a full bucket of grain holds about 1,500 cc of oxygen (arithmetic); extra absorber does no harm.) 3. Work fast: an opened pack starts in 20 minutes and is spent in about 5 hours. Reseal spare packets in a small jar. Label every bag with contents and date. - Absorbers are not edible; hand warmers are not a substitute. -

Bugs (USU, p. 95): oxygen held under 1% for 12 days kills every stage, so Mylar with absorbers kills weevils (🖼️ the common grain pests, FAO p. 78). ⚖️ Setting and running a fair ration Work out the ration (rule of thumb): 1. Weigh everything, item by item. 2. Count the days to the next harvest and add about 3 months of reserve. 3. Daily ration per person = stock ÷ (people × days), for each food. 4. Turn it into calories (1 lb dry grain ≈ 1,500 kcal) and compare with 2,100. The gap is what the garden, hunting, fishing, foraging and animals must make up. Example (our arithmetic): 3 adult-equivalents, 13 months (395 days). 900 lb of grain ÷ (3 × 395) ≈ 0.76 lb per person per day ≈ 1,100 kcal — half the need. Start the garden and the rabbits and chickens now. Keep it fair (rule of thumb, except where cited): - One standard scoop per food, marked with its weight. A written daily log: date, what went out, to whom, what is left. - Two people present whenever stores are opened. Keep stores locked and out of sight. - Make sure children, the sick, older people and pregnant and nursing women really get their share — give them smaller, more frequent portions (Sphere, p. 235). - Fuel, pots and water matter as much as food — lacking any one hurts as much as a short ration (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74). Store salt and spices: people eat more of a dull
setting-and-running-a-fair-ration

much as food — lacking any one hurts as much as a short ration (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74). Store salt and spices: people eat more of a dull diet when it tastes good (p. 75). - Grind just before eating (🖼️ Kearny's pipe-and-can grinder). Milling loses about 10% of wheat or corn (WHO, p. 75), and ground whole corn keeps only 6–8 weeks (Sphere, p. 232). If this goes wrong: one person losing weight faster → check they really eat their share (children and old people often give theirs away). Stores shrinking faster than the log → reweigh, check for rats and spoilage before suspecting people. 📚 Go deeper: Sphere, p. 235 — fair distribution; WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74 — rations, fuel, milling (scanned, not searchable); Kearny, p. 84 — a homemade grain grinder.

🔥 Cooking with little fuel A fuel shortage is a nutrition problem: one refugee pellagra outbreak happened partly because people had no fuel to cook the beans they were given (WHO Pellagra, p. 29). 1. Soak beans first (USU Dry Beans, p. 2). 2. Crack or grind grain — meal cooks much faster than whole kernels. 3. Boil briefly, let insulation finish it. Cook meal with at least 4 parts water to 1, boil briefly, then finish in a fireless cooker for 4–5 hours (Kearny, p. 89). 4. Build a haybox: a box packed with hay, wool or blankets around a lidded pot (🖼️ the parts; 🖼️ cut-away drawing). Beans and meat boil 20–25 minutes before going in (Practical Action, p. 5); old beans longer (USDA FB 771, p. 16). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Homemade Fireless Cookers, p. 4 — building one; Firewood guide — making the wood count.

Rose hips and many berries have over 300 mg per 100 g; cooking destroys it; breast milk covers a nursing baby (p. 33). Soak whole (unsplit) beans, peas, lentils or wheat 12–21 hours. 2. Drain and spread between damp cloths; keep them damp. 3. Eat when shoots are ½–1 inch (30–48 hours) — the shoot holds the vitamin. Don't over-wash rice or pour off its water. Strong tea, raw fermented fish and molds in damp food block thiamine (p. 17). Pellagra comes from corn-heavy diets with untreated corn (WHO Pellagra, p. 13); one outbreak began 4 months after peanuts were dropped from a ration. If corn is a staple, nixtamalize it (FAO, p. 19; Food from Scratch) and eat beans or meat with it. Rickets and our winter sun: 10–15 minutes of sun on a child's bare skin daily prevents it. with it. Rickets and our winter sun: 10–15 minutes of sun on a child's bare skin daily prevents it. Treatment: 5,000 IU vitamin D daily for 4–6 weeks, then 1,000 IU daily for 6 months, usually from fish-liver oil (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 46). Rule of thumb: at 42° N the November–February sun is too weak to make vitamin D, and the valley is often cloudy — store cod-liver oil or vitamin D, and get children into the summer sun. Iodine: adults need about 150 µg a day (WHO, pp. 36–37), and 250 µg when pregnant or nursing (WHO 2007). About ½ teaspoon of US iodized salt gives roughly 150 µg — you don't need more salt than that. The Pacific Northwest was historically part of the US "goitre belt" (rule of thumb) — store iodized salt sealed, dry and dark, and use fish and kelp from the coast. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Scurvy, p. 35 — the famine sprouting method; WHO Thiamine, p. 19 — forms of beriberi; WHO Pellagra, p. 8 — the rash and outbreaks; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 24 — goitre.

🦴 Starvation and refeeding slowly Recognize it (WHO Management of Nutrition, pp. 25–26; malnutrition; 🖼️ signs in children, mild to severe): - Marasmus — "skin and bones", an old man's face, loose "baggy pants" skin on the buttocks (🖼️ drawing). - Kwashiorkor — swollen feet and legs, peeling "flaky-paint" skin, thin loose hair, misery, no appetite (🖼️ drawing). - Adults — wasting and weakness, sometimes swelling. - For every severe case there may be about 10 moderate ones. Refeed low and slow: 1. Sudden big meals can cause fatal refeeding syndrome (rule of thumb). 2. Starter formula (WHO F-75) for a severely malnourished child, used for the first days until appetite returns: 25 g dried skim milk + 70 g sugar + 35 g cereal flour + 27 g oil + water to 1 litre, boiled 5–7 minutes. Or 300 mL fresh cow's milk + 70 g sugar + 35 g flour + 17 g oil + water to 1 litre (WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21). After it cools, WHO adds 20 mL of mineral mix per litre (potassium and magnesium — "it must be added") and 140 mg vitamin mix or a multivitamin; recipes on p. 61. 3. Small feeds every 2–3 hours, day and night (p. 22). No iron in the first week (p. 9). 4. Adults: WHO aims for about 40 kcal per kg of body weight
starvation-and-refeeding-slowly

feeds every 2–3 hours, day and night (p. 22). No iron in the first week (p. 9). 4. Adults: WHO aims for about 40 kcal per kg of body weight a day; once appetite returns, give ordinary food with added oil (WHO, p. 111). But if they've eaten almost nothing for a week or more, start lower — about 10–20 kcal per kg a day, building up over 4–7 days (UK NICE guidance). Feeding too much too fast can stop the heart (refeeding syndrome). 5. Dehydrated and starving: don't give full-strength rehydration salts. One ORS packet in 2 litres plus 50 g sugar and 40 mL mineral mix (ReSoMal) (WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 18). Note: these manuals are from 1999–2000; WHO updated its guidance in 2013, including some drug doses. F-75 and ReSoMal are still used — leave the drugs to someone trained. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21 — F-75 and F-100 recipes and charts; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 6 — recognizing malnutrition; WTND ch. 21, p. 12 — malnourished children.

🍼 Babies and toddlers in a shortage Breastfeeding first (WHO 2004, pp. 21–23): - Only extreme hunger lowers a mother's milk — feed the mother well. Keep nursing when mother or baby is sick, and nurse more often. - Weak or premature babies: express milk and feed it from an open cup (🖼️ removing milk by hand; 🖼️ cup feeding). - Substitutes only for babies with no breast milk, by cup, not bottle (p. 27). If a baby is due or small, store real infant formula as a backup: about 110 g a day, 3.3 kg (7¼ lb) a month (same page). If the milk has stopped or the mother is gone: - Relactation: a woman who stopped breastfeeding can make milk again, for her own or an adopted baby, without another pregnancy; even a woman never pregnant (a grandmother) can sometimes make some (WHO Relactation, p. 7; scanned). Frequent suckling brings the milk. - A healthy wet-nurse is next best (WHO 2004, p. 23). - Homemade dry-milk formulas in two old books are a last resort — see the last section. Babies 6–24 months: - Porridge thick enough to stay on the spoon, not thin gruel, enriched with mashed beans, oil, egg or greens. Flour from sprouted grain cooks thinner, so more food fits a small stomach (WHO Complementary Feeding, pp. 17–18). - Non-breastfed babies under one need 5

beans, oil, egg or greens. Flour from sprouted grain cooks thinner, so more food fits a small stomach (WHO Complementary Feeding, pp. 17–18). - Non-breastfed babies under one need 5 meals a day, not 3 (p. 37). - Non-breastfed toddlers: 200–400 mL milk a day if they eat other animal foods, otherwise 300–500 mL. Goat, cow or sheep milk — boil raw milk (WHO 2005, pp. 14–16). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Infant Feeding in Emergencies, p. 21 — keeping breastfeeding going; A Book for Midwives, p. 7 — cup feeding removed milk; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 14 — the first 6 months.

🌿 Wild food around the valley What the Takelma ate here. The Takelma people lived along the middle Rogue and south toward the Illinois River (Sapir 1907, p. 3). Their staple was the "black acorn" (Sapir, p. 8; California black oak; 🖼️ photo), pounded, sifted, leached with hot water on clean sand and boiled as mush (Sapir, p. 9). Camas (🖼️ photo) was pit-roasted on alder over hot stones, sometimes for days, then mashed into cakes for winter. Manzanita berries (🖼️ flowers and berries) were pounded to flour with sugar-pine nuts; tarweed and sunflower-type seeds were parched and ground. They also ate madrone berries, pine nuts, salmon, steelhead, trout, crawfish and freshwater mussels. ☠️ Foraging safety rules 1. Eat nothing not 100% identified — ideally confirmed by two people with a book. 2. Skip the whole wild-carrot family (white umbrella-shaped flower heads — 🖼️ poison and water hemlock photos; wild carrot, poison hemlock). Western water hemlock grows along valley creeks and kills fast, by seizures (PNW 109, p. 5; 🖼️ chambered root and stem, p. 1; 🖼️ look-alikes side by side, pp. 3–4). 3. Camas: dig only from a patch you watched bloom and marked plant by plant, only blue-flowered plants. Skip every white or cream-flowered plant — death camas is creamy-white and every part is poisonous (PNW 104, p. 2; 🖼️ WSU photos; 🖼️ Army drawing). 4. Always leach acorns. Always cook elderberries; never eat their stems, leaves or green berries (OSU, p. 4; 🖼️ elderberry drawing). 5. Never eat bracken fern — it holds a cancer-causing compound and an enzyme that destroys thiamine (WSU, p. 11; 🖼️ drawing). 6. Cook anything from ponds (wapato, cattail, watercress) — parasites (rule of thumb). 7. Throw out moldy, damp or discolored grain, and grass seed heads with black ergot spurs (USU, p. 66; rule of thumb; 🖼️ ergot photo). 8. Lean meat alone starves you. Living on rabbit or lean venison without fat causes "rabbit starvation" — keep fat in the diet (render lard; rule of thumb). 9. Try a new wild food in

you. Living on rabbit or lean venison without fat causes "rabbit starvation" — keep fat in the diet (render lard; rule of thumb). 9. Try a new wild food in a small amount first, and take no more than a third of a patch (rule of thumb). If someone may be poisoned: death camas causes drooling, mouth numbness, vomiting, weakness, confusion and an irregular heartbeat 1–8 hours after eating (PNW 104, p. 2). Keep them warm, on their side if drowsy, watch their breathing, and keep a piece of the plant (rule of thumb). ⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - "Two pounds of cooked grain per day" as an adequate diet (FEMA HS-4, p. 111). It should be about 1½–2 lb of DRY grain; 2 lb cooked is only about 800–1,200 kcal. The same page says "adults do not get rickets" — they do (it is called osteomalacia). Instead: plan from 2,100 kcal and the tables above. - Grain puree for babies under 6 months, and scarce cow's milk saved for them (FEMA HS-4, p. 114) — outdated and dangerous. Instead: breast milk, relactation or a wet-nurse; no animal milk or solids before 6 months. - Homemade skim-milk + oil + sugar infant formula (FEMA HS-4, p. 114; Kearny, p. 96) — a last resort only, when no breast milk, wet-nurse or real formula exists. It is not a complete infant food, and emergencies make all artificial feeding riskier (WHO 2004, p. 27). If you must: boiled water, a cup not a bottle, made fresh. Kearny himself says mother's milk is best. - "Ferns on toast" — Saunders 1920, pp. 146–147 recommends bracken. Don't (cancer, thiamine loss). - Camas with no death-camas warning — Saunders, pp. 43–45. Instead: follow rule 3 above. - Drug doses in the WHO 1999–2000 malnutrition manuals predate WHO's 2013 update. Use the feeding methods; leave the drugs to trained hands. 📚 Go deeper: WHO 2004, p.

above. - Drug doses in the WHO 1999–2000 malnutrition manuals predate WHO's 2013 update. Use the feeding methods; leave the drugs to trained hands. 📚 Go deeper: WHO 2004, p. 40 — why no animal milk before 6 months; WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21 — the feeding methods that still hold.

🌾 Flour from grain - Grow hulless varieties of oats and barley if you can — hulled types need dehulling. Wheat and corn are the easiest staples to grow and grind. Winter grains are sown in fall and cut the next summer: ¼–½ inch deep, about 1 foot apart each way (SARE, p. 2). - Harvest when the heads are fully tan and nodding and the kernels are too hard to dent with a fingernail. Cut about 10 inches below the heads. - Thresh by stomping the heads in a clean bin or on a tarp (🖼️ a threshing box); winnow by pouring the grain slowly in front of a fan (or in a breeze) so the chaff blows away. Repeat. (SARE handout, p. 1) - Dry to 12–13% moisture before storing — wetter grain heats, molds and draws insects. Field test: a dry kernel resists your thumbnail and cracks sharply between your teeth. (Peace Corps Small Farm Grain Storage, p. 55) If you dry it with heat, keep eating grain below 140 °F and seed grain below 113 °F (p. 53). - Store whole grain, grind as needed. Whole grain keeps for years; flour goes rancid within months once milled. A hand grain mill (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ a homemade pipe grinder) is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom

milled. A hand grain mill (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ a homemade pipe grinder) is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom one) and sift out the bran (Shifts and Expedients, p. 519). - Kill pests in stored grain: freeze small bags 2–3 days, or heat a ½-inch layer at 140–150 °F for 30 minutes (may weaken bread rise). Store airtight, and only when dry. (USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 14; 🖼️ the common grain pests, FAO p. 78; rice weevil) - A sealed, full container kills bugs on its own — they use up the oxygen. Keep the grain you dip into daily in a separate small container (Peace Corps, p. 279). 🌰 Acorn flour Our oaks — tanoak (the traditional favorite), California black oak, Oregon white oak and canyon live oak (🖼️ tanoak photo; 🖼️ oak and acorn drawing) — all make good flour, but every acorn must be leached to remove bitter tannins. A tanoak can drop over 200 pounds in a good year and bears some crop every year (NRCS Tanoak, p. 1). 1. Gather the second fall (late September–October); the first acorns down are mostly wormy. Dry them 2–5 days in the sun or 20 minutes in a 175 °F oven, door ajar. Whole, dry acorns keep several years — in sacks or jars, not plastic. (UCCE, p. 2) 2. Crack and shell them, and remove any moldy or wormy ones. Grind the nutmeats to a coarse meal or flour. 3. Leach — any one of these: - Hot: soak in hot water for an hour, drain, repeat several times (fastest). - Running water: a cloth bag of meal in cold running water for several hours. - Daily change: 3 parts water to 1 part meal in jars, kept cool; pour off the dark water and refill every day for about a week. - Traditional: pour nearly scalding water over fine flour in a hollow scooped in clean sand (Hupa, p. 38). 4. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of
acorn-flour

water over fine flour in a hollow scooped in clean sand (Hupa, p. 38). 4. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of the starch's binding power (better for bread); hot is faster. 5. Use it wet as mush/porridge, pat it into flatbread on a hot stone or pan, or dry it and replace ¼ to ½ of the wheat flour in bread (acorn flour has no gluten on its own). 6. Ground meal goes rancid in a warm room — grind only a few weeks' worth and keep it cold (UCCE, p. 2). Other local nuts need no leaching: hazelnuts (June–July, dry and eat raw; 🖼️ photo) and sugar pine nuts (October; pound the cones to free the seeds) — Hupa, pp. 39–40. Bay nuts (Oregon myrtle; 🖼️ peeled bay fruit) must be roasted at 350 °F for 30–45 minutes until dark-chocolate brown; they taste of coffee and contain a caffeine-like stimulant (UCCE, pp. 2–3). 📚 Go deeper: UCCE Foods from the Tanoak Forest, p. 2 — modern acorn and bay-nut processing step by step; Goddard, Life and Culture of the Hupa, p. 37 — how acorns were gathered, ground, leached and cooked just south of us; NRCS Tanoak guide, p. 2 — storage, leaching and acorn bread. 🌰 The local way: choosing oaks, storing, pounding, leaching in a sand basin and

🌿 Camas, cattail and other local starches - Camas bulbs (Camassia quamash — meadows, blue flowers in spring; 🖼️ photo) were a major food here. They must be pit-roasted or slow-baked 24–36 hours — long cooking turns the indigestible starch sweet. Dry cooked bulbs or cakes for storage. ⚠️ Death camas grows in the same meadows and its bulbs look the same. Flower color is not a safe test. Only harvest from a bed you have watched bloom and learned plant by plant; if there's any doubt, leave it. (USDA Great Camas guide, pp. 1–2; Wild-Plants\ death camas guide; 🖼️ death camas flowers and leaves) - Dig after flowering, take only the big bulbs, replant the small ones, and rest each patch a few years. 🌽 Corn: masa, tortillas and hominy Always cook dried corn with lime or wood ash ("nixtamal") before making it a staple — it unlocks the corn's niacin. People living mostly on untreated cornmeal get pellagra (FAO Maize, p. 13). - Masa with lime (food-grade slaked lime, cal): use lime 1% of the dry corn's weight (5 g of lime per 500 g of corn — weigh it if you can) and water 1½ times the corn's volume. Heat to just below a simmer (200–210 °F) until the skins slip off but the center is still firm (often under 30 minutes). Rest 8–12 hours in the liquid, then rub and rinse off the skins. Grind while cold (a metate or stone mill, with a little cold water; 🖼️ metate and hand mill); use the masa within a day. (Smithsonian method, pp. 1–3) Fresh corn needs less lime and cooking; old, hard corn more (FAO, p. 66). - With wood ash instead: boil shelled corn 15–30 minutes in weak lye water made from hardwood ashes until the hulls loosen, then rinse very thoroughly in running water until no lye remains. Lye is caustic — gloves and eye protection; never taste it. - Lye hominy with store lye (USDA) — use pure lye (100% sodium hydroxide, sold for soap-making), never a drain cleaner with other chemicals: 5 oz lye in 6 quarts cold
