Lye hominy with store lye (USDA) — use pure lye (100% sodium hydroxide, sold for soap-making), never a drain cleaner with other chemicals: 5 oz lye in 6 quarts cold water; stir in 5 quarts whole corn and let stand 15 hours. Wash and rub the corn in a cloth bag until hulls and black tips are gone, then boil 3–4 hours in salted water, changing the water once or twice to remove the lye taste. Makes 15–20 quarts. (FB 1236, pp. 20–21) - Corn tortillas: knead masa with a little water to a soft, play-dough feel, press balls flat between plastic or cloth, and cook on a hot dry griddle about a minute a side. Keep the masa under a damp cloth — dry masa cracks (Smithsonian, p. 3). - Hominy (whole kernels; 🖼️ an old hominy block; 🖼️ stone mortar and muller) and cornbread, mush, polenta and corn pone recipes: USDA Corn and Its Uses as Food (FB 1236, p. 11). To stretch wheat, use a scant cup of cornmeal per cup of flour in quick breads and bake longer. - If the kernels go mushy all the way through, they're overcooked and won't make masa — stop sooner next time (Smithsonian, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Smithsonian Nixtamalization — the full masa method; USDA FB 1236 Corn and Its Uses, p. 11 — mush, pone, cornbreads and

🍞 Leavening without store yeast or baking powder - Wild sourdough starter: mix equal weights of flour (whole-grain or rye starts fastest) and unchlorinated water in a jar. Every day, discard all but a little and feed it equal weights of flour and water (twice a day from day 4). Keep it at 70–82 °F. Usable around day 7, strong in 2–4 weeks — it's ready when it doubles within 4–6 hours of feeding and smells yeasty and pleasant. Throw it out if mold appears. (Illinois Sourdough 101, pp. 1–3) - Keep it going: save ½ cup each time you bake; the night before, feed it equal parts flour and water and leave it warm 6–8 hours. Store in glass, not metal, with the lid loose. (Alaska's guide warns against all metal; Illinois allows stainless steel but never copper, iron or galvanized.) (UAF Sourdough, p. 2) - Back-up: spread some starter thin, dry it until brittle, and store it airtight. Revive by crumbling into warm water overnight, then feeding. - Sourdough pancakes and muffins get ½ tsp baking soda dissolved in 1 Tbsp water, stirred in last. Never put soda in the starter itself — it can kill the yeast (UAF, pp. 2–3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) — liquid yeast keeps about two

🧂 Salt, 🍯 sweeteners and 🥓 fat - Salt from seawater (sea salt): seawater is about 3.5% salt — roughly 4–5 gallons per pound of salt in practice. Collect it away from harbors and outfalls, filter through cloth, boil down to a slush, then finish drying slowly; pour off the last bitter liquid for better taste. - Bigleaf maple syrup (OSU 2025 guide): tap after leaf drop and a hard freeze, through winter freeze–thaw days, until buds break. 5/16-inch spile in a 2-inch hole (🖼️ tapping, step by step); collect sap daily and boil it within 24 hours. Bigleaf sap is thin — about 80 gallons of sap per gallon of syrup (20 gallons ≈ 1 quart after ~8 hours of boiling). Syrup is done at 7 °F above the boiling point of water where you are — about 216 °F around Cave Junction's elevation (219 °F at sea level). (OSU EM 9163, pp. 2–8) Keep buckets lidded — "ropey" (stringy) sap is spoiled (🖼️ photos). Let syrup settle and pour it off the gritty "sugar sand"; to keep it on a shelf, bottle it at 180–190 °F into just-boiled jars (pp. 6, 8–9). - Honey: strain through progressively finer cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a

cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a pan instead. Solid ("granulated") honey is fine. (pp. 3–4) Honey replaces sugar cup for cup in baking (FB 1136, p. 23). - Lard and tallow: chill fat and render it within about a week. Melt slowly with a little water, stirring, at 235–245 °F (no copper pots), until bubbling stops and the cracklings float and turn chestnut-brown (cracklings); strain into clean jars, fill full, store cool and dark. (Minnesota, pp. 2–3) Leaf (kidney) fat makes the best lard; strong-tasting gut fat is for soap. Slightly rancid lard can be rescued by heating it with sliced potatoes until they're dark brown, then straining (pp. 2, 4). - Nut oil (hazelnuts, acorns): grind, boil with water, and skim the oil as it rises; clarify and store cool (Practical Action brief, p. 2). Discard moldy nuts first; store oil dark and airtight, never in copper (pp. 1, 6; 🖼️ hand oil presses, p. 3). - Butter: sour the cream mildly at 65–75 °F, churn at 52–66 °F until grains the size of wheat form, drain, wash twice in cold water, and work in ¾ oz salt per pound (USDA FB 876, pp. 23–24; 🖼️ the churn, p. 10; 🖼️ working the butter, p.

🥩 Jerky - Heat the meat to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F) before or right after drying — drying alone doesn't kill E. coli, Salmonella or trichinosis. Ten people caught trichinosis from cougar jerky in 1995 (PNW 632, p. 8); cougar and bear are hunted in our units (ODFW, pp. 67–68). Either dip strips 1½–2 minutes in simmering brine before drying, or heat the dried strips 10 minutes in a 275 °F oven (pp. 9, 17; 🖼️ oven-heated jerky, p. 14). - Dry at 145–155 °F (check with a thermometer; an oven with the door propped open works). Sun drying isn't recommended. Done when a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (pp. 9, 18; photos). It keeps 1–2 months. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely — tested methods and the hot-brine recipe; NDSU Preservation of Game Meats and Fish, p. 5 — game jerky, smoking and curing.

🥖 Staples - No oven thermometer? Put a scrap of white paper or ½ tsp flour on a tin plate in the oven; if it turns light golden brown in 5 minutes, it's right to start bread (FB 807, p. 15). Over a fire, cook on coals, not flames (OSU EM 9331, p. 4). - Danger zone: cooked food left between 40 °F and 140 °F for over 2 hours can make you sick (OSU EM 9331, p. 5). Basic yeast bread — per loaf (USDA FB 807, pp. 13–17): 1 cup lukewarm liquid, about 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp sugar or honey, up to 1 Tbsp fat, and yeast (or ½ cup active sourdough starter in place of yeast and part of the liquid). Knead until smooth and springy, let it double, shape, let it rise again, and bake at about 400 °F for 40–50 minutes, until it sounds hollow when tapped. Stop adding flour once the dough doesn't stick to unfloured hands — too much flour makes heavy bread. Rise it covered, at about 80 °F; it's ready for the oven when a light touch leaves a slight dent. Simple sourdough loaf: 1 cup active starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about

starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about 425 °F for 35–45 minutes. Poke test: a floured finger-dent that springs back halfway means bake now; one that stays means over-risen — bake at once. A preheated Dutch oven (lid on 30 minutes, then off) gives a good crust without a real oven (Illinois, pp. 5–6). Flour tortillas / flatbread: 2 cups flour, ¼ cup lard, 1 tsp salt, about ¾ cup warm water. Knead, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cook on a hot dry pan 30–60 seconds a side. Works with part acorn or barley flour. Barley flatbread with no yeast: FAO Barley, p. 63. Biscuits (USDA FB 1136, p. 23): 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder (or the soda and sour milk swap above), 2 Tbsp fat, ⅔–¾ cup liquid. Bake hot (about 450 °F) 12–15 minutes. Keep it all cold and handle it lightly. Too much soda makes them yellow and bad-tasting (p. 22). Crackling bread: for each cup of cornmeal, ¾ tsp salt and ½ cup cracklings left from rendering lard; pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg +

pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg + 2 yolks, ½ tsp salt, about ⅓ cup water (or the old way: one egg, a pinch of salt and enough flour for a very stiff dough). Knead 8–10 minutes, rest 10–20, roll paper-thin, cut ⅛–¼ inch strips. Cook fresh 2–4 minutes, dried 10–12. To store, dry until the noodles snap; keep airtight about a month (longer frozen). Hardtack (keeps for years): 3 parts flour to 1 part water (no salt — salt draws moisture and mold), stiff dough, ½ inch thick, prick with holes, bake 1 hour at 375 °F, then dry 3 more days. Old beans take longer; lentils and split peas need no soak. Beans + corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Cellar storage is in the Root Cellar guide; how much to put up is in the Food Security guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent botulism and poisoning - You can't see, smell or taste botulism. Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans and every vegetable except most tomatoes are low-acid. They go in jars only in a pressure canner. There is no tested way to can them without one, so dry, ferment, salt or cellar them instead. - Use a tested recipe, set for our elevation (about 1,300 ft): the 15-lb weight or 11 lb on a dial for pressure canning; water-bath times plus 5 minutes. - Boil home-canned meat and vegetables 11 minutes before anyone tastes them. - Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. -

Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. - Weigh curing nitrite exactly. Too much is poison. - Smoke and drying don't cook food. Cold-smoked fish is raw. Jerky must reach 160 °F.

☠️ Botulism: why low-acid food needs a pressure canner Clostridium botulinum spores are on most fresh food. Sealed in a jar of moist, low-acid food at 40–120 °F with no air, they can make a deadly toxin in 3–4 days (USDA Guide 1, p. 6). The food can look, smell and taste normal (PNW 361, p. 2). | Acid foods (pH 4.6 or lower) | Low-acid foods | | Fruit, jam, pickles, sauerkraut, tomatoes with acid added | Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans, every fresh vegetable, most soups and stews | | Boiling-water or steam canner | Pressure canner only | The spores die only at 240–250 °F, which takes a pressure canner (🖼️ what one looks like). A boiling-water canner would need 7–11 hours, and no such times have been tested (USDA Guide 1, p. 8). Signs of botulism, usually 18–36 hours after eating: double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, dry mouth and weakness, then paralysis spreading down to the breathing muscles (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 110). Bad cases need weeks on a breathing machine, so prevention is everything. No honey for babies under 12 months (p. 111). Boil before eating: 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft, so 11 minutes here, timed from a full boil. This destroys the toxin, not the spores (PNW 361, p. 2). No pressure

♨️ Running a pressure canner off-grid Choose a weighted-gauge canner. It never needs testing. A dial gauge must be tested yearly; one reading high gives unsafe food (PNW 421, p. 5). The canner must hold at least 4 quart jars. Every batch (USDA Guide 1, pp. 20–22; PNW 421, p. 9; 🖼️ step-by-step drawing): 1. 2–3 inches of hot water, or 4–5 inches for fish and other long processes. Jars on the rack (🖼️ photo). 2. Lock the lid, weight off. Heat until steam pours out, then vent a full 10 minutes. Put the weight on. 3. Start timing when the weight jiggles. If pressure ever drops below the target, bring it back up and start the whole time over. 4. Turn off the heat and let it cool by itself. Never cool it with water. At zero pressure, take off the weight, wait 10 minutes, and open the lid away from your face. On a wood stove, campfire or outdoor burner there is no tested method. Canner makers forbid outdoor LP burners and any burner over 12,000 BTU. In Utah State tests, canners boiled dry within minutes and warped, and cold outdoor air breaks jars and spoils seals (WSU flyer, p. 1). Never "can" in any oven (PNW 361, p. 2). If a wood range is your only heat (general practice: untested, so the risk is yours): - Water-bath

flyer, p. 1). Never "can" in any oven (PNW 361, p. 2). If a wood range is your only heat (general practice: untested, so the risk is yours): - Water-bath canning works if you hold a full rolling boil and restart the timer whenever it stops (USDA Guide 1, p. 18). - For pressure canning, practice first with jars of plain water. Use 4–5 inches of water. Control heat by sliding the canner between hotter and cooler parts of the stovetop, not by adding wood. Restart the timer every time pressure dips. Never walk away. - If you can't hold steady pressure, don't can low-acid food. Care (PNW 421, pp. 6–8, 12): stock spare gaskets and safety (overpressure) plugs now (🖼️ where they sit). Replace a gasket that's worn, stretched or hardened. Small steam leaks are fine if pressure holds; add extra water. Clean the vent with a string. 🥫 Jars, lids, storage and spoilage - Mason jars last for years; only the flat lid must be new (🖼️ jar, lid, sealing compound and band). Throw out chipped jars (PNW 361, p. 3). Mayonnaise-type jars are for acid foods in a water bath only, never a pressure canner (USDA Guide 1, p. 13). - One-time metal lids shouldn't be reused. Opening warps them and the sealing compound is spent. Unused lids keep about 5 years, so stockpile them. Buy from the maker; many other sellers' lids were poor in 2021 (FN2028, p. 1). - Reusable plastic lids with rubber rings (the Tattler type) sealed safely in tests reported by NDSU Extension. Follow the maker's directions exactly, which may include tightening the band as soon as the jar comes out (FN2028, p. 1). - If you must reuse a one-time lid (general practice, not tested): only on high-acid jars (jam, fruit, pickles, kraut), where failure shows as mold or fizzing, not hidden toxin. Never on low-acid food. Test seals after 12–24 hours, bands off. Press the middle: if it springs back, it's not sealed. Tap with a teaspoon: a ringing note means sealed; a dull one means not (USDA Guide 1, p. 25; 🖼️ photo). 🍑 Water-bath and steam canning; jam without pectin Water bath (USDA Guide 1, p. 18; 🖼️ illustrated steps): keep 1–2 inches of water over the jars. Start timing at a hard boil; if the boil stops, start over. At the end, take the lid off, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars out, and leave them alone 12–24 hours. Steam canner (saves fuel and water): approved for acid foods only, using a tested boiling-water recipe. The total time must be 45 minutes or less. Vent until a full column of steam shows, and never open it to add water (K-State MF3241, p. 2). Jam and jelly without bought pectin: - Apples, crab apples, gooseberries, some plums and grapes have their own pectin; strawberries, cherries and blueberries don't. For jelly, use ¾ ripe and ¼ under-ripe fruit (USDA Guide 1, p. 29). - Berry jam: 4 cups crushed berries and 4 cups sugar makes 3–4 half-pints. Boil hard to 217–218 °F, or until two drops run together off a cool spoon. Process 10 minutes here (USDA Guide 7, p. 6; PNW 652, p. 26). Feral blackberries ripen by the bucketful in July and August (general practice). - Don't cut the sugar. Too little gives a weak gel, mold and yeast (USDA Guide 1, p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 652 Boiling Water Canning Project Manual — fruit, tomatoes, jam and jelly step

☀️ Drying in our dry summers Trays and solar dryers are in the Root Cellar guide. - Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air. A solar dryer (🖼️ USDA solar drier; 🖼️ brick-and-plastic dryer plan) is dependable with 3–5 days in a row near 95 °F, which is an ordinary July to September here (PNW 651, p. 16). - Not in wildfire smoke. Bring trays in when smoke settles in the valley (general practice). - Dries well (photos): apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, grapes, huckleberries. Not blackberries. - No sulfite dips for anyone with asthma (p. 18). - Fruit leather from windfalls: heat the purée to 160 °F first (p. 20). - Done? Pack it loosely in covered jars 2–4 days, shaking daily. Moisture on the lid means dry it more (p. 18). - Kill insect eggs before storing: 160 °F for 30 minutes (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit by fruit; Wikipedia: Food drying.

🥩 Jerky and pemmican Safe jerky (PNW 632): 1. Slice lean meat into strips. 2. Bring it to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F): dip strips 1½–2 minutes in simmering brine before drying (p. 17), or heat dried strips 10 minutes at 275 °F (p. 9; 🖼️ photo). 3. Dry at 145–155 °F, checked with a thermometer (🖼️ which kind), until a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (p. 18; 🖼️ photo). 4. Keep it sealed; it's best within 1–2 months (p. 21). Don't sun-dry meat (USU, p. 59). Bear and cougar carry trichinosis; ten people caught it from cougar jerky (PNW 632, p. 8). Pemmican: lean meat dried by sun, wind or smoke (not salt-cured), pounded, and mixed with hot rendered fat. About 6 lb of meat makes 1 lb, and it keeps for years, depending on the fat (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). There's no modern tested recipe, so (general practice): do the 160 °F step, then dry the meat brittle; render the fat until it stops bubbling; use about equal weights of meat and fat; firm tallow (deer, elk, beef) keeps better than lard; fully dry any berries. Store it cool, dark and airtight; throw it out if rancid or sour. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely — tested methods and the hot-brine dip; Food From Scratch — jerky basics.

🥚 Lard, confit, eggs and vinegar - Lard: render slowly at 235–245 °F and don't let it scorch. The fuller the rendering, the less water and the better it keeps (Minnesota, p. 3). Steps are in Food From Scratch. - ⚠️ Confit and potted meat (meat sealed under lard) are airless and low-acid, exactly what botulism needs. No method is tested. Use them only short-term in a cold winter cellar, and boil before eating (general practice). - Eggs: fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs, wiped not washed, in 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, 2 inches over them, or in clear limewater (2 lb lime in 5 gallons boiled water). Prick the shell before boiling (USDA 1935, pp. 3–4). USDA says 6–9 months, FAO only 1–6 (FAO, p. 83); plan on the shorter. - Vinegar: yeast turns fruit juice to alcohol in 4–6 days. Then add 1 part unpasteurized vinegar to 4 parts juice, leave it open under cheesecloth at 70 °F or warmer, and don't disturb the "mother." It takes 3–6 months (USDA FB 1424, pp. 9–12; 🖼️ barrel "converter"). Only a titration test proves its strength (p. 30), so use it for cooking, never for canned pickles. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs — water glass and lime; USDA FB 1424 Making Vinegar.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Open-kettle canning: jars "filled to overflowing," turned upside down, never processed, even vegetables (Henley, p. 605; Household Discoveries, p. 542, p. 544), and cotton batting or mutton suet "as if hermetically sealed" (p. 549). Instead: process every jar (USDA Guide 1, p. 10). - Oven canning: jars can seal and explode, and the food never gets hot enough (FB 1186, p. 37). Instead: a pressure canner. - Paraffin seals on jam (mold toxins; USDA Guide 1, p. 30), on kraut fermented at 86 °F (FB 1438, p. 14) and on smoked fish (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 2). Instead: process jam; ferment at 60–75 °F under brine. - Borax, boric acid, salicylic acid (the folk "aspirin in the jar" trick) and salts up to 40% saltpeter (Henley, p. 363). Poisons. Instead: heat, acid and salt by a tested recipe. - "10:1 table salt and saltpeter," about ten times modern levels (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). Instead: the MSU amounts or a premix label. - Hot-smoking fish in 130–150 °F air for 2–3 hours (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 14). Instead: 150–160 °F inside the fish for 30 minutes (PNW 238, p. 2). - Jerky dried at 120 °F with no heat step, "almost indefinitely" keeping (NDSU, p. 5), and sun-dried jerky (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). 🥔 Root Cellars & Food Storage Without Power How to keep a year's harvest with no refrigerator: root cellars, storage rooms, pits and buried barrels, cooling with water and evaporation, sun and solar drying, curing and smoking meat, fermenting, and keeping eggs. The manuals are in Food-Storage\ (Root-Cellars-Pits, Cooling-Without-Power, Drying, Curing-Smoking, Fermenting-Eggs-Vinegar); canning and freezing are in Gardening-Food\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent food poisoning and losses - Low-acid food in sealed jars needs pressure canning — never "water bath" or "oven can" vegetables, meat or beans, and never can wild mushrooms. Follow the USDA canning guide exactly. - Cured meat needs exact amounts. Weigh salt and any curing salt (nitrite/saltpeter) — too little lets meat spoil, too much nitrite is poisonous. Follow one tested recipe; don't mix them. - Cold-smoked fish is not cooked. Hot-smoke fish to 150–160 °F inside for 30 minutes (PNW 238) unless it's heavily salted and dried. - Green potatoes are toxic (why) — store potatoes in the dark and cut away green parts. - Check stored food weekly. One rotting apple or potato spreads; remove it at once.

🌡️ The Illinois Valley problem: warm ground Old root-cellar books assume cold ground. Deep soil stays near the average yearly air temperature, and across most of the U.S. that's 49–58 °F; at 6 ft down clay still swings about ±11 °F through the year (MSU Earth Tempering, p. 2; 🖼️ ground-temperature map and chart). Here the yearly average is roughly 54 °F (rule of thumb, from Cave Junction's average highs and lows). So: - A cellar here idles around 50–58 °F. That's perfect for winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes, and fine for a few weeks of most other crops. - To get it down to the 32–40 °F that potatoes, carrots, cabbage and apples want, you must cool it with cold night air in winter: open the vents on cold nights, close them on warm days (USDA FB 1939 (1960), p. 5; Agriculture Canada Pub. 1478, p. 12; 🖼️ where the cold air comes in). November–February nights here regularly fall into the 20s and 30s. - In a 50–60 °F space, root crops keep only 3–4 weeks; packing them in damp (not wet) sand or soil cuts the shriveling, and a partitioned-off room or outdoor cellar let in to outside air about doubles the time (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29–30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below),

air about doubles the time (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29–30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — storage in a 50–60 °F space, p. 29; MSU Earth Tempering — ground temperature map, p. 2; PNW 548 — winter vegetables west of the Cascades.

🏗️ Building a root cellar The essentials (Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar, pp. 2–6; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar; 🖼️ plan of a 10×14 ft farm cellar): 1. Drainage first. Pick a slope or high ground. On the wet valley floor, build at or above ground level and heap earth over it rather than digging into a winter water table; lay a drain pipe along the footings (Novia, pp. 8–9; 🖼️ plan and section drawings). 2. Earth cover: at least 3½ ft of soil and straw over the roof (layers of ~6 in straw and 8–12 in soil), carried well past the sides. Add soil as the straw rots. 3. Two vents at opposite ends, about 12 in square for a 10×14 ft cellar (🖼️ how the air flows through; 🖼️ vents in a cellar cross-section): - Intake: brings outside air down to about 1½ ft above the floor. - Outlet: starts at the ceiling and rises well above the roof (warm air leaves high). - Both adjustable, and screened against rodents and insects. 4. Double doors about 4 ft apart act as an air lock. Face the door north and keep it shaded so summer sun doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13–14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel — it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around

doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13–14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel — it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around everything. 6. A thermometer and a humidity gauge inside (or a wet rag test: if things shrivel, it's too dry — sprinkle the floor). Simpler options: - Basement-corner storage room: about 10×10 ft with an outside window. Insulate the two inside walls and the ceiling (vapor barrier on the warm side), and run an intake duct from the window down to about 18 in above the floor (Pub. 1478, pp. 8–12; 🖼️ perspective view; 🖼️ cross-section). - Above-ground and part-underground cellars: plans in USDA FB 1939 (1960) (🖼️ partly underground cellar; 🖼️ outdoor cellar, side view). - Unheated outbuilding, porch or garage: works for squash, onions and dry goods — not for the cold & moist group. 📚 Go deeper: Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar — full plan, p. 2; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar — photo step by step; USDA FB 1939 (1943) — cellars, pits and banks; Wikipedia: root cellar.

🕳️ Pits, clamps, buried barrels — and the garden itself - Cone pit (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 16; 🖼️ cross-section): on well-drained ground, dig 6–8 in deep, line with straw or leaves, pile the vegetables in a cone, cover with straw, then 2–3 in of earth, thickened as winter comes. Leave a tuft of straw sticking out the top as a vent and cap it with a board. Open a pit all at once and use a new spot each year (FB 1939 (1960), p. 9). - Clamp (long mound) for potatoes: a straw bed, a vent duct along the bottom, about 8 in of packed straw and up to 12 in of soil; in mild climates use more straw and less soil (FAO Prevention of Post-Harvest Losses; 🖼️ clamp drawing). - Buried barrel or trash can: a clean food-safe barrel laid in the ground on a slant so water runs out, mouth facing the path, covered with straw and earth (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 18; 🖼️ barrel pit; 🖼️ buried trash can). Line or wrap it with ¼-inch hardware cloth against gophers and voles (rule of thumb). - Leave it in the ground (🖼️ in-garden and mound storage): parsnips, carrots, beets, leeks, kale, collards and rutabagas can stay in the garden through most Illinois Valley winters — in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in

❄️ Cooling without power - Springhouse: water from a spring or deep well sits near ground temperature — about 52–55 °F here (rule of thumb). Run it through an insulated tank or a shaded stone trough and stand crocks, milk cans and butter in it (USDA FB 976; 🖼️ insulated cooling tank). See springhouse. - Evaporative cooler — made for our dry summers: a screened cabinet covered in flannel or burlap, kept wet by wicks from a pan of water on top, in shade and breeze. In hot, dry weather it can hold about 50 °F inside; it works poorly in humid weather (USDA The Iceless Refrigerator). Bigger versions use a wall of wet charcoal, or a double brick wall with wet sand between (about 400 bricks keeps 220 lb of produce), wetted twice a day (Practical Action Evaporative Cooling, p. 2; 🖼️ charcoal cooler; 🖼️ brick cool chamber). The clay-pot zeer is the small version (Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools; 🖼️ how it works; 🖼️ pot sizes). - Ice house): ice packed in at least 15 in of sawdust on all sides, on a drained floor, keeps through summer (USDA FB 475, pp. 6, 12–13; 🖼️ insulation diagram). Valley ponds rarely freeze thick, but the bulletin shows freezing ice in metal cans on cold nights. Realistically a small ice store is a winter-only luxury here. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Iceless Refrigerator; Practical

☀️ Drying food Our hot, dry late summer is ideal drying weather. Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air; dependable drying needs several days in a row near 95 °F (PNW 651, p. 16). - Trays: wooden frames with food-safe screen (not galvanized); cover with cheesecloth or netting against insects; bring trays in at night so dew doesn't re-wet the food (USDA FB 984, pp. 13–14; 🖼️ screened solar drier). - Solar dryer: a dark box with a clear top, vents low and high, and screened trays — a 3×6 ft dryer serves a household of 4–6 (Practical Action A Simple Solar Dryer; 🖼️ layout); more designs in the Peace Corps solar food technologies manual and Practical Action Solar Drying (🖼️ cabinet and tent dryers). - Is it dry? Fruit is leathery with no moist center (photos); vegetables are brittle. Squeeze a handful of fruit: it should spring apart "like rubber bands." Then condition it at least 2–4 days in a covered jar, shaking daily — if moisture beads up, dry it more (USDA FB 984, p. 47; PNW 651, pp. 17–19). - Don't dry outdoors in wildfire smoke — ash settles on the food (rule of thumb). - Jerky: PNW 632 (🖼️ dry enough: cracks, doesn't snap). Store everything dry in sealed jars. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit-by-fruit and vegetable-by-vegetable;

🥓 Curing and smoking meat Dry-cured country ham and bacon keep without refrigeration once cured, smoked and aged. - Cure in the cold season: meat must stay 36–40 °F for the whole cure — warmer risks spoilage, colder stops the salt from soaking in (USDA Curing Pork Country Style, p. 5). Here that means December–February, in a cellar or shed vented on cold nights. Carver's bulletin covers curing where winters are too warm (Carver 1912). - The cure: about 8 lb salt + 2 lb sugar per 100 lb of meat, rubbed in, repeated after about a week; 1½–2 days per pound of ham (🖼️ parts of a ham; 🖼️ rubbing in the cure; Virginia Tech 458-223, p. 3; Kentucky ASC-213). Curing salt (nitrite) must be weighed exactly — use a commercial premix by its label. - Smoke with hardwood (never pine) at 100–120 °F for cured pork (Leaflet 273, p. 8). A barrel smoker at the top of a sloping covered trench, fire at the bottom, is the simplest smokehouse (USDA AWI-68; 🖼️ firebox plan). - Store: wrap cooled hams, bag in muslin or paper (🖼️ wrapped and bagged), and hang in a dark, dry, airy, rat-proof place; skipper flies don't breed below 45 °F (Leaflet 273, p. 8; 🖼️ ham pests). - Fish: dry-salting keeps longer than brining in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish

🥬 Fermenting, salting, eggs and vinegar - Sauerkraut: 2½% salt — 1 lb salt to 40 lb cabbage (about 3 Tbsp per 5 lb); pack in a crock) (🖼️ crocks and jars), weight it so brine covers the cabbage, skim scum. Ferment 3–4 weeks at 70–75 °F or 5–6 weeks at 60–65 °F; below 60 °F it may not ferment, above 75 °F it goes soft (USDA FB 1438, p. 14; USDA canning Guide 6). Old bulletins say 86 °F and paraffin seals — don't. - Salted vegetables (beans, greens, corn) in crocks: recipes in the 1918 Food Administration bulletin. - Eggs for months (USDA says 6–9, FAO only 1–6; plan on the shorter — see the Preserving guide): fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs in a crock of 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, with 2 in of liquid over them; or clear lime water. Prick the shell before boiling (USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs). - Vinegar: fruit juice → alcohol (yeast) → vinegar (air-loving bacteria). Leave the container open to air under cheesecloth and keep it at least 70 °F (USDA FB 1424; 🖼️ barrel "converter"). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1438 Fermented Pickles and Sauerkraut; USDA canning Guide 6 — fermented foods; Wikipedia: sauerkraut.

🐀 Keeping rats, mice and bugs out - Mice get through ¼-inch gaps. Use ¼-inch hardware cloth on vents and storage bins (rule of thumb); line corncribs and grain bins with galvanized hardware cloth (USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 10; 🖼️ rat-proof grain bin and walls). - Foundations: concrete curtain walls 2 ft below ground, and metal or stucco on lath 2 ft up the walls, stop burrowing rats (Rat Proofing, p. 8; 🖼️ concrete curtain wall). - Grain, beans and dried food in metal or glass with tight lids. Freeze dry beans and grain 2–3 days, warm them a day, then freeze again (freezing alone misses some eggs), or heat them, to kill weevils — not the old chemical fumigants (USU, p. 95). - Cats, traps and tidiness — no open feed, no clutter for nesting. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Rat Proofing Buildings and Premises; Food From Scratch — storing grain.

🌱 Your Seed Bank: Grow, Harvest and Save Seed How to keep a heirloom seed bank alive for good in the Illinois Valley: store it so it lasts, test it, plant each variety at the right time here, keep varieties from crossing, and save your own seed every year — including seed from the fruits (tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, squash, peppers). It ends with the calorie crops the kit is missing and how to propagate fruit trees and berries, whose seeds don't grow true. The manuals are in Gardening-Food\Seed-Saving, Gardening-Food\Fruit-Propagation and the rest of Gardening-Food\. Written for the Heaven's Harvest "10 Year" seed bank. The company's list has 39 varieties (they note some may be swapped when seed is short), so check your own packets — the rules below are by crop, so they still apply. ### The five rules of a seed bank 1. Don't plant it all. Plant part of each packet; keep the rest sealed as a backup. 2. Start saving seed in year one — the short-lived ones first: onions, leeks, sweet corn, peppers and okra keep only 1–2 years. 3. Test germination every winter so you know what still sprouts before you need it. 4. Know which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes,

🗄️ Keeping the seed bank alive Seed dies from heat and damp. Two rules from seed-storage research (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9): - Every 10 °F cooler roughly doubles seed life. - Every 1% less moisture in the seed roughly doubles it too (🖼️ chart: moisture, humidity and storage life). - Quick test for a storage spot: temperature (°F) + relative humidity (%) should add up to less than 100. (OSA, p. 17) Where to keep it here: - Not in a shed, garage, attic or vehicle — Illinois Valley summers top 100 °F. - Best: the coolest, driest room of the house, a closet on a north wall, or a dry root cellar. - Fridge or freezer only for very dry seed in an airtight jar. Let the jar warm to room temperature before opening, or moisture condenses on the cold seed. Very dry seed (about 5% moisture) held below 20 °F still sprouted well after 20 years. (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9) - Once you open a Mylar packet, reseal it, or move the seed into a glass jar with a desiccant packet (silica gel; 🖼️ chart: how the container affects sprouting). Label every jar with the variety and year. How long seed stays good in ordinary cool, dry storage (Univ. of Illinois seed life table, p. 2; McCormack, p. 17): | Years of good sprouting

🧪 Germination test ("rag doll") Do this every winter, and before planting any packet more than a year old (what germination looks like). (OSA, p. 18; Univ. of Illinois, p. 1) 1. Dampen a paper towel — damp, not dripping. 2. Lay out 10 seeds (more is more accurate) spaced apart, roll the towel up, and put it in a plastic bag with a little air. Label it. 3. Keep it warm: about 70 °F for most crops; 75–80 °F for peppers, eggplant, melons. Lettuce and celery sprout better with some light. 4. Check from day 3; remove sprouted and moldy seeds and count them. Slow crops (peppers, parsley-type seeds) can take up to 3 weeks. 5. Read the result: 10 of 10 — plant normally. 7–9 — sow thicker. 6 or fewer — this packet is failing: plant it now and save fresh seed this year. Fresh spinach, lettuce and pepper seed can be dormant for a few months — retest before giving up on it. 📚 Go deeper: OSA germination test, p. 18; McCormack — germination testing, p. 20.

🏡 Growing it here - Raised beds with good soil (🖼️ how they drain wet ground). Many valley soils are serpentine (high magnesium, low calcium) or slow-draining clay. Build raised beds, get a soil test before adding amendments, and add lots of compost. (OSU Soil Test Guide; Improving Garden Soils) - Water is the summer limit. Only 5–7 in of rain falls April–September. Rogue Valley gardens can lose ½ inch of water a day in hot wind (Growing Your Own, p. 21). Apply 1–1.5 in per watering (EC 871, p. 9), use drip lines, and mulch thickly. - Frost pockets: cold air drains to low ground. Plant warm crops on the warmest, sunniest ground you have, and keep row cover or old sheets ready for late-May frosts (🖼️ row cover on hoops). - Heat: lettuce, spinach and cabbage-family crops bolt or go bitter in July heat. Grow them in spring and fall, or under shade cloth on the north side of taller crops. - Deer and gophers: a 7–8 ft fence for deer; hardware-cloth bottoms on raised beds or wire baskets around roots for gophers (rule of thumb). - Bugs: encourage beneficial insects rather than spraying (PNW 550). 📚 Go deeper: Growing Your Own — Rogue Valley section, p. 21; Drip Irrigation in the Food Garden; Food Gardening with Less Water; Josephine County soil survey.

✋ Hand-pollinating and caging Squash, pumpkin and cucumber — save pure seed even when relatives grow nearby (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 12; 🖼️ male and female squash flowers; hand pollination): 1. In the evening, find male and female flowers that will open tomorrow (yellow showing at the tips; the female has a tiny fruit behind the flower). Tape or tie them shut (🖼️ taped flowers). 2. Next morning, once the dew is off, pick a male flower, peel back its petals, and rub its pollen onto the center of the opened female — use 2–3 males. 3. Tape the female shut again and tie a tag or yarn on its stem. Save seed only from tagged fruit. Corn: cover young ear shoots with paper bags before silks appear; when silks show, bag a tassel that's shedding pollen, shake the pollen into the bag the next morning, pour it onto the silks and re-bag (OSA sweet corn guide, p. 6; 🖼️ bags and tools). Cabbage family, carrots, peppers: cover them with a cage of row cover on hoops (🖼️ row cover on hoops). Cabbage-family plants need insects to set seed (they can't pollinate themselves), so put flies or bees in the cage — or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12–17; OSA

cage — or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12–17; OSA sweet corn hand pollination, pp. 5–8; Isolation Distances — caging, p. 17.

🍅 Saving seed from the fruits Fruit crops have wet seed (seed saving): let the fruit get riper than you'd eat it, scoop out the seeds, clean them, and dry them. (OSA, pp. 15–16, 21–24) Tomatoes — ferment them: 1. Pick fully ripe fruit from several healthy plants of the variety. 2. Squeeze the seeds and juice into a jar; add a little water if thick. Label it. 3. Leave it at about 70–80 °F for 2–3 days, stirring 2–3 times a day. A thin white mold on top is normal (keep stirring so it doesn't take over) — it eats the gel coat that keeps seed from sprouting. Stop before any seed sprouts, and keep it out of high heat (liquid in the high 80s °F can kill half the seed). (Tomato Seed Production, p. 11) 4. Add water and stir: good seed sinks; pour off the mold, pulp and floaters. Rinse in a strainer. 5. Spread thin on a plate or screen to dry (paper towels stick). Cucumbers: leave the fruit on the vine 4–5 weeks past eating stage, until it's big, yellow to orange-brown and slightly soft. Scrape the seeds and pulp into a jar and ferment about 3 days at 70–75 °F like tomatoes; good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop

🫘 Saving seed from dry crops These dry on the plant; harvest, thresh (beat or stomp the seed out), and winnow (pour in a breeze to blow off chaff). (OSA, pp. 19–24; 🖼️ threshing box; 🖼️ winnowing in front of a fan) - Beans and peas: let pods dry on the plant; pull plants when 70–80% of pods have turned color and finish drying under cover. Freeze shelled seed 3 days to kill bean weevils. (zine, p. 6) - Lettuce: let a few of the best plants bolt) (don't save from the first to bolt). When heads look fluffy ("feathered"), shake them into a paper bag; repeat a week or two later. In our hot summers, lettuce must flower by May or early June or seed set suffers. (OSA, p. 21; Climatic Considerations — Rogue Valley, p. 21) - Radish: dig the best roots, replant them, and let them flower; harvest when 60–70% of pods are brown and papery. (OSA, p. 23) - Spinach: sow early (it bolts as days lengthen); harvest when most seed is brown. (OSA, p. 23) - Onions and leeks: cut the seed head (umbel) when about a half-dollar-sized patch of black seeds shows; dry 10–14 days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Grow it in a block of

🥕 Biennials: seed in the second year Carrots, beets, onions, leeks, celery, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, collards, kale, turnips and rutabagas flower only after a winter (biennials; vernalization) — they need 8–12 weeks below 50 °F. (OSA, p. 4) - Leave them in the ground where winters rarely drop below about 14 °F — true for most of the valley, but use well-drained raised beds so roots don't rot, and watch for voles. December–January cold snaps of 5–10 °F still happen some years and kill most biennials: hill soil over them or cover them with row cover (Climatic Considerations, p. 21). - Or dig and store the best roots ("stecklings") at 35–38 °F and high humidity — in moist sand in a root cellar — and replant them in early spring. This lets you choose the best-looking roots. (OSA, p. 4; OSA Carrot Seed Production, p. 7; 🖼️ carrot stecklings trimmed for storage) - Carrots for seed: sow in June, not April, so roots are small going into winter (small roots survive cold better). (zine, p. 15) - Cabbage: overwinter a loose, full-size head; in spring cut an X in the top so the flower stalk can get out. Kale and collards: sow June 20–July 15 and overwinter them in place. (OSA, pp. 20–21) - Beets: small roots (1–1.5 in) overwinter best. (OSA Beet Seed Production; 🖼️ trimming beet tops)

🌾 Filling the calorie gap This kit is mostly vegetables — vitamins and variety, but not many calories. To live from a garden you also need: - Potatoes — the most food per square foot in this climate. Save your own "seed potatoes": keep healthy, egg-sized tubers cool and dark over winter (rule of thumb). - Dry beans — protein that stores for years. Your Provider and Blue Lake beans can be left to dry and eaten as dry beans. (OSU Preserving Dry Beans) - Winter squash — your butternut and pumpkin store for months. - Flour or flint corn — Golden Bantam is a sweet corn; it dries for parched corn but makes poor meal. - Grains (wheat, oats, barley) and garlic — see the Food From Scratch guide for growing, threshing and milling. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics — Food; Growing Your Own — amounts for a family of four, p. 9.

🍎 Fruit trees and berries: seeds don't come true An apple seed grows a new, different apple tree — usually a poor one. Fruit trees are kept true by grafting a twig ("scion") of the variety you want onto a rootstock (🖼️ whip-and-tongue graft, step by step). (Univ. of Minnesota Grafting and Budding; Univ. of Kentucky, p. 1) - Grow rootstocks from seed: apple and pear seeds need 70–90 days cold and moist) (in damp sand or a damp paper towel in a sealed bag in the fridge); peach 90–120 days. Then plant them; graft when the seedling is about pencil-thick. (Mississippi State Basic Grafting, p. 3) - Collect scionwood while trees are dormant (here, January–February, before buds swell): last year's growth, pencil-thick, a foot or more long. Wrap in damp (not wet) paper towel or sawdust in a sealed bag, label it, and keep it at 34–38 °F. Never store scions with apples or pears — the gas they give off ruins them. (Mississippi State, p. 3; Kentucky, p. 4; 🖼️ scion wood ready for storage) - When to graft: whip-and-tongue Feb–early March while dormant; cleft graft late Feb–March (🖼️ cleft graft); bark graft in spring once the bark slips (🖼️ bark graft). Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July–September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3–4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼️ T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed

(Mississippi State, pp. 3–4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼️ T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed often give usable fruit, but not the same as the parent (rule of thumb). - Berries and grapes are easier: - Raspberries and blackberries: bury a cane tip in late summer — it roots ("tip layering") — or dig suckers. (Virginia Tech, p. 4; 🖼️ tip layering; Layering) - Strawberries: root the runners. (Virginia Tech, p. 5) - Grapes: dormant hardwood cuttings. 🍄 Mushroom Guide How to identify, use, preserve and grow mushrooms in the Illinois Valley — and how not to die doing it. The field guides, poisoning reports and growing manuals are in Mushrooms\ (Identification, Poisoning-Safety, Uses-Growing-Preserving). Wild-Plants\ also has the Forest Service Wild Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest and death cap ID sheets. ### ⚠️ The rules that keep foragers alive 1. Only eat a mushroom you have identified with complete certainty — every feature, including the spore print and the base of the stem. "Pretty sure" is how people die. 2. No folk test works. Silver turning dark, a peeling cap, animals or insects eating it, soaking in salt water, cooking — none of these tell you anything. Cooking, drying, freezing and canning do not destroy the deadly toxins. (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 218) 3. The deadliest ones taste fine and make you sick late — 6 to 24 hours or more after eating. By then the toxin is already in your liver or kidneys. 4. Dig up the whole mushroom — the cup or bulb at the base is what tells you it's a deadly Amanita. Never eat unopened "buttons" of gilled mushrooms; nobody can tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in

tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked specimen in the fridge in case someone gets sick. (PNW/BC White Paper, p. 10)

🔎 How to identify a mushroom Check all of these, every time: - Underside: gills (thin blades), pores (a sponge of tubes — boletes), teeth or spines (hedgehogs), or blunt ridges (chanterelles). (See gills); 🖼️ labeled drawing of the parts; 🖼️ gills, pores, ring and cup.) - Stem base: dig it up. A cup (volva) or bulb at the base, plus a ring on the stem and white gills, means Amanita — leave all of them alone. (FB 796) (See volva) and ring); 🖼️ a death cap dug up, showing both; 🖼️ the "egg" the cup comes from.) - Spore print: cut off the stem of a mature cap, lay the cap gills-down on half white, half dark paper, cover with a glass, and wait a few hours. The color (white, pink, brown, rusty, purple-black) places the mushroom in its family. (Thomas Field Book; Atkinson, p. 373; pictures: Spore print; 🖼️ a spore print) - Where it grows: on wood or soil, under which trees (oak, tanoak, Douglas-fir, pine), alone or in clumps, and the season. - Flesh, smell and bruising: does it stain when cut? Is the flesh brittle or stringy? | Print color | Examples here | Note | | White | Deadly Amanitas, oyster, shiitake, matsutake, false chanterelle | White alone proves nothing — the death cap is white-spored (Hard, p. 40; GTR-576, p. 35) | | Yellowish white | Pacific golden chanterelle | (GTR-576, p. 38) | | Pink to salmon | Pluteus, Entoloma | (Hard, p. 255) | | Rusty to brown | Deadly Galerina, Cortinarius webcaps, poison pax | A brown print on a "shiitake" means Galerina (Cornell-UVM, p. 41) | | Purple-brown | Agaricus (meadow mushroom family) | (Hard, p. 327) | | Black | Inky caps | (Hard, p. 351) | Collecting, step by step: 1. Carry a basket, a knife, a trowel and paper bags or wax paper. Plastic makes mushrooms sweat and rot. (Thomas, p. 29) 2. Dig out the whole mushroom — don't snap the stem — so the base stays attached. 3. Keep each kind in its own bag. Some poisons sicken people even from a sauce the mushroom was cooked in (Bad Bug Book, p. 218), so one stray deadly cap in a basket of edibles is a real danger. 4. Note the tree, the ground, the date. Take a photo of the spot. 5. At home, sort on a clean table, make spore prints, and throw out anything you can't name with certainty — and wash your hands.

Poisoning timeline — deadly Amanita, Galerina, Lepiota: nothing for 6–24 hours, then violent vomiting and diarrhea, then a false recovery around day 1–2, then liver (and kidney) failure at day 3–5. 10–20% die even with hospital care. (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3) Sources differ on the death rate: BC public health says 10–30% even with treatment (BCCDC, p. 5); NAMA's records show about 11% of people who got sick (NAMA 2018–20, p. 3); FDA says 50–90% for people who reach care late, about 10% for those treated almost at once (Bad Bug Book, p. 219). Without a hospital, expect the worst. When did the symptoms start? 🚑 If someone may have eaten a bad mushroom - Get medical help immediately, even if they feel fine — the dangerous ones are delayed. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. - Bring the mushroom — leftovers, the uncooked ones, even scraps from the trash — in a paper bag (they rot in plastic). A photo is far less useful than a sample. (White Paper, p. 6; Michigan sheet, p. 2) - The main hospital treatment for amatoxin is aggressive IV fluids — NAMA calls it "by far the best single intervention" (NAMA 2018–20, p. 4; CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Liver drugs such as silibinin (from milk thistle) are tried, but proof is thin. Sources disagree on activated charcoal: FDA lists it as part of prompt treatment (Bad Bug Book, p. 229), CDC says it has no proven benefit for amatoxin, and NAMA says it's useless more than about 1 hour after eating. With no hospital: replace fluids constantly (oral rehydration solution — see the Medical guides), give activated charcoal only if they ate the mushroom within the last hour or so, and rest. Survival odds are much worse without a hospital — which is why rule 1 matters so much. - Don't be fooled by the false recovery. In the 2016 California outbreak, people sent home with "stomach flu" came back in liver failure (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). One Québec

🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms — never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Eat a few mouthfuls, not a plateful, of any wild mushroom, and not several days running — big servings cause reactions even with "safe" kinds like morels (White Paper, pp. 10–11). In 1991, 77 of 483 guests at a Vancouver banquet got sick from morels served raw (p. 10). - Fresh storage: in the refrigerator (40 °F or colder) in a paper bag — CDC's advice for morels (CDC 2024, p. 5). Don't freeze them raw — bacteria keep growing (NAMA 2018–20, p. 2). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow (dehydrator) until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying — spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2; USFS PNW-GTR-710, pp. 66–67) - No dehydrator? In warm, dry weather, dry on screens, threaded on fishing line, or in a single layer on a tarp, turning them; or use the warm air near a wood stove with a fan. Moving dry air matters more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note

matters more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4). - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. To steam: soak 5 minutes in 1 teaspoon lemon juice per pint of water, then steam whole 5 minutes, quarters 3½, slices 3, cool in ice water, pack and freeze (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2). - Never can wild mushrooms — only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times (OSU SP 50-919, p. 1). Improperly canned chanterelles gave diners botulism in Vancouver in 1987 (White Paper, p. 10). - Recipes from the old books — fine for cooking ideas once the mushroom is safely identified: McIlvaine's 15-page recipe chapter (p. 813), Mrs. Rorer's recipes in Atkinson (p. 379), Gibson (p. 321) and Thomas (p. 381). Skip their raw-mushroom salads and anything about canning. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Preserving Mushrooms SP 50-919 — freezing, drying and why only button mushrooms can be canned; Morels of Western North America — drying with and without power; McIlvaine recipe chapter — old-time cooking and drying methods.

🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4–6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax (🖼️ drill, plug, wax). Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6–18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8–12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell, p. 20; USDA Agroforestry Note 13, p. 3) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4–5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1–2 hours, mix in 5–10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662, p. 2; 🖼️ step-by-step photos) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again. Shiitake details: - Logs: 3–8 inches across and 2–4 feet long. A 4-foot, 8-inch log can weigh 80 lb. Cut from live trees roughly Thanksgiving to St. Patrick's Day, and inoculate within two weeks (Agroforestry Note 13, pp. 2–3). - Hole spacing: the sources differ — Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches

Hole spacing: the sources differ — Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches apart with one row fewer (p. 3). Either way, stagger the rows in a diamond pattern. - Spawn: one 5-lb bag of sawdust spawn does about 20–25 logs 4–6 inches by 3 feet (Cornell-UVM, p. 21). - Laying yard (🖼️ ways to stack logs): 75–100% shade all year — under conifers is best; the north side of a house or shed works for a few logs. Keep logs above 30% moisture; in a dry spell soak them a few hours or sprinkle them (Cornell-UVM, p. 23). - Harvest when caps are 60–75% open, edge still slightly curled under (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4; Cornell-UVM, p. 39). Logs keep producing for up to 6 years; about 10 logs feed a family. - Check every brown mushroom on your logs. Deadly Galerina can pop up on shiitake logs. Make a spore print: shiitake is white, Galerina brown; shiitake never has a ring (Cornell-UVM, p. 41; 🖼️ Galerina photo; Galerina vs. shiitake photos). Oyster details (UF SS662, pp. 2–4; 🖼️ bags as they colonize and fruit): incubate filled bags in the dark at 75–77 °F and 80–90% humidity until white all through (mycelium, 2–3 weeks); then give them light, about 68 °F, 90%

🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment — turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan — but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals, pp. 1–3) - Making the tea: simmering or boiling in water for 20 minutes to 2 hours breaks down the tough cell walls and releases the active compounds (VA, p. 1). - Who should be careful: people with leukemia or lymphoma, after a bone-marrow transplant, or on drugs that suppress the immune system — these mushrooms act on the immune system (VA, p. 3). - No panacea: in one mouse study a reishi extract made tumors grow faster (GTR-309, p. 31). 📚 Go deeper: VA Mycomedicinals — what the research shows for turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake; Agroforestry Note 13 — growing lion's mane on logs.The old mushroom books here (1895–1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. 🦌 Hunting, Trapping & Fishing for Food How to put wild meat and fish on the table year after year without emptying the hills and rivers: why the rules exist, local game and its habits, clean shooting and tracking, field dressing and cooling meat in our heat, butchering and using the whole animal, traps, snares and deadfalls, fishing, nets and fish traps, crawfish, mussels and lamprey, and the diseases that come with wild meat. The books are in Hunting\ (How-To, Game-Species, Butchering-Meat-Care, Disease-Safety), Trapping\ (Disease-Safety, Hides-Tanning) and Fishing\ (How-To, Nets-Traps, Mussels-Lamprey, Shellfish-Safety), with survival manuals in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. Seasons, hunting units, local waters and trapping rules are on Illinois Valley — Start Here. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Be sure of your target and what is beyond it. Bullets pass through game and keep killing. Never shoot at a sound, a color or movement. - Cook all wild meat through. Bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver can carry trichinella worms that survive freezing, smoking and drying. - Wear gloves to skin rabbits, rodents, beaver and anything with fleas (tularemia, plague). Never shoot a deer or elk that looks sick, and never eat its brain, spine, eyes or lymph nodes. - Check every trap every day at first light. Never set man-killing traps where people or pets walk. - Take the surplus, never the breeding stock. Never poison a

nodes. - Check every trap every day at first light. Never set man-killing traps where people or pets walk. - Take the surplus, never the breeding stock. 🌱 Take the surplus, never the seed Every year a wild population has two parts. The breeding stock is what the land can carry through the hard season. The surplus is the animals that will die anyway before next year's young are born. Take the surplus and the land feeds you again next year. Take the breeding stock and it doesn't (NY trapper manual, p. 13). Game laws were written to do exactly this, after the last time it went wrong. While ODFW and the state police still work, follow the rules. If enforcement stops, the reasons don't: - Elk nearly vanished from our forest. In 1910 the Forest Service called elk "very scarce" on the Siskiyou National Forest, and in 1932 it counted about 40. Elk mate in October, calve in June, and have one calf, so a shot-out herd takes decades to recover (Bailey 1936, p. 114; p. 115). - Deer: "unrestricted hunting soon cleans out the deer." Keep no more than about 5 does per buck. If does aren't each raising their usual two fawns, there are too few bucks or too many predators (Bailey, p. 120; written for mule deer, but it holds for blacktails). - Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird
take-the-surplus-never-the-seed

Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird only, because hens are nesting (ODFW bird regs, p. 32; p. 24). - Let small fish go. Fit traps with escape gaps (🖼️ drawing). A gill net's mesh should be about 0.4 × the girth of the fish you want; smaller mesh kills young fish before they spawn (FAO, p. 24; Twinework, p. 64). - Lost gear keeps killing for days or months, and nylon nets never rot. Mark and anchor gear, and tie one panel with cotton or plant twine that rots away (FAO, p. 59; Twinework, p. 41). - The Hupa weir. On the Trinity River, about 70 miles south, Hupa families built a salmon weir in late summer, fished it at night, and kept family fishing spots that were "always respected." The first high water swept it away (Goddard 1903, p. 34; p. 36). A weir left across a whole river all season would take the whole run. Leave gaps, and fish only part of each night and part of the run (general practice). Illinois River coho are federally threatened. 📚 Go deeper: NY trapper manual, p. 13 — surplus and carrying capacity; Bailey, p. 120 — how deer herds were shot out; Goddard, p. 34 —

🎯 Safe shooting, shot placement and tracking The four rules (Hunter ed, p. 40): 1. Point the muzzle in a safe direction. 2. Treat every gun as loaded. 3. Be sure of your target and what is in front of it and beyond it. 4. Finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot. Shot placement (Hunter ed, p. 61; CT DEEP, p. 3; 🖼️ where the organs lie in deer, elk, bear and small game): - Big game: heart and lungs, just behind the front shoulder, broadside. With a bow, a third of the way up the chest when the near leg is forward. - Never take head-on, rear-end, running or straight-away shots. A wounded, stressed animal suffers, and its meat tastes stronger. - Turkey (🖼️ gobbler and hen): head and neck. Rabbits and squirrels: head or chest (Ohio DNR, p. 2). Oregon's legal minimums are also humane-kill minimums: no .22 rimfire on deer, elk or bear; broadheads unbarbed and at least 7/8 in wide; bows at least 40 lb draw (ODFW big game regs, p. 22). Not a law, but keep bow shots to 40 yards or less (Hunter ed, p. 70). After the shot (Hunter ed, pp. 62–63): 1. Watch every move the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30–60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs.
safe-shooting-shot-placement-and-tracking

pp. 62–63): 1. Watch every move the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30–60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs. Wounded animals often head downhill toward water. Flag the trail; if you lose it, search in a circle or grid. 3. Approach from above and behind the head. If the open eye doesn't blink when touched with a stick, it is dead. 📚 Go deeper: Hunter ed manual, p. 61 — shot angles with drawings; Big Game Recovery — reading blood sign; CT DEEP — vital zones.

🔪 Field dressing and the gutless method Field dressing (PNW 517, pp. 7–8; Hunter ed, p. 64; 🖼️ step drawings; 🖼️ step photos): 1. Prop the animal on its back with its head slightly downhill. 2. Cut the hide from the inside out, so hair stays off the meat. Open the belly without cutting the stomach (rumen). 3. Cut the diaphragm and the windpipe. Tie off the colon before you pull it through. 4. Don't touch the dark-haired glands inside the hind legs, just below the hock. They taint the meat. 5. Drain the blood. If you must drag it, sew the cavity shut. Gutless method) — best on steep ground, alone, or in hot weather (Kentucky, p. 1; PNW 517, pp. 9–10; 🖼️ illustrated steps): 1. Skin the top side. Take off the front shoulder (no joint holds it on) and the hindquarter. 2. Take the backstrap and neck meat. Ease the tenderloins out last, without nicking the gut. 3. Flip the animal and repeat. You never open the body or saw the spine, which also avoids the spinal cord (chronic wasting disease). Drag the gut pile at least 25 ft from where you hang the meat (PNW 517, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: OSU PNW 517 Big Game from Hunt to Home — dressing and quartering with photos; Kentucky gutless method; Kentucky elk quartering.

🌡️ Cooling meat in our heat Heat is the enemy. Cave Junction's summer average is 67 °F and Grants Pass has hit 108 °F (Josephine soil survey, p. 5), and archery deer season falls in late August and September. - Get the meat below 40 °F within 24 hours (PNW 517, p. 6). - Hang it in a shady thicket at night. By day, wrap it in cold canvas and lay sleeping bags over it to hold the night's chill. Skin the carcass unless the night will freeze (Montana State, p. 2). - Don't wrap warm meat. Game bags, canvas and paper hold heat in. Keep it in moving air until it is below 40 °F (PNW 517, p. 11). - Meat from a warm day, or from an animal that ran hard or was wounded, should not be aged. Cut it up and preserve it as soon as it is chilled. - Scrape off blowfly egg clusters. Black pepper on moist spots and flapping cloth strips keep flies and ravens off (p. 12). - Birds: keep them at 40 °F or below (NDSU game birds, p. 2). - With no refrigerator, cut and preserve meat the same day: can it, cure it in winter, or make safe jerky (see the Preserving Food guide). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 517, p. 11 — cooling, game bags and flies; Montana State Field

🥩 Butchering, using the whole animal, and hides Bone it out (Wyoming B-884R, p. 2; p. 4): - Take the shoulder off along its natural seam, then the loin. Follow the hind leg's muscle seams into the sirloin tip, top, bottom and eye of round (🖼️ photos of each cut). - Grind the tough heel and trimmings, and preserve trimmings the day you cut them. - A 349-lb field-dressed cow elk gave 148 lb of boneless meat, about 42%. Use the whole animal: - Heart, liver, tongue and kidneys are good. Wash the heart and liver in cold water at once (PNW 517, p. 12). A healthy liver is smooth, wet and deep red-purple. Throw out a spotted or odd-colored liver; the muscle meat may still be fine (general practice). - Beaver, muskrat and raccoon are good eating: the quarters and back. The rib cage is usually discarded (Trapper Education Manual, p. 106; FM 3-05.70, p. 153). - Save the fat. People living on lean meat alone get sick ("rabbit starvation," (rule of thumb); see the Rabbits & Chickens guide). Brain-tanned buckskin), no chemicals (Farnham 1916, pp. 73–74; brain tanning)): 1. Soak the hide in water, or water and wood ashes, until the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼️ unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until
butchering-using-the-whole-animal-and-hides

ashes, until the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼️ unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until you can hold your hand in it. 3. Work the hide in it, and stretch it while it dries. Repeat until soft (🖼️ softening over a stake). 4. Smoke it over smoldering punky wood, never flame (p. 145). Use brains only from healthy animals, and wear gloves (chronic wasting disease). Bark tanning one heavy cowhide takes well over 100 lb of finely ground oak or hemlock bark, added 30–40 lb at a time over about 4 months (USDA FB 1334, p. 14); our tanoak was the old "tanbark" (general practice). 🪤 Trapping, snaring and deadfalls Where you set matters more than the trap (FM 3-05.70, pp. 127–128): - Set on a run (small, used by one species) or at feeding, watering and bedding spots. A trail is used by many species. - Funnel the run with sticks down to just wider than the animal (🖼️ drawing). Don't use freshly cut green wood, which smells of sap. Hide your scent with mud or smoke. - A squirrel pole carries several wire nooses 2–2¼ in across, set 1 in off the pole (p. 132; 🖼️ drawing). Check current ODFW rules first: western gray and Douglas squirrels are protected game in Oregon. Traps with no store-bought gear: the figure-4 and Paiute deadfalls need only sticks and cord (FM 3-05.70, p. 137; 🖼️ Paiute deadfall). Harding's 1907 Deadfalls and Snares shows many more (🖼️ spring-pole snare, 🖼️ trail snares). A box trap keeps rabbits unhurt ("the best for eating") and lets you release a cat, dog or hen unharmed (p. 146; 🖼️ drawing). Check every trap every day, at first light. Most furbearers move at night. Early checks mean less suffering, fewer escapes and less theft by other animals. Don't set more traps than you can check, and stay away from places where pets roam (Trapper Education Manual, p. 99; NY manual, p. 3). Keeping pets out (AFWA body-grip guide, pp. 9, 15–16): -

you can check, and stay away from places where pets roam (Trapper Education Manual, p. 99; NY manual, p. 3). Keeping pets out (AFWA body-grip guide, pp. 9, 15–16): - For raccoon, use sweet baits (marshmallow, molasses, corn syrup, corn) that dogs and cats ignore, not meat or fish. - Raise body-grip cubbies 4–6 ft up a tree (🖼️ cubby on a tree). - Set trail traps 5–6 ft in front of a fence crossing, not under it, so big dogs pass by (🖼️ trail-set drawings). Beaver: #330 body-grip traps or cable devices at slides, scent mounds and channels. Bait with fresh poplar, willow or cottonwood sticks. Use sliding-lock sets in water so the beaver drowns quickly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 138). 📚 Go deeper: Trapper Education Manual — sets, baits and running a trapline; Harding Deadfalls and Snares — illustrated improvised traps; AFWA dog-friendly sets — keeping pets safe.

🎣 Fishing, nets, fish traps and fish care While the rules are enforced (ODFW fishing regs, p. 19): one rod per person, lines closely attended (so no unattended set lines), and no snagging. Local waters and seasons are on Start Here. Nets and stream traps (AFH 10-644, pp. 311, 314): - Set a gill net at a slight angle to the current so debris washes off (🖼️ drawing). Check it at least twice a day. - In small streams, a brush or stake fence that funnels fish into a pen works. Leave a way through for most of the run (general practice) (🖼️ fish-trap layouts; 🖼️ maze traps). - Nets are knotted with the sheet bend, using a netting needle (🖼️ drawing) and mesh gauge (🖼️ drawing) (Twinework, p. 46). A fyke net (a netting hoop trap with wings) is the river version of a fish trap (p. 137). Fish care (NDSU, p. 2; NYSDEC, p. 4): 1. Bleed the fish by cutting the throat. Pull the gills and guts (🖼️ filleting drawing). 2. Scrape out the dark kidney along the backbone. Wipe it and keep it cold. 3. Don't let cleaned fish sit warm more than 2 hours. 4. Contaminants collect in fat: skin the fish and trim the fat (🖼️ where to trim). Smoke alone does not preserve fish. Hot-smoked fish must reach 150 °F inside (160 °F

Contaminants collect in fat: skin the fish and trim the fat (🖼️ where to trim). Smoke alone does not preserve fish. Hot-smoked fish must reach 150 °F inside (160 °F better) for 30 minutes, and still keeps only in a refrigerator (PNW 238, pp. 1–2). Without one, can it or salt it (see the Preserving Food guide). Mercury: Oregon has a statewide mercury advisory on bass, and Applegate Lake has one for resident fish. Sea-run salmon and steelhead carry fewer local contaminants. 🦞 Crawfish, mussels and lamprey - Crawfish (signal crayfish) come out at night. By day, look under stream stones. They grab offal tied on a string; pull them in before they let go. Cook all freshwater shellfish and fish (FM 3-05.70, p. 118). While the rules stand: open all year, no license, by hand, line with no hook, net, ring or trap, 100 a day (ODFW fishing regs, p. 22). - Freshwater mussels are famine food only. Some, like the western pearlshell (🖼️ shells), live over 100 years. About 1 in 100,000,000 larvae becomes a young mussel, and the larvae must ride on salmon or trout to survive (🖼️ life-cycle drawing). A bed stripped bare does not come back in a lifetime (Xerces, p. 12; p. 18). Taking them is illegal while the rules stand. - Pacific lamprey: leave it to the tribes (🖼️ photo on the ODFW Rogue fishes poster). The Hupa netted lamprey on warm spring nights and dried them over the fire (Goddard, p. 35). Tribes still prize it as food and medicine, but it is in steep decline (PLCI fact sheet, p. 1), and Oregon allows it only by tribal or Willamette Falls permit (ODFW, p. 22). 📚 Go deeper: Xerces Freshwater Mussels of the PNW — ID and why beds don't recover; PLCI fact sheet — lamprey and the tribes.

☣️ Disease and safety Trichinella in bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver: wild strains survive freezing (larvae lived 5 years in frozen bear meat), and curing, smoking and drying don't reliably kill them. Cook it through (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 142; NY manual, p. 26). Jerky is safe only if the meat reaches 160 °F (PNW 632, p. 8). Tularemia (rabbit fever) comes from rabbits, hares, beaver and muskrat, and from ticks and deer flies. An infected liver and spleen have white spots. As few as 10 bacteria breathed in can infect you, so don't make dust or spray while skinning. Wear gloves and cook thoroughly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92; Bad Bug Book, p. 64). It needs antibiotics for 10–21 days, depending on the drug (doxycycline 14–21) (CDC, p. 34). Chronic wasting disease isn't in Oregon yet but is in California, Idaho and Washington. Never shoot or eat a deer or elk that looks sick. Never eat the brain, eyes, spinal cord, spleen or lymph nodes. Bone out the meat, and soak tools in half bleach, half water for an hour (ODFW big game regs, p. 48; Hunter ed, p. 65; Kentucky elk guide, p. 2). Ticks: the western blacklegged tick (Lyme disease) lives here (🖼️ tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull

blacklegged tick (Lyme disease) lives here (🖼️ tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull a tick with fine tweezers close to the skin, straight up, no twisting, no heat or petroleum jelly (🖼️ removal photos). Treat clothing with permethrin (CDC, p. 50; ODFW fishing regs, p. 15). Plague): southern Oregon is one of the two US plague regions. Its main flea lives on the California ground squirrel, and a trapper caught plague from a cut while skinning a bobcat. Bag any flea-covered catch at once, spray insecticide in the bag and tie it shut (Plague in Washington, p. 4; Trapper Education Manual, p. 102). Hantavirus comes from deer mice. Never sweep or vacuum droppings. Soak them in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water for 5 minutes, then wipe up with gloves (🖼️ cleanup steps). Use snap traps, not live or glue traps (CDC 2021, pp. 11–12). Lead: fast-expanding lead bullets threw fragments 5–14 in from the exit hole, and lead turned up 18 in away. Rinsing didn't help. A solid copper bullet left few fragments, mostly within about 4 in. Trim wide, throw out bloodshot or bone-flecked meat, and grind one animal at a time (Minnesota DNR, p. 6; PNW 517, p. 1). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women

out bloodshot or bone-flecked meat, and grind one animal at a time (Minnesota DNR, p. 6; PNW 517, p. 1). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (general practice). Coastal clams and mussels: paralytic shellfish toxin and domoic acid aren't destroyed by cooking or freezing, and there's no antidote. Numb lips or tingling hands within hours means get help. With no state testing, leave coastal shellfish alone (ODA, p. 1; OHA, p. 1). Cold rivers: the Illinois and Rogue stay dangerously cold even in summer. Sudden cold water causes gasping (cold shock) and drowning, and water drains body heat 25 times faster than air. Strainers (logjams, overhanging branches) pin people under (OSMB handbook, p. 17; p. 14). 📚 Go deeper: CDC Tickborne Diseases — tick ID, symptoms and treatment; Minnesota Bullet Fragmentation — the X-rays; OHA PSP sheet — symptoms that mean get help now; Field Care guide — treating illness with no doctor.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - "You can eat these raw" for sea fish caught far offshore, and "there are no poisonous freshwater fish" (FM 3-05.70, p. 121). Ocean fish commonly carry worms, and mercury advisories apply here. Instead: cook all fish. - Poisoning fish with rotenone plants, lime or walnut husks (FM 3-05.70, pp. 148–150; AFH 10-644, p. 315). It kills every fish, the young salmon and the insects they eat, and ruins a stream for years. Never do it. - Bow traps and pig-spear traps (FM 3-05.70, pp. 138–140), which the manual itself calls deadly to people. Instead: snares, deadfalls and box traps, never near homes, trails or where children walk. - Smoked meat eaten "without further cooking," eating the brain (FM 3-05.70, p. 154), and sun-dried raw strips (p. 156). Smoked or dried bear still carries trichinella, and deer and elk brain carries chronic wasting disease risk. Instead: cook it through; jerky reaches 160 °F. - Ixodes dammini as the Lyme tick (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92), an old eastern name. Ours is the western blacklegged tick, Ixodes pacificus (CDC, p. 4). - A "minimum" 4-inch trim around the bullet path (PNW 517, p. 1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5–14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40–45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p.

1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5–14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40–45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p. 1). 🌰 Skills of the Valley's First Peoples How the peoples of this corner of Oregon and California lived well here for thousands of years, as how-to for a household with no stores: food through the year and how to keep it, fibers and baskets, houses and fire, tools, tending the land with fire, and the community ways that kept people fed and at peace. The skills come from the Takelma, whose country reached "perhaps as far west as Illinois river" (Sapir, p. 3); the Athabaskan-speaking peoples of Galice Creek and the Applegate (Sapir, p. 4); the Shasta of the upper Rogue (Kroeber, p. 344); and the Karuk, Hupa, Yurok and Tolowa to the south. No book here names the people of the upper Illinois Valley itself. These are living nations: after the wars of the 1850s the Takelma were moved to the Siletz reservation (Sapir, p. 7), and the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians, Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians, Karuk Tribe and Tolowa Dee-niʼ Nation still gather, weave and burn today (NRCS Beargrass, p. 4; KBO, p. 8). This guide covers everyday skills, not ceremonies. in Southern-Oregon\Food-From-Scratch\Wild-and-Local-Staples; Chesnut in Medical\Medicinal-Plants. ### The short version - Death camas grows with camas and the bulbs are "very nearly identical"; poisonings come in late summer, when stems are broken off (Chesnut, p. 333). Dig only plants you marked while they bloomed blue. - Leach every acorn until sweet; tannin is "deleterious to health" (Chesnut, p. 349). Cook every elderberry (OSU, p. 4). - Never eat raw buckeye (Chesnut, p. 384), yew or dogbane (AIB 415, pp. 50, 113), fresh iris roots (NRCS Douglas Iris, p. 1) or carrot-family roots: water hemlock kills (PNW 109, p. 1). - Poison oak's oil is in every part, even in winter, and its smoke has put people in intensive care (OSU PNW 108, pp. 2, 4). Learn it before you gather, weave or burn. - Most old ways of taking salmon and deer are illegal today: weirs, nets, spears, snares, dogs, fire drives (ODFW, p. 21; ODFW Big Game, p. 21). They are here so the knowledge survives. - No burning in fire season. The Karuk burned "in the fall before it starts in to rain" (Harrington, p. 116); now burn only outside fire season, on burn days (DEQ, p. 1), small, with experienced people and a fire line (KBO, pp. 43–44). - Never dig old village sites or graves, or carry off mortars, points or bones.
