🌰 Acorns: from tree to mush The modern short method is "Acorn flour" in Food from Scratch; here is the local way. Which oaks: tanoak was "most esteemed" (Goddard, p. 37) and bears some crop every year, over 200 lb on one tree (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). Black oak was the Shasta's first choice, then Oregon white oak (Dixon, p. 51), whose mush is "more slimy" (p. 54) and which ripens in one year, August–November (NRCS Oregon Oak, p. 1). Canyon live oak is "poisonous when raw" and needs "more washing" (Chesnut, p. 355). How many: "some 400 or 500 pounds" was a family's "year's supply" (Chesnut, p. 348); the NRCS says 500 to 2,000 lb (tanoak, p. 1). A 150-year-old black oak gives about 100 lb in a medium crop (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16), so 500 lb is five big black oaks (arithmetic). Acorns lack protein (Chesnut, p. 347): add salmon or meat. 1. Gather soon after they fall; the first drops are often "unsound because of insects, immaturity" (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16). 2. Dry them in the sun ("The roof of the house is often used", Goddard, p. 37); store them "in the shell, in large baskets" under an upturned basket (Kroeber, p. 126), safe from mold and "robbing squirrels" (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). 3. Shell them on a rock, tapping with a stone, and dry the meats again (Goddard,
acorns-from-tree-to-mush

basket (Kroeber, p. 126), safe from mold and "robbing squirrels" (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). 3. Shell them on a rock, tapping with a stone, and dry the meats again (Goddard, p. 37); rub off the thin inner skin by hand, a step "often overlooked" (Kroeber, p. 351). 4. Pound on a flat stone set in the floor, inside a bottomless basket hopper "wider at the top and entirely open at the bottom" (Sapir, p. 9), held down by your legs over its rim; lift the pestle with the wrist turned and let it fall straight (Kroeber, p. 125). Grind to powder: oily meal won't leach otherwise (Chesnut, p. 349). 5. Sift on a tilted, shallow basket; pound the coarse bits again (Goddard, p. 38).
acorns-from-tree-to-mush

Leaching in a sand basin 1. Scoop a saucer in clean sand and build up the rim (Goddard, p. 38). The Shasta raised theirs 6–12 in off the ground on sticks and pine needles (Dixon, p. 53). 2. Spread the meal about 2 in thick (same page); lay a cedar sprig or small tule mat on top so pouring doesn't scour it (Chesnut, p. 350). 3. Pour on water "nearly scalding hot", gently: "As fast as it soaks away more water is added until the material loses its bitter taste" (Goddard, p. 38); "A couple of hours are usually required" (Chesnut, p. 349). Use clean, safe water (KBO, p. 9). Taste it: done is sweet, with no bitterness or pucker. 4. Slap your palm onto the drained dough, lift it, and wash the sand off its underside in warm water (Dixon, pp. 53–54). Dried, the dough stores and was traded to "the Rogue River people" (p. 54).
leaching-in-a-sand-basin

Stone-boiling mush and baking bread 1. Pick stones that "did not splinter or disintegrate when heated and suddenly cooled" (Dixon, p. 54). Never heat wet or porous river rocks; they can burst (rule of thumb). Rinse off the ash; lift them with green-wood tongs (Chesnut, p. 350). 2. Dough and "a little water" in a tight basket or pot, hot stones in, then more water and stones, "vigorously stirred" (Goddard, p. 39) so they can't burn through (Kroeber, p. 125; Stone boiling). With salt "it is quite agreeable" (Goddard, p. 39). 3. Bread: small cakes on a flat rock tilted toward the fire, eaten with salt (Dixon, p. 54); a loaf on leaves in an earth oven about 12 hours turns sweet (Chesnut, p. 351).
stone-boiling-mush-and-baking-bread

Telling camas from death camas - Fruit and stem: death camas has a "less rigid stem" and smaller capsules of "three nearly distinct valves"; camas has one "ellipsoidal capsule". The bulbs "are very nearly identical", and late summer, "when the stems are often broken off", is when poisonings happen; two of three cases Chesnut knew were fatal (Chesnut, p. 333). - Death camas: bulb with "blackish scales"; V-shaped leaves "edged with stiff hairs"; stem 6–18 in; flowers "greenish to yellowish-white" in April–May (PNW 104, pp. 1–2). - Not colour alone: great camas can be "creamy-white to deep blue-violet" (NRCS camas, p. 2), so skip every white or cream flower. Not smell: death camas bulbs "do not give off an onion-like odor", which tells them from wild onion (PNW 104, p. 2); no book here says camas smells of onion, so smell can't separate the two. - The safe way: mark blue plants in bloom, dig them after seed set, and pull every death camas out of your beds, as the traditional camas tenders did (NRCS camas, p. 4).
telling-camas-from-death-camas

Tending a camas bed and pit-roasting Lift the turf in small sections, take only the larger bulbs, break up and replant the rest, put the turf back, and dig each patch "only every few years" (NRCS camas, p. 1). Replant bulblets ½–1 in deep and big bulbs 4–6 in (p. 3). A family of five needed about 2.7 ha (6.7 acres) (p. 2). The Takelma dug with a sharpened hardwood stick with a deer-horn handle (Sapir, p. 9). Raw camas is gluey and tasteless, cooked very sweet (Chesnut, p. 340), because "lengthy cooking" turns its starch to sugar (NRCS, p. 2): 1. Dig a pit, fill it with alder brush with stones on top (Sapir) or line it with stones (Chesnut), and burn it until the stones are hot (Sapir, p. 9; Chesnut, p. 340; Earth oven). 2. Lay alder bark or pine needles on the hot stones, then the bulbs, more needles, then earth; Chesnut's cooks kept a small fire on top overnight (same pages). Oak bark "burns slowly without flame" (Chesnut, p. 354). 3. "The succeeding day, if the roots were not yet well cooked, a fire was again built" (Sapir, p. 9). Camas takes 24–36 hours (NRCS, p. 2), until soft and sweet all through (rule of thumb). 4. Mash into cakes and dry them for winter (Sapir, p. 9); soak dried bulbs overnight before eating (NRCS,
tending-a-camas-bed-and-pit-roasting
p. 2), until soft and sweet all through (rule of thumb). 4. Mash into cakes and dry them for winter (Sapir, p. 9); soak dried bulbs overnight before eating (NRCS, p. 2).
tending-a-camas-bed-and-pit-roasting

Other bulbs and roots - Brodiaeas and mariposa lilies were "roasted in the ashes or boiled in baskets" (Goddard, pp. 40–41; Dixon, p. 52). Same death-camas rules. - Soaproot, famine food only: raw, it holds "the poisonous substance sapotoxin" (Chesnut, p. 331). The Hupa pit-cooked it "for about two days" (Goddard, p. 40); baked overnight it was "a significant food to the Karuk" (NRCS Soaproot, p. 1), but Chesnut found no clear sign it was eaten in Mendocino (p. 331). Try a little first (rule of thumb). Death camas is also called "soap plant" (PNW 104, p. 1): learn the plant, not the name. - Yampah roots taste nutty (Saunders, p. 31), but it is in the water-hemlock family: leave it to an expert. Tule rootstocks were "pounded into a kind of flour" (NRCS Tule, p. 1).

🫐 Seeds, nuts and berries Sugar-pine nuts (Sugar pine): in October families went "men and women together, to the tops of the ridges" and camped; cones were "pounded until the seeds loosen" (Goddard, p. 40). Gather fallen cones (rule of thumb). To keep them, the Shasta steamed the nuts in leaves in a covered pit of hot stones and water "for several hours", dried them, and later pounded them into cakes or mixed them with powdered salmon (Dixon, pp. 54–55). Hazelnuts: gather "as soon as ripe, for the bears are very fond of them": June–July by Goddard (p. 39), early autumn by the NRCS, so summer into early fall. Eat them raw or roasted, pound them into cakes "with berries, meat, or animal fat", or boil them for oil (NRCS hazelnut, p. 1). Pinole (parched seed meal): beat the seeds into a basket with a wicker beater, winnow and pick them clean, toss them with live tanoak coals in a basket tray, "constantly shaken and tossed to prevent the burning of the seeds and the basket", and grind (Goddard, p. 41). One kind at a time, with salt (Chesnut, p. 321; Pinole). For tarweed, "gathered in the fall" (Chesnut, p. 413), the Takelma first burned the stalks "to remove the pitchy substance", and ate the meal dry (Sapir, p. 10). Manzanita: the Hupa took berries "dry and powdery" in midsummer
seeds-nuts-and-berries

413), the Takelma first burned the stalks "to remove the pitchy substance", and ate the meal dry (Sapir, p. 10). Manzanita: the Hupa took berries "dry and powdery" in midsummer and later, dried them on sand, pounded them in the hopper and separated the flour from the seeds (Goddard, p. 41); the Takelma mixed the flour with sugar-pine nuts and stored it (Sapir, p. 10). Cider: scald ripe, sound berries "until the seeds are soft", crush, add an equal amount of water, pour at once over dry pine needles or straw in a sieve basket and let it drain (Chesnut, p. 394); drink it within four days (NRCS manzanita, p. 2). ⚠️ Too much whole fruit can kill: "The bowels become stopped with great masses of seeds and pulp" (Chesnut, p. 394). Huckleberries: evergreen huckleberries ripen "around October or November", "even tastier after freezing"; dry them in sun or smoke, mash, press into cakes and wrap in leaves or bark (NRCS Evergreen Huckleberry, p. 1). Elderberries: the NRCS says Native Americans ate them "raw, cook, or dry" (NRCS Blue Elderberry, p. 1); this guide follows OSU: cook every berry, never eat stems, leaves or green berries (OSU, p. 4). Others: thimbleberries, blackcaps, blackberries, currants, gooseberries (Goddard, p. 42); serviceberries dried for winter (Dixon, p. 55); salal, leaving some fruit on each plant (GTR-513, p. 76); drying: Preserving Food.

🐟 Salmon, lamprey and other fish The Takelma took trout, steelhead, coho and Chinook, crawfish and mussels (Sapir, p. 10). On the Klamath "there is scarcely a month in the year when some variety of salmon can not be taken" (Kroeber, p. 123). How it was done (illegal today): - Dip net at an eddy: from a platform over a backwater, a triangle of poles held a bag net with a fan of strings across its mouth, gathered to a cord in the fisherman's hand; when a salmon shook them he lifted the net (Dixon, pp. 56–58). "A single night's vigil sometimes produced a hundred salmon [...] a winter's supply" (Kroeber, p. 123). - Weir: "in a shallow, gravelly spot", stakes slanting downstream, a pole lashed at water level and guyed to shore with grapevines, weighted brush upstream, and "long willow fish-traps" in the gaps (Dixon, p. 56; Fishing weir). The Hupa built theirs in alternate years (Goddard, p. 34). - Also two-pronged harpoons (Kroeber, p. 124) and bone hooks baited with crawfish (Sapir, p. 10). Never poison: "No poisons [...] were used" (Goddard, p. 36). Drying and storing the catch: 1. Skin, take off head and tail, gut, and split at the backbone (Sapir, p. 11); wipe the blood with ferns and leaves (Goddard, p. 36). 2. Cut it "into three or more layers", held open with sticks (Goddard,
salmon-lamprey-and-other-fish

split at the backbone (Sapir, p. 11); wipe the blood with ferns and leaves (Goddard, p. 36). 2. Cut it "into three or more layers", held open with sticks (Goddard, p. 36), or roast it on split-hazel spits (Sapir, p. 11). Smoke and dry it over the fire; the Takelma "never salted" it. 3. Store slabs in baskets (Kroeber, p. 123), or bone it, rub it "to powder between the hands" and pack it in leaf-lined baskets (Dixon, p. 55) or tule sacks (Kroeber, p. 352). 4. Use it all: heads crushed into cakes for winter hunting trips, bones pounded for soup (Dixon, pp. 53, 55), dried eggs, "no form of food more concentrated" (Goddard, p. 36). Dried salmon "is very hard and nearly tasteless, but rather satisfying" (Kroeber, p. 123). Dry it until brittle (rule of thumb): smoke alone doesn't keep moist fish (PNW 238, p. 1), and lightly field-smoked fish keeps "2 weeks to a month" (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 17). Safe methods: "Fish: smoking, canning and salting" in Preserving Food. Lamprey, slit "many times to the skin" and dried over the fire (Goddard, p. 36), are now in steep decline and tribal-permit only (PLCI, p. 1): leave them to the tribes. The law today: game fish by angling, "using a hook and line" (ODFW, p. 16); no snagging, spearing, netting, trapping or clubbing them, and salmon, steelhead
salmon-lamprey-and-other-fish

them to the tribes. The law today: game fish by angling, "using a hook and line" (ODFW, p. 16); no snagging, spearing, netting, trapping or clubbing them, and salmon, steelhead and trout by day only (p. 21). Suckers and other nongame fish may be taken by hand, bow or spear; lamprey and mussels may not (p. 22). Legal gear: Hunting, Trapping & Fishing.

🦌 Deer, elk and small game How it was done (mostly illegal today): - Takelma deer fence: small gaps, each with a "finely spun" grass-rope snare; before daybreak men and dogs drove the deer while shoulder blades rattled over the gaps; near creeks or salt licks, with up to "one hundred and fifty" snares (Sapir, p. 11). Shasta and Takelma also made beargrass snares, used with fire (NRCS Beargrass, p. 3). - Shasta drives: in autumn, fences with nooses in the openings; after the oak leaves fell, fire set in broken circles, with women rattling deer bones at the gap and hunters hidden in the brush (Dixon, p. 59). - Stalking: the Shasta hunter wore a whole deerskin with head and antlers (Dixon, p. 59); the Hupa hunter hid his scent by "bathing and smoking with green fir boughs" (Goddard, p. 32). - Trail snares "where there is but one road to the feeding ground, salt-lick, or watering place" (Goddard, p. 32); deer "seem to have been snared more often than shot" (Kroeber, p. 124). Robins were snared with twine "baited with acorns" (Goddard, p. 33). The law today: no dogs, artificial lights, traps, snares or poison for game mammals (ODFW Big Game, p. 21); bows for deer and elk pull at least 40 lb, with unbarbed broadheads at least 7/8 in wide (p. 22). Scent control and patient stalking
deer-elk-and-small-game

(ODFW Big Game, p. 21); bows for deer and elk pull at least 40 lb, with unbarbed broadheads at least 7/8 in wide (p. 22). Scent control and patient stalking are still yours. More: Hunting, Trapping & Fishing. Use the whole animal. "None of the animal was wasted": marrow bones saved, sinews kept for bowstrings, the brain dried for "dressing the hide", spare meat cut in strips and cured over a fire (Goddard, pp. 32–33); elk antler made spoons and wedges. Deer fat went into "hard dough-like cakes" for winter (Sapir, p. 11); bones were pounded for winter soup, and bear meat boiled before drying (Dixon, p. 55; trichinella: "Disease and safety" in the Hunting guide). Hides were worked soft with "deer brains and water", or the hair loosened for leather by burying the hide "in wet sand for several days" (Goddard, p. 46); full steps: "Tanning hides" in Clothing & Leather. Sinew: take the back sinew or hind-leg tendons (the finer shank tendons make bowstrings) (Pope, pp. 11–12); dry them, pound them into fibres, wet them and twist or lay them on: "the moistened sinew is sticky and it hardens when dry" (FM 21-76, p. 151; Tendon).

🧵 Fibers, cordage and nets Iris cord, the local net and snare fibre: 1. Gather leaves "in the fall when fully mature"; plants "under oaks" beat those "under pines" (Goddard, p. 45). 2. Take only the two fibres near the leaf edges, drawing the leaf past your thumb against a mussel-shell "thumbnail" (Goddard, p. 45), and scrape them "clean of all tissues" (NRCS Douglas Iris, p. 1). 3. Roll them between palm and thigh into two-ply cord (Goddard, p. 45; 🖼️ twisting fibres). 4. Expect slow work: "it takes nearly six weeks to make a rope twelve feet long" (NRCS, p. 1). An iris deer rope was "near 20 feet long" and "about half an inch in diameter" (same page). ⚠️ "Fresh iris roots may be toxic" (same page). Dogbane: "The stems are cut in the fall; they are then split open and the long, silky fibers removed", then twisted into string (NRCS Indian Hemp, p. 1); Shasta string was "either of iris or Apocynum fibers" (Kroeber, p. 349). The leaves are poisonous "even when they are dry" (AIB 415, p. 50). Others: willow inner bark, "collected in spring", for rope (Chesnut, p. 344); fishing line of grass "rolled together by hand" (Sapir, p. 10). No book here covers nettle fibre; see "Linen, nettle and native fibers" in Clothing & Leather. Test a new fibre: tie "an overhand knot [...]
fibers-cordage-and-nets

by hand" (Sapir, p. 10). No book here covers nettle fibre; see "Linen, nettle and native fibers" in Clothing & Leather. Test a new fibre: tie "an overhand knot [...] If the knot does not break, the material is usable" (FM 3-05.70, p. 201); finger-spun cord 1/32 in thick can hold "20 to 30 pounds or more" (AFH 10-644, p. 275). Nets were knotted on a mesh stick from a shuttle (Goddard, p. 46), both often elk antler, with grooved stones for weights (Kroeber, p. 124).

🧺 Baskets The local style is twining: "Substantially the only technique is simple twining", patterns laid on top, and "Three-strand twining is customary for starts and strengthening courses", reaching north to "the Athabascan tribes on the Umpqua River" (Kroeber, p. 128; Basket weaving). The upright sticks (warps) are hazel or willow; the strands woven round them (wefts) are split root or grass (Sapir, p. 12). | Material | Used for | When | How to prepare | | Hazel shoots | Warps | Spring, "as soon as the sap is well started", from a patch burned 1–3 summers before | Peel while fresh; dry in the sun (Goddard, p. 48; Harrington, p. 161). A simple twined basket, from a Karuk weaver's own account, "from the time the warp sticks were first held together" (Harrington, p. 165): 1. Soak the root strands, with a bowl of water by you to wet them often (p. 167); keep the sticks wet "by letting them slip through the wet hand"; no fine work on a windy day, as "the material dries too rapidly" (Goddard, pp. 52–53). 2. Start: two hazel sticks together, tips opposite; two more the same way; hold the four in your left hand and lay four more crosswise on top (Harrington, pp. 165–166). 3. Lash the cross: from a corner, run a root strand diagonally across, then under; turn the bundle over and repeat until both groups lie flat and tight (pp. 167–177). 4. Two-strand twining, one round, four sticks at a time: one strand passes inside, one outside, crossing between groups (pp. 177–178; 🖼️ Mason's

groups lie flat and tight (pp. 167–177). 4. Two-strand twining, one round, four sticks at a time: one strand passes inside, one outside, crossing between groups (pp. 177–178; 🖼️ Mason's drawing). To join a strand, twist old and new together once "so it will not come loose again" (p. 177). 5. Three-strand twining: "I take the hindmost one all the time [...] it goes over two sticks and passes under one. Every once in a while I pull it tight" (p. 180). 6. Add sticks as the bottom widens, "whenever there seems to be a gap"; chew the butt end soft so it won't back out; add most on the bottom, few once the sides start up (p. 180). 7. Hold it inside-down on your thigh for the bottom, then against your knee; press each twist down with your left thumb (p. 181). Pattern: lay beargrass on the outside of the root strand and twine them as one (p. 182). 8. Finish: add three-strand rounds wherever it needs strength (Kroeber, p. 128); trim the stick ends only when all weaving is done, or bend them down and wrap them with willow, as some Hupa did (Mason, p. 99). Start easy with an open-twined plate, rows "about an inch apart" (Goddard, p. 51); a close pine-root cooking basket "is water-tight and will last many years" (p. 52). Mats: "overlapping tule mats

with an open-twined plate, rows "about an inch apart" (Goddard, p. 51); a close pine-root cooking basket "is water-tight and will last many years" (p. 52). Mats: "overlapping tule mats made homes well-insulated and rain-proof" (NRCS Tule, p. 1). 📚 Go deeper: Harrington, pp. 161–191 — the whole Karuk basket, with photo plates.

🏠 Houses and sweathouses The winter house was dug in, with a plank roof: - Takelma: split sugar-pine boards; a floor "a foot and a half to two feet below the surface", stamped smooth; corner posts and cross-beams lashed with hazel fibre; a door raised about 3 ft with an earth ramp and notched-pole ladder; a central fire and smoke-hole (Sapir, p. 13). Poorer families used pine bark (p. 14). - Shasta: a pit about 16 by 20–23 ft, no more than 3 ft deep; the dug earth heaped as walls and lined with cedar-bark slabs; sugar-pine roof boards "split out with wedges", with eaves that "protected the earthen walls" (Dixon, pp. 44–45; metres converted, arithmetic). Copy the porch: its door "always at the extreme corner", so "all direct draught into the house was stopped"; it held firewood, nets and spears (p. 45). - Hupa: about 20 ft square over a pit 12 ft square and 5 ft deep, cedar planks on end, a round door "closed by a plank slid from within" (Goddard, p. 23); roof planks laid double "with a good projection to carry the rain away from the walls", and poles over the fire for smoking fish and venison (p. 24). Planks without a saw: split logs with elk-horn wedges "driven home with stone mauls" into planks "two or more feet wide and two and a half
houses-and-sweathouses

and venison (p. 24). Planks without a saw: split logs with elk-horn wedges "driven home with stone mauls" into planks "two or more feet wide and two and a half to three inches thick" (Goddard, p. 25); the wedge's edge was "produced by rubbing on stone" (Kroeber, p. 136). With steel: "Splitting and laying your own shingles and shakes" in Shelter Building. Before digging a pit house, read "Quake rules for earth walls" in Natural Building, and ditch it so winter rain runs away (rule of thumb). Summer: a brush shelter round a fire (Sapir, p. 13). Firewood: big logs that burn all night, fed small pieces (Harrington, p. 260); mix fast-burning manzanita with slow wood (Chesnut, p. 393; Firewood guide).

The sweathouse: for cleanliness and warmth The Takelma sweathouse was partly underground and earth-covered; hot stones went in through a side hole and water was poured on them; women used "a small temporary stick structure covered over with blankets" (Sapir, p. 14). The Shasta sweat lodge was "a small hemisphere of pine bark and skins thrown over a few bent willows" (Kroeber, p. 348). To build one: bend willow poles into a dome about 5 ft high and across, cover it with blankets, put a pit of stones heated almost red-hot inside, and pour water on them. Drink "plenty of water"; "Half an hour of this is enough for most persons" (Seton, pp. 340–341; Sweat lodge). ⚠️ Keep it short, cool down slowly rather than plunging into a cold river, keep out anyone sick, pregnant or with heart trouble, and never leave a child alone in one (rule of thumb).

🔥 Making, keeping and carrying fire Hand drill (Fire making): 1. Wood: the Hupa used cottonwood root "well seasoned by hanging in the sweathouse" (Goddard, p. 48); buckeye wood also made drills (Chesnut, p. 384). 2. Hearth: "about a foot long one inch wide and three fourths of an inch thick", with "Several small shallow holes" near one edge and a groove from each hole to the edge. Drill: "about fifteen inches long and one-half inch in diameter" (Goddard, p. 48). Tinder: "finely shredded cedar bast" at the groove; the Takelma carried hearth, drill and tinder in the quiver (Sapir, p. 12). 3. Spin the drill between flat palms "with downward pressure" (Pope, p. 16); when your hands reach the bottom, bring them back to the top fast (rule of thumb). "Soon little glowing dust runs down the notches and ignites the prepared tinder" (Goddard, p. 48). The bow drill is easier to learn: "Fire and light without stores" in Make-Do Household (rule of thumb). Keep fire rather than make it. The Karuk drilled fire "Only once in a long time"; they kept big logs burning and carried fire: "They pack fire along in a bowl basket" with earth in it, to warm themselves where they cut wood (Harrington, p. 260). A fire bundle of "dry punk or fibrous barks (cedar) encased in a bark" carries coals, with "just enough"
making-keeping-and-carrying-fire

it, to warm themselves where they cut wood (Harrington, p. 260). A fire bundle of "dry punk or fibrous barks (cedar) encased in a bark" carries coals, with "just enough" air to keep them burning slowly (AFH 10-644, pp. 228–229). ⚠️ Carried coals start wildfires: carry none in the dry months (rule of thumb).

🏹 Tools: bows, arrows, points, wedges and soaproot The local bow was yew, "so thin that only the sinew backing kept it from breaking" (Kroeber, p. 127), with sinew laid "in several layers [...] over a glue consisting of steel-head salmon skin" (Sapir, p. 23). The Hupa laid it on "while the wood is green", bound it until dry, and seasoned the bow in the sweathouse (Goddard, p. 42); it was "effective for game up to fifty or seventy-five yards" (p. 43). Ishi's way, step by step. Ishi was Yahi, from Mill Creek far south in California, not local, but Pope's account is the fullest in the library: 1. Length: the stave across your chest from right hip to left hand, arm out at 45°; limbs three or four fingers wide. Season the split stave flat in a warm, sheltered place; scrape it to shape, finish with sandstone (Pope, p. 10). 2. Back it: soak strips of back or hind-leg tendon in warm water for hours; glue the back (boiled salmon skin) and let it dry; chew the wet sinew "soft and pulpy" and lay it in overlapping parallel lines; bind with bark for one night; when "thoroughly dry and hard", days later, scrape it smooth (p. 11). 3. Season again "for days or weeks". String: shank tendons chewed into fine threads and rolled into "a very tight, simple twist
tools-bows-arrows-points-wedges-and-soaproot

hard", days later, scrape it smooth (p. 11). 3. Season again "for days or weeks". String: shank tendons chewed into fine threads and rolled into "a very tight, simple twist one-eighth of an inch thick", dried taut (p. 12). His bows of 44 and about 54 in pulled 40 and 45 lb; yew "produced the best weapon", and tanoak, red cedar and juniper also served (p. 10). ⚠️ Yew is "probably one of the most toxic of all poisonous plants", and children are poisoned by "the scarlet fruit" (AIB 415, p. 113). The Army's quick bow uses "Dead, dry wood" (FM 3-05.70, p. 141): a different, unbacked bow. Arrows: Hupa shafts of syringa with a serviceberry foreshaft and three hawk feathers bound with sinew, 30–36 in long (Goddard, p. 44); Ishi used straight hazel shoots "about a yard long", peeled and seasoned in a bundle (Pope, p. 15). Straighten each bend by warming it over embers or a hot stone and pressing with the thumbs ("To burn or discolor the wood was evidence of bad technique"), smooth it between two sandstones (pp. 15–16), and set the point in heated pine resin bound with sinew (p. 22). Points: press off flakes with "a piece of antler lashed to a stick of wood about fifteen inches in length", the stone on a buckskin pad in your palm (Goddard, p. 44; Knapping). A
tools-bows-arrows-points-wedges-and-soaproot

with "a piece of antler lashed to a stick of wood about fifteen inches in length", the stone on a buckskin pad in your palm (Goddard, p. 44; Knapping). A deer point took Ishi about half an hour, and his people guarded their eyes from the flakes (Pope, p. 21): wear eye protection (rule of thumb). Use stone found loose in a creek, never from an old site. Small stone points don't meet the 7/8-in broadhead rule for deer. Soaproot (Chlorogalum) grows "up into southwestern Oregon". The bulb was soap "for washing the body, hair, baskets, and utensils"; its fibre coat makes brush bristles, and the cooked, mashed bulb glues them to a handle and glues feathers to arrows (NRCS Soaproot, p. 1; Chesnut, pp. 331–332). Dig it after it seeds, drop the seeds back in the hole and leave some bulb (NRCS Soaproot, p. 2). Other glues: boiled salmon skin (Pope, p. 11), sturgeon glands (Goddard, p. 43), pine resin (pitch glue: Make-Do guide). Needles were bone or hardwood with an eye, threaded with sinew (Sapir, p. 12).

🌲 Tending the land with fire "All that they used to do was to burn the brush at various places, so that some good things will grow up," says the Karuk text Harrington took down. "They do not set the fire for nothing" (Harrington, pp. 115–116; Cultural burning). Why they burned: - Acorns: easier gathering, fewer "diseases and [...] acorn pests", straight shoots, fewer "major conflagrations that would destroy the oaks", more seed plants (NRCS black oak, p. 2). A March burn gave "a bumper crop of sound" acorns beside unburned trees bearing unsound ones (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16). The Karuk burned under tanoaks "lest it be brushy where they pick up acorns", but not "too hard" (Harrington, p. 116). - Basket plants: hazel burned "in summer" was cut "the second summer afterwards" (p. 115); beargrass was picked "the next summer, in July" (p. 116), its new leaves "stronger, thinner, and more pliable" (NRCS Beargrass, p. 6). - Food, game, safety: huckleberries "grow up good" (Harrington, p. 115); oak savannas stay open, with better wildlife habitat (KBO, p. 7); and seasonal fire "can also reduce the occurrence of the larger, more destructive wildfires" (KBO, p. 7; Lake & Long, p. 7). What fire harms: manzanita "does not come up"; tanoak "is not good when it is burned off, the tree dies"; "they are careful lest the trees burn" (Harrington, p. 117).

What fire harms: manzanita "does not come up"; tanoak "is not good when it is burned off, the tree dies"; "they are careful lest the trees burn" (Harrington, p. 117). Black and white oaks survive light fire (KBO, p. 45); hot fire kills beargrass roots (GTR-513, p. 133). | What you tend | How often | Source | | Oak woodland underburn | Every 3–5 years | KBO, p. 42 | | Beargrass patch | About every 3 years; at least every 20 | NRCS Beargrass, p. 6; Lake & Long, p. 5 | | Hazel for basket sticks | Burn, then cut the second summer | Harrington, p. 115 | | Camas prairie | Yearly, after digging | NRCS camas, pp. 1, 4 | | Death camas in a camas bed | Mid-spring, three years running | PNW 104, p. 2 | When: then and now. The Karuk burned "in summer [...] when everything is dry [...] in the fall before it starts in to rain" (Harrington, p. 116); others "in the fall or early winter" (NRCS black oak, p. 2). That timing is inside today's fire season. Open burning is legal "outside of fire season [...] on burn days only"; Josephine County's burn line is 541-476-9663, and fines run "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1). Oak burners now go "prior to leaf out in the spring

days only"; Josephine County's burn line is 541-476-9663, and fines run "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1). Oak burners now go "prior to leaf out in the spring or after leaf fall in the autumn" (KBO, p. 45), and this library's rule is no open burning June–October, until real rain ("Burning on purpose: wet season only" in the Wildfire guide). So: after the fall rains or before spring green-up, on a burn day. How to burn safely (KBO, pp. 43–44): 1. Plan, get the permits, tell the neighbours; it takes "experienced personnel". 2. Thin and pile the brush first, to bring fuel "to safe levels"; rake to bare soil for 2 ft around oaks, snags and logs you want to keep. 3. Clear a fire line "approximately 12 to 24 inches in width" to bare mineral soil all the way round. 4. Burn when "neither too dry nor too wet", never "too windy, or during an inversion"; "Start by igniting small test patches". Keep a crew with water and hand tools on the line (rule of thumb). 5. Patrol "until the fire is dead out", check old stumps and duff for heat, and come back "in the hours and days following". 6. You owe for what your fire burns: under Yurok law a man whose hillside burn destroyed another man's hidden valuables was held liable for them (Kroeber, p. 59). 🤝 Community ways that worked Share the catch. Each Shasta fish dam belonged to one family, but its owners "were obliged to give to any one who asked for them as many fish as he could carry" (Dixon, p. 56). "The single hunter always shared his game with others on his return: the chief, however, had no greater share than others"; the hunter kept the hide and legs (Dixon, p. 60). A Hupa village followed its headman "because from him they received food in time of scarcity" (Goddard, p. 68). Clear rules and limits. Shared fishing spots went in 24-hour turns, changing "about the middle of the afternoon" (Kroeber, p. 59); no new fishing place could open below an old one, which "must have very closely restricted the total number" (p. 60); the Hupa weir went in alternate years (Goddard, p. 34). Take big camas only and rest the patch; leave some soaproot "for wildlife and future production" (NRCS Soaproot, p. 2); pull beargrass a few leaves at a time. Take no more than a third of a patch (rule of thumb). Pay instead of fight. A Takelma man who was struck would often "keep cool" and ask for payment instead of hitting back. In serious quarrels a go-between, whose "person was deemed inviolate", carried each side's exact words until the offender paid; the injured side then gave back "a
community-ways-that-worked

instead of hitting back. In serious quarrels a go-between, whose "person was deemed inviolate", carried each side's exact words until the offender paid; the injured side then gave back "a nominal present" "to cement the new friendship" (Sapir, p. 21). Among the Hupa, a respected man proposed the settlement, witnesses were called if facts were disputed, and "After the settlement is accomplished the parties must be friends" (Goddard, p. 69). Yurok law put it plainly: revenge "causes two liabilities to lie where one lay before", and once payment is accepted the claim "is irrevocably and totally extinguished. Even the harboring of a sentiment of injury is thereafter improper" (Kroeber, p. 44). Putting this to work: "Settling disputes and dealing with theft" in Community & Barter. Trade skills and teach the children. A man could "make use of his neighbor's skill" in bow-making (Goddard, p. 42). "Children are seldom punished or handled roughly when small"; they learned from "the father and grandfather at night, and by the grandmother, the great source of wisdom, by day", and "The girl soon begins to weave little baskets" (Goddard, p. 62).

💊 Medicine plants: go carefully The old books are full of plant remedies; almost none are tested, and some use the most poisonous plants here (death camas, iris root, dogbane, yew). This guide repeats none: read "Medicinal plants — go carefully" in Medical READ-ME-FIRST and use the Field Care guide. Bathing, soaproot soap and short sweats here are for cleanliness only.
medicine-plants-go-carefully

⚖️ Respect and the law - Public land: the Forest Service and BLM keep permit lists for forest products (GTR-513, p. 17), and digging wild camas "is rarely appropriate or legal except under salvage situations" (NRCS camas, p. 3). Plant your own camas and soaproot beds (NRCS Soaproot, pp. 1–2). - Tribal and private land: tribes already lack "access to ancestral lands" (KBO, p. 8). Ask before gathering, and don't strip a known weaving or camas site (rule of thumb). - Village sites and graves: "Oregon law protects American Indian graves and certain sacred American Indian objects on both public and private lands. It is illegal to remove, injure, or destroy these" (ODFW Today's Hunter, p. 33). "Do not disturb" a find; report it to the Forest Service or BLM on federal land, or the State Police; for human remains call OSP at once, 800-452-7888 (p. 34; ARPA; NAGPRA). The old stone mortars found in Shasta country "are never used by the Shasta" (Kroeber, p. 349). Leave mortars, pestles and points where they lie. - Fish, game and fire: see the law notes in the salmon, deer and burning sections. Sudden oak death rides "on tools, tires or shoes" (NRCS tanoak, p. 3): clean your gear between tanoak groves (rule of thumb).

🐇🐔 Rabbits & Chickens for Meat and Eggs How to keep meat rabbits and a self-renewing chicken flock with no feed store, vet or hatchery: breeds, hutches and coops, local predators, feeding on hay, greens, grain and scraps, breeding and kindling, hatching chicks under hens, eggs, summer heat, common diseases, slaughter and butchering, manure, and keeping the breeding lines going for years. The books are in Small-Livestock\ (Rabbits, Chickens, Slaughter-Processing) and Animals\ (Poultry, Rabbits-Other, Veterinary, Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst losses - Lock birds in every night behind hardware cloth, not chicken wire, buried at least 12 inches. A weasel kills several birds at once and fits through a ¼-inch gap (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 3, 6). - Heat kills rabbits. Plan litters for spring and fall, not July–August, and have shade, airflow and water ready before 100 °F days (USDA FB 1730, p. 31). - Never feed heated, moldy or sprayed greens, or plants from where dogs and cats go. Scotch broom and foxglove — everywhere here — are toxic (WSNWCB, p. 55). - Keep breeds that can renew themselves. Hybrid layers and Cornish-cross broilers rarely go broody and won't rebuild a flock (FAO, p. 10). - Rabbit meat alone is not a diet — it is very lean. Eat it with fat and starch. - The old bulletins' medicines are poisons (sodium fluoride, carbon tetrachloride, nicotine,

Rabbit meat alone is not a diet — it is very lean. Eat it with fat and starch. - The old bulletins' medicines are poisons (sodium fluoride, carbon tetrachloride, nicotine, DDT, lindane). See the last section.

🐇 Choosing breeds and starting stock Rabbits: - New Zealand or Californian — by far the leading meat breeds, for steady color and growth (🖼️ meat breeds). Most meat rabbits are butchered by 10 weeks (OSU EC 1651, p. 1). - Start with 2–3 does per buck (6 does and 2 bucks is typical). Buy from several different breeders to avoid inbreeding. Pick thick-boned rabbits, as deep as they are wide (EC 1651, p. 2; 🖼️ body shape to look for). Chickens (USDA FB 1508, p. 6; FB 1363, p. 8): | Breed | Good for | Notes | | Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island Red, Wyandotte, Orpington, Australorp | Eggs and meat | Most make good mothers — the best choice for a self-renewing flock (🖼️ Buff Orpington) | | Leghorn, Ancona, Minorca | Eggs | Fly over fences; "fickle mothers" (🖼️ Leghorn flock) | | Brahma, Jersey Giant, Cochin | Meat | Sit well but are clumsy on eggs | | Commercial hybrids, Cornish-cross | Short-term only | "Very low mothering ability and broodiness" (FAO, p. 10) | 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1651 — meat breeds and picking breeding stock; USDA FB 1508, p. 6 — back-yard chicken breeds; Practical Poultry Raising — low-input flocks.

🏠 Hutches and coops Rabbit hutches (USDA AIB 358, pp. 8–10; OSU EC 1654, p. 2; 🖼️ two-compartment hutch; 🖼️ building plans): - About 2 ft high, no more than 2½ ft deep; 3 ft long for small breeds, 4 ft for medium, 6 ft for large. At least ¾ sq ft per pound of rabbit. - Scrap lumber and hardware cloth work. Give each hutch) shade, a rain-proof roof and no drafts. - Water bottles or nipples, not crocks (crocks get fouled). No cedar shavings. - A resting board on part of a wire floor prevents sore hocks (R-41, p. 26). Colony or ground pens (rule of thumb): they save wire and work, but rabbits dig out (bury mesh or a 2-ft wire apron; cover the top), catch coccidiosis and tapeworm from soil, and you lose track of matings. Does in heat ride each other and conceive less (R-41, p. 41); extra bucks fight — castrate or remove them (p. 67). Keep breeding does in their own hutches; put only growing fryers on grass in movable pens. Chicken coops (OSU EC 1644, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ coop photo): - 3 sq ft per bird in the coop with a run, 8–10 sq ft without one. - Raise the coop 1 ft off the ground. Roosts 2 ft high, 5–10 inches of pole per bird (🖼️ roost layouts). - Run of

8–10 sq ft without one. - Raise the coop 1 ft off the ground. Roosts 2 ft high, 5–10 inches of pole per bird (🖼️ roost layouts). - Run of 1×2-inch mesh, top covered, fence buried 6–12 inches (Kentucky says 12+). - A movable pen (a chicken tractor) puts birds on fresh grass and breaks the parasite cycle. 📚 Go deeper: USDA AIB 358, p. 10 — scrap-lumber hutch plans; OSU EC 1654, p. 1 — cages, drafts and bedding; OSU EC 1644 — coop design for Oregon.

🦝 Predators of the Illinois Valley Who did it? (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 2–3) — all of these live here: | Predator | What you find | | Bobcat | Whole bird eaten or gone; leftovers covered with leaves and grass (coyotes and foxes don't do this; here a cougar also covers its kills, usually bigger ones like goats or deer (general practice)) | | Raccoon | Head, crop and breast eaten; heads pulled through the wire; eggs carried 50+ yards | | Fox | Bird gone; a few drops of blood and feathers | | Opossum | Feeding started at the vent | | Weasel or mink | Several birds killed, bloody, little eaten. A least weasel fits a ¼-inch hole | | Hawk or owl | Daytime (hawk) or night (owl) losses from open runs | Keeping them out (ID-245, pp. 5–6; 🖼️ photos): 1. Hardware cloth, buried at least 12 inches. Chicken wire keeps chickens in, not raccoons out. 2. Lock birds in every night. Feed them inside at dusk and they learn to go in on their own. 3. Cover the run against hawks and owls, and remove perches within 100 yards. Hawks and owls are federally protected — don't shoot them. 4. A guardian dog (such as a Great Pyrenees) that stays with the flock works day and night (raising one). 5. Rabbits too: hawks swoop

🌾 Feeding on little bought feed Rabbits without pellets (USDA AIB 358, p. 12): - Leafy legume hay (alfalfa, clover, vetch) + whole grain (oats, wheat, barley, rye, sorghum, buckwheat, soft corn) + salt. - Roots all year, especially winter: carrots, turnips, beets, mangels, sweet potatoes, Jerusalem artichokes (FB 1730, p. 11). - Expect 3–9 oz of feed per rabbit a day, and slower growth than on pellets — home mixes are hard to balance (OSU EC 1655, p. 1). Feeding greens safely (FB 1730, p. 12; R-41, pp. 37–38): 1. Fresh, once a day, only what they eat in 4–5 minutes, in a manger, never on the floor. 2. Dew-wet greens are fine. Greens that sat in a pile and heated are dangerous. 3. Never forage from where dogs or cats defecate (tapeworm, coccidiosis), or that was sprayed. 4. Change the diet slowly. A big feed of lush greens can kill rabbits used to pellets. Chickens on scraps, greens and range: - Mix each day's table scraps into a grain mash. Give greens all the time (clippings, cabbage, lettuce). No onion tops, geranium leaves or strong-flavored scraps — they taint eggs (FB 1508, pp. 26–27). Scraps are a supplement: too many lower laying (PNW 477, p. 4). - Winter greens: sprouted oats. Soak oats 24 hours in a pail with small holes in the bottom, keep moist and rinse
feeding-on-little-bought-feed

too many lower laying (PNW 477, p. 4). - Winter greens: sprouted oats. Soak oats 24 hours in a pail with small holes in the bottom, keep moist and rinse daily until they sprout (FB 1508, p. 27). - Foragers eat insects, worms, snails, seeds, grass and leaves; village hens' crops held 72% household waste (FAO, pp. 17–18). You can grow fly maggots on wet seed husks or dung (p. 24) — black soldier fly larvae are a common choice (rule of thumb). - With a dairy goat or cow: layers can live on skim milk or buttermilk to drink, all the grain they want, and oyster shell — about 4–5 gallons of milk a day per 100 hens (FB 1841, pp. 23–24). - Calcium always: oyster shell, limestone or crushed baked eggshell. The flock's own shells aren't enough, and short hens start eating their eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 117). Grit or gravel for confined birds (FB 1508, p. 28). Our dry season: scavenged feed dries up (FAO, p. 36) — here, roughly July–October when the grass browns. Store hay, grain, squash and roots for summer as well as winter (rule of thumb). Toxic plants: rhododendron, nightshades, foxglove, Scotch broom, poison oak, tansy, black locust, false hellebore, snowberry, clematis (WSNWCB, p. 55). Penned birds are at more risk — they eat what they're given (p. 54). Also never feed
feeding-on-little-bought-feed

broom, poison oak, tansy, black locust, false hellebore, snowberry, clematis (WSNWCB, p. 55). Penned birds are at more risk — they eat what they're given (p. 54). Also never feed moldy feed, avocado, raw dried beans, green or sprouted potatoes, or rhubarb leaves (rule of thumb). Water: a doe and her 8-week litter of seven drink about a gallon a day in summer (FB 1730, p. 12). Fresh water for chickens every day (FB 1508, p. 28; 🖼️ homemade waterers). A hen drinks about a pint a day, double in heat, and a day without water can stop laying for weeks (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA AIB 358, p. 12 — rabbit feeds without pellets; FAO, p. 17 — scavenging flocks and home-grown feed; USDA FB 1841, p. 23 — home-grown grain and milk rations.

🐤 Hatching and raising chicks With a broody hen — the dependable way without power (USDA FB 1363): 1. Broody hens cluck and ruffle up when approached. After she has stayed on the nest 2–3 days, move her at night to a quiet nest with dummy eggs (p. 9). 2. Set 10–13 eggs in cold weather, 13–15 in warm (p. 3). Use fresh eggs — quality drops after 5 days, and 3-week-old eggs rarely hatch (p. 5). 3. Candle on day 7 and day 14 (hold each egg to a bright light in the dark) and remove clear ones (p. 18; 🖼️ the air cell on days 7, 14 and 18; 🖼️ candling). 4. Chicks start pipping the evening of day 19 and are out by day 21 (FB 1538, p. 11). Don't help them out — those that can't hatch alone rarely thrive (p. 15). Incubators (only if you have steady power) (FB 1538, pp. 11, 16): fan type 99.5–100 °F, about 57% humidity, eggs turned 5–6 times a day; still-air about 102 °F at egg height. Turn at least twice a day from day 2 to day 18 (FB 1363, p. 3). Homemade: a foam cooler (🖼️ photos) with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99–100 °F, or a double cardboard box with the bulb in a chimney touching nothing (fire risk) — plan on hatching no more
hatching-and-raising-chicks

with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99–100 °F, or a double cardboard box with the bulb in a chimney touching nothing (fire risk) — plan on hatching no more than half the eggs. Brooding: - With the hen: shut hen and chicks in a brood coop (🖼️ drawing) at night (rats, cats). Move the coop weekly to fresh short grass (FB 1538, p. 18). Raise chicks on ground old birds haven't used for a year (p. 17). - Without a hen: start at about 95 °F. Chicks crowding to the heat are cold; panting with open mouths are too hot (p. 22; 🖼️ what each looks like). Wire across corners stops piling and smothering. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1363 — setting hens and choosing eggs; USDA FB 1538, p. 11 — incubation and brooding; Wikipedia: egg incubation — pictures of embryo development.

🥚 Eggs: how many, which hens, storing On little bought feed, expect far fewer eggs (FAO, p. 9): | How the hens live | Eggs per hen per year | | Scavenging only | 20–30 | | Scavenging + shelter and disease control | 40–60 | | Some feed | about 100 | | Fully fed | 160–220 | So two eggs a day (730 a year) takes 7–8 part-fed hens, or 25+ scavengers (our arithmetic). Which hens to keep (USDA FB 1727): hens lay most in year one and about 20% less in year two. Eat early molters and non-layers in June–July; keep hens still laying in August–September for a second year and for breeding (p. 5). A non-layer has a shrunken, dull, dry comb) (p. 8), pubic bones close together, only two fingers from the keel (p. 9; 🖼️ layer vs. non-layer), and yellow returning to beak and shanks (p. 10). Storing eggs: - Collect at least once a day. Wash only dirty eggs, in water 20 °F warmer than the egg (OSU EM 9350, p. 5). - Clean, unwashed eggs keep 2–3 weeks at cool room temperature, longer in a cold cellar (rule of thumb). - Spring surplus: water glass or limewater crocks keep eggs 6–9 months (USDA 1935, p. 3; FB 1508, p. 32). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1727 — telling layers from loafers, with

surplus: water glass or limewater crocks keep eggs 6–9 months (USDA 1935, p. 3; FB 1508, p. 32). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1727 — telling layers from loafers, with pictures; USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs — water glass and lime; Root Cellar guide — storing eggs cool.

🌡️ Heat, smoke and fire season Rabbits (USDA FB 1730, p. 31): - Newborn litters and does late in pregnancy suffer most. - Signs: fast breathing, wet mouth, slight bleeding from the nostrils. - Do: shade and airflow (🖼️ a cooling basket for young rabbits). Wetting hutch tops and floors cools the hutch 6–10 °F. Lay a sick rabbit on a feed sack soaked in cold water. Chickens (FAO, p. 27): they have no sweat glands and cool by panting. Severe stress above 104 °F (40 °C); 115 °F (46 °C) kills most. They eat less, drink more and lay smaller eggs. Give shade, airflow and cool water; white paint reflects up to 70% of the sun's heat on a roof. Heat-stressed birds peck each other. Wildfire smoke (PNW 783, p. 10): watch for coughing, open-mouth breathing, watery eyes, weakness. Keep water clean and fresh, cool them, mist down dust, and put off stressful jobs (weaning, moving). Evacuation plan: Illinois Valley page. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1730, p. 31 — rabbits in hot weather; FAO, p. 27 — heat and housing; PNW 783, p. 8 — evacuating or sheltering stock.

🩺 Common diseases with no vet Rabbits: - Quarantine new rabbits a month, downwind, and do their chores last (OSU EC 1654, p. 1). - Watch for: runny nose and matted front paws (snuffles; 🖼️ photo), crusty ears (ear mites), diarrhea, sores. - The common killers — coccidiosis, pneumonia and enteritis — come mostly from poor sanitation (R-41, p. 52). Keep floors dry, clear droppings, keep droppings out of feed and water (p. 57). - Bloat or diarrhea with no fever: more hay and roughage; beware fermented or spoiled feed (p. 57). - Snuffles: cull (p. 56) — it spreads. - At butchering: white spots on an enlarged liver = liver coccidiosis (p. 56). Throw that liver away. Chickens: - Coccidiosis: bloody droppings, droopy young birds; at death the two blind guts (ceca) are swollen with blood (FB 1652, pp. 52–53; 🖼️ life cycle). If you stocked amprolium, it treats it; chicks kept off their droppings (wire or slat floors, fresh ground) get less (Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 317). - Marek's disease (paralysis; 🖼️ swollen nerves) strikes at 12–25 weeks (UF PS044, p. 7). No cure — cull, and hatch from survivors' lines (rule of thumb). - Lice and mites: ruffled feathers, scabs, fewer eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132; 🖼️ louse, 🖼️ mite). Give a dust bath of fine dry soil and wood ash, keep nests

Lice and mites: ruffled feathers, scabs, fewer eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132; 🖼️ louse, 🖼️ mite). Give a dust bath of fine dry soil and wood ash, keep nests clean with fresh straw (rule of thumb). - Burn or deeply bury birds that die of disease (FB 1652, p. 13). - Gloves and eye protection with lye or lime disinfectants (FB 1538, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 312 — poultry diseases with no vet; Raising Healthy Rabbits and Raising Healthy Poultry — illustrated care; USDA FB 1652 — disease signs (ignore its drugs).

🔪 Humane slaughter and butchering Killing — practice on a carcass first; the AVMA says neck dislocation is humane only when done by trained people on small animals (AVMA, p. 44): - Rabbit: hold the hind legs, thumb just behind the ears, fingers under the chin; stretch and raise the head sharply (🖼️ how to hold it). Or a heavy blow at the base of the skull (FB 1730, p. 52). - Chicken: hang it head-down in a killing cone and cut the side of the neck (Kansas State EP71, p. 1). Chickens (EP71, p. 1; UMN EB 385): 1. No feed for 8–10 hours before. 2. Scald at 140 °F for 30–40 seconds, dunking up and down; a little detergent helps. Pluck at once. 3. Gut (🖼️ step by step), then chill in ice water to 40 °F (UMN, p. 6); keep unfrozen under 4 days (EP71, p. 2). - Don't eat a bird with lumps or spots on the liver, fluid in the body, or orange fat on a thin carcass. - Pinfeathery birds: wait a week or two (UMN, p. 1). Allow 1–2 gallons of water per bird (OSU EM 9273, p. 2). Rabbits (FB 1730, pp. 52–55): 1. No feed the day before (R-41, p. 77). 2. Hang by a hook through the hock tendon of one hind leg; cut off the head at once to

52–55): 1. No feed the day before (R-41, p. 77). 2. Hang by a hook through the hock tendon of one hind leg; cut off the head at once to bleed. 3. Remove tail, free hind foot and front feet, then peel the skin off like a sock (🖼️ steps). 4. Gut. Heart, kidneys and liver are good food. Stretch the pelt on a wire frame to dry (🖼️ pelt on a stretcher); tan with salt-alum (FB 1334, p. 27). - Yield: a 4–4½ lb fryer at 8 weeks dresses to 50–59% of live weight, 78–80% of that edible (p. 47). Keeping the meat: pressure-can it (soak dressed rabbit 1 hour in salted water first) (USDA canning guide 5, p. 5), or dry thin strips (CVM, p. 90) — 16 oz raw makes about 4 oz jerky (PNW 632, p. 7). 📚 Go deeper: UMN Home Processing of Poultry — illustrated plucking and gutting; USDA FB 1730, p. 52 — slaughter and skinning with drawings; UF Humane Euthanasia — putting down a sick animal.

🌱 Manure for the garden - Rabbit manure has about 2% nitrogen — more than most farm manures — and won't burn plants: dig it straight in (USDA Rabbit Manure, pp. 4–5). A doe and her litters make about 6 cubic feet a year (9 with bedding); a buck about 3. Raise earthworms in the pile under the hutches (vermicomposting) — they cut odor and flies (p. 6). - Chicken manure: compost it at least 120 days (🖼️ compost bins) before use, and never put it raw on seedlings or growing plants. Spread raw litter in fall, after harvest, so winter rains leach out the salts (Idaho CIS 1194, pp. 2, 6) — our wet winters suit this. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Value and Use of Rabbit Manure, p. 6 — composting and worm beds; Idaho CIS 1194 — the 120-day rule and spreading rates.

🧬 Keeping the lines going for years How many feed a family (our arithmetic from the sources): - A doe at full production raises about 28 fryers a year — roughly 60 lb of carcass, 48 lb of meat (FB 1730, pp. 19, 47). Each pound of fryer takes 3½–4½ lb of feed. Rabbit twice a week for four people ≈ 100 fryers ≈ 4 does + 1 buck; keep 6 does and 2 bucks to cover losses and smaller litters on home feed. - FAO's village flock: 15 hens laying 30 eggs each = 450 eggs, some set under broodies (FAO, p. 36). About half of each hatch is cockerels — eat them at 12–20 weeks before they compete for feed (rule of thumb). Avoid inbreeding: - Inbreeding isn't harmful in itself, but it quickly brings out hidden defects; beginners usually inbreed just to avoid getting a new buck (FB 1730, p. 20). Keep at least two unrelated bucks and trade bucks with neighbors every few generations (rule of thumb). - Roosters: one per 12–15 Leghorn-type hens, 10–12 Rock or Wyandotte, 10 or fewer of the heaviest; with 20–30 hens keep two and alternate them (FB 1508, p. 10). FAO replaces the cock with a new cockerel every year (p. 36). Trade for an unrelated rooster every 2–3 years, or keep 2–3 hen families and rotate roosters (rule of
keeping-the-lines-going-for-years

FAO replaces the cock with a new cockerel every year (p. 36). Trade for an unrelated rooster every 2–3 years, or keep 2–3 hen families and rotate roosters (rule of thumb). - Keep records of matings and litter sizes (🖼️ a hutch card); breed from the best mothers. Don't live on rabbit. It is high in protein but low in fat (EC 1651, p. 1). People who live mainly on lean meat get "rabbit starvation" within 1–2 weeks — nausea, diarrhea, weakness and a craving for fat that more lean meat won't fix. Keep protein under about a third of calories and pair rabbit with fat (egg yolks, chicken fat, lard, nuts) and starch (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1730, p. 20 — inbreeding and selection; FAO, p. 36 — a self-renewing village flock; Food Security guide — fitting meat and eggs into a ration.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Sodium fluoride dusted on setting hens for lice — FB 1363, p. 9. It is poisonous. Instead: a dust bath of dry soil and wood ash, clean straw in the nest. - Poisons as wormers and mite killers in FB 1652: carbon tetrachloride (p. 63, p. 77), nicotine sulfate (p. 78), DDT (p. 49), phenothiazine (p. 79), kerosene emulsion and carbolineum (p. 7). Instead: use the bulletin for signs and prevention only; rotate ground, keep litter dry, cull. Also nicotine sulfate painted on roosts in Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132 — don't. - Lindane for rabbit ear mites — Peace Corps Livestock Manual Vol 4, p. 341. Banned and nerve-toxic. - "Salt-acid" tanning with concentrated sulfuric acid — FB 1730, p. 60. Instead: salt-alum (p. 61; FB 1334, p. 27). - Formalin for tanning and preserving paws in R-41, pp. 81, 83 — toxic; use salt-alum. Ipil-ipil (leucaena) as feed (p. 37) — toxic in quantity (not grown here anyway). Many drugs R-41 names won't be available. - Cresol disinfectant — FB 1508, p. 31. Toxic. Instead: scrub, sun and dry; lime with gloves and goggles. - "Don't mix your own rabbit feed" (OSU EC 1655, p. 1) is right while pellets exist. After that, home-grown feed is the only choice — expect slower growth and smaller litters, not failure. 📚

🐐 Milk Goats, Home Dairy & Bees How to keep dairy goats healthy with no vet or feed store, get clean milk and keep it without a fridge, turn it into butter, ghee, yogurt, kefir and cheese, and keep honey bees for honey and wax. The books are in Animals\Goats-Sheep, Animals\Dairy-Cheese, Animals\Bees and Animals\Veterinary, with the old farm butter and cheese bulletins in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools and milk cooling in Food-Storage\Cooling-Without-Power. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Raw milk can carry brucellosis, tuberculosis and Listeria (which causes miscarriage). Pasteurize milk for children, pregnant women, the old and the sick: 145 °F for 30 minutes, or 161 °F for 15 seconds, then cool it fast (UMN, p. 1). - Never give honey to a baby under 1 year — infant botulism (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 108). - Never feed hedge or garden trimmings. Yew kills before any sign shows; rhododendron, azalea and oleander poison goats (WSU, p. 2). - Oregon is short of selenium. Keep a covered selenium goat mineral out all year, and never let sheep eat goat mineral — its copper poisons them. - Shut goats in every night (cougars) and put an electric fence around the hives (black bears). - Anyone who has had a whole-body reaction to a sting must not work bees without epinephrine at hand.

🐐 Choosing and feeding milk goats What to expect: a doe giving about 1,000 lb (about 500 quarts) in a 10-month lactation is a fair milker; 1,600 lb or more is excellent (USDA FB 920, p. 5). That is about 1½ quarts a day (our arithmetic). Two does bred a few months apart keep milk coming all year (rule of thumb). Breeds (FB 920, p. 10): Saanen, Toggenburg, Nubian and Alpine (🖼️ Saanen, 🖼️ Toggenburg, 🖼️ Nubian, 🖼️ Alpine). Nubians give the richest milk, best for butter and cheese. LaMancha and the small Nigerian Dwarf are newer (rule of thumb). Feeding (FB 920, pp. 25–26): - Goats browse: they prefer leaves, twigs and weeds to grass. - Grain: about 1 lb for every 3–4 lb of milk. - One doe for a year: about 500 lb of hay and 450 lb of grain with 6 months of pasture; about twice the hay with none. One acre of good pasture carries 2–3 goats for a 5–6-month season. - House the buck away from milking does — his smell gets into the milk. Here (rule of thumb): pasture browns from June to the October rains and winter is mud, so plan hay for both. Browse: blackberry, willow, maple and oak leaves. Goats eat poison oak; its oil rubs off their coats onto your hands. Change feed slowly, over 7–10 days. Plants that

for both. Browse: blackberry, willow, maple and oak leaves. Goats eat poison oak; its oil rubs off their coats onto your hands. Change feed slowly, over 7–10 days. Plants that kill goats — mostly hungry goats in unfamiliar brush (the "where" column is local knowledge, rule of thumb): | Plant | Where | What happens | | Western azalea, rhododendron, laurel | Along valley creeks and serpentine meadows; gardens | Drooling, vomiting (rare in goats — a red flag), bloat, tremors, collapse; activated charcoal may help (WSU, p. 15) | | Pacific yew, garden yew | Shady creek forest; hedges | Often fatal before any sign (AIB 415, p. 113) | | Oleander | SW Oregon yards | All parts very poisonous (OSU, p. 12) | | Chokecherry, cherry | Wilted or frosted leaves | Cyanide (AIB 415, p. 26) | 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 920 Milk Goats — breeds, rations, housing; USDA AIB 415 — western poisonous plants in color.

🏠 Fences, shelter and minerals - Fences: no barbed wire. Field fence traps horned heads. Electric works once goats are trained: two hot wires held mature does but not kids (OSU EC1646, pp. 1–2). - Shelter: a dry three-sided shed with fresh air but no drafts, and something to climb (🖼️ shelter, 🖼️ climbing structure). Keep goats dry and out of cold wind (FB 920, p. 35). - Cougars: shut goats in a shed or barn every night (ODFW, p. 2). Selenium (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1–6): - Most Oregon livestock are low in selenium (🖼️ map). White muscle disease was first described here, in 1958. It strikes kids 3–8 weeks old: stiffness, trembling, weak hind legs, can't stand or suckle, heart failure. Low selenium also causes abortion, stillbirth and more mastitis. - Free-choice selenium mineral salt is simplest. Keep the feeder covered — rain leaches selenium out. - Injections (such as Bo-Se) need a vet, last under a month, and an overdose kills. - Stock a year or more of selenium goat mineral now (rule of thumb). Copper: copper oxide wire particles help control barber pole worm in goats, but copper poisons sheep. Never feed goat mineral to sheep, and don't use low-copper sheep mineral for goats (UF VM271, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9094 — selenium salt vs injections; OSU EC1646 — fences and sheds.

🥛 Clean milk: milking, cooling, pasteurizing Milking (Lincoln Univ, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ milking stand): 1. Clip the udder hair. Squirt the first milk into a strip cup and look for clots every milking. 2. Dip the teats; wipe each goat with her own towel. Milk without wringing the teats; dip again after. 3. Filter, and chill to 38 °F within an hour. Cold raw milk keeps 12–14 days. Cooling without power (USDA FB 976, pp. 6, 15; 🖼️ cooling tank): a can of 85 °F milk set in 3 times its volume of 37 °F water only gets to about 50 °F — use more water and stir. Spring water is often as warm as 65 °F; check it with a thermometer. In our 95 °F summers, milk you can't chill should become yogurt, cheese or ghee the same day (rule of thumb). Why pasteurize: raw milk and soft raw-milk cheeses spread brucellosis, TB and Listeria; hard, aged cheeses are safer (Zoonoses, p. 92). Young children should not get raw milk; yogurt resists contamination better (WHO, p. 16). Plant poisons pass into milk too — lupine can cause birth defects in people (WSU, p. 15). Pasteurizing at home (UMN, p. 1): 1. Use a double boiler, or a pot set in a pan of water, so the milk doesn't scorch. 2. Heat to 145 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring,

If it drops below 145 °F, restart the 30 minutes (rule of thumb). UMN's own home method has a safety margin: stir until an accurate thermometer reads 165 °F, then cool at once. 3. 🧈 Cream, butter and ghee Goat cream barely rises, and goat butter is pure white (FB 920, p. 7), so sour the whole milk and churn it. Cow milk can be skimmed from a shallow pan 4 inches deep after 36 hours (ILCA, p. 38; 🖼️ drawing). Butter from soured whole milk (ILCA, p. 60): 1. Let the milk sour until it tastes pleasantly sour. Fresh milk churns slowly and loses fat. 2. At 59–79 °F, rock or shake it in a closed vessel until butter grains form (🖼️ small churns). Colder can take 5 hours. Butter from cream (USDA FB 876, p. 23): ripen it at 65–75 °F until mildly sour, then churn at 52–66 °F for 30–40 minutes until the grains are wheat-sized. Drain the buttermilk (🖼️ photo) and wash the butter twice. Salted to 3% (about ½ oz per pound (our arithmetic)), butter keeps up to 4 months sealed, cool and dark (ILCA, p. 49). Ghee keeps a year without a fridge (Practical Action, p. 4): 1. Boil butter gently until the water is gone and the milk solids turn golden brown. 2. Let it settle; strain through boiled cheesecloth. 3. Store airtight, dark and cool — not in iron or copper, which speed rancidity. It keeps more than 12 months at room temperature. 📚 Go deeper: ILCA Rural Dairy Technology — village dairying with no power;

🧀 Yogurt, kefir and cheese Yogurt (Practical Action, pp. 1–3): 1. Heat milk to 176–185 °F and hold 15–20 minutes, stirring. Cool fast to 104–113 °F. 2. Stir in 20–50 g of live yogurt per liter (about 1½–3 tablespoons per quart (our conversion)). 3. Keep warm 4–6 hours — a haybox or a cooler with jars of hot water works — then chill. 4. Keep a "mother culture" going; replace it if flavors go off. Kefir needs no warm box (ILCA, p. 59): heat milk to 185 °F for 30 minutes and cool it, add kefir grains, and leave about 12 hours at room temperature (72 °F). Reuse the grains; they multiply (rule of thumb). Lemon or vinegar cheese (queso blanco, paneer) (ILCA, p. 50; 🖼️ step chart): 1. Heat milk to 180 °F, or a simmer. 2. Stir in lemon juice, about 3 mL per 100 mL of milk (about 2 tablespoons per quart (our conversion)), diluted with equal water — or vinegar. Curds form at once. Settle 15 minutes. 3. Drain in a cloth, salt, press overnight. Keeps about 3 days cold, 5 in brine (Practical Action, p. 1). Cottage cheese with no bought culture (USDA FB 1451, pp. 6–7): 1. Let skim milk clabber at about 75 °F (about 30 hours) until clean and pleasantly sour. 2. Cut it in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot

pp. 6–7): 1. Let skim milk clabber at about 75 °F (about 30 hours) until clean and pleasantly sour. 2. Cut it in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot water to bring it to 100 °F; hold about 30 minutes, stirring gently. Drain in a cloth, rinse cold, salt. A gallon makes about 1½ lb. 3. Homemade starter: set several boiled pint jars of fresh milk at 75 °F (🖼️ starter jars). Keep the one that curdles in about 30 hours with a smooth curd and a clean, sharp sour taste, and carry it on daily. A simple rennet cheese (FB 920, p. 8): stir a junket tablet dissolved in cold water into 1 gallon of milk at 88 °F. Cut the curd after 30 minutes, warm it to 98 °F, bag and press it (🖼️ homemade lever press), and rub with salt for several days. Ready at 10 days. Making your own rennet (Book of Cheese, pp. 55–56): 1. Take the stomach of a young kid, lamb or calf that has had nothing but milk. Clean it, blow it up, dry it. 2. Cut it open and soak it in 3–5% salt water (about 4–7 oz salt per gallon (our arithmetic)) for days to weeks. 3. Filter, add more salt, and keep it cool and dark (stone jugs, colored glass) — light destroys it. 4. Strength varies and

A full deep frame holds about 5 lb | | Source | FAO, pp. 44–45 | AH 335, pp. 72–73; 🖼️ plans; 🖼️ cutaway | Forage and the summer dearth (AH 335, p. 21 lists western bee plants). Here (rule of thumb): manzanita and willow bloom February–March, bigleaf maple in April, and blackberry in June–July is the main flow. A dearth follows from late July to the fall rains, when robbing and yellowjackets peak: reduce entrances (🖼️ entrance reducer), never spill syrup or leave comb out (OSU EM 9186, p. 4), and keep water within half a mile (rule of thumb). Swarms) are free bees: - They come mostly March–June: the old queen and half the bees hang in a cluster for an hour or so (AH 335, p. 38; 🖼️ resting swarm). Swarming bees are full of honey and gentle (Langstroth, p. 41). - Shake the cluster into a box of old comb (🖼️ hiving a swarm); close it at
bees-hives-forage-swarms-feeding

resting swarm). Swarming bees are full of honey and gentle (Langstroth, p. 41). - Shake the cluster into a box of old comb (🖼️ hiving a swarm); close it at dusk. A bait hive of old dark comb catches swarms by itself (rule of thumb). - Your own colony swarms when it has more than 6 frames of bees and is crowded: split it when swarm cells appear (OSU EM 9186, p. 11; 🖼️ swarm cells). - Package bees from California will stop after a collapse, so swarms will be the only new bees (p. 14). Feeding (AH 335, pp. 49–51): 1:1 sugar syrup in spring; thick 2:1 for new colonies and fall stores; dry sugar on the inner cover in a late-winter emergency. Feed late in the day with narrowed entrances. Never feed honey from unknown hives — it spreads disease. A broodless colony eats about 4 lb of honey a month (p. 72); the book's 90-lb winter store is for cold climates, and here plan on about 60 lb: an average colony eats about that between the fall and spring flows (p. 72), and our long summer dearth eats into stores too (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FAO Bees and Forest Livelihoods — building top-bar hives; USDA AH 335 — swarming, feeding, wintering.

🦠 Bee health: varroa and foulbrood Varroa mites are the main killer; unchecked they double every month (HBHC, p. 5; 🖼️ mites on bees and larvae). Here they peak in August–September, as the winter bees are raised (rule of thumb). Counting mites (HBHC, pp. 9–10): 1. Shake bees from 1–3 brood frames (not the one with the queen) into a tub. 2. Scoop ½ cup (about 300 bees) into a jar of rubbing alcohol or soapy water, shake, and count the mites. 3. Mites ÷ 300 × 100 = mites per 100 bees. Treat at 1+ in winter and spring, 2+ in summer and fall. Controls with nothing bought (pp. 39–40): cut out capped drone) brood 2–3 times in spring, or force a brood break by caging the queen 1–2 weeks or making a split. Oxalic acid dribble (p. 29): 35 g, weighed (roughly 2⅓ level tablespoons if you have no scale (rule of thumb)) in 1 liter of 1:1 syrup; 5 mL on the bees in each occupied gap between combs, 50 mL at most per colony, best with no capped brood (late fall, winter). Corrosive: gloves and goggles. Vaporizing it is extremely dangerous. Stockpile pure oxalic acid dihydrate now (rule of thumb). American foulbrood (AFB) — the disease that means burning: - Signs: spotty brood; sunken, darker, pierced cappings; foul smell (FAO 2006, p. 10; 🖼️ dead larvae
bee-health-varroa-and-foulbrood

now (rule of thumb). American foulbrood (AFB) — the disease that means burning: - Signs: spotty brood; sunken, darker, pierced cappings; foul smell (FAO 2006, p. 10; 🖼️ dead larvae in cells). - Matchstick test: push a matchstick into a dead larva and draw it out slowly. About an inch of ropy brown goo means AFB (FAO Forest, p. 150; 🖼️ photo). - Then: burn combs, frames, honey and dead bees in a pit about 3 ft deep and fill it in; scorch the inside of the boxes until slightly brown. Shaking the bees onto clean new combs can save them (FAO 2006, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: HBHC Tools for Varroa Management — mite counts and every treatment; FAO Honey Bee Diseases and Pests — photos of brood diseases, mites and wax moth.

🍯 Honey, wax, bears and stings Honey with no extractor (FAO Forest, p. 91; Practical Action, p. 3): take only sealed comb and leave winter stores. Cut it as comb honey, or crush it and strain through coarse, then fine, cloth. Keep everything bone-dry — honey over 19–20% water ferments. Don't heat it; crystallized honey is fine. Beeswax (FAO Forest, pp. 112–113): melt comb in water, strain through sacking, and let the wax cake float and set; repeat through finer cloth. A solar melter (a black box with a glass lid) also works. Wax is highly flammable — never heat it dry over a flame (🖼️ double boiler). Beeswax candles need a thicker wick than tallow (Practical Action, p. 2). Bear fence (UF ENY-2060, pp. 1–5): bears come for the brood, and come back. Run three electric wires at 8, 20 and 32 inches on heavy T-posts every 8 ft, at least 3 ft from the hives, with a 6-ft ground rod (🖼️ step photos; 🖼️ finished fence). Test for 6,000–8,000 volts and keep plants cut back 2–3 ft. Bait the wire with foil smeared with bacon grease so a bear's nose gets the first shock (rule of thumb). Stings: pain and swelling at the spot are normal; scrape the stinger out at once (rule of thumb). A whole-body reaction (anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, faintness) follows 0.3–7.5% of stings

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Phenothiazine mixed into salt as a constant dewormer — FB 920, p. 26. Breeds resistant worms. Instead: FAMACHA-targeted deworming. - Iodoform in mineral oil put into the uterus — FB 920, p. 30. Outdated. Instead: never pull the afterbirth (KSU, p. 13). - Caustic-stick disbudding — FB 920, p. 34. It runs into eyes and burns other kids or the doe. Instead: a hot iron. - Pasteurizing at 140 °F (60 °C) for 30 minutes — Zoonoses, p. 31. Too low. Instead: 145 °F for 30 minutes or 161 °F for 15 seconds. - Paraffin heated to 240 °F for dipping cheese — FB 1191, p. 15 (220 °F in Book of Cheese, p. 287). Fire and burn hazard. Instead: melt wax in a pot set in water, never unattended. - Soft cheese from raw milk — Book of Cheese, p. 167; FB 920, p. 8. It carries Listeria and brucellosis. Instead: pasteurize milk for soft cheese. - Bee drugs — AH 335, p. 132. The 1980 book predates varroa in the US (1987). Instead: the HBHC varroa guide. - Killing colonies over burning sulfur to take the honey — Langstroth, p. 264. Instead: take only surplus honey. 🐴 Horses, Mules and Draft Animals How to keep, feed, handle, ride, shoe and pack horses, mules and donkeys, and how to put them to work in harness — written for a time when there may be no feed store, vet or farrier. The manuals are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ (Care-Feeding, Riding-Training, Hoof-Care-Shoeing, Packing-Travel, Draft-Harness). Horse health, vital signs, colic and first aid are in Animals\ and the Animals and vet care section of the Illinois Valley page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - A horse can kill you without meaning to. Stay where it can see you, speak before you touch it, keep a hand on it as you move around the hindquarters, and never stand directly behind or in front of it. - Never wrap a lead rope or reins around your hand or body, and never tie a horse with a knot you can't pull loose. Never tie with a chain lead. (4-H Horse Project PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety) - Wear a helmet and boots with a heel when riding. - The old books here (1867–1940s) teach good handling and shoeing but also harsh "breaking" methods and dangerous old medicines (purges, firing, chloroform). Use them for skills, not for doctoring.

🐎 Choosing an animal - For a first horse, pick an older, calm, well-trained one over a young or green horse — the 4-H manual says 6 to 18 years suits most purposes, and "a young horse and an inexperienced rider do not learn together" (PNW 587, p. 24). For hard work, not much under 5; with good care many stay useful past 20 (USDA FB 779, p. 8). Check it sound before you take it: walk and trot it on hard ground, look for limping, swellings, bad feet and bad habits. (USDA How to Select a Sound Horse; 🖼️ points of the horse; 🖼️ where unsoundness shows; conformation) - Age by the teeth: after about 12 years the front teeth turn triangular and slant forward. (USDA AIB 353, p. 18; PNW 587, p. 48; 🖼️ mouths from 4 to 8 years; 🖼️ 14- and 22-year-old mouths) - Mules are tough, sure-footed, eat less and handle heat and rough country better; they tend to stand and fight rather than bolt. A well-trained mule is very steady; a badly trained one is hard work. Donkeys need shelter always — their coats aren't waterproof, which matters in our wet winters. (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and
choosing-an-animal

Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and rarer. Mules are hardy but can still founder, and they fret if stabled long or kept alone. Donkeys live just over 30 years and should be kept with a companion. (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 15–19; 🖼️ points of the donkey) 📚 Go deeper: 4-H Horse Project (PNW 587) — choosing a horse, breeds, behavior; USDA How to Select a Sound Horse — unsoundness, blemishes and vices to check; Donkey Care Handbook — how donkeys and mules differ from horses; USDA Mule Production — breeding and raising mules.

🌾 Feeding and water - Total feed: 1.5–2.5% of body weight a day, most of it hay or pasture. Never less than 8–10 lb of hay a day for a 1,000-lb horse; an idle horse holds weight on about 18 lb of good hay. (Nebraska G1781, pp. 1–2; FM 25-5, p. 101) - Weigh a horse with a string: weight (lb) = heart girth (in) × heart girth (in) × body length (in) ÷ 330. Body length is point of shoulder to point of buttock. (G1781, p. 1; 🖼️ where to measure) - Working horses: about 1.1 lb grain + 1.25 lb hay per 100 lb of body weight a day, grain split into 3 feeds. Keep each grain meal under about 5 lb for a 1,000-lb horse. Feed by weight: a quart of oats ≈ 1 lb, a quart of corn ≈ 1.7 lb. (USDA FB1419, p. 9; G1781, p. 3; UGA B1356) - Water: 5–15 gallons a day, double in heat or hard work (an idle horse drinks about 10–12 — G1781, p. 4). Give an exhausted horse small drinks every 5–10 minutes until it recovers. In cold weather, take the chill off the water or salt the feed (1–2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: horses eat about 1½–3 oz a day of loose salt-mineral, which beats

feed (1–2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: horses eat about 1½–3 oz a day of loose salt-mineral, which beats a block. 🦷 Teeth and worms - Teeth: check at least yearly (twice for older horses). Sharp edges form on the outside of the upper molars and inside of the lowers — float (rasp) them (🖼️ how to hold the float) or the horse drops feed and loses weight. (PNW 587, p. 46; Merillat Animal Dentistry) - Signs of tooth trouble: dropping grain while chewing, holding the head sideways, eating slowly, whole grain in the manure, losing condition (G1781, p. 4). - Worms: don't deworm blindly every 8 weeks. Adults need 1–2 treatments a year (one in fall for bots and tapeworms); youngsters 3–4. When dewormers run out: pick up manure, don't overgraze, rotate pastures and graze with cattle or sheep. (Penn State/SARE, pp. 1–2) - Know your high shedders: most horses carry few worms; a few shed most of the eggs. Penn State's line: deworm a horse whose fecal egg count is over about 300 eggs per gram; over 500 is a "high shedder" (Penn State, pp. 1–2). Foals need a special schedule — ask the books, not guesswork. - Kill eggs without drugs: a manure pile that heats to 130–150 °F kills most parasites, flies and weed seeds (OSU EC1558, p. 16; 🖼️ covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass

p. 16; 🖼️ covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass it to horses — worm them together (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16). 📚 Go deeper: Penn State Managing Equine Parasites — the egg-count method and when to treat; 4-H PNW 587 — teeth and aging; Merillat Animal Dentistry — floating and dental work by hand (old book: skills only).
