🦶 Hoof care and shoeing - Pick out the feet every day (🖼️ how). A healthy frog feels like firm rubber (🖼️ parts of the hoof). Thrush) (black, stinking rot in the frog) comes from wet, dirty footing — trim away dead tissue, apply an antiseptic, and get the horse onto dry ground. In our wet winters, give horses a dry gravel or wood-chip standing area. (TM 2-220, p. 97; PNW 587; OSU EC1558, p. 2) - Hooves grow about ⅜ inch a month. Trim barefoot horses every 6–12 weeks, donkeys and mules every 6–10; the Army reset shoes every 3–6 weeks (🖼️ untrimmed vs. trimmed). (NMSU B-707, p. 2; Donkey Care Handbook, p. 14; TM 2-220) - Going barefoot (when shoes and nails run out): leave the sole, balance the wall, round off the outer edge so it doesn't chip (🖼️ using the rasp), and check weekly. Most horses do fine barefoot on soft ground; hard rocky work wears feet faster than they grow. (TM 2-220, p. 98) - Making and fitting shoes: TM 2-220 The Horseshoer teaches forging shoes from bar stock, fitting and nailing (🖼️ nailing and clinching), and even shoeing in the field with a ground fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference (🖼️ the foot from the side; farrier). Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. Taking shoes off

fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference (🖼️ the foot from the side; farrier). Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. Taking shoes off for good (TM 2-220, p. 97): 1. Pull the shoes, then trim to balance and round the edge of the wall. Leave the dead sole. 2. Expect the hoof to break away and the horse to go a bit tender for the first few weeks. It isn't serious and passes as new horn grows. 3. On rough, rocky pasture, leave the front shoes on for the first few days while the horse settles, then pull them. 4. Even shod horses do better with 2–3 months a year barefoot. Mud is the enemy here. Wet ground softens hooves and soles, leading to cracks, stone bruises, abscesses and thrush; mud also causes "mud fever" (scratches) — crusty scabs on the lower legs (OSU EC1558, p. 2). For the dry lot, lay down twice as much footing as you have mud: landscape fabric, 3 inches of ¾–1½-inch crushed rock, then 6 inches of gravel or sand or up to 12 inches of wood chips (p. 5; 🖼️ photo). Field tips from the Army farrier: store horseshoe nails wrapped in an oiled cloth in a watertight can, and a worn rasp can be re-sharpened with a three-cornered file and re-hardened (TM 2-220, p. 99)

🤠 Handling, saddling and riding - Leading: from the left side, right hand near the halter, slack folded (never wrapped) in your left hand. If the horse rears, let go with the hand nearest the halter so you stay on the ground. (PNW 587, p. 51) - Tying: use a quick-release knot (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ step by step), about 3 ft of rope, tied at or above withers height to something solid. Any rope around the neck gets a bowline (it can't tighten), never a slip knot. Untie before taking the halter off. (PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety, p. 3) - Saddle fit: with pad and rider on, the gullet must clear the withers. After a sweaty ride, even sweat marks = good fit; dry spots = pressure. A sliding saddle needs a breast collar, not a tighter cinch. Dry spots with raised skin lead to saddle sores and white hair — fix the fit now (UF Saddle Fit, p. 3). - Cinching): snug it gradually until a flat hand just slips under, walk the horse a few steps, then recheck after a short ride — many horses puff up their bellies. On the trail, stop after 1–2 miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼️ holding the reins), sit deep with heels

miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼️ holding the reins), sit deep with heels down. The 4-H manual (PNW 587) and FM 25-5 walk through riding step by step. - Starting young horses: handle foals early and teach them to lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2–3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with a bowline. (USDA FB1368) - Holding a horse for treatment: have a helper hold up another foot while you work on a leg; a twitch on the upper lip works for short jobs — tighten it only enough to stay on and take it off as soon as you can (PNW 587, p. 30). - Tack repair: cutting leather, hand-stitching with waxed thread and riveting are in TM 10-430 The Saddler and Hasluck's Harness Making (🖼️ sewing awls; 🖼️ stitching clamp). 📚 Go deeper: 4-H PNW 587 — handling, safety knots, tack, saddling and riding; UF Saddle Fit — checking tree fit and sweat patterns; The Saddler TM 10-430 — hand-repairing saddles and tack; USDA Breaking and Training Colts — gentling and starting young horses.

🩺 Health checks and first aid Normal vital signs at rest — the sources differ a little, so learn your own horse's normal by taking it twice a day for a week (PNW 587, p. 28; 🖼️ vital-signs chart): | | Temperature | Pulse (beats/min) | Breaths/min | | 4-H PNW 587 | 99–101 °F (102+ = sick) | 32–48 (over 50 = distress) | 8–20 | | Raising Healthy Horses | 99–101.5 °F | 40–48 | 10–14 | | UGA B1356 | 99.5–101.5 °F | 32–36 | 8–12 | Take the pulse under the jawbone for 15 seconds × 4. A pinched fold of neck skin should flatten in 1–2 seconds; gums should be pink and moist; a healthy horse passes several piles of manure a day (PNW 587, p. 28). Act fast (no vet coming? treat these as emergencies) — temperature 102 °F or more, signs of colic, a deep puncture, a wound near an eye, joint or tendon, severe lameness, choking, off feed 12–24 hours, worsening cough, persistent diarrhea, or a mare in trouble foaling (PNW 587, p. 29). Colic (belly pain) — looking at or kicking at the belly, pawing, rolling, getting up and down, sweating, little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ a horse in colic): - Take away all feed. — food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4–5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet; a horse can lose up to 4 gallons of blood without severe stress. Eyes: rinse gently with saline (1 teaspoon salt in a pint of boiled water — Raising Healthy Horses, p. 9) or weak-tea-colored dilute betadine. Donkeys hide illness. A dull donkey off its feed is an emergency — it can fall into hyperlipaemia (fat flooding the blood) and die. Coax it to eat with fresh grass or favorite food and warm water. 🚜 Harness and draft work - What an animal can pull all day: about one-tenth of its body weight in steady draft (a big horse pulling 150 lb at 2½ mph ≈ 1 horsepower). Donkeys pull about a fifth of their weight for 3–4 hours. A cart donkey should pull no more than twice its weight, cart included, on the flat. (Peace Corps Animal Traction, p. 20; Donkey Care Handbook) Sources differ: Starkey quotes 15% of body weight as normal pulling power for horses (Starkey, p. 118). - Collar fit: a flat hand should just pass between the collar and the windpipe (🖼️ drawing). A short collar chokes; a long one bruises the shoulders. Give each horse its own collar and wipe it after every use. Sore shoulders are the #1 harness problem. (USDA FB1419; FM 25-5; 🖼️ where collar sores form) - Harness, hitching, driving pairs and teams, carts, plows and sledges: FM 25-5, Mounted Instruction for Field Artillery, the Peace Corps Animal Traction manual and Starkey's Harnessing and Implements (🖼️ harnessing options). Big-team hitches and eveners: Sommerfeld's How to Hitch Horses (🖼️ five-horse evener; 🖼️ eveners for four horses). Preventing sore shoulders, step by step (USDA FB1419, pp. 17–20): 1. Fit: flat hand at the windpipe, fingertips at the sides of the neck just above the shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip

17–20): 1. Fit: flat hand at the windpipe, fingertips at the sides of the neck just above the shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip sweat pads — they cause more sore shoulders than a clean, smooth collar. 3. Set the hames snug so the pull comes about one-third of the way up from the point of the shoulder (🖼️ point of draft; 🖼️ hames). 4. Spring toughening: for the first 2–3 weeks of work, wash the shoulders after work with warm water and mild soap, then rinse with cold water with a little salt in it. 5. At midday, lift the collar forward, wipe off sweat and dirt, and let the shoulders cool. 6. Allow for winter hair and extra flesh when fitting a collar in spring — the fit changes as the horse works down. Harness care: hang it in a dry room; wipe the collar face after every use; once a year take it apart, soak 15 minutes in lukewarm water with mild soap, clean, oil and restitch. 🏠 Shelter, Building & Repair The best shelter you will ever have is the house you already live in — if you keep the water out. This guide covers keeping an existing house sound (roof leaks, flashing, gutters, rot and insects), heating one warm room, reglazing windows, durable local woods, hand-tool carpentry, splitting your own shakes, drying lumber, log and earth building, chimneys, earthquake and wildfire hardening, and emergency tarp shelters. The books are in Shelter-Building\ (House-Repair, Carpentry-Timber, Earth-Natural-Building, Wildfire-Quake-Hardening). Hand tools and saws are in Blacksmithing-Tools\Hand-Tools; quake and fire guides are in Earthquake-Tsunami\ and Wildfire\; cob, straw bale, light straw-clay, hempcrete, earth and lime plasters, making lime and thatch are in the Natural Building guide and Natural-Building\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Roof work kills. Use scaffolds, ladders or a safety rope (USDA FB 1751, p. 24). Never work on a wet or mossy roof, or alone (rule of thumb). - Old houses hold lead paint (before 1978) and asbestos (old shingles, siding, pipe wrap). Don't sand, cut, heat or burn them. Scrape paint wet and keep children away (rule of thumb). - Carbon monoxide. Any fuel heater without a chimney needs an open window — 1 sq in per 1,000 Btu (MSU E-1669, p. 3). Keep a battery CO alarm by the beds. - Cascadia will shake hard. Brick chimneys were damaged in most

— 1 sq in per 1,000 Btu (MSU E-1669, p. 3). Keep a battery CO alarm by the beds. - Cascadia will shake hard. Brick chimneys were damaged in most big U.S. quakes (FEMA 232, p. 144), and heavy unreinforced earth walls can collapse. Build light, keep earth walls low and single-story, and bolt the house to its foundation (FEMA 232, p. 168). - Wildfire comes as embers. Screen vents with 1/8-in metal mesh, keep gutters clear, and keep firewood 30 ft from the house (OSFM, p. 8; FEMA P-737, p. 23). - Never use the old poisons the old bulletins recommend — DDT, arsenic, pentachlorophenol, coal-tar creosote. See the last section.

🏚️ Finding and patching roof leaks Inspect the roof regularly for breaks, missing shingles, choked gutters and damaged flashing (USDA FB 1751, p. 22) — every fall before the rains, and after big storms (rule of thumb). Finding the leak (p. 22): - A wet spot near a chimney or outside wall usually means bad flashing or loose mortar. - Under an open roof, the drip can land well downslope from the hole. Follow the stain uphill. - If you see daylight from the attic, push a straw through the hole so you can find it from outside. - South-facing slopes wear out faster. Check them most often. Emergency patches: - Missing wood shingle: cut a piece of tin-can metal, paint it on both sides, and slide it under the course above. Don't loosen the good shingles. Cut old nails with a long, thin cold chisel, and dab roofer's cement on any exposed nail heads (p. 22). - Metal roof or gutter, no solder: plug small holes with roofer's cement. For big holes, stick canvas or several layers of cloth over the hole with thick paint, then give it several more coats (p. 23). - Bigger damage: tarp it (see the tarp section) until you can repair it. 💧 Flashing, gutters and keeping water away Roofs leak most where two surfaces meet: valleys, chimneys, dormers and walls. Flash these with galvanized or copper sheet (FM 5-426, p. 119; valleys at p. 124; 🖼️ valley flashing drawings (ignore its red-lead paint); 🖼️ chimney flashing). Flashing over window and door heads should run at least 4 in up behind the siding above the drip cap (USDA AH 73, p. 163; 🖼️ where flashing goes). Move the water away from the house (AH 73, pp. 8–9, 169): - Downspouts should empty onto splash blocks at least 3 ft long that carry water away from the foundation (🖼️ drawing). - The top of the foundation should sit at least 8 in above the ground. - A crawl space needs at least 18 in between the soil and the floor joists, with vents on opposite sides (FB 1993, p. 3). - Grade the soil so it slopes away from the walls, and clean gutters every fall (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Wood-Frame House Construction (AH 73) — illustrated flashing, gutters, foundations and crawl spaces; FM 5-426 — valley flashing. 🔥 One warm room: drafts, plastic and heat With little fuel, heat one room, not the house. The relief-shelter order of priorities in winter (IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting, p. 30): 1. Clothing and bedding first. 2. Waterproofing (the roof). 3. Bedding up off the damp floor. 4. Windproofing. 5. Then heat one room. Make a plastic-curtained buffer (a lobby) between the warm room and the cold rest of the house. Insulate floors and walls with straw sandwiched between plastic. Treat any stove in a small room as a fire risk. Seal the drafts (HUD, In the Bank or Up the Chimney, pp. 36–37; 🖼️ caulking drawings): - Caulk wherever two different materials meet: drip caps over windows and doors, frame-to-siding joints, sills, siding corners, where wood meets the foundation, pipe and wire holes, and where a chimney meets siding. - Stuff wide cracks (like the sill) with oakum or fiber first, then caulk. Plastic storm windows (HUD, p. 42): tape clear plastic over the inside of the window frame (easier, and it lasts longer), or tack it outside with 1/4 × 1 1/4 in wood slats. Pull it tight and trim the extra. Heaters without a chimney make carbon monoxide. Leave 1 sq in of open window for every 1,000 Btu of heater output. 🪟 Reglazing and saving windows ⚠️ Paint on windows made before 1978 almost certainly contains lead. Don't sand it dry or heat it until it scorches. Scrape it wet, collect the chips, and keep children away (rule of thumb). Replacing a pane (NPS Brief 9, p. 5; 🖼️ window parts named): 1. Dig out the old putty without gouging the wood. Soaking the glass in linseed oil loosens putty stuck to it. 2. Pull the glazing points (the small metal tabs) and lift out the glass. 3. Lay a thin bed of putty in the rabbet (the groove the glass sits in) and press the pane in. 4. Push in new glazing points. 5. Run a final bead of putty and bevel it with a putty knife so water runs off. 6. Paint when the putty skins over, usually in 2–3 days. Lap the paint slightly onto the glass to seal it. Where window rot starts: the sill, the sill-to-jamb joints, the bottom-rail corners and the muntin (glass-bar) joints — wherever water sits. The sill must slope outward. Cracked putty lets water soak the joints (NPS Brief 9, p. 2). Saving partly rotted wood: let it dry, brush on 2–3 coats of boiled linseed oil, 24 hours apart, fill cracks with putty, then paint (p. 5). Rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by themselves — dry them spread

Rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by themselves — dry them spread flat outdoors or keep them in a can of water (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Preservation Brief 9 — reglazing, sash cords, weatherstripping and sill repair. 🐜 Rot, termites, carpenter ants — and woods that last Dry wood does not rot. Decay needs wood wetter than about 30% moisture. Air-dried wood is at or below 20%, and decay already in the wood stops if it's kept dry (Wood Handbook, p. 314; 🖼️ rot fungi). What rots houses and draws termites (USDA FB 1993, p. 7): wet, unventilated crawl spaces; scrap wood left on the soil; wood touching soil (especially dirt-filled porches); wood buried in masonry near the ground; no gutters or roof overhang; roof and plumbing leaks. The fixes (FB 1993, p. 3): no wood touching soil, an 18-in crawl space, vents on opposite sides (or roll roofing laid over the soil), and an inspection every winter or early spring. Termites build earthen tubes up foundations (🖼️ photo): break them, and block the route with mortar or pitch. Carpenter ants (USFS R10-TP-128, pp. 4, 7; 🖼️ winged ants): - More than 20 ants indoors, especially in winter, means a nest inside the house. - Their frass looks like sawdust mixed with insect parts (🖼️ photo). - They don't eat wood — they hollow out wet, softening wood. Fix the moisture, find and remove the nest wood, keep firewood and debris away from the house, and store food sealed. Which woods last (heartwood only; Wood Handbook, Table 14-1, p. 316): | Decay resistance | Western species |

Use their heartwood for sills, posts, shakes and anything touching the ground. Port-Orford-cedar killed by root disease still has sound, durable heartwood (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1993 Decay and Termite Damage in Houses — spotting decay and termite tubes (ignore its poisons); Wood Handbook ch. 14 — decay, insects and durable species; USFS Carpenter Ants — finding the nest. 🪚 Hand-tool carpentry and drying lumber Square a corner with 6-8-10 (FM 5-426, p. 48; 🖼️ the same idea with 3-4-5): 1. Measure 6 ft along one line and 8 ft along the other. 2. Move the lines until the diagonal between those two marks is exactly 10 ft. Never use less than 6 ft. 3. When the whole rectangle is laid out, check that both diagonals are equal (🖼️ drawing). Batter boards hold the lines (p. 46; 🖼️ batter boards). Handsaw basics (Disston, p. 10): start on the waste side of the line with your thumb against the blade, and draw back a few times to make a groove. Crosscut at about 45° to the board with full-length strokes. Support the waste piece so it doesn't splinter off. Hewing a log flat (An Ax to Grind, p. 52): hew green, freshly cut logs — dry logs hew badly. Set the log on V-notched yokes about knee high. Snap a chalk line, score down to it with a single-bit axe, then flatten with a broadaxe (🖼️ step-by-step drawings). Roofs and joints: rafter lengths by the step-off method (FM 5-426, p. 108) or the steel square (Brace and Mayne, p. 199; 🖼️ rafter pitch); mortise-and-tenon joints (Griffith, p. 105; 🖼️ drawing). Air-drying lumber (OCHA/IFRC/CARE Timber, pp. 45, 68): - A 1-inch (2.5 cm) board takes about a year to air-dry, depending

🖼️ rafter pitch); mortise-and-tenon joints (Griffith, p. 105; 🖼️ drawing). Air-drying lumber (OCHA/IFRC/CARE Timber, pp. 45, 68): - A 1-inch (2.5 cm) board takes about a year to air-dry, depending on species. Thicker takes longer. - Stack it off the ground on bearers, with stickers (spacer sticks) between every layer (🖼️ stacking drawing). - Seal or paint the ends — they dry fastest and crack. - Cover the top loosely so air still moves through. Wood shrinks most along the growth rings, about half as much across them, and hardly at all along its length (Wood Handbook, p. 84). Green wood opens gaps as it dries. 📚 Go deeper: FM 5-426 Carpentry — layout, framing, rafters and roofing; USFS Handtools for Trail Work, p. 46 — adzes and broadaxes; Timber in Humanitarian Operations — felling, drying and joining timber. 🪵 Splitting and laying your own shingles and shakes Splitting (NPS Brief 19, p. 2): 1. Cut the log into bolts as long as the shingle, then quarter them. 2. Rive off thin boards along the grain with a froe and mallet (or an axe) (🖼️ froe drawing; 🖼️ photos). 3. For a taper, flip the bolt end-for-end after each split. 4. Use heartwood only. Sapwood rots fast. 5. Old shingles were 3/8–3/4 in thick, 3–8 in wide and 14–36 in long, smoothed with a drawknife so rain doesn't sit in the grain. If a split runs off to one side, start again from the other end of the billet and split back to meet it (Beard, p. 115). Laying wood shingles (USDA FB 1751, pp. 6–7) on a roof of 1/4 pitch or steeper (flatter roofs are hard to keep tight): | Shingle length | Show to the weather | | 16 in | 5 in | | 18 in | 5 1/2 in | | 24 in | 7 1/2 in | - Gaps of 1/4 in between dry shingles, 1/8 in between green ones. - Two rust-resistant nails per shingle, no more than 3/4 in from the edges and 1–2 in above the next butt line. - Break joints by at least 1 1/2 in from the course below. - Double the first course at the eaves

For our wet winters, nail shingles to spaced 1×4 slats (spaced the same as the exposure) instead of solid boards. Air reaches the underside so they dry out, and it takes less lumber (FB 1751, p. 6). 🏕️ Log buildings Cutting the logs (USDA FB 1660, pp. 5–6): - If you will peel the logs, fell in winter. Spring-cut logs stain and decay. - Logs over 20 ft are heavy and seldom needed. - Season them stacked in the shade with air around them. Peel them — bark has no practical advantage and invites beetles (🖼️ peeling with a drawknife or bark spud). Foundations: - Wicks sets cedar posts in holes at least 3 ft deep, or uses stone piers — large flat stones or cobbles bedded firmly and chinked with small stones. Hew the sill logs flat on top (Wicks, pp. 15–17). - Keep the bottom logs high and dry. Wicks cuts posts off 10 in above ground; later Forest Products Lab guidance is 12–18 in, with eaves of about 24 in on a one-story cabin (that bulletin is not on the drive). A sill log touching soil is already rotting or soon will be (NPS Brief 26, p. 8). Notching: the common corner notches — saddle, V, dovetail, square — are drawn in NPS Brief 26, p. 5 and FB 1660, p. 12. Notches that cup upward hold rain and rot first (Brief 26, p. 9), so cut the notch in the underside of the upper log (rule of thumb). Blocking: wood slabs or stones wedged into the gap. 2. Soft packing: moss, oakum or clay. 3. Daub: clay mixed with lime, troweled on wet. 🧱 Earth building — with the Cascadia caution ⚠️ Heavy, unreinforced earth walls can collapse in a big quake. The Peace Corps handbook calls for steel reinforcement in footings and walls in earthquake areas (Building Homes of Earth, pp. 70–75). In southern Oregon, keep earth walls low, light and single-story, or use earth only as infill or inside walls within a braced wood frame (rule of thumb). Ribbon test for building soil (Building Homes of Earth, pp. 24–25; 🖼️ drawing): roll damp soil into a cigar shape and squeeze it out between thumb and finger into a ribbon. | Ribbon length | What it means | | 8–10 in | Lots of clay — walls last only if you stabilize or temper it | | 2–4 in | Medium clay — often good | | No ribbon | Too little clay | | Springs back like a sponge | Organic topsoil — unusable | Adobe bricks (USDA FB 1720, pp. 9–10): 1. Puddle clayey loam with water. Mix in no more than 1 part loose straw to 5 parts mud. Too much straw, or manure, weakens the brick. 2. Mould the bricks (🖼️ forms; 🖼️ step by step). After a few days, stand them on edge. 3. Dry them 2–3 weeks under cover from rain. Never let uncured brick freeze. 4. Lay them in mud mortar with 1/2–1 in joints.

Adobe works in wet climates only if the walls are kept dry and the site never floods (p. 3) — so give it wide eaves and a raised foundation. Rammed earth (USDA FB 1500, pp. 9, 11–12): - Right moisture is about 7–14% water by weight (p. 8): a squeezed handful should break apart when dropped. - Ram it in 4–5 in layers between forms (🖼️ rammers; 🖼️ forms). - The foundation is masonry as thick as the wall (generally 18 in), at least 12 in above ground so rain can't splash the earth, with a damp-proof course on top. 🧯 Chimneys and stovepipe Building or checking a masonry chimney (USDA FB 1889; 🖼️ whole-chimney diagram): - It should rise at least 3 ft above a flat roof and 2 ft above any ridge within 10 ft (p. 4). - It needs a fire-clay flue lining and a footing on solid ground below the frost line (p. 6). - Keep 2 in of air between the chimney masonry and any wood framing (p. 8). - Smoke test before use: build a smoky fire at the base, cover the top tightly with a wet blanket, and look for smoke leaking through the walls. Fix every leak first (p. 10). - Stovepipe must never pass through floors, closets or hidden spaces, or enter the chimney in the attic (p. 10). Single-wall stovepipe needs 18 in from anything that burns; only proper shielding allows less (CMHC, p. 36). Repointing loose chimney mortar: rake it out and refill with 1 part portland cement, 1 part lime and 6 parts sand (FB 1751, p. 24). When cement runs out, use lime and sand, about 1:3 — and keep hard cement off soft old brick (rule of thumb). Cleaning and chimney fires: see the Firewood guide. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1889 Fireplaces and Chimneys — flues, footings, clearances and cleanouts; CMHC Guide to Residential Wood Heating — current clearances. 🌎 Earthquake and wildfire hardening Earthquake (FEMA 232): - Masonry chimneys are heavy, rigid and often brittle. They have been damaged in most moderate to severe U.S. earthquakes, and a damaged chimney becomes a falling hazard. Light flues do better (pp. 144–145). Don't put beds beside a brick chimney (rule of thumb). - The best-value retrofits: bolt the sill plate to the foundation, and sheathe crawl-space cripple walls (the short stud walls between foundation and floor) with plywood. Replace decayed sill wood while you're there (pp. 168–170; 🖼️ sill bolts; 🖼️ cripple-wall bracing). - Check your house: look under it for bolts in the sill — no more than 6 ft apart on a one-story house, 4 ft on a two-story (Living on Shaky Ground, p. 15). Wildfire — embers cause up to 90% of house ignitions and can fly miles ahead of a fire (OSFM, p. 5). They blow into vents and light the debris in gutters (FEMA P-737, p. 13): - Vents: cover with 1/8-in metal mesh, or fit ember-rated vents (OSFM, p. 8). 1/16-in mesh stops more embers but clogs; replace or cover any 1/4-in mesh (Oregon BCD, p. 5). - Gutters: metal gutters with noncombustible leaf guards. Mesh guards still let pine needles build up, so check and clear them (FEMA P-737, pp. 45–46). - Woodpiles at least 30 ft from the house, on bare or

guards. Mesh guards still let pine needles build up, so check and clear them (FEMA P-737, pp. 45–46). - Woodpiles at least 30 ft from the house, on bare or gravelled ground (P-737, p. 23). ⛺ Emergency tarp and plastic shelters Fixing plastic so it doesn't tear (IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting, p. 26): - Spread the load. Plain nails pull straight through. Nail through wooden battens, or use washers or bottle caps (sharp side away from the plastic), or fold the plastic over a rope. - Fold the sheet over on itself wherever you fasten it (🖼️ good and bad fixings). Keep it tight and sloped (p. 29): a loose sheet flaps in the wind and holds puddles, and both tear it. Keep nail heads flush, smooth anything that touches the plastic, and keep branches and hot metal (stovepipes) away. Tarping a damaged roof (rule of thumb): run the tarp over the ridge so rain can't get under its top edge, and hold it down with battens nailed through it, not with nails alone. Out in the open: a poncho lean-to needs only a poncho, 2–3 m of cord, three stakes and two trees (FM 21-76, p. 49; 🖼️ drawing). For fallout shelters, see the Nuclear Fallout guide. 📚 Go deeper: IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting — fixing, repairs and warm rooms; Beard — bark and brush lean-tos up to pole houses; Kearny Expedient Shelter Handbook — quickly built earth-covered shelters.

Don't cut, break, sand or burn it. 🧱 Natural Building: Cob, Straw, Clay, Hemp & Lime Building walls, plasters and floors from local earth, straw, hemp and lime that stand up to Cascadia shaking, wet winters and fire season — plus burning your own lime and thatching sheds. The books are in Natural-Building\ (Cob-Earth, Straw-Bale-Light-Clay, Hemp-Lime, Plasters-Lime-Floors, Roofs-Thatch, Quake-Moisture). The soil ribbon test, adobe, rammed earth, log chinking and quake retrofits are in the Shelter guide; cordwood and earthbag how-tos are only in the Appropedia archive in Manuals\DIY-Appropedia. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Never build earth or straw walls where floods reach. Cob walls collapsed outright when floodwater rose up them (DSIR 1922, p. 19). Our river soils flood (Soil Survey, p. 17). - Keep the roof light and off the earth walls. The deadliest quake failure is walls falling out and the roof falling in (Minke, p. 13). One storey. - Quicklime burns eyes and skin, and damp quicklime can start a fire. Goggles and gloves; store it airtight (NBS Circular 30, p. 10). - No cement or plastic over earth or straw. They trap water and rot the wall from inside (NPS Brief 5, p. 5; BSD-112, p. 12). - Loose straw is tinder. In fire season plaster bales promptly, sweep up straw daily, and never thatch a house with a stove (rule of thumb). - Serpentine rock can carry natural

straw is tinder. In fire season plaster bales promptly, sweep up straw daily, and never thatch a house with a stove (rule of thumb). - Serpentine rock can carry natural asbestos. Never crush or sieve it dry (rule of thumb).

🧭 Choosing a system for our conditions The key advice: in Cascadia country, build a braced timber frame that carries a light roof, and use earth or straw only as infill or a skin. Keep it one storey. Never build on floodplain soils. Shaking forces grow with weight, and mud-walled houses have caused the most quake deaths (PA EQ Housing, p. 2). The safest layout puts the roof on its own posts (Minke, p. 38): if the walls fall, the roof stays up. 🌎 Quake rules for earth walls Minke's 10 mistakes that collapse earth houses (p. 12): (1) no ring beam; (2) lintels too short; (3) too little wall between a door and a window; (4) openings too close to corners; (5) no plinth; (6) windows too wide for their height; (7) walls too thin for their height; (8) poor mortar — part-filled joints, or joints over 15 mm (⅝ in); (9) too heavy a roof; (10) a roof not fixed to the walls. Shape and size: square beats rectangle, circle beats square; split an L-shape into separate blocks (Minke, p. 9). Walls no taller than 11.5 ft, no unsupported wall longer than 23 ft, no gables, wall tops tied together (PA, p. 3). Doors and windows (Minke, p. 41; PA, p. 3): - Windows no wider than 4 ft, nor more than ⅓ of the wall's length. - Openings at least 2 ft from corners; wall between openings at least 3¼ ft and ⅓ of its height. - Lintels bear 40 cm (Minke) or 50 cm (PA) into the wall each side — use 20 in, or make the lintel part of the ring beam. - Doors open outward, with a big window or second door opposite as an emergency exit. Ring beam: a closed timber ring with stiff corners, tied down by vertical wooden rods from the foundation up to

big window or second door opposite as an emergency exit. Ring beam: a closed timber ring with stiff corners, tied down by vertical wooden rods from the foundation up to a double timber ring beam (Minke, p. 35; 🖼️ PA timber bond-beam drawings). Block walls also need vertical bars at corners, openings and every 5 ft (CSEB manual, p. 12). Siting: don't cut into a slope, build on one, or sit below a steep one; level a platform well back (Minke, p. 8). Avoid fill, river banks, landslide ground and slopes over 20° (CSEB, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Minke — plinths, ring beams and separate roofs, drawn; CSEB manual — bands and reinforcement step by step. 🎩 "A good hat and good boots": keeping walls dry "Giv'un a gude hat and pair of butes an' 'er'l last for ever" — cob asks only for dry foundations and a good roof (Williams-Ellis, p. 46). Boots — raise the wall off the ground: | Wall | Stone or masonry base above ground | | Cob | About 2 ft (Williams-Ellis, p. 56) | | Earth walls in quake country | At least 12 in, on a footing 8 in wider than the wall and 16 in deep (Minke, p. 34) | | Plastered straw bales | At least 6 in; 8–12 in better (BSD-112, p. 6) | Don't lay a smooth damp-proof layer on the plinth — in a quake the wall slides off. Key it with vertical wooden rods every 12–20 in and a rough plinth top (Minke, p. 34). Hat: an overhang, a pitched roof and nearby shelter can cut the rain on a wall tenfold (BSD-112, p. 5; 🖼️ how walls get wet). Minimum overhangs: 16 in on one storey, 24 in on two, with gutters (p. 11); here, go wider (rule of thumb). Hip the roof rather than build tall earth gables (Williams-Ellis, p. 57). Splash zone: puddles and splash hollow out the base ("coving"); rising ground water makes walls erode and bulge (NPS Brief 5, p. 4). Grade the ground away, dig a

57). Splash zone: puddles and splash hollow out the base ("coving"); rising ground water makes walls erode and bulge (NPS Brief 5, p. 4). It hangs on nails that rust, cracks, lets water in and stops the wall drying (NPS Brief 5, pp. 3, 5). ⛏️ Local materials: clay, sand, straw and stone Clay — the Pollard soils. Under the loam topsoil is red subsoil about 50% clay; the typical profile is half a mile south of Kerby (Soil Survey, p. 157). They cover high terraces and hillsides in the Illinois River and Deer Creek valleys (p. 18) and are rated "too clayey," with moderate shrink-swell (p. 223): a fat clay that needs lots of sand. Use the ribbon test in the Shelter guide and a shrink box — pack damp soil in a 2-ft box; more than ¼ in of shrinkage means it will crack (PA Mud Plasters, p. 4). Be wary of serpentine clay. Brockman soils, on alluvial fans in the valley (🖼️ photo), formed from serpentinite and are "very sticky and very plastic" (Soil Survey, p. 141). Expect bad cracking; make test bricks first, and keep it damp (rule of thumb). Sand and gravel: the Takilma and Kerby low terraces are cobbly loam over extremely gravelly sand (p. 18). Screen out stones over ¼ in (5–6 mm) for blocks and plaster (PA Soil Blocks, p. 10). Straw, never hay. Building straw is the dead stalks of wheat, barley or oats (BSD-112, p. 3). Hay molds (rule of thumb), and leftover grain draws mice and birds that tunnel in (Beard, p. 80). Grain straw comes from the Klamath Basin and Willamette Valley; buy

3). Hay molds (rule of thumb), and leftover grain draws mice and birds that tunnel in (Beard, p. 80). Grain straw comes from the Klamath Basin and Willamette Valley; buy tight, dry, bright bales and store them off the ground under cover (rule of thumb). Limestone and marble: see the deposit table under Making lime. 📚 Go deeper: Josephine County Soil Survey — maps of clay and gravel; PA Soil Blocks — shrink and drop tests. 🏺 Cob, step by step Cob is mostly aggregate held by about one-fifth clay: old Devon cob tested at 24% stones, 52% sand, 21% clay, about 1% straw (DSIR, p. 16). Here, use it for infill between frame posts, garden walls and small sheds — not tall load-bearing walls. Cob); 🖼️ old Devon cob cottages. Season: Devon built March to September (Williams-Ellis, p. 56). Here, build May–September and get the roof on before the October rains (rule of thumb). 1. Plinth: stone, about 2 ft high, keyed with wooden rods (see above; 🖼️ drawing). 2. Mix: heap the earth beside the wall and pick out big stones. Four people turn the heap with forks, treading all the while; one sprinkles water, another straw. Turn it twice (p. 53). 3. Lay: tread it onto the wall in diagonal layers, working the heels, overhanging the base about an inch for paring (pp. 54–55). 4. Lifts: about 2 ft; each takes 2–3 weeks to dry, so work several walls in turn. Pare each lift plumb when firm (p. 55). 5. Thickness: 18 in minimum, one storey only (p. 57). 6. Openings: wooden lintels well tailed in (20 in each side); frames fixed to wooden blocks built into the cob (p. 61). 7. Corners crack, so round them (DSIR, p. 16). 8. Top: a closed timber ring beam (🖼️ drawing), then a light hipped
cob-step-by-step

wooden blocks built into the cob (p. 61). 7. Corners crack, so round them (DSIR, p. 16). 8. Top: a closed timber ring beam (🖼️ drawing), then a light hipped roof with good eaves. 9. Dry: don't render the outside for one to two years; protect it from frost and rain meanwhile (Williams-Ellis, p. 56). Labor: eight mostly green men took three months to raise one cottage's walls (p. 49). 📚 Go deeper: Williams-Ellis Cottage Building in Cob — mixing, lifts, finishing; DSIR Building in Cob and Pisé — regional methods and why cob fails. 🌾 Straw bale Bales (BSD-112, p. 3): two-string 18 × 14 in; three-string 24 × 16–18 in; 32–40 in long; at least 7 lb per cubic foot. Straw is fine up to about 20% moisture; rot begins at 25–30% (CMHC 00-103, p. 2). Straw-bale construction. How it works: plaster skins (lime or cement 1–1½ in, earth 2–3 in) carry 95–99% of the load; the bales insulate (BSD-112, p. 4). Here, use bales as infill in a timber frame (rule of thumb). Building it: toe-up 6 in or more, with a capillary break between foundation and plaster (CMHC, p. 3); wide overhangs and gutters; careful flashing at window and door sills and heads, where rain gets in (BSD-112, p. 11); earth or lime plaster straight onto the straw. The wet-coast warning (CMHC 00-103, pp. 2–3): the walls that rotted had two or more of these: minimal overhangs; no capillary break; heavy indoor wetting; bales below grade; poor splash protection; a north-facing wall. Straw in floors rotted to "nothing but a pile of black compost." On the rainy coast a north wall stayed damp from humid air alone; CMHC urges "extreme caution" with north walls in high-rain climates. Never put straw under a floor. Fire: a wall of 7.5 lb/ft³ wheat bales with 1 in of earth plaster each side passed a 1-hour fire test and the hose stream. The plaster: 3
straw-bale

a floor. Fire: a wall of 7.5 lb/ft³ wheat bales with 1 in of earth plaster each side passed a 1-hour fire test and the hose stream. The plaster: 3 parts clay, 2 chopped straw, 6 sand, in two ½-in coats (Intertek, pp. 13, 16). Fire-season site rules (rule of thumb): plaster within days; rake up loose straw every evening; keep water and a hose on site; no grinding or welding near straw; store spare bales well away from buildings — FEMA puts sheds holding combustibles 50 ft or more from a house (FEMA P-737, p. 23). 📚 Go deeper: BSD-112 Building Science for Strawbale — moisture, overhangs, plaster; Intertek fire test — photos and plaster mix. 🪵 Lighter systems: straw-clay, hempcrete, wattle, bags, blocks, cordwood Light straw-clay (slip-straw) (CMHC 05-109, pp. 2–3; Light clay): clay-coated straw packed into forms around a timber frame. It carries no load, dries fast (no vapour retarder over it), and insulates R-0.8 to 2.1 per inch. It settles about 7% as it dries, so top it up. Four hours of propane torch burned only 2 in in, and it is ductile — it soaks up quake energy. Method (general practice): dip straw in thick clay slip, tamp it into 12-in forms on the frame, and let it dry through a summer before plastering. Hempcrete (Hempitecture, pp. 6, 9, 11; Hempcrete): binder (lime plus pozzolan) to hemp hurd 1.5 to 1 by weight — 50 lb of binder, 33 lb of hurd, about 6 gallons of water. A squeezed ball should hold when tossed 2–3 ft. Use within 30 minutes, out of the sun; place 2 in at a time, tamping hardest along the forms. Walls are 8–12 in, R-2.2 to 2.5 per inch, and need diagonal bracing since they can't be sheathed in plywood. Gloves and eye protection (p. 3). Reality (general practice): hurd means retting and breaking stalks by hand, and the binder needs lime. Wattle and daub (quincha): poles and woven sticks packed with earth — the most flexible earth system; one survived a heavy Guatemala quake (Minke, pp.

and the binder needs lime. Wattle and daub (quincha): poles and woven sticks packed with earth — the most flexible earth system; one survived a heavy Guatemala quake (Minke, pp. 13, 28; 🖼️ a wattle-and-daub store). It cracks as the wood moves and holes harbor insects, so patch it yearly. Keep poles out of the soil, where they rot (PA, p. 3). Earthbags: test houses used jute or cotton tubes of earth, given 4 coats of lime against rot, with a ring beam and the roof on separate posts (Minke, p. 30). Plastic bags rot in sunlight within months — plaster them soon (general practice). Earthbag construction. Pressed blocks (Compressed earth block): the mix is right when a ball dropped from shoulder height breaks into a few pieces (PA Soil Blocks, p. 10; 🖼️ pressing a block). A 50%-clay soil like Pollard subsoil needs lime: try blocks at 5, 7 and 9% lime by weight (p. 8). Keep lime blocks damp a week and don't use them for 37 days (p. 12). Cordwood: seasoned log rounds laid crosswise in mortar — heavy, unreinforced, so for sheds, not houses (general practice). Cordwood construction. 📚 Go deeper: Hempitecture manual — forms and packing; Minke — wattle and daub, earth-filled bags. 🎨 Earth plasters, lime plaster, limewash and floors Earth plaster (PA Mud Plasters, pp. 3–5; Earthen plaster): 1. Aim for 10–15% clay — at least 3 parts sand to 1 clay — plus straw chopped to 1–2 in, about 85 lb per cubic yard. Try test patches. 2. Brush off dust and wet the wall. Throw on a clay-rich first coat up to ¾ in thick; scratch it. 3. When dry, dampen it and add a thinner, sandier finish coat (🖼️ photo). Shade the work; skip hot, windy days. 4. Limewash it. Lime-soil plaster is 1 hydrated lime : 2 clayey soil : 3–6 sand (p. 4). - Fill holes with dry earth bricks in slurry, not wet mud, which shrinks (Irish Thatch guide, p. 50). Lime plaster and stucco: - Mortar: 1 lime putty : 3 sand (NPS Brief 2, p. 2; 🖼️ mixing it, photos). - Stucco: base coats 1 lime : 3 sand with 6 lb of goat or cattle hair (½–2 in) per cubic yard; finish 1:3 without hair (NPS Brief 22, p. 15; 🖼️ stucco layers drawn). Best is ⅜-in scratch and brown coats, then a ⅛-in finish (NPS Brief 21, p. 3; 🖼️ plastering tools). - Cure slowly: mist and cover with burlap for 3 days; plastic only if tented off the wall (NPS Brief 2, p. 11). Limewash yearly to fill hairline cracks

tools). - Cure slowly: mist and cover with burlap for 3 days; plastic only if tented off the wall (NPS Brief 2, p. 11). Limewash yearly to fill hairline cracks before they let water in (NPS Brief 22, p. 7); one coat lasts about a year (Irish guide, p. 50). Make the first coat watery so it soaks 2–3 mm in (Minke, p. 49). Tint with ochre or umber (rule of thumb). Earthen floors (Peace Corps, pp. 139–141): 1. Dig out topsoil to 6–7 in below the finished floor and tamp — but don't ram swelling clay. 2. Lay 4 in of tamped sandy gravel (6 in over swelling soil) against rising damp. 3. Ram two 1½-in layers of stabilised earth; the top one with enough lime that a nail barely scratches it. 4. Cure it damp several days. Seal with oil, hot beeswax or tallow. Old floors were painted with ox blood (DSIR, p. 17). Farm-made stabilisers (PA Additives to Clay, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ a bark-stabilised render): dung (up to a third, fermented several days); horse urine; fresh blood with lime; casein from soured milk; glue from boiled skins and bones; linseed oil; oak bark tannin (here, oak or tanoak (rule of thumb)). Use animal products only from healthy animals — anthrax. Often none is needed. 📚 Go deeper: PA Mud Plasters and Renders — mixes and two-coat work;

🔥 Making lime Mortar mixes, concrete, lime concrete and pozzolans are in Mortar, Concrete & Roads. ### ⚠️ Lime burns - Quicklime is hazardous (PA Lime, p. 1) and "highly caustic" (Irish guide, p. 50). Alkali burns, as from plaster and cement, are worse than acid burns (ATP 4-02.11, p. 118). - Lime in an eye: flood it with clean water at once and keep rinsing at least 20 minutes (p. 118). Plain water only. - Goggles, gloves, long sleeves. Slake in an open tub, never a closed one; keep children away (rule of thumb). - Damp quicklime heats up and can start a fire. Store it airtight (NBS Circular 30, p. 10). - Burn lime only in the wet season, never in fire season (rule of thumb). Stone: at least 95% calcium carbonate; marble and shells work too (PA Lime, p. 1). Known deposits (DOGAMI Ore Bin 1958, p. 5): | Deposit | Where | Notes | | Lime Rock (Holton Creek) | ~2 mi southeast of Kerby | Marble, over 98% | | Elder Creek | Near Takilma | Burned for the old Takilma smelter | | Jones Marble Quarry | ~4 mi west of Williams | Over 99% | | Turvey | ~4 mi west of Williams | 95% | | Grizzly Gulch | 2 mi south of Oregon Caves | Small; may now be inside the

99% | | Turvey | ~4 mi west of Williams | 95% | | Grizzly Gulch | 2 mi south of Oregon Caves | Small; may now be inside the park, which was enlarged in 2014 — check before digging (rule of thumb) | | Oregon Caves | National monument and preserve | "Not available" — never quarry there | Get the landowner's or agency's permission (rule of thumb). Burning (PA Lime, pp. 1–2; Lime kiln): break stone to 4–6 in and hold it at about 1,830°F (1,000°C) for several hours. The simplest burn — a ring of logs with limestone heaped on top — gives under 1,100 lb of lime (🖼️ loading a kiln). A shaft kiln must be at least 6 times as tall as it is wide (PA Kiln, p. 1; 🖼️ building drawings); stone and fuel go in the top, lime comes out the bottom. A wood-fired kiln used about ½ cord per ton of lime (NBS Circular 337, p. 117; 🖼️ old shaft kilns). Underburn rather than overburn: overburned lime is yellow, heavy and won't slake; underburned stone can go back in (p. 13). Slaking (NBS Circular 337, p. 119): 1. Test: barely cover two or three fist-sized lumps with water. Crumbling in under 5 minutes = quick-slaking; 5–30 = medium; over 30 = slow. 2. Quick: add lime to plenty of water, never water

or three fist-sized lumps with water. Crumbling in under 5 minutes = quick-slaking; 5–30 = medium; over 30 = slow. 2. Quick: add lime to plenty of water, never water to lime, and hoe hard at the first steam. Medium: water to half-cover. Slow: moisten, wait, add water a little at a time. Too hot and it "burns"; too much water "drowns" it (NBS 30, p. 11). 3. Sieve the putty and keep it under water at least two weeks before plastering (p. 119). Pit-slake dolomitic) lime much longer, or it swells in the wall (PA Lime, p. 3). 4. Always add sand — putty alone cracks to pieces (NBS 30, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: PA Small Vertical Shaft Lime Kiln — drawings and a day-by-day build; PA Testing Lime — field tests for homemade lime. 🏚️ Thatch — for sheds only - Pitch 45° or steeper (Irish guide, p. 18). - Material: any stiff, hollow-stemmed grass or reed at least 3 ft long (p. 19). Thresh grain straw clean or mice dig in; lay it 10–12 in thick (Beard, p. 80). - Life: reed wears about ¼ in a year, so 6 in of cover lasts about 24 years (Irish guide, p. 31). A re-thatch can weigh 3 tonnes — check the timbers (p. 41). Fire: most thatch fires start at the chimney — cracked flues, sparks, stovepipes through the thatch (pp. 61–62). Oregon calls even untreated shakes "not desirable" (Oregon BCD, p. 3). Thatch only sheds 50 ft or more from the house (FEMA P-737, p. 23), never a dwelling with a stove. Thatching. 📚 Go deeper: Irish Thatch guide — materials, fixing, repair, fire prevention; Beard — a simple thatched roof. Pictures: 🖼️ fixing a course with scollops, Irish guide p. 31.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Hot pitch or tar "skirting" on cob bases (Williams-Ellis, p. 61). Coal tar causes cancer; use a high stone plinth and limewash. - Cement-lime render as "probably the best" for cob (same page). Use lime or earth (NPS Brief 5, p. 5). - Powdered glass in the wall base against rats (p. 62). Use render over wire mesh (same page). - "Salamanders" (open coke braziers) to speed lime setting indoors (NBS Circular 30, p. 11). Carbon monoxide kills. - Hot bitumen cut with kerosene in plaster (PA Mud Plasters, p. 4). Fire and fume hazard; not needed. - Copper sulphate ("bluestone") on thatch (Irish guide, p. 41). It irritates eyes and skin and poisons streams. - Whitewash called "fireproof," tinted with chrome yellow (Household Discoveries, p. 270). It isn't fireproof, and chrome yellow is a lead pigment. Use ochre and umber. - Tall unreinforced cob — "no apparent limit" to height (Williams-Ellis, p. 57). Both old cob books pre-date quake design; follow the quake rules above. 📚 Go deeper: Minke — plasters and paints that work on earth; NPS Brief 5 — why cement fails on earth walls.

🏗️ Mortar, Concrete & Roads How to lay brick and stone, pour and patch concrete, and keep a gravel road passable when no paving crew is ever coming: lime, cement-lime, earth and fire-clay mortars; concrete mixed by hand; what you can honestly build without store cement; why asphalt can't be made at home and how to patch what's left; and roads, ditches and culverts. Burning lime is in "Making lime" in the Natural Building guide. The main books are in Shelter-Building\Concrete-Masonry (Army FM 5-428 Concrete and Masonry; Gillmore's 1864 Limes, Hydraulic Cements and Mortars), Shelter-Building\Roads (FHWA Gravel Roads; Army FM 5-436 Paving and Surfacing) and Natural-Building\Plasters-Lime-Floors. Work out quantities with the Practical Math guide, the Calculator and the Unit Converter. ### The short version - Wet cement burns skin slowly: "you may not feel anything for several hours" (CAWST, p. 38). Goggles, gloves, long sleeves; rinse an eye with clean water at least 15–20 minutes. - Less water makes stronger concrete. About 6 gallons per 94-lb sack (VITA, p. 290); never loosen a stiff mix with water alone (VITA, p. 296). - Keep concrete wet at least 7 days. Never kept damp, it ends at about 60% of its strength (Peace Corps Wells, p. 249). - Mortar must be softer than the brick, or the bricks crack instead of the joints (NPS Brief 2, p. 4). 1 cement : 1

(Peace Corps Wells, p. 249). - Mortar must be softer than the brick, or the bricks crack instead of the joints (NPS Brief 2, p. 4). 1 cement : 1 lime : 6 sand suits most new work (FM 5-428, p. 196). - Plain lime hardens only in moist air, never under water or in wet ground (Gillmore, p. 76). Wet places need hydraulic lime, a pozzolan or cement. - Cement keeps 6 months to a year, even covered; lumpy cement is dead (Wells, p. 235; CAWST, p. 74). - Asphalt can't be made at home: it's left over from refining crude oil (FM 5-436, p. 15). Plan on gravel. - A gravel road lives on drainage: crown it ½ in per foot (4%), never over 6%, and keep ditches and culverts clear (FHWA, p. 22).

🧪 Lime for mortar: what's new beyond burning it Stone, burning, slaking and the quicklime safety box are in "Making lime" in the Natural Building guide. Four more things matter once lime goes into mortar: - Plain ("fat") lime hardens only in moist air. It sets by drying, then slowly taking carbon dioxide from the air; "Dry carbon dioxide will not react with dry slaked lime", so soak the work often while it sets (NBS Circular 30, pp. 11–12). It "will not harden under water", so it's "unsuitable for masonry under water, or for foundations in damp soils", and it shrinks too much to use without plenty of sand (Gillmore, p. 76). - Wood-burned lime is the good stuff: lime burned cooler is better, "why wood-burned lime generally commands a higher price" (NBS Circular 30, p. 8). Kilns at Rockland burned hemlock, pine, spruce and fir, 4 cords per 100 barrels of 230–240-lb lime, 42–48 hours in the heat (Gillmore, p. 149): about ⅓ cord per ton (arithmetic). - Magnesian (dolomitic) lime slakes slowly, never "burns", works smoother and made the stronger mortar in the Bureau's tests (NBS Circular 30, pp. 13–14). - Hydraulic lime sets in wet places. Limestone with under 12% clay gives slightly hydraulic lime; 18–25%, eminently hydraulic (PA Lime, p. 3). It slakes slowly with little heat or steam and swells far less (Gillmore, p. 77).

with under 12% clay gives slightly hydraulic lime; 18–25%, eminently hydraulic (PA Lime, p. 3). It slakes slowly with little heat or steam and swells far less (Gillmore, p. 77). Looks tell you little: "insist upon having some of the stone actually burned" (NBS Circular 30, p. 8). Test it: Gillmore sank one cake of stiff paste in water at once and another after it set in air, and timed their hardening (p. 86). Paste that firms up under water within days is hydraulic; paste that stays soft is fat lime (rule of thumb). Make hydraulic lime from fat lime and clay ("twice-kilned"; Gillmore, pp. 92–93): 1. Mix well-slaked lime with smooth potter's clay: about 10% clay gives "moderately hydraulic" lime. 2. Roll balls 2–3 in across and dry them completely; damp clay stays inert. 3. Burn at a bright red heat with a good draft. The balls can ride on top of an ordinary lime burn. Judge the heat with the heat-colour chart in the Blacksmithing guide. 4. Grind to powder and keep it dry. Pozzolans (the Roman trick). A pozzolan "is a substance which, when mixed with lime and water, hardens as a cement" (PA Quake Housing, p. 4): fine silica and alumina that react with slaked lime (Wood Handbook, p. 275). - Lightly burned clay: "Artificial pozzuolana is produced whenever clay is subjected to a slight calcination";
lime-for-mortar-what-s-new-beyond-burning-it

4): fine silica and alumina that react with slaked lime (Wood Handbook, p. 275). - Lightly burned clay: "Artificial pozzuolana is produced whenever clay is subjected to a slight calcination"; the Romans used brick and tile dust, and forge scale and the ashes from under a lime kiln's grate work too (Gillmore, p. 99). In France, clay was dried and baked in an ordinary lime kiln with 1 measure of charcoal to 16–18 of clay (p. 100). Volcanic ash and rice-husk ash also work (PA Lime, pp. 3–4). - Mixes: harbour mortar at Algiers was 1 lime putty : 1 sand : 1 pozzolana (Gillmore, p. 110); test mortars used 2 pozzolana : 1 lime (p. 296). Use fat lime, not hydraulic, and let the mix stand a while before the last remixing (p. 309). - Be honest: those used volcanic pozzolana, and pozzolans "should be tested first" (FM 5-428, p. 33). Brick dust is weaker: make test cakes, keep them damp and give them weeks before trusting a wall to it (rule of thumb). Stretching scarce cement: in 1:4 or 1:5 mortar "at least one-third of the cement may be replaced by slaked lime without loss of strength" (Henley's, p. 694); lime up to 15% of the cement's weight also makes it more watertight (NBS Circular 30, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Gillmore, pp. 91–101 — four ways to

p. 694); lime up to 15% of the cement's weight also makes it more watertight (NBS Circular 30, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Gillmore, pp. 91–101 — four ways to make lime set under water; NBS Circular 30, pp. 11–18 — how lime mortar hardens; PA Testing Lime, p. 2 — field tests. Pictures: Hydraulic lime.

Strength runs from 2,500 psi (M) to 75 psi (K) (NPS, p. 7); it is rarely the problem. The one rule: softer than the brick. Harder mortar "will not 'give'", so the bricks crack and spall instead (NPS Brief 2, pp. 3–4). Granite can take strong mortar; soft brick wants lime (p. 7). Bagged masonry cement has no lime and "can damage historic masonry" (p. 6).

instead (NPS Brief 2, pp. 3–4). Granite can take strong mortar; soft brick wants lime (p. 7). Bagged masonry cement has no lime and "can damage historic masonry" (p. 6). Sand and water: clean, free of salt and clay, rounded river sand packing best; it's 1 binder to 3 sand because good sand is about 30% air (NPS, p. 4). Two sizes of sand beat one (NBS Circular 30, pp. 14–15); screen it under ¼ in (Peace Corps Homes of Earth, p. 103). Salty water makes white bloom and weak mortar (FM 5-428, p. 196). Mixing by hand (FM 5-428, pp. 196–197; NPS, p. 10; 🖼️ photos): 1. Measure every part with the same bucket; sand damp and loose. 2. Cement-lime: mix the dry parts first, add half the water, mix 5 minutes, then the rest a little at a time. 3. Lime putty: put the sand into the putty. Beating it with a mallet or ax handle and chopping with a hoe makes it work better. Lime and sand alone keep "indefinitely" covered damp; once cement goes in, they don't. 4. Use it in time: remix mortar that stiffened by drying, but throw out any that has begun to set; use it within 2½ hours above 80 °F, 3½ below (FM 5-428). Repointing old walls, NPS says 30 minutes to 1½ hours, no added water. 5. Never use mortar

set; use it within 2½ hours above 80 °F, 3½ below (FM 5-428). Repointing old walls, NPS says 30 minutes to 1½ hours, no added water. 5. Never use mortar that froze; add no "antifreeze" (FM 5-428, p. 197). Wet the bricks, not the blocks: wet clay brick that drinks fast; never wet concrete blocks (FM 5-428, p. 194). Earth blocks: if 20 drops of water in a 1-in circle vanish in under 1½ minutes, wet them (Peace Corps, p. 104). Earth, chimney and firebrick mortars: - Adobe: "mud without straw", ½–1-in joints; 1 cu ft lays 25–30 bricks of 4 × 10 × 16 in (USDA FB 1720, p. 10). Never repair adobe with lime or cement mortar (NPS Brief 5, p. 7). - Stabilised-soil mortar for pressed blocks: low-clay soil, sieved, with twice the blocks' stabiliser. Test two blocks mortared together: no open cracks after a day; after 7 days, dropped from shoulder height onto a corner, some cracks should run through the blocks (Peace Corps, p. 104). - Chimneys: cement mortar "is more resistant to the action of heat and flue gases than lime mortar": 1 portland : 1 lime : 6 sand, and "Firebrick should be laid with fire clay" (FB 1889, p. 8). In quakes, masonry chimneys need four ½-in bars grouted full height, and factory-built ones are "the better choice for light-frame houses" (FEMA
mortar-mixes-sand-and-mixing

laid with fire clay" (FB 1889, p. 8). In quakes, masonry chimneys need four ½-in bars grouted full height, and factory-built ones are "the better choice for light-frame houses" (FEMA 232, p. 145). - Firebrick: fire clay and water "to the consistency of thick cream"; grind old firebrick to get fire clay. Dip each brick, tap it home, joints as thin as possible (FM 5-428, p. 279). No fire clay? Crushed firebrick with "your purest clay", or clay alone as a last resort (VITA, p. 355); a lime kiln used about 1 fire clay : 1 crushed firebrick (PA Shaft Kiln, p. 2).

🪨 Laying stone and repointing old joints Rubble stone walls (FM 5-428, pp. 236–238): biggest stones in the footing, as long as it is wide, in about 2 in of mortar; each stone on its broadest face; wet porous stones first; pack tight and fill gaps with small stones and mortar; one bonding stone through the wall every 6–10 sq ft; stagger the joints; nothing bigger than two people can handle easily. Quake caution: "double-faced walls, without tie stones and with rubble infill should be strictly avoided" (PA Quake Housing, p. 4), and the house code "essentially prohibits the use of rubble stone masonry" (FEMA 232, p. 124). Use stone for footings, low garden walls and terraces, and build houses of braced timber (rule of thumb). Repointing loose joints (NPS Brief 2; FM 5-428, p. 284): 1. Stop the water first: fix leaking roofs and gutters (NPS, p. 2). Work with the wall at 40–95 °F, in shade (p. 7). 2. Rake out with hammer and chisel to 2–2½ times the joint's width, about ½–1 in for brick; grinders chew brick edges (p. 9; 🖼️ right and wrong). 3. Pick the mix: scrape old mortar with a screwdriver, then a cold chisel; scratch the brick with a fingernail. The new mortar must not be harder than the brick (p. 14). FM 5-428's Type S suits hard modern brick only. 4.
laying-stone-and-repointing-old-joints

cold chisel; scratch the brick with a fingernail. The new mortar must not be harder than the brick (p. 14). FM 5-428's Type S suits hard modern brick only. 4. Brush out dust and dampen the joint, no standing water (p. 10). For cement-lime, prehydrate: wet the dry mix just enough to hold a ball, let it stand 1–2 hours, remix stiff; it shrinks much less (FM 5-428, p. 284). 5. Pack ¼-in layers, each "thumb-print hard" before the next; tool the last at thumb-print hardness (NPS, p. 11). Brush off smears with bristle or nylon, never wire, after it dries but before it sets, about 1–2 hours (p. 12). 6. Mist it and keep it under burlap 3 days (p. 11). Try a 3 × 3 ft test patch first (p. 9).

🧮 Concrete: what it is and the mixes Concrete is cement, sand, gravel and water. "The amount of water used to mix these ingredients is by far the most important factor in determining the final strength" (Wells, p. 234). Beginners use too much, and once it sets "there is no simple non-destructive test" of strength (VITA, p. 284). | Cement : sand : gravel | Use | Source | | 1 : 2 : 3 | Small jobs and repairs; 6 gal water a sack; a sack makes about 5 cu ft | VITA, pp. 291–292; FM 5-428, p. 116 | | 1 : 2 : 4 | Water tanks, reinforced floors, walks, fence posts | Brace & Mayne, p. 263 | | 1 : 2½ : 5 | Foundation walls | p. 273 | | 1 : 3 : 4 | House footings, 5–7 gal water a sack | Peace Corps, p. 71 | | 1 : 3 : 6 / 1 : 4 : 8 | Cellar and barn floors, walks / big heavy foundations | Brace & Mayne, p. 263 | | 1 : 1 : 3 | Water troughs (or 1 cement : 3 bank-run gravel) | p. 279 | | 1 : 3 : 2 | Thin toilet slab (more sand than gravel) | Hesperian, p. 20 | For ordinary work "1:2:4, 1:2:3, 1:2.5:5 …
concrete-what-it-is-and-the-mixes

| p. 279 | | 1 : 3 : 2 | Thin toilet slab (more sand than gravel) | Hesperian, p. 20 | For ordinary work "1:2:4, 1:2:3, 1:2.5:5 … all work equally well" (Wells, p. 234). Water per 94-lb sack: 5 gallons for floors that take hard wear; 6 for anything watertight (tanks, septic tanks, driveways); 7 for footings and foundation walls (VITA, p. 290). Count water already in wet sand (USDA AH 73, p. 10). Checking the wet mix: - Shovel test: stab the pile into ridges. Ridges stand = good; crumbles = too dry; ridges slump = too wet (CAWST, p. 75). - Rock test: rod a bucketful 25 times and drop a smooth, round 4-in rock on it; a dent of about 1½ in is right for footings (Peace Corps, p. 71). - Slump cone: walks, culverts and pavements should sag 1–3 in (VITA, pp. 295–296). - Too wet? Add sand and gravel in proportion. Too stiff? Add water and cement. "Do not add just water … this will weaken the concrete" (VITA, p. 296).

🪣 Sand, gravel and water for concrete - Sand from beaches, dunes and riverbanks is often too fine; scrape off about 1 ft and look for coarser sand below (Wells, p. 235). - Biggest stone: no more than ⅕ of the thinnest part, ¾ of the gap between bars, ¼ of a slab's thickness; about ¾ in suits most work (Wells, p. 236; VITA, p. 284). Mixed sizes beat one size (Brace & Mayne, p. 263); chunky crushed rock or rounded creek gravel is best, not flat or splintery (VITA, p. 285). - Jar test: 2 in of sand in a clear jar, water to ¾ full, shake a minute, wait 3 hours. A silt layer over ⅛ in (3 mm) on the sand means weak concrete (VITA, p. 285). - Washing: in a drum, cover with water, stir, let stand a minute, pour off; once or twice removes most silt (Wells, p. 236). Dirt, clay, mica, salt and rotted plants all weaken concrete (FM 5-428, p. 19). - Stone test: break some with a hammer; concrete is only as strong as its stone (Wells, p. 236). Never crush serpentine (greenish, soapy rock) for gravel: it can carry asbestos (rule of thumb). - Damp sand swells: "20 buckets of bone dry sand" plus 2 of water make "about 27 buckets of damp sand" (Wells, pp. 236–237). Squeeze test (6–8 in
sand-gravel-and-water-for-concrete

of thumb). - Damp sand swells: "20 buckets of bone dry sand" plus 2 of water make "about 27 buckets of damp sand" (Wells, pp. 236–237). Squeeze test (6–8 in into the pile): falls apart = damp, 0–2% water; clings = wet, 3–4%; glistens = very wet, 5–8%; cut the mixing water to match (FM 5-428, p. 313). - How much paste? Fill a pail with your gravel, then with water: that much water is the room for sand and paste (VITA, p. 291). Drinkable water is fine; water with algae is not (FM 5-428, p. 18). - Cement: store it off damp floors, away from outside walls, sacks stacked close (Wells, p. 235); lumps can't be broken up and used (CAWST, p. 74).

🏋️ Mixing, forms, steel and placing by hand Hand mixing (FM 5-428, p. 117; VITA, pp. 293–294): 1. On a clean, tight, wetted platform, spread the sand, the cement over it, then the gravel. 2. Turn it dry at least 3 times, till it's one colour. 3. Make a hollow, add water slowly, and turn at least 3 more times. 4. Get it into the forms within 20 minutes. One person mixes about a cubic yard an hour; rinse tools at day's end (Wells, p. 247). Forms: - "They always seem too strong … Once the concrete is poured, it is too late" (Peace Corps, p. 73). Flat work: 2×4 or 2×6 edges, stakes every 4 ft; walls: wire ties every 2½ ft up the studs (VITA, pp. 296–297). - Leave nail heads sticking out; oil or grease rough boards inside unless it will be plastered (Wells, pp. 241–242). - Forms fail from pouring walls too fast, too few nails, loose ties and old or undersized lumber (FM 5-428, p. 101). Watch them while you pour (p. 102). Steel: concrete resists squeezing but breaks when stretched; steel is the opposite (Wells, pp. 243–245). - Bars clean of loose rust, at least 1 in from the forms, about two-thirds of the way through the pour from the loaded side; reinforced parts at least 3 in thick, 4 better. - Grid no
mixing-forms-steel-and-placing-by-hand

least 1 in from the forms, about two-thirds of the way through the pour from the loaded side; reinforced parts at least 3 in thick, 4 better. - Grid no wider than 3 times the thickness; tie crossings with wire; overlap bars 20 times their diameter; hook smooth rod ends; prop the grid on small stones. - Quake country: footing bars all the way round, lapped 24 in for ½-in bar (FEMA 232, p. 67). Heavy woven fence wire can go in block-wall joints (Peace Corps, p. 75). - Big or heavily loaded work "can become too complicated for a person without special training" (Wells, p. 243). Placing: don't let it fall more than 3–5 ft (FM 5-428, p. 11). Rod it and tap the forms, but too much tamping sends the stones to the bottom (Wells, p. 248). New on old: clean, damp, some stones showing, no puddles (FM 5-428, p. 132); after a stop of more than a few hours, "clean, score, and wet the top" (AH 73, p. 11). Finish with a wooden float for grip; trowel too much and it "will not wear well" (Brace & Mayne, p. 270).

💧 Curing, cold and heat Concrete hardens by a slow reaction with water, not by drying. Once dry it stops, and it "cannot be re-wetted in the field to re-start the hardening process" (Wells, p. 249). | Kept damp for | Strength it finally reaches (Wells, p. 249) | | Not at all | About 60% of what it should | | 3 days | About 80% | | 7 days | Almost 100%, and more as long as it stays moist | Kept moist a month, it's "about twice as strong" as open-air cured (VITA, p. 299). - How long: at least 7 days in a temperate climate (VITA, p. 298). - How: wet burlap or sacks, straw, damp earth or sand, or plastic weighted down; sprinkle so it never dries between; flood a slab inside a little earth dam; keep wooden forms wet (FM 5-428, pp. 146–149). - Stripping and loads: footing forms not before 48 hours (Peace Corps, p. 70); wall forms after 4–5 days; light loads after 7 days (Wells, p. 249). Loosen forms with wooden wedges, never a steel bar (FM 5-428, p. 158). - Lime mortar dried too fast never carbonates properly (NPS, p. 5): keep it damp too. Cold (FM 5-428, pp. 152–158): protect concrete whenever it's 40 °F or colder; thin work (under 12 in) should be 55 °F going in. Heat
curing-cold-and-heat

5): keep it damp too. Cold (FM 5-428, pp. 152–158): protect concrete whenever it's 40 °F or colder; thin work (under 12 in) should be 55 °F going in. Heat the water (max 180 °F) and if needed the sand and gravel (max 150 °F), and mix those first, then the cement. Never pour on frozen ground. Keep it above freezing at least 3 days: concrete that freezes young is permanently weakened, and homemade concrete (not air-entrained) is hurt more easily. Cover it with straw (AH 73, p. 12). No "antifreeze", and no unvented fuel heater in a heated tent: carbon monoxide (pp. 156, 158). For mortar, warm the sand and water and protect the work from frost (NPS, p. 6). Hot (FM 5-428, pp. 149–152): keep concrete under 90 °F; hot, dry wind is worst. Shade the materials, use cold water, sprinkle the gravel, wet the forms, steel and ground just before pouring, work early or at night, and loosen the forms soon and keep it wet. In this valley, pour in spring and early fall when you can (hard winter frosts, hot dry summers) (rule of thumb).

🏡 Footings, slabs, posts and troughs - Footings (USDA AH 73, pp. 11–12): twice as wide as the wall, as deep as the wall is thick, never under 6 in, below the frost line. Dug too deep? Fill with concrete, "never replace dirt". Post footings 24 × 24 × 12 in with a pedestal. In high-rain country bring the foundation wall 18 in above ground (Peace Corps, p. 72). Big "plums" of stone save cement, bedded apart in the wet concrete, porous ones wetted (Henley's, p. 692). - Slab floor (AH 73, p. 22): at least 4 in of tamped gravel, a vapour barrier, wire mesh, and a slab at least 4 in thick. - Walk (Brace & Mayne, pp. 268–270): dig 8 in; tamp 6 in of gravel or cinders as you fill; 4 in of 1:2:4; a 1-in topping of 1 cement : 1 sand bonded with pure cement; slope it to drain; groove it into blocks; keep it covered and wet 2–3 days. Lay floors in small sections (p. 271). - Fence posts (pp. 280–284): 6 in square at the base, 4 in at the top, 7 ft long; 1:2:4; four wires 1 in in from the sides, ends hooked; forms off after 3 days; keep wet, don't use for 2 weeks. - Water trough: rich 1:1:3; outer form on at least 10 days, kept covered and
footings-slabs-posts-and-troughs

sides, ends hooked; forms off after 3 days; keep wet, don't use for 2 weeks. - Water trough: rich 1:1:3; outer form on at least 10 days, kept covered and wet (p. 279). Toilet slab: "Latrines step by step" in the Sanitation guide. Blocks: a day in the mould, 5 more days sprinkled under cover, 4 weeks before use (Henley's, p. 697). How much to mix (Wells, pp. 237–238): finished volume × 1.5 = dry materials, plus 10%, split by the parts; a sack is 1 cu ft. A 10 × 10 ft slab 4 in thick is 33 cu ft; × 1.5 + 10% = 55 cu ft of 1:2:3 = about 9 sacks of cement, 18 cu ft of sand, 28 of gravel, and about 55 gallons of water (arithmetic). VITA's 5 cu ft a sack gives 7 sacks, so 9 leaves a margin. It weighs about 4,800 lb at 144 lb per cu ft (see the Practical Math guide) (arithmetic).

🩹 Patching and repairing concrete - New concrete (FM 5-428, pp. 161–163): repair within 24 hours of stripping. Chip honeycomb back to solid with square edges, keep it wet several hours, brush in creamy cement-and-water grout, fill in layers no thicker than ½ in, scratching each. A thin coat over honeycomb spalls off. Flat patches go at least 1 in deep, never feathered. - Old concrete (pp. 163–164): "far better to remove too much old material than not enough". Cut edges straight down 1–2 in, leave 1 in around any bar, keep it wet overnight ("a good bond will not form without it"), ram in a stiff mix in layers, and start curing at once. - Slabs and paths (FM 5-436, pp. 179–181): for spalls, brush on thin cement paste, then pack 1 cement : 2 sand wet just enough to stick when squeezed. For broken pieces, cut a rectangle with the top 2 in of the old edge straight down, soak it and patch. Cement-bound macadam: fill the hole with broken concrete or gravel 1½–2½ in, flat sides down, ram it, and work in a thick grout of 1 cement : 2–2½ sand. In an emergency, ram in damp soil from the bottom up. - Leaking tank: chip out the crack and plaster cement paste inside and out (CAWST, p. 80).
patching-and-repairing-concrete

🏛️ Concrete without store cement: the honest picture Portland cement can't be made on a homestead. A precise, finely ground mix of limestone and clay must be burned to a white heat where it starts to melt; "The ordinary temperature of lime-kilns would be far too low" (Gillmore, p. 69). Natural cement comes from limestone that happens to hold the right clay (Brace & Mayne, p. 262); only a test burn shows if any local rock does. | Binder | Hardens | Good for | Not for | | Fat lime | Slowly, from the outside, in moist air | Mortar, plaster, floors and fill in dry places | Wet ground, under water, early loads (Gillmore, p. 76) | | Hydraulic lime or lime + pozzolan | Under water, slowly | Footings and linings that stay wet | Work that dries out in the air (Henley's, p. 694) | | Earth stabilised with lime | Over weeks | Blocks (cure 37 days), floors | Wet bases (PA Soil Blocks, p. 12) | Lime concrete (hardens only in air): 1. About 1 hydrated lime : 3 sand : 6 coarse stone (3–4 in), what a lime kiln used as fill under its floor (PA Shaft Kiln, p. 2). 2. Slake the lime fully and make it into mortar with the sand before adding stone; hot quicklime concrete "has grown into disrepute"
concrete-without-store-cement-the-honest-picture

its floor (PA Shaft Kiln, p. 2). 2. Slake the lime fully and make it into mortar with the sand before adding stone; hot quicklime concrete "has grown into disrepute" (Gillmore, p. 230). 3. Use a bit more mortar than there are gaps in the stone (pail test above; p. 229). 4. Ram it in layers about 6 in thick until a thin film of water shows under the rammer (p. 231). 5. Keep it damp for weeks; don't load it early (rule of thumb). Lime-pozzolan concrete: the same steps with the lime-pozzolan or hydraulic-lime mortar from the first section. It's the only homemade kind that hardens in wet ground. Before trusting a footing to it, cure a few test blocks damp for a month and break them beside a store-cement block (rule of thumb). Save store cement for what only cement does: wells and cisterns, toilet slabs, footings in wet ground, and repairs (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Gillmore, ch. 7, pp. 229–262 — concrete with lime and cement. Pictures: Roman concrete.
