🌾 Rushlights: Gilbert White's measured method A rushlight is the white pith of a rush, held up by one strip of its skin, dipped in fat and burned like a thin candle (Rushlight). Gilbert White weighed, counted and timed them in Letter 26 of The Natural History of Selborne (1775). He used "the common soft rush", found "in most moist pastures, by the sides of streams, and under hedges", best "in the height of summer", and "the largest and longest are best" (White, p. 205). Soft rush (Juncus effusus) grows in wet pastures and ditches around the valley (rule of thumb). Making them (White, p. 206): 1. Cut the longest rushes and put them in water at once, "for otherwise they will dry and shrink, and the peel will not run". 2. Peel off the green skin, leaving "one regular, narrow, even rib from top to bottom" to hold up the pith. 3. Bleach and dry: lay them on the grass to "take the dew for some nights", then dry them in the sun. 4. Dip them in "scalding" fat (a knack learned by practice): bacon-pot skimmings, salt settled out in a warm oven. "A little wax" makes them cleaner and burn longer; "mutton-suet would have the same effect". White's numbers: "about six pounds of grease will dip a pound of rushes" (p. 206). A pound of dry rushes held
rushlights-gilbert-white-s-measured-method

and burn longer; "mutton-suet would have the same effect". White's numbers: "about six pounds of grease will dip a pound of rushes" (p. 206). A pound of dry rushes held "upwards of one thousand six hundred" (p. 207). A rush 2 ft 4½ in long burned "three minutes short of an hour", a longer one an hour and a quarter (p. 206), with "a good clear light" (p. 207). "One pound and a-half of rushes completely supplies his family the year round", since working people went to bed by daylight in summer (p. 207). (Arithmetic:) that is about 2,400 rushlights and 9 lb of grease a year; at White's cautious half hour each, 1,200 hours, over 3 hours a night on average. Burning them (rule of thumb): hold the rush slanting in a clip or split stick on a heavy base, over a tin or a dish of sand to catch drips; move it up as it burns; never leave one alight in an empty room. Leave two ribs of skin on and it burns slower and dimmer, like the old "watch-lights" (White, p. 207): a night light.
rushlights-gilbert-white-s-measured-method

🫒 Lamp oils: what burns and what doesn't Good: kitchen fats, "lard, bacon grease, vegetable shortening, or vegetable oil" (ORNL-4941, p. 44), and non-drying oils like olive oil, which "become rancid and thicken ... but do not dry up" (HD p. 366). HD names lard oil, neat's-foot oil (boiled from cattle feet), olive, colza and rape-seed oil together (p. 367). Animal and fish oils are "very similar to the nondrying vegetable oils", though fish oil can smell "very offensive" (pp. 366–367); Northwest peoples burned the eulachon, or candlefish, for light (Shifts, p. 94). Hard fats like tallow need a soft-fat lamp whose flame warms the dish (below). Not good: drying oils like linseed (flax) "oxidize ... into a hard, resinous varnish" (HD p. 366): expect a gummed, crusted wick. The book doesn't test this in a lamp; it follows from the varnish (rule of thumb). The catch with vegetable oil: it is safe, "but their disadvantage is that they do not rise in the wick-carrier" (WHO, p. 106). So keep the wick short, the flame just above the oil (ORNL-4941, p. 309), or float it. As the oil drops, top it up or lower the wick holder (rule of thumb). Clarifying and storing: let oil settle a few days and pour off the top; to dry it, boil gently, stand, filter through cloth and heat briefly to 100 °C (212
lamp-oils-what-burns-and-what-doesn-t

Clarifying and storing: let oil settle a few days and pour off the top; to dry it, boil gently, stand, filter through cloth and heat briefly to 100 °C (212 °F) (Oil Extraction, pp. 5–6). Wet oil sputters (rule of thumb). For rancid or smelly animal oil, filter it through a burlap bag lined with flannel with charcoal quilted between, or stir clean charcoal lumps into it over a slow fire and strain (HD p. 367). Store it "in lightproof, airtight and moisture-proof containers in a cool place", never copper (Oil Extraction, p. 6), and don't leave lamps filled for months (Kearny, p. 104). Burn the old oil, eat the fresh (rule of thumb). Pressing oil: rape seed is 40–45% oil, mustard 25–45%, sunflower and sesame 25–50%, safflower 30% (Oil Extraction, p. 1). Dry and clean the seed, throw out mouldy ones, dehull sunflower (p. 1); soft seeds and nuts can be hand-pressed, hard ones need a ram press (p. 2). A cage press (a perforated metal cage under a plunger) can be driven by a screw or a car jack: raise the pressure slowly, and beware a leaking hydraulic jack's "poisonous hydraulic fluid" (p. 3). Nut meats: boil, add salt, skim (p. 2). Every pint burned is a pint not eaten: press for food first (rule of thumb).

Never gasoline or mixed fuels in an open lamp - The jar lamps are safe only with kitchen fats: "DO NOT USE KEROSENE, DIESEL FUEL, OR GASOLINE — USE ONLY FATS OR OILS OF THE KINDS FOUND IN THE KITCHEN" (ORNL-4941, p. 309). Knocked onto dry paper, the flame goes out by itself when the fuel is "a cooking oil or fat" and the wick is small (Kearny, p. 104). - Good kerosene gives off no burnable vapour below 110 °F (HD p. 91). Gasoline does even in freezing weather, so a little of it makes kerosene far more dangerous, and fuel mixed into cooking oil spills and burns like fuel (rule of thumb). Never use a can that ever held gasoline (WHO, p. 106). - Test doubtful kerosene outdoors (HD p. 92): a tablespoon of it on a cup of water heated to 110 °F, and a lit match. "If the oil takes fire it is unsafe."
never-gasoline-or-mixed-fuels-in-an-open-lamp

🪔 Lamps you can make Fuel use: with the smallest practical wick, about 1 oz of oil or fat in 8 hours (Kearny, p. 104), or "about 3 ounces ... in 24 hr" (ORNL-4941, p. 308). 1 lb of fat lasts about 128 hours, five days and nights (arithmetic). Wicks: cotton string, cloth or rag; in the bush, plant fibres, beaten bark or peeled rush (Shifts, p. 91). Flat kerosene wicks: "Save old felt hats", or hem a strip of cotton stocking or flannel about three times the burner's width (HD pp. 139–140).
lamps-you-can-make

Wire-stiffened jar lamp From Oak Ridge's tested drawing (🖼️ ORNL-4941, p. 309): 1. Base: two bent nails, about ½ in shorter than the jar is wide, tied one across the other so it won't rock. 2. Wick: cotton string "slightly less than ⅛-in. in diameter". Tie a fine wire (window-screen wire) round the nails at its middle, and wind its ends in opposite directions up the string so it stands stiff. 3. Oil: fill the jar no more than half full of cooking oil or fat, with the "flame from end of wick ... just above oil surface". 4. Reflector: foil ⅔ of the way around the jar and under its bottom. Hang it on light wire by a loop "large enough for finger". 5. Light it with a match tied to a stick. To put it out, drip oil on the wick. Keep spare wire and string.
wire-stiffened-jar-lamp

Floating-wick lamp From the drawing (🖼️ ORNL-4941, p. 310): 1. A block of soft pine ½ in narrower than the inside of the jar (2½ in for a 3-in jar), about ¾ in high. 2. A V-notch across the top: 5 even saw cuts, then whittle it out, leaving about 3/16 in under it. Bore a snug wick hole through the bottom of the notch with a knife point, from both sides. 3. A wick 1/16–3/32 in thick (thin cotton string or twisted threads). Float it on oil in a half-full jar with the same reflector. When not in use for days, take the wood out of the oil. Shifts floats a wick on "bottle wire and three bits of cork": "half an inch of wick is enough to last all night"; but rats can upset a lamp and carry off the burning wick (p. 93).
floating-wick-lamp

Hunter's lamp and soft-fat lamps - Hunter's lamp (slut lamp; Seton's names are "slot-lamp, grease-jet, hunter's lamp"): cotton cloth or twisted rag in a clam shell of oil or melted grease. Better, push the wick through a hole in a thin, flat stone in the grease to hold it up; better still, use a tin for "a steadier lamp, as well as a much larger light" (Seton, p. 239). - Soft fat (too stiff to climb a wick, too soft to mould): lay the wick so it rests on and overhangs the edge of the dish; "the flame soon heats the side sufficiently to melt a portion of the fat" (Shifts, p. 91). - Open flames: stand them in a tin tray on something that can't burn, away from drafts and children (rule of thumb).
hunters-lamp-and-soft-fat-lamps

Can lanterns and candle holders - Tomato-can lantern: a big hole in the bottom for the candle, the sides punched full of small holes from inside; it "will not go out in the wind" (Seton, p. 239). A candle pushed up through a hole in the side of a can makes "a boxed light, shining ahead like a searchlight" (Seton, p. 240). - Jar lantern: "a candle, a glass jar, and light wire to hang the lantern" (FEMA H-4, p. 76). To carry a candle, stick a short one in a tumbler with its own drips (HD p. 99). A tin candlestick's socket seam must be folded, not just soldered, or it will "melt apart" (Thatcher, p. 117).
can-lanterns-and-candle-holders

🛢️ Kerosene lamps while the kerosene lasts Storage and heaters: "Kerosene and propane" in the Fuel guide. Keep it in a metal can marked KEROSENE, not red, never an old gasoline can, outside the house away from where children play (MSU E-1669, p. 4). Good kerosene is "clear and nearly colorless, like water" (HD p. 92). 1. Each morning, by daylight: clean, fill, trim (HD p. 138). Never fill a lamp while it is burning (p. 93) or hot. Fill to within about ½ in of the top, since "the oil expands with heat and runs over"; wipe it dry (p. 139; p. 92). 2. Trim by rubbing the char off with a finger or burnt match: "Don't cut it; you can't cut it even" (p. 92). The wick must reach the bottom (p. 138); renew it "every month or two, no matter how fresh it looks" (p. 92). 3. Keep the burner's air holes clear; once a month, boil the burner in washing soda or lye water (p. 92). 4. Light it low and turn it up slowly; if steam fogs a cold chimney, keep it low till that clears (p. 139). Too high or too low, it smokes; set the screw back a touch so the wick won't creep up (p. 94). 5. Turn it low before blowing it out and when carrying it. Use lamps with "a
kerosene-lamps-while-the-kerosene-lasts

set the screw back a touch so the wick won't creep up (p. 94). 5. Turn it low before blowing it out and when carrying it. Use lamps with "a broad, solid base", and don't light one that has stood part-empty a long time (p. 93). Chimneys and spares: the right chimney gives "perhaps twice as much" light; a cold draft or the flame touching a hot chimney cracks it (p. 93). Toughen new ones by boiling 10–15 minutes in strong salt water, wrapped in cheesecloth, and cooling them in the water (p. 139). Keep "two or three extra chimneys and burners, and a yard or two of wicking", with lamps all alike so parts swap (p. 138). For a night light, don't turn a lamp low (it throws off unburned carbon); use a small lamp turned up (p. 94). Kerosene-soaked rags in a heap can catch fire on their own (p. 138). Pressure lanterns are brighter but "noisy", "hot" and "troublesome to start" (Rural Lighting, pp. 3–4), and burn about 5 litres a week at six hours a night (pp. 6–7). No kerosene lamps in a small closed room: "They produce gases that can cause headaches or even death" (Kearny, p. 104).
kerosene-lamps-while-the-kerosene-lasts

🔆 Getting more light from a little flame - Reflect it: "Use reflective material such as aluminum foil, mirrors, or white boards to concentrate a weak light where it is needed" (Kearny, p. 104). With foil on three sides and the bottom of a jar lamp hung between you and your book, a flame "smaller than that of a birthday candle" is enough to read by (same page). - A reflector stand: a tin sheet nearly 2 ft tall bent into a half cylinder 6–8 in across, with a shelf for the lamp and two small mirrors angled behind, let Shifts' author "write or sketch with facility during many hours of the weary night" (pp. 92–93). A mirror also throws light "down a well or other deep, dark recess" (HD p. 96). - Light, clean walls: "dirt absorbs and masks light", and washing gets back 5–10% more light than dry wiping (TM 5-683, p. 131). Ceilings should be the lightest, off-white, not shiny; dirt can halve the light in a year (Navy CE, p. 181). Wash lamp soot off walls, chimneys and reflectors (rule of thumb); a clean, right-sized chimney can double a kerosene lamp's light (HD p. 93). - Task lighting: one small light close to the work and everyone at one table, not a lit room (rule of thumb). For light to work by, build the fire up

Task lighting: one small light close to the work and everyone at one table, not a lit room (rule of thumb). For light to work by, build the fire up on a base 18 in to 2 ft high (Shifts, p. 92). - Pine knots and fatwood: "a roll of birch bark, a pine knot, or some pine-root slivers, in a split stick of green wood" (Seton, p. 239); resinous splints burn in a rest, nearly upright if very resinous (Shifts, pp. 93–94). Finding fatwood: "Fire and light without stores" in the Make-Do guide. It's smoky: fireplace or outdoors only, and no torches outdoors in fire season (June–October) (rule of thumb).

🧯 Fire, fumes, burns and children Putting out a fire: - Burning wax or fat in the pot: heat off, then a metal lid or damp cloth. "On no account try to extinguish burning wax with water as it will intensify the fire" (Practical Action, p. 3). - A burning lamp: wrap it tightly in "a heavy woolen rug" to smother it. Burning oil on the floor: sand or earth, never water, "as it will only spread it". Clothes on fire: don't let the person run; wrap them in wool (HD p. 95). - Don't throw a burning lamp out of the window, though that page says to: you'd carry an open fire across the room, spill burning oil on yourself and the floor, and the window may be shut. Smother it where it stands (rule of thumb). - Keep a bucket of sand or earth by the lamps and the candle pot (FEMA H-4, p. 76). Where lamps go: a safe lamp is "short and heavy", with "two flat sides" so it won't roll, a screw-on metal lid and thick glass, and never at a table's edge; light bottle lamps "could easily topple, igniting the clothes of a child" (WHO, p. 106). "Keep lamps and matches out of reach of children" (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 22). Hanging lamps: the books disagree. FEMA says hanging helps "prevent lamps
fire-fumes-burns-and-children

(WHO, p. 106). "Keep lamps and matches out of reach of children" (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 22). Hanging lamps: the books disagree. FEMA says hanging helps "prevent lamps from being knocked over" (H-4, p. 76); WHO says "not to hang the lamps on walls" (p. 106), where a lamp on a nail sits by a sleeping child; a barn lantern on a pulley stays above the hay forks (Handy Farm Devices, p. 115). Our rule: hang lamps from an overhead wire, away from walls, curtains, shelves and beds, above head height, with nothing that burns above them or within their swing; an earthquake will set them swinging (rule of thumb). Children and kerosene: fuel and lamp oils are the commonest child poisons in poorer countries, kerosene alone up to 16% of cases, mostly children 1 to 3 years old (WHO, p. 145). Child-resistant caps are "the only proven intervention"; use dark containers, as kerosene "may be easily mistaken for water" (p. 152), and dyeing it blue cut poisonings in Australia (p. 153). "Never keep kerosene, gasoline, or other poisons in cola or soft drink bottles" (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 29). If swallowed: do not make them vomit (same page), and no activated charcoal (Book for Midwives, p. 12); see the Field Care guide. Carbon monoxide and soot: - "Any time you have an open flame, it
fire-fumes-burns-and-children

vomit (same page), and no activated charcoal (Book for Midwives, p. 12); see the Field Care guide. Carbon monoxide and soot: - "Any time you have an open flame, it may generate carbon monoxide"; it has no colour or smell, usually no symptoms, and "unconsciousness and death can occur without warning". Never fall asleep with a lamp burning (FM 21-76, p. 182; Carbon monoxide poisoning). - Signs: headache, dizziness, confusion, yawning, weariness, nausea, ringing ears, sudden collapse. Get the person into open air; keep them still and warm (TC 21-3, p. 40). - Put flames near where air leaves the room, and put them all out if it must be shut up (Kearny, p. 104). - Soot: a lamp turned too high or too low smokes, and soot in the lungs is "exceedingly harmful" (HD p. 94); all lamps and candles "contribute to indoor air pollution" (Rural Lighting, p. 4). Burns from hot wax and fat: keep children away from the candle pot and turn pot handles in. Put a burn in clean, cool water (not ice) right away, for no longer than 20 minutes; "Never put ice, grease, fat ... on a burn" (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 22). Leave cooled wax stuck to the skin; it comes off as the burn heals (rule of thumb). Big or deep burns: "Burns" in the Field Care guide. After a

⛽ Fuel Guide How long gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane keep, how to tell when fuel has gone bad, what can be rescued, how to store fuel for the long haul — and how to get fuel out of gas-station underground tanks, drums and vehicles when there's no grid power. The manuals are in Fuel\ (Fuel-Quality-Storage, Station-Tanks-Pumping, Military-Fuel-Handling, Other-Fuels). Wood gas, biodiesel and alcohol fuel are in Homestead-Skills\Fuels. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent fires and deaths - Gasoline vapor explodes. No flames, smoking or sparks within 50 feet of open fuel. Use only pumps made for gasoline — ordinary electric motors spark. (FM 10-67-1, p. 21) - Static sparks ignite fuel. Touch bare metal with your bare hand before opening any cap. Keep the nozzle touching the can or tank the whole time you pour. Fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed or on carpet (rule of thumb). (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–23) - Never climb into a tank sump, manway or tank. Fuel vapor pushes out oxygen and can kill without any smell or warning; the lids are heavy. Work from ground level. 🔍 Is this fuel still good? - Jar test: pour a sample from the bottom of the can or tank into a clean clear jar. Good fuel is clear and bright. Let it stand 15 minutes. Haze, droplets or a second layer at the bottom = water. Water fully settles out in about a day. (FM 10-67-2, p. 36; p. 97; 🖼️ Army samplers that reach the bottom) - Bad signs: darker color, a sour or varnish smell, or a drop on glass that leaves a sticky film when it dries (gum). Gum sticks valves and clogs carburetors. - E10 with a bottom layer has phase-separated (E10 blends): the bottom is ethanol plus water, not just water. E10 at 60 °F holds only about 4 teaspoons of water per gallon (3.8, to be exact) before this happens — less in the cold. Humid air rarely causes it; rain and water sitting in tanks do. (EPA phase-separation memo, p. 2; pp. 4–5) What the jar tells you: | You see | It means | Do this | | Clear and bright | Good fuel | Use it | | Haze or tiny droplets | Water mixed in | Let it settle a day, take fuel off the top, filter | | A separate bottom layer | Free water — or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see

🔧 Rescuing old fuel (FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing, p. 97) - Water and dirt can be fixed: let the fuel settle a few hours to a day, then pour or siphon off the top (Siphon), leaving the bottom inch behind, and filter it. The Army lets gasoline and diesel settle at least 2 hours after a tank is filled; water drops out in about 24 hours. - Phase-separated E10: the layers won't remix. Drain off and discard the bottom layer. The top is weaker (lower-octane) gasoline — fine for lawn, farm and older carbureted engines. - Stale but clean gasoline: blend it with fresh. The Army mixes a small test batch ("pilot blend") first and tests it. In its worked example, gummy old gasoline needed about 6 parts fresh to 1 part old to come back within limits. (FM 10-67-2, p. 98; 🖼️ blending-ratio graph) Rule of thumb: 1 part old to 4 or more parts fresh for mildly stale gas, and use it in simple engines (generators, mowers, older trucks) — not modern high-compression or turbo engines. The staler it is, the more fresh fuel it needs. Blending can't save fuel that's bad in many ways at once. (FM 10-67-2, p. 97) - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. 🛢️ Diesel care - Water is the enemy. Drain water from the bottom of tanks and drums regularly, and check for it every time you gauge — the Army checks with water-finding paste every time and drains water the day after new fuel comes in, before it rises high enough to be drawn into the outlet. Keep drum bungs tight and covered so rain can't seep in. (FM 10-67-1, p. 141; 🖼️ gauging the water in a tank) - "Diesel bug": yeast, fungus and bacteria grow where fuel meets water — brown, black or gray slime that clogs filters and eats tanks. A puddle of water in the tank bottom is enough to feed big colonies, and it's worst in hot, humid weather. Prevent with zero water and a biocide; badly slimed tanks must be drained and scrubbed. Tanks left unused for a long time collect water at low points. (DoD UFM 3-460-03, pp. 29–30) - Expect old station diesel tanks to be corroded inside. EPA found moderate or severe corrosion in 83% of the diesel tanks it inspected, and ethanol had crept into 90% of the diesel samples. (EPA Corrosion in USTs with Diesel, p. 8; p. 10; 🖼️ photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every
diesel-care

photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every day (a heater or tractor) so the fuel turns over. Keep spare filters. (FEMA P-1019, p. 91) - Cold gelling: thin diesel with No. 1 diesel or kerosene (the Army blends kerosene in for winter — FM 10-67-2, p. 98) or add a cold-flow additive — before it gets cold; additives won't un-gel it. Additives don't change the temperature at which wax first clouds the fuel; they only help it keep flowing through filters a few degrees colder. (NREL Biodiesel Handling Guide, p. 29) "Summer" diesel bought in July can gel on a frosty valley morning — buy diesel in the season you'll burn it. (Alberta, p. 12) - Substitutes: diesel engines can run on No. 2 heating oil, which is nearly the same fuel (FEMA P-1019, pp. 91, 106). Kerosene and Jet A are close to No. 1 diesel. Kerosene is "dry" (low lubricity) and harder on modern injection pumps; older mechanical-pump diesels tolerate substitutes best. (Rule of thumb) Pictures: Diesel fuel, Heating oil, Cloud point (the temperature where wax first clouds the fuel), Jet fuel. 📚 Go deeper: DoD UFM 3-460-03 Petroleum Fuel Systems Maintenance — water, microbes and tank cleaning; EPA Corrosion in Diesel USTs — what's

🏪 Getting fuel out of gas-station tanks Why this matters here: a 2016 emergency exercise in Portland on a Cascadia earthquake found it would have catastrophic impacts on Oregon's petroleum infrastructure and make resupply very hard. Once delivery trucks stop, the fuel already in local station tanks may be all there is. (NASEO Petroleum Shortage Planning, pp. 7–8) What's under the concrete (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets; North Dakota training; cutaway drawings: 🖼️ station tank, pump and piping, 🖼️ diesel tank equipment): - Each tank is usually 8,000–20,000 gallons, about 8–10 ft across, with its bottom roughly 10–14 ft below the pavement. (Rule of thumb) - Fill pipes sit inside small round spill buckets (5–25 gallons, lids 1–2 ft) (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 7; 🖼️ photo of the lids; 🖼️ spill-bucket photo). The cap colors usually tell you the fuel: white = regular, blue = mid-grade, red = premium, yellow = diesel; orange marks vapor-recovery pipes, not fuel. (Rule of thumb — check by gauging.) - A large manhole (3–4 ft lid) right over each tank covers the turbine-pump sump — the pump, piping and leak sensor (🖼️ sump photos). Other small risers are the tank gauge, spare ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy — get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below.

ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy — get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below. Expect fuel vapor when you open them. (EPA, pp. 5, 8) - Bail out the spill bucket first. Rain and snowmelt fill them; if you open the fill cap under water, the water runs into the fuel. Wipe it and do it twice. (EPA, p. 8) - Water-finding paste on the tip changes color where there's water in the bottom; fuel-finding paste smeared where you expect the fuel line makes the reading sharper. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to gallons. (EPA, pp. 6–7) Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. A

(EPA, pp. 6–7) Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. A check valve just under that pump keeps the line full ("primed") between uses. (Vermont, p. 3; 🖼️ suction-system diagram) - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in the sump, usually 240-volt, ¾–2 hp (rule of thumb), plus the dispenser's electronics. That takes a stout generator. Connect only through the station's transfer switch — never by backfeeding. (🖼️ transfer-switch diagram; Transfer switch) Several states have paid to prewire stations with generator hookups or "quick connects" (Florida required some by law in 2006). (NASEO, pp. 71–73; Florida SB 528 analysis) If the owner is around, work with them: they know their tanks and may already have a generator hookup. Step 3 — no power: pump it up by hand. - A siphon won't work — the fuel is below you, and a siphon only flows downhill. - Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut when the tank is about 95% full). The drop tube ends close to the tank bottom — within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the

tank bottom — within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the separate gauge port is another way in. (Vermont, p. 5; EPA Inventory Control, p. 7; 🖼️ drop-tube valve photos) - Suction lift is the limit. Air pressure can push water up at most about 33 feet in a perfect vacuum at sea level, and real pumps do far worse; gasoline's own vapor pressure cuts the lift further, especially when it's hot. (FM 10-67-1, pp. 485, 487) Hand and 12-volt suction pumps typically lift gasoline 10 feet or less (less in hot weather — gasoline boils in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or low tank, use a pump that goes down into the tank — a 12-volt submersible fuel-transfer pump rated for gasoline on a long hose — or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. (Submersible pump, Hand pump) - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge, pump into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel. Bonding and grounding, the Army way (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–22; drawings: 🖼️ bond wire and ground wire, 🖼️ grounding a tank truck, 🖼️ bonding a farm tank; Static electricity, Ground)): - Bond = connect the two metal things (nozzle to can, pump to tank) so no spark can jump between them. 🚗 Drums and vehicles - Drums: a rotary or lever drum hand pump threads into the 2-inch bung; the Army's have a bonding wire and a strainer. Keep the drum grounded, and cover the pump's suction pipe when it's not in use. (FM 10-67-1, p. 353; 🖼️ drum pumps in a 55-gallon drum) - Open bungs slowly on a drum that's sat in the sun or been bumped around — pressure can spray out fuel and vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14; 🖼️ drum bungs and chimes) - Cars and trucks: most modern fillers have an anti-siphon screen or rollover valve, so a hose won't reach the fuel. It's usually easier to disconnect the fuel line at the engine and let the car's own fuel pump push fuel into a can (key on, or power the pump relay) — or drain from the fuel-filter or tank fittings underneath. Older vehicles and many diesel trucks have no screen. (Rule of thumb) - Gas in old vehicles goes stale too — jar-test it before trusting it. Drum pump. 🔥 Kerosene and propane Kerosene heaters (CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety, pp. 1–2): - Only water-clear 1-K kerosene (Kerosene), never gasoline (even a little is dangerous). Store it in blue cans that have never held gasoline, away from other fuel cans. - Refuel outdoors with the heater off and cool, and don't fill above the "full" mark — that space lets the fuel expand. - Keep it at least 3 feet from furniture and clothes. - Unvented heaters make carbon monoxide: run it with the room's door open to the rest of the house, and crack a window about an inch if the door must be closed or the house is tight. - Keep the wick clean and set at the right height. - If it flares up, don't carry it and don't throw water on it. Use its shut-off switch; if that fails, get everyone out. Propane (Texas RRC Propane Safety Tips; Propane, Gas cylinder): - Store cylinders outdoors and upright, never in a closed building; vapor is heavier than air and pools low. (p. 4) - Never put your head over a tank's valves — the relief valve can pop. Liquid propane causes frostbite on skin and eyes. (p. 4) - Keep big tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance.

🌲 When the stored fuel runs out These are big projects — read the books before you build anything. - Wood gas: in World War II, cars, trucks and stationary engines in Europe ran on gas made by burning wood in a sealed canister. FEMA's plans fit 4-stroke gasoline engines of 10–150 hp; a diesel can run mostly on wood gas with a little diesel to light it. ⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 590; how it works: 🖼️ the four strokes drawn, Four-stroke engine, Two-stroke engine) 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2–3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it — water or gum?), fuel filter and line. (MAVCC, pp. 595–598; 🖼️ drawings) 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. (MAVCC, pp. 599–600; 🖼️ spark-tester drawing) 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression — a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. With a compression gauge, crank at least six times before you read it. 🚜 Diesel engines Diesels have no spark plugs — squeezing the air makes it hot enough to light the fuel. So a diesel needs compression and clean fuel with no air in the lines. (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 5; 🖼️ gasoline and diesel strokes side by side; Diesel engine) Diesels usually need less maintenance than gasoline engines because they have no ignition system. (FM 5-424, p. 114) Won't start or keeps dying: suspect air in the fuel lines (an "air lock"), an empty tank or a clogged filter. (Practical Action, p. 12) Bleed the air out (p. 16): 1. Fill the tank with clean diesel and open the tank valve. 2. Loosen the bleed screw on the fuel filter (and on the injection pump) until fuel runs out in a steady stream with no bubbles. Tighten it. 3. Loosen the injection line nut at the injector and crank the engine until fuel comes out without foam. 4. Tighten the nut and check every joint for leaks. What the smoke and symptoms tell you (Practical Action, pp. 11–14): | Symptom | Common causes | | Lots of black smoke | Faulty injector (p. 14) | | Overheating | Low coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank
diesel-engines

coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank or lines, clogged air cleaner, wrong valve timing, overload, lots of stopping and starting, idling when not needed | | Burns oil | Worn or wrongly fitted piston rings, worn cylinder, damaged seals or head gasket | | Knocking or noise | Poor-quality fuel, loose connecting rod, worn or badly adjusted parts | Cleaning an injector nozzle: soak the nozzle valve and body in clean diesel, scrub the soot off with a copper (not steel) wire brush, and check the needle slides freely. (Practical Action, p. 15; 🖼️ injector valve, taken apart; 🖼️ cleaning the spray holes; Fuel injection) Don't run a diesel generator lightly loaded for long. It runs too cool, soot builds up in the engine and exhaust ("wet stacking"), and over time this can permanently damage it. (FEMA P-1019, p. 150) Give it a real load when you run it. Diesel fuel catches fire less easily than gasoline, but once burning a diesel fire is fierce (Practical Action, p. 6). 🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust — and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course, p. 25) - The four chain rules: sharp, depth gauges set right, correctly tensioned (more bar and chain trouble comes from wrong tension than anything else), and well oiled. The chain should not hang below the bar but should still turn freely by hand. (USFS, p. 31; 🖼️ parts of the chain; 🖼️ right and wrong tension; Saw chain) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. If the chrome is chipped, file until the chip is gone. (USFS, pp. 33–34; 🖼️ filing angles; 🖼️ file height and direction) - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. Never file one lower than the tool. (USFS, p. 34; 🖼️ what the depth gauge does; 🖼️ gauge tool and rounding off) - After several hand filings, the angles

🔋 Generators Where to put it (CPSC, p. 1): - Outdoors, far from doors, windows and vents, exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put a battery-powered CO alarm in the house. (Engine-generator, Carbon monoxide poisoning) - In rain, run it under an open, canopy-like roof on dry ground where water can't puddle under it. Dry your hands before touching it. - Use heavy outdoor extension cords rated for more than the total watts on them, with all three prongs and no cuts. Don't pinch them in doors or windows. - Turn it off and let it cool before refueling. Keep its fuel outside living areas. - Set it nearly level — the Army 3 kW set allows no more than 15° of tilt — on planks or timbers if the ground is soft. (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) Maintenance (rule of thumb — the generator's own manual comes first): oil change every 50–100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20–30 minutes once a month. Machines that sit idle for long periods should be "exercised" on a schedule to keep oil moving and moisture out. (TM 5-683, p. 41) Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second — rule of thumb).

⚙️ Electric motors: testing and repair When a motor won't run, check the simple things first, in this order (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, pp. 24–25; know the parts first: 🖼️ cutaway of an induction motor, 🖼️ main parts laid out, Induction motor): 1. Power: is the right voltage reaching the motor terminals? Check fuses, breakers and the switch. 2. Load: take the belt off. If the motor now runs, the machine it drives is stuck. 3. Bearings: power off, turn the shaft by hand. If it won't turn freely, a bearing is dry, worn or stuck. 4. Thermal protector: many motors have a red reset button; others reset themselves once cool. A tripped protector means something else is wrong — find it. 5. Starting switch: a motor that hums but won't start, yet runs if you spin the shaft by hand, has a fault in its starting circuit (see below). 6. Windings: a burned winding has a strong burned smell, and you may see charred insulation. Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed (Illinois, p. 28; 🖼️ capacitor-start motor; 🖼️ the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged

motor; 🖼️ the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure. Replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage (rule of thumb). Switch contacts can be dirty, burned or pitted, or a wire can burn in two. (Illinois, p. 24) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance; a high reading between any two leads means an open winding. (Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 237) - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. Write readings down — a steady fall over months warns of trouble even above the minimum. (TM 5-683, p. 54) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). 🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14–15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) (Brushed DC motor, Diode) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need high speed (rule of thumb: about 1,500+ rpm — step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field — they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 11; 🖼️ how an alternator makes current; 🖼️ testing the rotor) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it about 1–5% faster than its synchronous speed — e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1820–1890 rpm. Output rises with the extra speed. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 54) On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. 🛠️ Reusing a generator for water or wind power When the gasoline and diesel are gone, a portable generator still holds two valuable machines: an engine and a generator head (the part that makes electricity). There are two ways to keep using them. 1. Keep the whole set and change the fuel. FEMA's wood-gas plans say stationary engines on wood gas "run electric generators, pumps, and industrial equipment" (FEMA Wood Gas Generator, p. 19). A generator sits still, so it needs a gas cooler and a second filter that a moving vehicle wouldn't, and hot gas costs power: about 1% for every 10 °F above 70 °F (p. 28). Most portable generators have engines of 15 hp or less; for those FEMA says to use a 6-inch fire tube with a narrowed throat (p. 67). The rest (building it, and the carbon monoxide danger) is in the Fuel guide. 2. Take the generator head off and turn it with water or wind. The rest of this section is about that.
reusing-a-generator-for-water-or-wind-power

What's inside: two kinds of portable generator Standard generators (the open-frame kind) have a generator head bolted to the engine: - A spinning rotor makes the magnetic field and a still stator around it makes the power, so the output comes straight off the stator wires (NEETS 5, pp. 64–66; 🖼️ rotating-field alternator with exciter). - The rotor's field is fed through brushes and slip rings, or with no brushes at all: a small exciter and diodes spinning on the shaft feed it (ESHA Small Hydro Pt 2, p. 31; 🖼️ brushless alternator). The Army's 3 kW set is the brushless kind; its book gives the normal winding resistances (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 26). - A voltage regulator (AVR) holds the voltage steady by changing the field's strength, because the speed has to stay fixed for the frequency (NEETS 5, p. 78). Many cheap heads instead use a capacitor on an extra winding to make their field (rule of thumb). - Speed sets the frequency: a 2-pole head must turn 3,600 rpm for 60 Hz, a 4-pole head 1,800 rpm (NEETS 5, p. 76; 🖼️ 2-pole vs 8-pole). Almost all portable sets are 2-pole, 3,600 rpm (rule of thumb). - Most heads have only one bearing. The other end of the rotor is bolted onto the engine's crankshaft, so a head taken off the engine needs a new shaft end and
whats-inside-two-kinds-of-portable-generator

heads have only one bearing. The other end of the rotor is bolted onto the engine's crankshaft, so a head taken off the engine needs a new shaft end and bearing before a belt can drive it (rule of thumb; the hydro handbook notes horizontal generators "usually have a single bearing", DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 57). Inverter generators (the quiet, closed-case kind). There is no manual for one in the library; this is how they are generally built (rule of thumb): - The engine's flywheel is the rotor: a ring of magnets spinning around a stator with many poles. It makes three-phase AC whose voltage and frequency both rise with speed, and there may be several separate sets of windings (for the inverter's own power, for battery charging). - A rectifier turns that into DC, and the inverter board turns the DC into steady 120-volt, 60 Hz power. The board usually also works the throttle and needs signals from the engine, so it rarely works without its engine. - The magnet-and-stator part is the same family as the flywheel alternator on small engines (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 370; 🖼️ flywheel alternator parts), and it behaves like any permanent-magnet alternator: voltage rises in step with speed (Piggott Axial Flux Alternator, p. 15).
whats-inside-two-kinds-of-portable-generator

Which parts are worth saving | Part | Best use | Watch out for | | Magnet alternator (from an inverter generator) | Charging batteries from a slow water wheel or wind rotor: rectify it to DC, then a diversion controller | Test it first (below). Keep its magnets away from iron and don't drop it | | Wound-field generator head (standard generator) | A fast turbine, like a Pelton wheel on a good drop, belted up to its speed | Wants 3,600 rpm; voltage holds but frequency swings with the load | | Engine | Wood gas (above), or turning a pump, mill or saw directly | Same care as any engine (top of this guide) | | Voltage regulator, capacitors | Stay with the generator head | Discharge capacitors before touching | | Inverter board | Rarely reusable without its engine; keep for parts | Can hold a deadly charge | | Bearings, pulleys, frame, outlets, breaker, wire | Your hydro or wind build | Check bearings (below) |

Taking it apart safely 1. Drain the fuel, unplug the spark plug wire, and work outdoors or with the doors open (rule of thumb). 2. Discharge every capacitor (inverter board, voltage regulator, capacitor-excited heads): the charge left in capacitors "is, in many cases, sufficient to cause a lethal shock." Use a shorting probe with its ground clip on first, touch each terminal several times, and keep your hands off the metal (NEETS 21, pp. 32–33; 🖼️ shorting probe). Short a stored capacitor's terminals with a wire; "CHARGED CAPACITORS CAN KILL" (p. 34). 3. Photograph and tag every wire, and punch-mark the frame and end bells so they go back the same way (Navy Construction Electrician, p. 255; 🖼️ punch marks). 4. Turn the shaft by hand before opening anything: binding means a bent shaft, bad bearings or debris (same page). 5. Taking a magnet flywheel off: hold it with a holding tool (the nut's thread direction depends on which way the engine turns), then use a puller, not a hammer: "Too much hammering will jar the magnetism out" (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2, pp. 58–59; 🖼️ flywheel pullers). Don't drop it, store it away from iron, and pick metal chips off the magnets (p. 60; MAVCC, p. 374). 6. Pulling a rotor out of a stator: lift the brushes first, support the rotor only by its shaft, and slide thin
taking-it-apart-safely

off the magnets (p. 60; MAVCC, p. 374). 6. Pulling a rotor out of a stator: lift the brushes first, support the rotor only by its shaft, and slide thin cardboard into the gap to protect the windings (Navy Construction Electrician, p. 256; Kuphaldt Vol 6, p. 174). 7. Bearings: leave good ones on the shaft; pull with the puller on the inner race (see "Electric motors: testing and repair" above; Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 224).
taking-it-apart-safely

Testing what you salvaged - Spin it and measure. Turn the shaft with a drill, a lathe or a rope at a speed you can count, and read the AC volts across the output wires. On a magnet alternator the voltage goes up in proportion to speed, so one reading tells you what it makes at any rpm (Piggott, p. 36). - Speed from frequency: Hz = rpm × number of poles ÷ 120, so a multimeter that reads Hz is a tachometer (same page). - DC after the rectifier ≈ 1.4 × the AC reading, minus about 1.5 V (same page). To charge a 12 V battery you need about 14 V DC. - Short two output wires and turn it: a good one becomes stiff but smooth; "If it trembles as you turn it then there is a fault" (Piggott PMG Manual, p. 42). No meter? A 3-volt flashlight bulb across two wires will glow when you turn it (p. 40). - A wound-field head makes little or nothing until its field is fed: spin it with the field wires on a 6-volt battery (Kuphaldt Vol 6, pp. 174–175), or flash the field as described in "Motors as generators" above. - With an ohmmeter: slip ring to shaft should read open (otherwise the rotor is grounded); ring to ring should match the spec (open = broken winding, low
testing-what-you-salvaged

generators" above. - With an ohmmeter: slip ring to shaft should read open (otherwise the rotor is grounded); ring to ring should match the spec (open = broken winding, low = shorted); each diode reads low one way and high the other. Never test diodes with a 110-volt test lamp (Alternator Servicing, pp. 17–19). The Army's brushless set: flash the field; if the voltage holds under load the stator and rotor are good; if not, test the diodes on the exciter rotor (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 95). - Megger the windings to the frame (minimums under "Electric motors" above). A head rated for standby use "may not hold up under continuous operation at full load", so run it well below its rating (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 59).
testing-what-you-salvaged

Matching it to a water wheel or wind rotor - The 3,600-rpm head is the hard part. "The 2-pole generator with a speed of 3600 rpm is too high for practical use with a microhydropower system"; 1,800-rpm heads are the usual choice (NRCan Micro-Hydropower Systems, p. 24). - Water: a Pelton wheel turns fastest on a high drop. Its buckets work best at about half the speed of the jet (ESHA Pt 2, p. 20), so an 8-inch Pelton on 100 ft of drop turns about 1,060 rpm, and needs about 3.4 to 1 to drive a 3,600-rpm head (arithmetic). Many small turbines run under 400 rpm and need a speed increaser (p. 28). Water wheels are slower still (NRCan, p. 23). - Wind: an 8-ft rotor in a 7 mph wind turns about 167 rpm (Piggott, p. 9); a 3,600-rpm head would need about 22 to 1 (arithmetic), which isn't practical. "Almost every small wind generator on the market uses a directly driven permanent magnet generator" (DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems, p. 12): use the magnet alternator, or build Piggott's (above). - Belts: the speed ratio is generator rpm ÷ turbine rpm (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 81); pulley diameter × rpm is the same on both shafts (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, p. 17). V-belts are the best choice and slip instead of breaking things if the
matching-it-to-a-water-wheel-or-wind-rotor

diameter × rpm is the same on both shafts (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, p. 17). V-belts are the best choice and slip instead of breaking things if the turbine jams (DOE, p. 85). Don't go below the smallest pulley for the belt size, about 3 in for an A belt and 5.4 in for a B (p. 86; 🖼️ table). Size the belts for 1.4–1.5 times the turbine's power (p. 89), make the distance between shafts adjustable because belts stretch, and expect to lose 3–6%, up to 10% if loose (pp. 95–96). Don't mix old and new belts, and mark the generator and its base so it goes back in line (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M, pp. 19–20). - Mounting: a car wheel-bearing hub makes a good bearing for a homemade alternator (Piggott, p. 15; 🖼️ mounting it). Driving the shaft directly needs careful alignment and a coupling that flexes a little (Illinois, p. 17). - Runaway: with no load, a turbine and generator can reach two to three times normal speed (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 61), and a disconnected magnet alternator's voltage "may become dangerously high" (Piggott, p. 37). Always keep the dump load on (rules above).
matching-it-to-a-water-wheel-or-wind-rotor

Hooking it up - To charge batteries: a three-phase rectifier (six diodes, one pair per wire) turns the output into DC (Kuphaldt Vol 3, p. 122; 🖼️ three-phase bridge), then a diversion controller and the battery. For a long wire run, rectify to a high voltage and step it down at the battery (NCAT Micro-Hydro, p. 18). - For heat and lights only, use the AC as it comes: heating doesn't care about frequency (DOE Vol 1 Pt 1, p. 153); hot water is the best place for the spare power (see Storing Energy Without Batteries). - Not for motors or electronics unless something holds the frequency steady: "Fluctuating frequency will destroy small motors and solid state equipment" (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 56). - A three-phase head on one phase gives only about a third of its rating (same page). - What to expect: magnet generators are over 80% efficient (NRCan, p. 25); the whole system is the turbine × the belt × the generator (ESHA Pt 2, p. 26). The water sets the limit: watts ≈ gallons per minute × feet of drop ÷ 10 (see the creek hydro section of the Off-Grid Power guide), and Oregon's water law applies (above).

🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone — from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for at least 20 minutes (longer for an eye that still stings). Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide). - Never throw water on burning wax or fat — it spreads the fire. Cut the heat and smother it with a metal lid or damp cloth.

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing — it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (see the soap section below). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day — diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose — use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (p. 2). - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs. - Wash hands with soap (🖼️ how-to drawing; Hand washing) before handling food or eating, after the toilet, after cleaning up a child or caring for a sick person, and after touching animals or garbage. Hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol) only works on hands that aren't visibly dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies — chlorine, latrines and hygiene after

on hands that aren't visibly dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies — chlorine, latrines and hygiene after disasters; Army FM 21-10 Field Hygiene and Sanitation — keeping a group healthy in the field; EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, p. 2 — the bleach-drops table.

🧼 Soap from fat and ashes 1. Make lye from ashes. Use hardwood ashes (they make the best lye); ashes of paper, cloth or garbage won't work (VITA, p. 342). Fill a bucket with ashes (🖼️ VITA's leaching drawing; Lye), pour on boiling water and stir, top up with ashes and water, then let it stand 12–24 hours and carefully pour off the clear liquid (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 2). 2. Check the strength. Lye that floats a fresh egg or a potato is right. Too weak? Run it through fresh ashes again, or boil it down. (VITA, p. 343) 3. Make soft soap. Boil ½ cup of ash lye for every cup of clean fat until it is thick, rubbery and foamy. Age the brown jelly at least a month before use. (VITA, p. 344) Ash lye is potash, which only makes soft soap; hard bars need store lye (caustic soda), or boiled soap "salted out" with salt water (USDA 1940, p. 3; Practical Action, p. 4). Hard soap with store lye (USDA): weigh 2½ lb clean fat, melt it and let it cool to lukewarm. Dissolve 5½ oz lye in 11 oz cold water (lye into water, never water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after
soap-from-fat-and-ashes

water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after 24 hours; let them harden a week or more out of the sun. (USDA 1940, p. 3) - Clean kitchen grease first: melt it with about an equal amount of hot water, stir, let it cool, and lift the clean fat off the top (USDA 1940, p. 3). - Is it done? Cool a drop on a plate. Clear = ready. Weak and grey = needs more lye. A grey skin that slides on the plate = too much lye — add more fat (Practical Action, p. 3). - New ("green") soap is still caustic. Wear gloves to handle it and let bars cure at least 3 weeks (Practical Action, p. 4). - Keep children away and don't breathe the fumes. Splashes: water, lots of it (some old books say vinegar — use water). | Soap problem | Likely cause (Practical Action, p. 4) | | Won't thicken | Not enough lye, too much water, too cool, not stirred enough, or too much liquid oil | | Oily layer on top as it cools | Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye

top as it cools | Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye from ashes, soft and hard soap, recipes; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 342 — leaching lye and soft soap with drawings; CAWST Soap Making Fact Sheet — modern measured recipes; MSU Making Soap at Home — store-lye bars.

👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1–2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda — wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic — gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard)), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun — sunlight helps disinfect. Stains (USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics): - Treat it while fresh, and try cold water first — hot water and soap set many stains. Test any remover on a hidden seam. (pp. 4, 6) - Blood: soak in cold water until the stain turns light brown, then wash in warm soapy water. Strong salt water (about 2 cups salt per gallon) loosens old stains. Never hot water. (p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8).

(p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8). - Chlorine bleach destroys wool and silk, and rots cotton if left on more than a minute or two (p. 5). 🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt (or a 50-50 mix of the two). No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles (chew stick), or wrap rough towel around a finger. Use thread as floss. (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 2; Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63 — gum care and keeping teeth without a dentist; Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17 — teeth, gums and mouth.
personal-care

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads (photos): several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). Change pads several times a day; a homemade tampon must be changed at least 3 times a day or it can cause a serious infection (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5, p. 4). - A pad that buttons on: a sleeve of heavy cotton about 4½ × 9½ inches with two button wings, plus removable folded towel liners about 6 × 8 inches. Wash and add bleach if you have it; dry in the sun, never under the bed — damp pads mold and cause itching. (WASHplus pattern — 🖼️ step-by-step drawings) - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun. 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus Making Reusable Menstrual Pads — sewing pattern with drawings; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5 — periods and staying clean.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives More detail (water washing, washing cloth wipes safely, which plants to avoid) is in Paper, Ink & Toilet Paper. - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap — the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠️ Learn poison oak first — it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. (🖼️ drawing) It grows as a shrub or a climbing vine, and the roots and stems carry the oil too (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). Also avoid stinging nettle. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9184, p. 24 — poison oak photos and control; FM 3-05.70 Survival, p. 514 — poison oak and other plants to avoid.

🚽 Toilets when the water is off - Don't flush if the sewer lines might be broken, even if your pipes look fine. A septic system can keep working if nothing leaks or backs up. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, pp. 4–5) - Twin-bucket toilet (Bucket toilet): two 5-gallon buckets marked "pee" and "poo". The poo bucket is lined with a heavy (3 mil or thicker) black bag; after each use, cover it with about ½ cup of sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper or peat. Keeping urine out of the poo bucket is what stops the smell. (OSU, pp. 2–3) - Emptying: dilute urine with wash water and pour it on the ground, a different spot each time. Fill the poo bucket no more than half, then double-bag it with gloves on and store it sealed, away from food and water. In the country you can bury it — never within 100 feet of a well, spring or creek. (OSU, p. 3) - Hand-washing station: a jug of clean water with a spigot, a catch bucket, and soap in the toe of a sock tied to the jug — one by the toilet, one by the kitchen (OSU, p. 3). - Trench latrine (🖼️ drawing; Pit latrine) for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover

latrine (🖼️ drawing; Pit latrine) for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover each use with soil; fill it in when the contents are 1 foot from the top (WHO/WEDC, p. 56). Hot ashes tipped into a pit cut smell and flies (Practical Action VIP Latrine, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics: Sanitation — twin-bucket setup and supply list; WHO/WEDC Technical Notes, p. 55 — trench, family and borehole latrines; Practical Action Compost Toilets — longer-term options; EPA Composting Toilets — how they work.

🔥 Fire and light without stores For candles, wicks, lamp oils and homemade lamps in detail, see Light Without the Grid. - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps — smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (🖼️ drawing) (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun (🖼️ drawing); touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool (🖼️ drawing); or a bow drill (🖼️ drawing) — drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192–194, and the Army survival manuals — FM 21-76, ch. 7). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable
fire-and-light-without-stores

Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\. - Dipped candles: dip wicks in melted tallow, cool, dip again until thick enough (🖼️ hand-dipping drawing) (Household Discoveries, p. 98). 2 parts beeswax to 1 part tallow is firmer than plain tallow (p. 99). Melt wax in a pot set in hot water, not over the flame (Practical Action Candlemaking, p. 3). - Rushlights: peel rushes and dip the pith in tallow like a candle (Household Discoveries, p. 99). How much light you get (lumens, roughly — Practical Action Rural Lighting, p. 3): candle 1 · wick oil lamp 1–10 · hurricane lantern 10–100 · mantle lamp ~1,000 · a 1-watt white LED 25–50 in that old table — a modern 1-watt LED gives about 80–150 (Off-Grid Power guide). 📚 Go deeper: FM 21-76 Army Survival Manual, ch. 7 — tinder, fire lays and fire without matches; Seton Book of Woodcraft, p. 192 — the classic bow-drill method; Practical Action Candlemaking — dipping, pouring and molding; Practical Action Rural Lighting — lamps, LEDs and batteries compared.

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (🖼️ pine drawing) (it's flammable — heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3–4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard — for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. Plain heated resin works as glue too (FM 3-05.70, p. 455). - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste — for paper and labels. - Casein (milk) glue — skim-milk curd mixed with slaked lime and two other chemicals — makes wood joints as strong as the wood — water-resistant but not waterproof. Full recipe: VITA, p. 313. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax–oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in. - Waterproof boots (USDA): melt together 1 lb petroleum jelly + 2 oz beeswax, or 12 oz tallow + 4 oz cod oil. Apply warm (never hotter than your hand can bear), working it into the welt and sole edge, where shoes leak most. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 12–13) 📚 Go deeper: Henley's Twentieth Century Formulas (1916) — hundreds of glues, pastes and cements; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 313 — casein glue; USDA Care of Leather, p. 10 — oiling and waterproofing shoes and harness.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams (🖼️ drawing), backstitch where it must be strong (🖼️ drawing), whipstitch for edges (🖼️ drawing), and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way — 🖼️ drawing). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Mend early — a few stitches on a weak seam or loose button save a big patch later. Shrink new patch cloth first and cut it on the straight of the weave. Darn with yarn raveled from a seam allowance, and don't pull it tight (it puckers). (USDA ABCs of Mending, pp. 4–8) - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow — choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Shoe care: work grease in well where the sole meets the upper, and let shoes dry somewhere warm, not hot. Re-sole before the welt and insole wear through — after that they're rarely worth fixing. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 10–11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet): shut the water off first, then replace the washer (🖼️ cut-away drawing). A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). If the washer screw is stuck, put on a drop of kerosene and tap it; if the head splits, deepen the slot with a hacksaw. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, pp. 4–5) - Toilet tank keeps running: usually a leaky, waterlogged float or a worn flapper/ball (🖼️ ball cock drawing; Ballcock). A tank should empty in about 10 seconds. (pp. 9–11) - Clogged drain: put a little water in the sink and plunge hard; if that fails, open the trap) under the sink (🖼️ drawing) and dig out the grease and hair with a bent wire (p. 12). - When you shut off the water for repairs, open the highest faucet so a vacuum can't suck dirty water back into the pipes from a tub or toilet (p. 12). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply — never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe (🖼️ drawing). Thaw drains from the low end upward. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, p. 14.) 📚 Go deeper: USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs in the Home — faucets, valves, tanks, clogs and thawing, with drawings; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater — using wash water

Bulging or leaking capacitors (photos) are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. - Look before you plug in — about 2 minutes finds most visible faults: loose or corroded connections, stray solder or wire bits (shake it and listen), charred resistors, and a white crust at an electrolytic capacitor's seal (🖼️ how one is built). A discolored or leaking transformer means a short somewhere. If anything smokes or sizzles when powered, pull the plug at once. (NEETS 6, pp. 210–211) - The simplest explanation that fits all the symptoms is usually right (Kuphaldt, p. 37). Multimeter quick tests (touch the probes together first — the meter should read near zero ohms — Kuphaldt Multimeters, p. 30) - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode (🖼️ test drawing): conducts one way only — about 0.5–0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor (🖼️ ohmmeter test): test it like two

open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor (🖼️ ohmmeter test): test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. Avoid the lowest ohms range (R×1), which can damage small transistors. (NEETS 7, p. 111) - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. (NEETS 6, p. 171) Resistor color code (🖼️ chart): black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1–2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow–violet–orange–gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. - Put the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal (the pad or lug), not the thin wire; a little fresh solder on the tip helps the heat flow. 🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F). - Building one (Haybox; 🖼️ cut-away drawing): a wooden box, old trunk or bucket with at least 4 inches of packing all round the pot, below it and in a thick cushion on top. Crumpled newspaper, packed hard, is the best cheap packing. Use a pot with straight sides and a tight lid, sized to the food — a big half-empty pot cools fast. (USDA FB 771, pp. 6–9) (The 1919 bulletin suggests asbestos — never use it.) - Times: boil beans or meat 20–25 minutes first, then 2–2½ hours in the box; soft foods need only a few minutes' boil and about 25 minutes in the box. It cuts fuel use by about 40%. (Practical Action Fireless Cookers, pp. 2, 5) - Meat and beans are the riskiest — don't leave them in the box too long, and reboil before eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p.

🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. Never store food in trash bags, paint cans or chemical drums. Containers of 20–30 lb are easy to lift and get used up before bugs move in. (USU Food Storage in the Home, pp. 11–12) - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls. Seal cracks, keep food off the floor, and keep the store room between freezing and 70 °F — cooler keeps longer (USU, p. 9). - Clay-pot cooler (zeer): a small clay pot inside a bigger one with wet coarse sand between, and a wet cloth on top (🖼️ how it works). Evaporation keeps vegetables cool — it works best in hot, dry weather, which suits our summers. Keep it in shade with a breeze and wet the sand three times a day. (Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler, pp. 1, 6) 📚 Go deeper: USU Food Storage in the Home — containers, storage rooms and shelf life; Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler — making and using a zeer pot; WSU Root Cellars — storing vegetables and fruit without power.

💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (🖼️ drawing; SODIS) (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water — let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\. - Clear enough? Stand the full, open bottle on a page of large print (letters about ½ inch high) and look down through it. If you can read it, the water is clear enough. - Fill ¾, shake 20 seconds, then top up — the air helps kill germs. Lay bottles flat, on metal roofing if you have it. Drink straight from the bottle so it isn't re-contaminated. - Not green or brown bottles; replace scratched, cloudy ones (about yearly). SODIS does nothing for chemical pollution. (Eawag SODIS Manual, pp. 26, 86–87) - In long rainy spells, boil or use stored or rainwater instead (p. 27). 📚 Go deeper: Eawag SODIS Manual, p. 26 — step by step, with a question-and-answer section from p. 85; OSU Survival Basics: Water, p. 3 — boiling and bleach; CAWST Biosand Filter Manual — build a filter for cloudy water.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants (🖼️ common roaches; German cockroach): powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds (🖼️ drawing), and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. Cover water barrels and screen their vents so they don't breed there (Practical Action Household Water Treatment, p. 2). - Lice (🖼️ drawing; head louse, body louse): comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb (🖼️ drawing) every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. Body lice live in clothing seams — wash clothes and bedding at least weekly (FM 21-10, p. 96). - Ticks (🖼️ western blacklegged tick photo; Ixodes pacificus): check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers. Grip close to the skin and pull with gentle, steady force without crushing it, and protect your fingers with cloth or gloves (FM 21-10, p. 98). 📚 Go deeper: Army FM 21-10 Field Hygiene and Sanitation, p. 96 — lice, ticks, mites and other pests; USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 13 — pantry pests.For hundreds more recipes — cleaners, polishes, glues, inks, waterproofing, pest control and home remedies — see the classic formula books in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do\.
