⚒️ Blacksmithing and Hand Tools How to set up a simple forge, pick the right scrap steel, forge and heat-treat it, and make or repair basic hand tools — chisels, punches, tongs, knives, axes — plus how to sharpen and re-handle the tools you already have. The full books are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ (Blacksmithing, Heat-Treating-Steel, Hand-Tools); axe and crosscut-saw manuals are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws. Farm blacksmithing (plow shares) and a short Practical Action brief are in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries - Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Assume everything near the forge is hot; pick things up with tongs, and set hot pieces down where no one will grab them. - Eye protection at the anvil, grinder and when quenching. Never use a cracked grinding wheel, never wear gloves at the wheel, stand aside when you switch it on. (Navy Steelworker, p. 22) - Never heat galvanized (zinc-coated) metal indoors — the fumes cause "metal fume fever." Strip the zinc first (rule of thumb: soak overnight in vinegar) and work outdoors. Drinking milk does not help, despite old advice (TM 10-440, p. 60 still recommends it — ignore that). - Quench oil can catch fire. Use a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an

a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an oil fire — smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) Oil fires usually start when there's too little oil for the piece. (Practical Action Blacksmithing, p. 3) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide — work outdoors or under an open-sided roof. - Fire season: Illinois Valley summers are dry. Keep a full water bucket or trough by the forge for embers as well as quenching (Practical Action, pp. 1–2), clear dry grass and leaves well back from the forge, and never leave a fire unattended. (Rule of thumb) - Oily rags can catch fire by themselves. Throw them out or keep them in a bucket of water. (USFS An Ax to Grind, p. 34)

🔥 A simple forge and anvil Rule-of-thumb setups; the books have full plans. - Forge: anything that holds a fist-sized pile of burning fuel with air blown up into the middle — a brake drum or steel tub lined with clay, or a brick or stone hearth with a pipe coming in at the bottom (the "tuyere"). The ICS Shop Equipment book and the Peace Corps manual show how to build forges and bellows. (ICS, p. 21; drawings: 🖼️ brick forge, 🖼️ tuyere, 🖼️ village forges, 🖼️ how a bellows works; Forge) - Air: a hand-crank blower, homemade bellows, a hair dryer or a small fan with a valve or gate to control it. Too much air wastes fuel and burns steel. (🖼️ hand-built fan and pump designs; 🖼️ a blower) - Fuel: charcoal (easy to make — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels), or coal turned to coke in the fire. Keep the fire clean: rake out clinker (glassy lumps), and work in the hot center. Screen coke to get rid of dust before you use it. (Practical Action, p. 2; Charcoal, Coke), Clinker)) - Anvil: a real anvil is best, but a chunk of railroad rail, a big block of steel, or a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. Set the face at about knuckle height when you stand with your arm hanging. Practical Action also shows a stone with an

The Peace Corps puts car springs, axles and torsion bars in the medium-carbon group; Practical Action calls coil springs, leaf springs and torsion bars high carbon. Test each piece and treat springs as hardening steel either way. Practical Action also warns that rebar often has a bit more carbon than true mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 5) - Quick test: heat the tip to light cherry red and quench it in water. If a file skates over it like glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. (Peace Corps, p. 32) - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams

🧪 Hardening and tempering 1. Anneal (soften) old steel before reshaping it cold or filing it: heat slowly to red, then bury it in dry wood ashes, lime or powdered charcoal and leave it until cold. (Selvidge, p. 56; Annealing)) 2. Harden: heat evenly to cherry red — rule of thumb: just past the point where a magnet stops sticking to it — and quench. - Plain carbon steel (springs, files, most scrap): water or brine (about ¾ lb salt per gallon) cools fastest and most evenly. Thin or very high-carbon pieces (files, knives) can crack in water — warm oil (80–150 °F; vegetable oil works) is gentler. (Steelworker, pp. 35–36) - Alloy steels: oil only. - Keep the piece moving in the quench. Steam and gas bubbles otherwise cling to it and leave soft spots, which can later crack or warp. (Selvidge, p. 57; Steelworker, p. 35; 🖼️ a quench tank; Quenching) - The steel is now glass-hard and brittle — temper it right away, before it's fully cold. The Navy Steelworker manual takes parts out of the quench at about 200 °F — still too hot to touch — rather than letting them cool through the "cracking range" below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven)

🛠️ Making basic tools - Cold chisel (first real project): a 6–8 inch piece of coil spring or axle. Straighten it, draw one end to a wedge, grind or file the edge to about 60°, harden and temper to purple at the edge (one-heat method). Leave the striking end soft. (TM 10-440, pp. 33–34; 🖼️ forging a chisel; Chisel) - Hot chisel vs cold chisel: a hot chisel is left soft and used only on hot steel; a cold chisel is hardened and tempered and used only on cold steel. Don't swap them. (Practical Action, p. 4; 🖼️ hot and cold chisels side by side; 🖼️ hot and cold cutters) - Center punch / drift: same steel, drawn to a round taper; temper the point straw to brown. - Tongs: two matching pieces of mild steel, forged with jaws and a boss, punched and riveted together. Richardson Vol 2 and Selvidge have patterns. (Step drawings: 🖼️ Drew, 🖼️ ICS) - Knife: from an old file or saw blade. 🪓 Keeping hand tools working Hanging an axe handle (USFS An Ax to Grind): - First check whether you need a new handle at all — often just a new wedge will do. (An Ax to Grind, p. 28) - Line the edge up with the center of the handle. Laid flat, the blade should touch the table one third of the way from the heel. (p. 24; 🖼️ a correctly hung ax) - Saw the wedge slot about two-thirds of the depth of the eye. Drive the head on by striking the end of the handle on a block, not the head. (pp. 30–31, photographed step by step: 🖼️ p. 30, 🖼️ p. 31) - Drive a hardwood wedge in until it stops, leaving ¼–½ inch, then trim. No metal wedges, screws or epoxy. Soaking a loose head in water only works for a day. (pp. 32–33; 🖼️ wedging, pictured) Soaking the head in linseed oil is a better temporary fix. (p. 33) - Good handle woods: straight-grained ash (Oregon ash grows here), hickory, oak. (Rule of thumb) The grain should run straight along the handle and in line with the wedge slot. (p. 26; 🖼️ good and bad grain; Oregon ash, Hickory) Sharpening: - Never sharpen an axe on a fast dry bench grinder — it draws the temper (the edge turns blue). Use a file (cuts on

Use a file (cuts on the push stroke only; lift on the return, wear gloves and use a knuckle guard), a slow wet grindstone, then a whetstone. File until a burr forms, then switch sides. 🧵 Clothing, Textiles, Leather & Shoes How to keep a household clothed and shod for years with no stores: dressing for our cold-wet winters, heavy mending, sewing machines, wool from sheep to yarn, linen, natural dyes, weaving, knitting, tanning, and boots and moccasins. Simple stitches, darning, tire sandals and boot-grease recipes are in the Make-Do Household guide; this guide goes further. The books are in Clothing-Leather\ (Sewing-Mending, Knitting-Hats-Gloves, Spinning-Weaving-Dyeing, Tanning-Hides, Shoes-Boots, Cold-Weather-Clothing), Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do, Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools and Trapping\Hides-Tanning. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Wet, not cold, is what kills here. Wear wool under a waterproof shell, no cotton in the winter rain, and change to dry socks at least twice a day (TC 21-3, p. 12). - Fleece and nylon melt onto skin. Wear wool or cotton at the stove, at the forge and near any fire (rule of thumb). - Never use the old poisons in tanning, fur and dye recipes: arsenic, mercury chloride, chrome, sulfuric or oxalic acid, gasoline, burning sulfur. Brains, bark, salt, alum, soap and smoke are enough. - Wear gloves with brains (deer and elk can carry chronic wasting disease) and lime (rule of thumb), and never put cut or cracked hands in alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather

alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather burns easily. Dry boots slowly; leather hotter than your hand can bear is almost sure to burn (USDA FB1183, p. 9).

🌧️ Dressing for our cold-wet winters Our winters are "cold-wet" — near freezing, freeze-thaw, rain, wet snow, slush and mud — the hardest weather to dress for. You need a waterproof or water-repellent, windproof outer layer over insulation, and waterproof footwear. "Cold-dry" weather (below 14 °F) is colder but easier (TC 21-3, p. 6; 🖼️ cold-wet vs cold-dry). On the valley floor most winter nights are in the 20s–30s °F, with weeks of rain from November to March (rule of thumb). The COLD rule (TC 21-3, p. 10; 🖼️ drawing; FM 21-76, p. 176): | | Rule | Why | | C | Keep clothes clean | Dirt and grease clog the air spaces | | O | Avoid overheating | Better a little cool than sweaty; shed a layer before you work | | L | Wear it loose and in layers | Trapped air insulates; a tight outer layer crushes it (🖼️ drawing) | | D | Keep it dry | Wet clothing carries heat away far faster than dry | Wool, not cotton. Cotton underwear, T-shirts, jeans and flannel lose what little warmth they have when wet and pull heat from the body. Wool keeps you warm when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too — their blood vessels
dressing-for-our-cold-wet-winters

when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too — their blood vessels don't narrow in the cold the way the hands' do (rule of thumb). Feet (TC 21-3, pp. 12, 41–42): trench foot (🖼️ photo) comes from days of cold, wet feet, not from freezing; in bad cases the skin dies and amputation follows. 1. Change to dry socks at least twice a day. 2. Dry and massage your feet. 3. Dry leather boots whenever you can. 4. Wear socks that aren't tight, and only one pair of cushion socks at a time. Drying clothes (TC 21-3, p. 14; FM 21-76, p. 177): - Hang items separately, high in the shelter, away from the stove and steaming pots. Nylon melts if dried too close. - Pin damp socks inside your outer layer as you walk. Never put damp clothes in a sleeping bag. - Dry leather slowly; boots can dry between the sleeping-bag shell and liner. Bedding: wet down loses much of its warmth. No bag? Sew two layers of cloth and stuff them with dry leaves, pine needles or moss (FM 21-76, p. 177). Wool blankets beat heavy cotton quilts (Household Discoveries, p. 53). 📚 Go deeper: TC 21-3 Cold-Weather Soldier's Handbook — layers, feet, drying clothes, cold injuries; FM 21-76

🪡 Mending and hand sewing Hand-sewing basics (TM 4-42.21, pp. 17–22): - Cut thread about 36 inches, never more than a yard (it tangles). Cut it; never bite or break it. - Basting (🖼️ drawing) holds work in place for a while. Backstitch (🖼️ drawing) is the strong seam. Catch (cross) stitch (🖼️ drawing) holds hems invisibly. Whipstitch (🖼️ drawing) binds raw edges. - Darns are for holes under 1 inch; patches for bigger ones (pp. 39, 43; 🖼️ four darns; 🖼️ top patch). Cut a top patch 2½ inches bigger than the hole all round, with ½ inch turned under, its grain matching the garment's. Mend early (ABCs of Mending, pp. 5–6): overcast fraying seams, tape-stay pocket corners, rework raveled buttonholes with buttonhole stitch (🖼️ drawing), and sew buttons on with a thread "shank" so the cloth isn't strained. Canvas, packs, tarps and leather (TM 4-42.21, pp. 71–74): - Use a triangular sailmaker's needle (🖼️ drawing), pushed with a sewing palm (a leather strap with a metal pad — 🖼️ putting one on). - Pull the thread across a cake of beeswax, and rewax it as you go (🖼️ drawing). - Cut 2-strand thread 6 times the seam length, 4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl — the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼️ threading the awl; 🖼️ the finished stitch; Lockstitch):
mending-and-hand-sewing

4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl — the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼️ threading the awl; 🖼️ the finished stitch; Lockstitch): 1. Thread the awl, leaving ½ inch out of the needle. Pull out enough thread to reach the end of the seam. 2. Push the needle through; pull all that slack through to the underside; hold it and withdraw the needle. 3. Push the needle in a stitch-length away and pull it halfway back, forming a loop underneath. 4. Pass the slack thread through the loop. Pull the needle out, then pull handle and thread equally hard to lock the stitch in the middle of the cloth. Repeat. Waxed thread for leather (The Saddler, p. 15; Hasluck, p. 36): twist 3–6 strands of flax (linen) thread. Taper each end first by untwisting it on your thigh and pulling it apart. Saddler's wax works best near 75 °F; cold wax is brittle. For shoes use waxed flax, never cotton — it is stronger, and the wax seals the stitch holes (FB1183, p. 9). 📚 Go deeper: TM 4-42.21 General Fabric Repair — every hand stitch, four darns, patches, canvas and webbing; USDA ABCs of Mending — darns and patches for every fabric. ✂️ Fibers, first garments and sewing machines Tell the fiber before you trust a salvaged garment (Turner, p. 95): | Burn a few threads | Fiber | | Burns fast, little ash, no smell | Cotton | | Burns slowly, black ball of ash, smells like burning feathers | Wool | | Melts and drips into a hard bead | Synthetic — keep it away from fire (rule of thumb) | Boiling a sample in weak lye (in an enamel pot) destroys wool but leaves cotton — so never wash wool with lye or chlorine bleach (rule of thumb). A first garment with no pattern (Turner, pp. 122–123): a kimono nightgown takes cloth twice the shoulder-to-floor length, plus a hem. Fold it crosswise, lay the drafted pattern on the fold, and cut the neck with the garment on the wearer. Its long straight seams (French or felled) are good machine practice. To remake old clothes, rip, wash and press first, and check the cloth is worth the work (Make-overs from Coats and Suits, p. 4). Lice live in seams: hang infested clothes in the cold, then beat and brush them. This does not kill the eggs (FM 21-76, p. 177). Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4–12; 🖼️ two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting

Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4–12; 🖼️ two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting kerosene or cleaning fluid into every hole and bearing, then oil each one freely. Never oil the tension discs. Never use gasoline indoors. 2. A stuck screw: soak it with cleaning fluid. "Left is loose, right is tight" (p. 5). 3. Replace a dirty wool wad in a long-bobbin oil well with raw wool (p. 8). 4. Then one drop per hole after each day's work, and now and then when idle (p. 10). 5. Skipped stitches: usually a needle of the wrong length or set wrong — the short groove faces the shuttle point. Sharpen a dull needle on a fine emery stone; scratch marks on the machine to record the needle length (pp. 11–12). Many electric heads from about 1900–1960 fit a treadle cabinet, run by a 3/16-inch leather round belt if the hand wheel has a belt groove. Stock spare needles, bobbins and belts now (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Turner Sewing and Textiles — seams, measuring and simple garments; USDA FB1944 — cleaning and adjusting machines.

🐑 Wool: from sheep to yarn Shearing (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 81–82; 🖼️ handling the fleece; Sheep shearing): once a year when spring warms. If cold, wet weather follows, house the sheep 10–14 days or leave some wool on. Shear white sheep first, keep colored wool apart, and never throw hay over sheep's backs — it ruins the fleece. Here, shear in late April–May as the rains ease (rule of thumb). Washing without felting: - Raw fleece: soak a few ounces at a time in warm water with mild soap for about 30 minutes. Don't stir it or it felts. Rinse in water of the same temperature (CSU 4-H Spinning, p. 17). - Finished woolens: lukewarm suds (about 95 °F), rinses the same temperature. Never boil, rub, wring or twist; squeeze, pull to shape and dry away from the fire (USDA, p. 9; Household Discoveries, p. 206). - Local soap: the bulb of soaproot lathers "like ordinary soap" and has no alkali, which suits wool better than lye soap (Chesnut, p. 332). It grows on dry, rocky slopes here (rule of thumb). Carding and combing (CSU, p. 17; Hooper, p. 43): carding (🖼️ hand cards) gives soft, fuzzy yarn; combing gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal
wool-from-sheep-to-yarn

gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal dog comb, or your fingers. Make a drop spindle) (CSU, p. 16; 🖼️ spinning with distaff and spindle): 1. Sand a 12-inch, ½-inch dowel to a point at one end. Cut a ⅛-inch notch 1 inch from the blunt end as a hook. 2. Glue a 2–3-inch wooden disk (the whorl) 1½ inches from the point. Spin it like a top; if it wobbles, re-center the whorl. Spin and finish (CSU, pp. 18–19): 1. Tie on an 18-inch leader of yarn. Twist the spindle and draw the fibers out as the twist runs up. Too much twist makes drafting hard; too little and the yarn falls apart. 2. Wind a skein around a chair back and tie it in 4 places. Soak it 20 minutes and hang it to dry with a weight. A balanced skein hangs straight. Angora rabbits give wool from a hutch: shear every 10–12 weeks, leave ½ inch of wool in winter, and keep newly shorn rabbits warm (USDA Handbook 309, p. 61). 📚 Go deeper: CSU 4-H Spinning — spindle, washing, carding, skeins; Hooper Hand-loom Weaving — carding, distaff and spindle.

🌾 Linen, nettle and native fibers Fiber flax (USDA FB669; 🖼️ the plant): 1. Climate: moderately cool, damp weather while growing and a dry spell at harvest. Heat and drought make it ripen early and short (p. 7). Here, sow very early on moisture-holding soil, or irrigate (rule of thumb). 2. Sow thickly — about 6 pecks an acre — so stalks grow tall and unbranched (p. 11). 3. Pull, don't cut, when the stalks yellow and the lower leaves drop (p. 12). 4. Ret to rot the gum that holds fiber to stalk: spread it on grass 2–8 weeks, turning once (dew retting), or weight bundles under soft water 6–15 days and watch closely — "a few hours' delay often causes loss" (pp. 16–17). 5. Dry the straw, break it (🖼️ a flax brake), then scutch (beat) out the woody bits (Hooper, p. 37). Native fibers: - Douglas iris: the leaf edges are "as fine and strong as silk" and made the strongest nets and snare rope (🖼️ twisting fiber into cord) — about six weeks' work for a 12-foot rope (Chesnut, p. 343). - Hemp dogbane: good fiber, but poisonous to livestock (AIB 415, p. 50). - Stinging nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch

nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch like flax (rule of thumb; no book here covers nettle fiber). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB669 Fiber Flax — growing, retting, breaking and scutching; Chesnut (1902) — native fiber and soap plants of our region.

🎨 Natural dyes with safe mordants Mordant with alum (USDA, p. 10): for each pound of dry wool, dissolve 4 oz alum and 1 oz cream of tartar in 4–4½ gallons of soft water. Bring it slowly to the boil, simmer 1 hour, and leave it overnight. The Navajo used raw alum, or water from burned green juniper needles (Navajo Native Dyes, p. 19). Skip the "chrome" mordant on the same USDA page — it causes cancer (see the last section). | Color | Plant | How | | Dull greenish yellow | Oregon grape roots, stems and leaves | With raw alum (Navajo, p. 39; USDA, p. 24) | | Soft brown | Alder bark peeled in fall | No mordant needed (Navajo, p. 23; Worst, p. 207) | | Black | Tannin (oak or tanoak bark, sumac) plus "iron liquor" | Steep iron filings in vinegar for days; mop it onto tanned leather (FB1334, pp. 19–20) | - Use enamel pots — tin or aluminum changes the color (Navajo, p. 12). - Test fastness: sun a sample half-covered with cardboard (USDA, p. 6). - Dye pots are never used for food again (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Navajo Native Dyes — plant dyes with only alum or juniper ash; USDA Home Dyeing with Natural Dyes — mordanting and dye recipes. 🧶 Weaving and knitting The simplest loom (Hooper, pp. 60–61): the one part every loom needs is the cross in the warp (🖼️ securing the crosses) — alternate threads cross between two rods so they can't tangle. A board with the warp wound around it and two rods holding the cross is a working loom. For 10-yard warps, build a warping board (🖼️ drawing) at least 6 ft × 1 ft with smooth hardwood pegs 1 inch thick, and tie cords through both crosses before taking the warp off, or it "will be irretrievably spoiled" (pp. 64–68). The next step up is the foot-power loom (Worst, p. 11; 🖼️ parts named). Picture: Warp and weft. Knitting habits from the WWI sock drives (Nicoll, pp. 25–26): - Join yarn without a knot: ravel both ends 3 inches, remove half the strands of each, overlap them and rub between damp palms. - Cast on (🖼️ drawing) and off loosely. Press with a damp cloth and a cool iron — wool scorches. - Tie a few needlefuls of the same yarn to each article for darning later (🖼️ repairing knitting). 🦌 Tanning hides Hold a hide until you can work it (USDA FB1334, p. 8): salt it with 1 lb of salt per lb of hide; it keeps 3–5 months. Never let it freeze or heat. Work in wooden barrels, never iron (🖼️ tools). Lime takes off the hair in 6–16 days (🖼️ unhairing); a gallon of vinegar removes the lime (pp. 10–14). Bark tanning) — sole and harness leather (pp. 14–16): 1. Per hide, steep 30–40 lb of oak or hemlock bark, ground no coarser than corn, in 20 gallons of boiling water. Use rain water, and keep it away from iron. 2. Strengthen the liquor every 5 days; then bury the hide in wet bark for 6 weeks, and again for about 2 months. 3. It is done when a cut edge shows no white streak. Sole leather needs 2 months more. 4. Finish with dubbin (equal parts tallow and neatsfoot or cod oil), slicking (🖼️ drawing) and staking (🖼️ drawing). Local bark: tanoak bark "has high tannin content" and was once used widely to cure leather (USDA NRCS, p. 2); Oregon white and black oak bark also work. Sudden oak death kills tanoak and is under quarantine in Curry County, next door: don't haul tanoak bark, wood or leaves out of infested areas (rule of thumb). 👢 Boots, shoes and moccasins Boot care (USDA FB1183, pp. 9–12): - Wet boots: wash off mud, grease work boots while damp, stuff with paper, dry slowly. - Harder grease in summer, more grease in winter (p. 12); recipes are in the Make-Do guide. - Soles: stand them 15 minutes in warm grease, no hotter than your hand can bear (FB1334, p. 16). A home repair kit (FB1183, p. 9): last holder, 3–4 iron lasts, hammer, pincers, knives, rasp, awls, sole and heel nails, flax thread, bristles and wax. Half-soling sewn shoes (Leno, p. 131; Bower, p. 29): 1. Wet the new leather. 2. Take off the old sole without cutting the welt. 3. Carry the new sole well back into the waist (the narrow middle). 4. Cut a channel deep enough to bury the stitches, and sew with stout, well-waxed thread. Pegged soles: one well-driven row of pegs usually holds; two rows make a stiff, tiring sole (Leno, p. 109). Fit: measure the foot's length seated, then trace it on paper standing — it lengthens under load, and the difference sets the allowance (p. 45; 🖼️ measuring diagram). Leno also covers pumps (turnshoes) and leggings. Moccasins in a wet climate (Farnham, pp. 260–266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted,"

climate (Farnham, pp. 260–266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted," because the leather is spongy. Improve them: - Add a rawhide sole, or sew on a thick "tap" that runs up the sides (p. 266). - Shape them by wetting and wearing them until dry (p. 264). - For uppers, 10–12 oz cotton duck rubbed with paraffin and ironed is waterproof and wears well. Deadly; old mounts and furs may still carry it (ATSDR Arsenic). Instead: salt, dry, cold storage. - Chrome tanning — FB1334, p. 17; the bulletin itself says the spent liquor "probably would be fatal to farm animals" (p. 19). Also the chrome (dichromate) dye mordant — USDA dyes, p. 10. Chromium(VI) causes cancer (ATSDR Chromium). Instead: bark or alum. - Sulfuric acid "salt-acid" pickle — FB1334, pp. 27–28; Farnham, p. 113. Burns and fumes. Instead: salt-alum. - Oxalic acid tan liquors — Farnham, p. 116; Household Discoveries, p. 409. Poisonous. Instead: brains, bark or alum. - Gasoline baths for furs — FB1334, pp. 25–26; Farnham, p. 150. Fire and fumes. Instead: lukewarm soapy water (rule of thumb). - Burning sulfur to bleach sheepskins — Farnham, p. 151. Toxic fumes. Instead: keep the natural color. - Formaldehyde and borax-heavy "pickles" in old taxidermy recipes (rule of thumb). Instead: salt and alum. - "40 to 45 percent of body heat" lost from the head — FM 21-76, p. 176. 📜 Paper, Ink & Toilet Paper How to make the paper, ink and toilet paper a household goes through once the stores are gone: paper by hand from rags, plants and scrap paper; iron-gall and soot inks; pens, pencils and slates; keeping paper and books from mold; and what to use instead of toilet paper, tissues and paper towels, and where each may go. The two papermaking and ink books are in Homestead-Skills\Paper-Ink: Watt's The Art of Paper-Making (1890), whose chapter "Making Paper by Hand" covers the vat, mould and sizing, and the Bureau of Standards' Inks (Circular 426, 1940). The old recipe books are in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do and the toilet books in Sanitation-Hygiene\Latrines-Toilets. Where no book covers a step, this guide says (rule of thumb). ### The short version - Rags make the best paper. Linen and cotton, cooked soft in weak lye or lime and pounded to pulp; there is "no better material" than linen (Watt, p. 20). - Lye burns skin and can blind. Gloves, goggles, no aluminum pots, children away; flush splashes with lots of water (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 1). - Scrap paper is the easy win: soak, pound, form again (Leland, p. 159). - Iron-gall ink is tannin + iron + a little gum: oak galls, tanoak bark or sumac leaves, with rusty nails in vinegar (Practical Action Natural Dyeing, p. 4). Keep tannin and

ink is tannin + iron + a little gum: oak galls, tanoak bark or sumac leaves, with rusty nails in vinegar (Practical Action Natural Dyeing, p. 4). Keep tannin and iron about equal by weight; too much iron eats paper (NBS Inks, p. 35). - Soot ink never fades and doesn't harm paper (NBS, p. 37): use it for records that must last. - Never add mercury ("corrosive sublimate") or chromates as old recipes do. A few cloves or a little alcohol stop mold (Household Discoveries, p. 422). - Washing with water is the cleanest toilet paper, 2 cups to 3 quarts a time (Compendium, p. 10). Cloth wipes belong to one person and are washed hot. Only toilet paper goes into a septic or flush toilet (EPA, p. 6). - Learn poison oak and stinging nettle before you wipe with any leaf. Wipe front to back and wash your hands (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 18, p. 10).

🧺 What paper is, and fibers that work Paper is "a composition of linen, cotton, or other vegetable fibre reduced to powder and then combined with size, which is a kind of glue" (Leland, p. 112). Beaten fiber spread thin on a screen felts into a sheet; the size (glue) lets it take ink. | Fiber | How good | Notes | | Linen rags, flax waste, hemp, old rope | The best: long, strong, flexible (Watt, p. 20) | Already retted and boiled, so it needs "but little chemical treatment" (same page) | | Cotton rags | "Strong and flexible", a little spongy (p. 20) | Worn-out sheets, shirts, flour sacks | | Straw (wheat, oats, rye, barley) | Short; "cannot of itself make a strong paper" (p. 20) | Cut 1–2 in (p. 99); mix with rag pulp (rule of thumb) | | Corn stalks and husks, reeds, bean stalks, hop vines, poplar, willow | On Watt's list of paper materials (p. 26) | Long cooking; try a small batch (rule of thumb) | | Cattail, milkweed | Ithaca Hours were printed on "locally made … cattail (marsh reed) paper" (FRB Cleveland, p. 2); milkweed used "to some extent" (Saunders, p. 256) | Cut cattail only from clean water; learn waterhemlock first (Food from Scratch) | | Waste paper | The easiest (Watt, p. 104) | See "Recycling"

🔥 Cooking fiber soft Boiling in alkali removes grease, dirt and the "cementing substances" around the fibers; linen rags lose a fifth to a third of their weight (Watt, p. 45). ⚠️ Lye "can cause blindness if splashed into the eye" (Practical Action, p. 1): gloves, long sleeves, goggles, children away, no aluminum (CAWST, p. 2); flush splashes with plenty of water. Wet lime is caustic too (rule of thumb). 1. Liquor: wood-ash lye ("Soap from fat and ashes" in the Make-Do guide); potash "affects but slightly" the fiber itself (Watt, p. 19). Or slaked lime, gentler on fine rags (p. 50), which helps pulp "felt together better" (Lime circular, p. 25). 2. How much: mills used about 5 lb of lime and 3 lb of soda ash per 100 lb of rags (Watt, p. 49), under 1 oz of lime and ½ oz of washing soda per pound (arithmetic). For ash lye, thin egg-floating lye with about 4 parts water (rule of thumb). 3. Simmer until a fiber pulls apart easily in your fingers, the old test for "tender" rags (Watt, p. 147). Mills boiled 2–6 hours under steam pressure (p. 49); an open pot takes half a day or more (rule of thumb). 4. Rinse until the water runs clear and the fiber stops feeling slippery, "until free of soda" (Lime circular 337, p. 92). Gloves on until

or more (rule of thumb). 4. Rinse until the water runs clear and the fiber stops feeling slippery, "until free of soda" (Lime circular 337, p. 92). Gloves on until then. 5. No fuel? Old mills retted rags, piling them damp until tender, with "considerable loss of fibre" to rot (Watt, p. 147).

🔨 Beating fiber into pulp - It is slow. Stamping rods took "forty pairs of stamps for twenty-four hours to produce one hundredweight of paper" (Watt, pp. 147–148). Pound wet fiber with a wooden mallet on a hardwood block, or in a mortar as Leland does (p. 159); plan on an hour or more for a few dozen sheets (rule of thumb). - Don't chop fibers short: cut fiber makes paper that "will be tender" (weak). Long pulp makes strong paper, shorter pulp fine writing paper; grasses beat in half the time of rags (Watt, p. 129). - Ready when a pinch shaken in a jar of water makes an even cloud (rule of thumb): "a fine paste, not … lumpy and stringy, but soft" (Leland, p. 113).

🪟 The mould, deckle and vat In Watt (pp. 147–149) the mould is a wooden frame "neatly joined at the corners", with ribs a little over an inch apart and fine wires along it, "about fifteen or twenty in an inch". The deckle, a loose frame on top, "must fit very neatly or the edges of the paper will be rough". The vat was a warmed tub "about 5 feet square and 4 feet deep"; felts of wool cloth go between wet sheets. Build a small one (rule of thumb, after Watt): 1. Make two identical frames of straight, dry 1×2 wood, a bit bigger inside than your sheet (about 9 × 12 in for letter paper), corners glued and pegged square. 2. On one (the mould), fit thin ribs about 1 inch apart, flush with the top, and tack fine window screen tight over them (fiberglass, brass or bronze; steel rusts and stains). 3. The other frame is the deckle; it must sit snugly on the screen. Oil or wax all the wood. 4. Vat: a washtub or tote longer than the mould. Felts: two dozen pieces of wool blanket or flannel.
the-mould-deckle-and-vat

📄 Forming, couching, pressing and drying 1. Charge the vat with clean water and pulp, and stir before every sheet to keep it "uniformly mixed" (Watt, p. 148). More pulp, thicker sheets (rule of thumb). 2. Dip the mould with its deckle and lift "as much of the pulp as will form a sheet of paper" (same page). 3. Hold it level as it drains, "otherwise … the sheet of paper would be thicker on one part than another". Shake gently front to back, then side to side, "propelling the pulp in four directions" (p. 149). Lift off the deckle. 4. Couch (say "cooch"): turn the mould face down onto a damp felt, press, and lift it away. Lay another felt on top; keep stacking felt, sheet, felt (same page). 5. Press hard: the mill used "a very powerful press" (same page); at home, boards above and below and a car jack under a beam, a cider press or heavy stones (rule of thumb). Then take the sheets off the felts, press them gently to remove felt marks, and next day separate and press once more (same page). 6. Dry slowly, hung over lines; cow-hair ropes "do not stain the paper" (p. 150), and slow loft drying was thought best (p. 145). In wet winters, dry indoors away from direct stove heat (rule of thumb). 7. Smooth: mills "hot-pressed" sheets
forming-couching-pressing-and-drying

paper" (p. 150), and slow loft drying was thought best (p. 145). In wet winters, dry indoors away from direct stove heat (rule of thumb). 7. Smooth: mills "hot-pressed" sheets between pasteboards with hot iron plates (p. 150); a warm flatiron over a cloth does the same (rule of thumb). | Problem | Likely cause | | Thick and thin patches | Mould not held level (Watt, p. 149) | | Rough, ragged edges | Deckle too loose (p. 148) | | Weak paper that tears | Fibers chopped too short (p. 129) | | Ink spreads like on a blotter | Not sized yet (p. 136) | | Sheet sticks to the screen | Pulp too thin, or mould not pressed firmly onto the felt (rule of thumb) | 📚 Go deeper: Watt, ch. 🧴 Sizing: making paper take ink On unsized paper a pen stroke "would spread in all directions" (Watt, p. 136). Starch stirred into the pulp won't fix it: blotting paper is made "with starch alone" (p. 199). Hand-made paper was dipped in gelatine size after drying (p. 150). - Size from hide scraps: cover clean skin clippings with water and hold at 180–190 °F, "very important that the liquid should not actually boil", for 12–16 hours (pp. 140–141). Skim, strain, and stir in dissolved alum, which "greatly improves its sizing property, besides preserving it" (p. 141); more in warm weather (p. 143). Hide scraps and alum: Clothing & Leather guide. - Quicker: boil "clean parchment cuttings until they form a clear solution" and strain through muslin (Henley's, p. 508), or use "1 ounce of good glue in 1 pint of hot water" (Household Discoveries, p. 271). - Sizing: warm the size to lukewarm (Watt, p. 143); lay dry sheets in one at a time, each evenly wet; press out the extra, separate, press again, dry slowly (p. 150). - Thin paper needs stronger size. Sizing is "one of the most difficult and uncertain" jobs, upset by heat and damp (p. 143): test a few sheets first. - Starch brushed on the surface helps: bond paper was surface-sized with starch, "an additional barrier against the penetration of the ink" (NBS Inks,
sizing-making-paper-take-ink

143): test a few sheets first. - Starch brushed on the surface helps: bond paper was surface-sized with starch, "an additional barrier against the penetration of the ink" (NBS Inks, p. 39). Brush thin cooked starch onto dry sheets (rule of thumb). - Size and starch feed silverfish (Leland, p. 144); a few drops of clove or other essential oil keep paste from molding (Household Discoveries, p. 59).

♻️ Recycling scrap paper, cardboard and mending Re-pulping: tear scraps small and soak them a long time, changing the water now and then; pound the soft mass in a mortar, boil it, and "to give it consistency, add flour-paste or gum" (Leland, p. 159). - Handwritten paper is easier than print: "a little soda-ash will discharge ordinary writing ink", but printer's ink is carbon and leaves grey pulp (Watt, p. 104), fine for wrapping, card and the outhouse. Mills used 10–20 lb of soda ash per 100 lb of paper, boiled 12–24 hours (p. 105). Washing soda: "Laundry" in the Make-Do guide. - Cardboard: paste sheets together with size, or lay several wet sheets on each other as you couch (Watt, p. 200). Leland's paste for it has "a little alum and glue and a few drops of oil of cloves" to stop souring (p. 151). Papier-mâché: newspaper strips in flour paste, several layers, dried in the sun (A Book for Midwives, ch. 25, p. 6). - Mending: fill holes with pulp worked to a fine paste (Leland, p. 113); patch tears with thin paper and a paste of ½ tsp each starch and flour cooked thick with boiling water, which "will not mold or discolor paper" (Lee's, p. 204). - Waxed paper: rub paper on a hot iron plate with beeswax (Henley's, pp. 507–508). Dirty pages: rub with stale

which "will not mold or discolor paper" (Lee's, p. 204). - Waxed paper: rub paper on a hot iron plate with beeswax (Henley's, pp. 507–508). Dirty pages: rub with stale bread (Household Discoveries, p. 60).

✒️ Iron-gall ink Iron and tannin from galls make a pale ink that the air turns black (NBS Inks, p. 7); it "turned black on the paper" (Household Discoveries, p. 416), darkest in about a week (NBS, p. 26). - Tannin: oak galls (the old imported kind held 60–70% tannic acid); crush, steep "in hot, not boiling, water", and strain (Household Discoveries, p. 416). Also sumac leaves (Practical Action, p. 4), tanoak bark, "high tannin content" (Tanoak guide, p. 2), and walnut hulls or maple bark (Trapper manual, p. 46). Local tribes blackened basket material with fresh oak bark, water and rusty nails (Chesnut, p. 354). - Iron: "rusty nails and a cupful of vinegar" in a bucket of water for "a couple of weeks" (Practical Action, p. 4), or iron filings in ½ gallon of vinegar for several days, some always left undissolved (USDA FB 1334, p. 19). - Copperas (green vitriol) is iron sulfate and "contains no copper"; blue vitriol (bluestone) is copper sulfate. Don't mix them up (NBS, p. 36). Good copperas is pale green; rusty means air has spoiled it, so keep it tightly closed (p. 20). The balance matters. Government record ink has about 31 g of tannin (tannic plus gallic acid) to 30 g of iron sulfate per liter (NBS, p. 13), about 1 oz of each per quart (arithmetic). With too little tannin,
iron-gall-ink

g of tannin (tannic plus gallic acid) to 30 g of iron sulfate per liter (NBS, p. 13), about 1 oz of each per quart (arithmetic). With too little tannin, writing "may become rusty in a comparatively few years" (p. 26); iron sulfate "caused decided weakening of the paper", tannin did not (p. 35), and some old manuscripts have crumbled to their margins (p. 34). When unsure, use less iron. With galls and copperas (Household Discoveries, p. 417): 2 oz crushed galls, 1 oz gum arabic, 1 oz copperas, 16 oz soft water; stand 2 weeks, shaking often. That is about 1.3 oz tannin to 1 oz copperas, close to the government balance (arithmetic). Leave out the "5 grains of corrosive sublimate" the book adds: it is mercury. Use a few cloves. Tannin tea: 2 oz crushed galls (or a double handful of chopped tanoak bark or dried sumac leaves) steeped overnight in 1 pint of hot, not boiling, rain water; strain through cloth. 3. In a glass jar, add iron water a spoonful at a time, testing a stroke on paper after each; stop when the strokes dry dark and stop improving. "Some experiments will be required" (Household Discoveries, p. 417). 4. Stir in a little gum or thin hide-glue size, which

Stir in a little gum or thin hide-glue size, which keeps the black from settling and fastens it to the paper (NBS, p. 8). Add a few cloves and bottle it. - Rain water (distilled is best); hard water uses up the ink's acid (NBS, p. 18). Glass or a glazed crock: "avoid the use of metal vessels … Iron, especially" (p. 77). - It "corrodes steel pens" (Household Discoveries, p. 416): wipe nibs. Travelers pressed such powders into "ink stones" (Henley's, p. 409).

🖤 Soot ink and other inks Carbon ink is the oldest: lampblack (soot) or charcoal held in glue, gelatin or gum; India-ink cakes are that paste dried, then rubbed with water (NBS Inks, p. 7). Carbon "cannot be bleached by any amount of exposure to intense light" (p. 37) and is unlikely to harm paper (p. 38). Homemade India ink (Household Discoveries, p. 419): boil an old kid glove (or a clean hide scrap) "until it forms a thick size"; hold a cold plate in a candle flame and, while it is still warm, mix the soot with the size. Test: let lines dry bone dry and sponge them. "If the ink runs, it is of poor quality." - Grind it fine and stir before each dip; coarse carbon settles (NBS, pp. 37–38). Never mix it with iron-gall ink: acid makes the carbon settle (p. 38). - A tenth part glycerine keeps India ink liquid (Henley's, p. 409); it works better with a brush than a steel pen (p. 408). - Printing ink is carbon in boiled linseed or nut oil (Household Discoveries, p. 422). The Wintu and other tribes "used the soot from burnt oak galls to make tattoos" (Tanoak guide, p. 2). - Sumac ink: "The berries and leaves of red or staghorn sumac boiled together in water make a permanent black ink" (Seton, p. 334). The Navajo

(Tanoak guide, p. 2). - Sumac ink: "The berries and leaves of red or staghorn sumac boiled together in water make a permanent black ink" (Seton, p. 334). The Navajo dyed black with three-leaved sumac (Navajo Native Dyes, p. 67), but three leaflets is also poison oak: pick no three-leaflet shrub unless someone who knows both shows you (rule of thumb). - Berry juice fades: dyes "have the unfortunate habit of fading" (NBS, p. 7), fine for children's pictures. Invisible ink: fresh milk shows when gently heated (Household Discoveries, p. 420).

🧊 Keeping ink, and bringing back faded writing - Mold: "a little alcohol or a few drops of any essential oil or a few cloves will prevent mold"; thin thickened ink with water or strained strong coffee (Household Discoveries, p. 422). - Air spoils ink: keep bottles nearly full, corked and dark (NBS, pp. 23–24). Make small batches; a two-year supply may end up "too full of sediment" (p. 24). - Freezing: a little alcohol prevents it (Household Discoveries, p. 422). Inks frozen solid at about 0 °F came back when thawed and shaken, and no bottle broke; they were about ⅚ full (NBS, p. 25; arithmetic). Leave headroom and keep ink indoors in frost (rule of thumb). Restoring faded iron-gall writing. It leaves rust in the strokes, so it can be brought back (faded dye ink leaves "literally nothing behind", NBS, pp. 32–33). "A 2- or 3-percent solution of tannic acid", or gall tea, turns the rust black: "by far the best treatment" (p. 33; Household Discoveries, p. 422). 1. Brush it on softly, or trace the letters with a pen dipped in it; rinse briefly in clean water and dry, or the whole sheet darkens in time (p. 33). 2. Try a corner first. For a treasured paper, think twice: NBS advised against treating the Declaration of Independence (p. 34). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 426 Inks —

🪶 Pens: reed, quill and brush Reed or bamboo pen (VITA, p. 360): 1. Take dry bamboo or stiff reed about 6 in × ⅜ in. Whittle one end to width and shave it thin so it flexes, keeping the tip on the hard outer side. 2. Cut the tip straight across, then shape it "by gently writing on the sandpaper with the dry pen". 3. For an ink hole, rest the knife point at least ⅛ in up from the tip and twist to drill a hole about 3/32 in. 4. For a reservoir pen, bind a thin bamboo cover plate on with a rubber band or fine wire (p. 361). Quill pen (rule of thumb; no book here shows how): take a big goose or turkey wing feather; soak the barrel, harden it in hot sand for a minute, strip the lower barbs and scrape off the outer skin and inner pith. Cut a long scoop on the underside, a short slit up the point, and trim the tip square and thin. Recut it as it wears. Brush: India ink "applies well with a brush" (Henley's, p. 408). A gold nib "cannot be rusted" by any ink (NBS, p. 18).
pens-reed-quill-and-brush

✏️ Pencils, charcoal, chalk and slates - Hoard pencils. An 1871 traveler gave up ink (it dries, clogs and corrodes pens) and "trusted simply to the powers of a good HH. pencil" (Shifts and Expedients, pp. 31–32). Pencil "lead" is graphite and clay, "not lead (the metal)" (Kuphaldt, p. 97). - Don't make real lead pencils from melted lead in reeds, as an old book does (Shifts, p. 217). Lead fumes poison: never melt lead indoors, and keep children away (ODFW, p. 27). - Sharpener: a block with coarse sandpaper on one side and fine on the other (Household Discoveries, p. 62). - Charcoal: a burnt stick marks well enough to lay out a tepee (Seton, p. 467). For drawing sticks, char peeled willow twigs in a tin with a nail hole, like char cloth ("Fire and light without stores" in the Make-Do guide), in the stove during fire season (rule of thumb). - Soapstone, chalk and slate pencils mark iron (ICS, p. 55). Stop smudging with "a light wash of gum of any kind, diluted varnish, or even milk" (Leland, p. 259). Slates save paper. Children learned their tables "upon their slates or on the blackboard" (Ray's Primary, p. 11); a "stick or chalk board" is a toddler's toy (WHO/UNICEF, p. 2); a kitchen slate keeps the list of supplies running low (Household Discoveries, p. 69). - Blackboard paint:

11); a "stick or chalk board" is a toddler's toy (WHO/UNICEF, p. 2); a kitchen slate keeps the list of supplies running low (Household Discoveries, p. 69). - Blackboard paint: 1 lb shellac in 1 gal alcohol, with 4 oz each of fine lampblack, powdered emery and ultramarine (Henley's, p. 491). Lacking those, a smooth dark board or flat stone takes chalk or soapstone (rule of thumb). - Wax tablet: a shallow tray of beeswax, written on with a point and smoothed to erase (rule of thumb); beeswax takes "any sharp-pointed instrument" (Household Discoveries, p. 421). - Birch bark: no book here covers it, and paper birch is not a valley tree (rule of thumb). Smooth bark or leaves take scratched letters, as India's palm leaves did (Shifts, p. 504).

📚 Keeping paper and books from mold - Damp breeds "molds and fungi". Keep books on "open, airy, well-lighted shelves"; after a wet spell wipe the covers and set them "in the sun or before a fire for a few hours"; camphor, wrapped in paper, in closed boxes (Henley's, p. 127). In our wet winters, check monthly (rule of thumb). - Light and damp age writing; mold destroys "both ink and paper" (NBS, p. 27). Store records dry and dark, off the floor and away from outside walls (rule of thumb). - Insects: oil of lavender or cedar on the shelves; silverfish "loves starch" (Household Discoveries, p. 59). - Records that must last: soot ink or balanced iron-gall ink on rag paper, never berry or dye ink (NBS, pp. 7, 37).

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives: water, cloth, leaves, cobs There are two ways: wash ("typically … 0.5–3 litres", about 2 cups to 3 quarts) or wipe with "paper, leaves, corncobs, rags or stones" (Compendium, p. 10; arithmetic). Agree as a household what you'll use, and plan a supply that lasts (Sphere, p. 143). Water: pour from a squeeze bottle or jug with one hand and wash with the other, then wash your hands with soap (rule of thumb). The wash water carries feces: keep it out of the urine bucket; small amounts may soak into the soil (EcoSanRes, p. 38). Pour-flush toilets suit water-washers (Hesperian ch. 7, p. 35). Cloth wipes ("family cloth") belong to one person each: shared towels spread disease (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 153; pink eye, Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 16, p. 3). Cut soft cotton (flannel, old T-shirts) 6–8 inches square, a day's worth plus spares each; many families use cloth for urine only (rule of thumb). Used cloths go in a lidded bucket ("Toilet paper alternatives" in the Make-Do guide). Wash them like cloth diapers: 1. Rinse in cold water, then wash with soap ("Menstrual pads and diapers" in the Make-Do guide). 2. Wash above 140 °F, or soak in 0.05% bleach (about 2 Tbsp of 6% bleach per gallon): "Dishes, laundry and periods" and the bleach-strength table in the Sanitation guide. 3. A

A little vinegar in the last rinse, as for diapers (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 15, p. 23). Dry in full sun. 4. Wash water goes to the latrine or wastewater system, not the garden (Oregon DEQ, p. 12), and never into a creek. Wash a sick person's cloths separately, with bleach (rule of thumb). Leaves: no book in the library recommends any particular leaf for wiping. Leaves are a normal choice (Compendium, p. 29), but which leaf is up to you. Rub a new one on your inner arm and wait a day before trusting it (rule of thumb). - ⚠️ Poison oak: "leaves of three, let it be"; vine or shrub, "all over low elevation in western Oregon"; "the roots and stems also contain the oil" (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). "All parts, at all times of the year" cause the rash, bare winter stems too (FM 3-05.70, p. 514). Rash care: Injuries guide. - ⚠️ Stinging nettle grows on moist forest floors and riverbanks; its hairs sting "for hours or cause blisters" (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). - Thimbleberry (rule of thumb): big soft leaves on "a thornless, wideleaved shrub, 3 to 8 feet high, with showy

"for hours or cause blisters" (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). - Thimbleberry (rule of thumb): big soft leaves on "a thornless, wideleaved shrub, 3 to 8 feet high, with showy white flowers" (Chesnut, p. 369), in forest shade (OSU EC 1306, p. 4). - Mullein (rule of thumb): first-year rosettes of "wooly basal leaves" on roadsides and dry open ground (USFS PNW-GTR-513, p. 131); gentle enough to put on wounds (AFH 10-644, p. 90), but the hairs bother some people (rule of thumb). 🧼 Wiping, handwashing and children - Wipe from front to back: "Wiping forward can spread germs, amebas, or worms into the urinary opening and vagina" (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 18, p. 10; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 10, p. 7). - Teach children "to wipe or wash carefully, and to wash their hands after using the toilet. Girls especially should be taught to wipe from front to back"; wash babies after they defecate (Hesperian ch. 7, p. 11). - Wash hands after the toilet and after cleaning up anyone else (OSU, p. 4), with soap "or an alternative such as ash" (Sphere, p. 143). Put a tippy tap by every toilet ("Handwashing and water for hygiene" in the Sanitation guide).
wiping-handwashing-and-children

🧣 Handkerchiefs, towels and reusing paper - Handkerchiefs, not tissues. Someone with a cold "should cover his nose and mouth when he coughs or sneezes, and wash his hands often", and should not blow but "just wipe" the nose (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 13, p. 13). Each person keeps their own, washed hot like cloth wipes (rule of thumb). - Flour sacks make dish towels and dishcloths (Household Discoveries, p. 68); hem old sheets into napkins (rule of thumb). - Paper bags wrap things, then wipe up milk or grease and go in the fire; waxed box liners wrap cheese and lunches (p. 67). Newspaper goes under carpets, wraps woolens against moths and covers plants on frosty nights (p. 68); damp, it polishes windows (p. 275). - Paper too far gone: shred it for the bucket toilet, or burn clean paper in the cooking fire, never in the open June to October ("Garbage, sickroom and birth waste" in the Sanitation guide).

🎒 On Foot: Backpacking and Travel When the Roads Are Empty With no fuel and no car, walking is how a household reaches Grants Pass, the coast, family or a trade. This guide covers planning, loads and packs, feet, water and food on the move, camp, wildlife, cold rivers, snowy passes and staying safe on the road. Miles, travel days and route files are in other guides, and this one links to them. Its new books are in Southern-Oregon\Travel-On-Foot: the Army's Military Mountaineering (TC 3-97.61, 2025) and Foot Marches (ATP 3-21.18, 2017), Horace Kephart's Camping and Woodcraft (1916, two volumes), ODF's fire-season rules, OSU's poison-oak bulletin and a National Park Service trip planner. The older Foot Marches (FM 21-18) and Knapik's Load Carriage are in Southern-Oregon\Bicycles-Carts\Trailers-Carts; the Air Force survival handbook (AFH 10-644, the whole book despite "Signaling" in its file name) is in Southern-Oregon\Comms-Signals\Visual-Sound-Signals. ### The short version - Cold rivers kill. Wade alone only where it is knee-deep or less and the current mild (TC 3-97.61, p. 345). Unbuckle hip and chest straps first (p. 344), never tie yourself to a rope, and "if in doubt, turn back or wait for help" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). Oregon rivers stay "dangerously cold" in warm weather (OSMB, p. 17). - Feet first. Cover a hot spot the minute you feel it (Knapik, p. 49); change socks at noon and

rivers stay "dangerously cold" in warm weather (OSMB, p. 17). - Feet first. Cover a hot spot the minute you feel it (Knapik, p. 49); change socks at noon and never "walk them dry" (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 144–145). - Carry less: plan family loads on 10–20 kg (22–44 lb) (World Bank, p. 65). - Plan by time, not miles: about 15 miles a day on roads (what the walking-routes tool assumes), plus an hour per 1,000 ft of climb (FM 3-97.6, p. 72). Late December has only about 9 hours of daylight (arithmetic). - Water: 2–4 quarts a day when cool, 4–8 in the mountains, never over 1¼ quarts an hour (NY hunter manual, p. 81; FM 3-97.6, p. 17; FM 21-10, p. 56). Treat every drop. - No fires in fire season. ODF's 2026 rules ban "campfires, cooking fires and warming fires" from May 15 (ODF closure, p. 1). Eat cold, or use a stove in a cleared spot. - Leave a written plan; turn back early. Leaving "a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather conditions is foolhardy" (AFH, p. 427). And "Travelling alone is dangerous" (p. 426).

Distance, hills and daylight - Miles and days from Cave Junction are in "Travel times from Cave Junction" in the Bicycles & Carts guide and "Walking out" in the Start Here guide; print directions and maps from Walking-Routes\WALKING-ROUTES.html. All assume 15 miles a day with a pack. - Hills: the Bicycles guide has the Army rule (a third more distance, an hour per 1,000 ft up). Checks: 800 ft of climb an hour "is good work", and "If you cannot talk without catching your breath ... you are going too fast" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 146); distances are "reduced by half over average gradients of 10 percent" (🖼️ FM 21-18, p. 66). - The first days are hardest: stiff legs on day two; poor sleep, constipation and sore feet by day three (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 142–143). Make the first days 8–10 miles (rule of thumb). - Daylight at Cave Junction (arithmetic, 42° N): about 9 hours on December 21, 10 in mid-November and late January, 12 at the equinoxes, 15¼ on June 21. A 15-mile day takes 7½–8 hours with rests, so plan 10–12 miles in midwinter. Start looking for camp "at least two hours before sunset" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 212). - Season: snow can fall in any month above 5,000 ft, and flash floods run "many miles downstream" of the rain (FM 3-97.6, p. 15). Choosing a route Where there are no bridges, "keep away from streams and follow the ridges between them" (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 49–50), and "Travel on trails rather than taking shortcuts through the brush" (AFH, p. 446). The library's back-road routes climb high Forest Service roads, such as Grayback Road (FR 4611) toward Grants Pass and Medford and Sanger Peak Road (FR 4803) toward Crescent City; US-199 stays lower. The route files give no heights, so read each climb off a topo map (rule of thumb) ("Reading a topo map" in the Navigation guide). No book on the drive gives camping limits on public land; the Forest Service has long allowed about 14 days in one spot (rule of thumb).
choosing-a-route

The plan you leave behind, and when to turn back Leave a note "stating departure time, destination, route of travel, personal condition, and available supplies", and carry "sufficient water to reach the next probable water source" (AFH, p. 427). The NPS trip-plan form is in "Getting un-lost" in the Navigation guide. Turn-around rules to write on the plan (rule of thumb): 1. A turn-around time: if you aren't at the pass, ford or planned camp by then, go back. 2. A river above the knee, or rising: "Not every river or stream can be crossed safely" (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). 3. Snow above the knee on a pass and no snowshoes; smoke or a fire column ahead; a hot east wind in fire season. 4. Water down to half with no sure source ahead; someone hurt, sick or limping; a checkpoint that says no.

Caches "Bears will demolish any such pile [of stones] that one man could build." Hang the bundle from a peeled pole between two trees 15–20 ft up, trees "too slender for a bear to climb, yet too stout for him to shake" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 233). Hide damp-proof things under an old, half-buried log, away from camp so one raid or fire doesn't take both (p. 236). Dried food needs a "completely waterproof" container (AFH, p. 369).

🚶 Pace, rests and walking technique The day's rhythm. On roads this guide follows FM 21-18; on steep trails and in cold, the newer books' shorter stops. 1. Start in fewer layers, a little chilly (AFH, p. 428); stop to fix laces, straps and layers in the first half hour (ATP 3-21.18, p. 25). 2. On roads: rest 15 minutes after the first 45, then 10 in every hour, feet up (FM 21-18, p. 48). 3. On steep trails and in cold: "shorter breaks taken more often are better ... especially in colder weather" (TC 3-97.61, p. 109); "Long halts eat up daylight; they stiffen the muscles; and they cause chills" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 142). Lean the pack on a tree or bank. 4. At any long stop, put on a layer: "It is much easier to keep a warm body warm" (ATP, p. 25). 5. Halfway: a 15-minute stop in which everyone changes socks (FM 21-18, p. 91). - Uphill: slow and steady, zigzagging rather than charging straight up (TC 3-97.61, p. 107). The rest step: pause on the straight rear leg, "so the bone, not muscle, supports the weight" (ATP, p. 25; 🖼️ TC 3-97.61, p. 108). - Downhill: bend the knees; "Even one pole can be very helpful". Go straight down scree in short shuffling steps, heels dug in; never walk below someone on a loose

- Downhill: bend the knees; "Even one pole can be very helpful". Go straight down scree in short shuffling steps, heels dug in; never walk below someone on a loose slope (TC 3-97.61, p. 109). - Heat: don't march "at the hottest time of day" (FM 21-18, p. 61); 3½ mph with 40 lb or more is "hard work" (FM 21-10, p. 57). Heat illness: "Heat and cold in the Valley" in the Field Care guide. Drop no wrappers; they tell others who passed (FM 21-18, p. 84).

Fitting and loading a pack - The hips carry the load: "A waistband will support 80 to 90 percent of the weight" cinched "around the pelvic girdle" (AFH, p. 454); in one test a frame and wide hip belt cut shoulder pressure from 203 to 15 mm Hg (Knapik, p. 31). - Heavy things close to your back, balanced side to side; high on easy ground, lower on rough ground ("low or midway"); rain gear and first aid on top (AFH, p. 453; TC 3-97.61, p. 156). - Nothing dangling: "flip-flops" and "stick-outs" snag in brush and can throw you off a log bridge; the best pack is one roomy sack holding everything (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 126). - Adjust at every rest (AFH, p. 450). Numb, tingling arms ("rucksack palsy"): move the straps or use a frame and hip belt (Knapik, p. 47). Lift a heavy packboard by sitting against it and rolling to your knees; never drop it (Packboard, p. 1).
fitting-and-loading-a-pack

Boots and socks - Fit: a thumb's width past the big toe, and a finger under the unlaced tongue (🖼️ FM 21-18, pp. 107–108). Pressure means too small, rubbing too big. Carry spare laces (p. 109). - Break boots in before the trip, alternating with an old pair and taping known hot spots (ATP 3-21.18, p. 110). Dry them slowly with a warm cloth inside; on freezing nights keep them in the sleeping bag (FM 21-18, p. 107). Resoling: "Boots, shoes and moccasins" in the Clothing guide. - Socks: "The wool cushion-sole sock is best"; dry damp ones inside your shirt (FM 21-18, p. 109). A thin nylon or polyester liner under the wool cuts blisters (Knapik, p. 48). - Wet feet: stop "and wring out the hose; do not 'walk them dry'" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 144). No dry socks left: grass insoles an inch thick, made fresh daily (AFH, p. 191).
boots-and-socks

Blisters Prevention: two socks, good insoles, a lighter load, distance built up slowly, and "Cover skin when hot spots appear" (Knapik, p. 47). A hot spot is "a localized warm or burning sensation"; cover it with moleskin or tape at once (p. 49). Draining: the books disagree. TC 3-97.61 says "Never drain blisters unless" infected (p. 49); FM 21-18 drains all of them (p. 102); Knapik leaves small ones and drains big ones on weight-bearing spots (p. 50). This guide follows Knapik: 1. Small (under 5 mm, about 3/16 in) and not painful: leave it whole, inside a doughnut of moleskin (Knapik, p. 52). 2. Big and tight on the sole or heel: wash around it, flame a needle, prick it at the edge, press the fluid out and leave the skin on; cover past the edges (🖼️ FM 21-18, p. 102). 3. Torn open: take off the loose roof and treat it as a wound (Knapik, p. 51); see "Wounds and infection when there's no hospital" in Field Care. 4. Spreading redness or pus: infection, which can become cellulitis or blood poisoning (Knapik, p. 48). Rest the foot.
blisters

Trench foot and frostbite - Trench foot comes from days in wet, cold boots at 32–50 °F, sitting or standing still, laced tight (FM 21-18, p. 106): an ordinary valley winter. Early on, feet are pale, numb and not painful, so check each other. Prevent it with dry socks and boots daily; in wet boots, wiggle the toes. Treat gently: feet "should not be rubbed or massaged"; clean, dry, raise, and carry the person (same page). Mild cases heal with about 24 hours of drying (TC 3-97.61, p. 54). - Frostbite (high passes in winter): warm small spots with body heat, hands in armpits, bare feet on a companion's chest; no massage, fire or snow (FM 21-18, p. 105). Don't thaw deep frostbite on the trail: "it is safer to walk on frozen feet" (p. 106).
trench-foot-and-frostbite

A daily foot routine | When | What | Source | | Before the trip | Toenails "short and square, and straight across"; boots broken in | 🖼️ FM 21-18, p. 100 | | Each morning | Clean, dry, powdered feet; tape known hot spots | p. 101 | | At halts | One boot off at a time; rub, powder, dry socks; loosen laces over the arch | ATP, p. 110 | | Evening | Wash feet and dry them well; dry socks and boots; look for red, swollen spots | Kephart Vol. 2, p. 144; ATP, p. 110 | Rub healthy feet only. A stress fracture needs two or three weeks of rest (FM 21-18, p. 107).

🧥 Clothing, cold and heat What to wear is in "Dressing for our cold-wet winters" in the Clothing guide. On the trail: - Three layers: one next to the skin that moves sweat, an insulating one, and a wind-and-rain shell. Wool "provides warmth when wet"; soaked clothing loses heat "several hundred times faster" than dry; cotton is a poor choice (NY hunter manual, p. 77). - Start cool; "Do not sit around when overheated and damp ... But do not muffle up on the march" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 145). Dry underwear and socks at night "are as warm as an extra blanket" (p. 104). Carry spare socks, hat and gloves, and a poncho or "extra-large plastic trash bag" (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). - Hypothermia creeps up from wet brush, wind and "Resting against cold surfaces"; chocolate, peanuts or raisins help (NY hunter manual, p. 82). Heat: a hat and light clothing that covers the skin (p. 77). Treatment of both: Field Care. Smoke: the Wildfire guide.
clothing-cold-and-heat

too much plain water dilutes the blood's salt (Field Care). - Don't eat snow: it "will contribute to loss of body heat" (TC 3-97.61, p. 46). Running short? "physical activity must be reduced" (p. 75); walk in the cool hours (rule of thumb).

Finding, carrying and treating water - Finding: streams, springs, rain; a short tube fills a bottle from a trickle off rock; "Water is scarce above the timberline" (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). By a muddy pond, dig a hole "about 18 inches across and down about 6 inches below water-level, a few paces from the pond", bail it three times, then take the clearer water (Seton, p. 292). Still treat it. Summer ridges are dry: plan refills at creeks and springs on the topo map (rule of thumb). - Skip water below farms or mine tailings (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). "Never drink from the well of an abandoned farm" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 214); "It is not true that running water purifies itself" (p. 213). - Carrying: wide-mouth bottles; bladders "can break and have freezing issues" (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). Sleep with your water on freezing nights (p. 75). - Treating: "Virtually all surface waters are microbiologically contaminated", and Giardia and Cryptosporidium "thrive in domestic and wild animals" (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). A 1-minute boil kills them; tablets miss Crypto and work slower in cold water; many filters don't stop viruses (p. 76). Methods: "Step 3 — Kill the germs" and "After a wildfire" in the Water Purification guide.
finding-carrying-and-treating-water

🍞 Food on the move - How much: a loaded march burns over 300 calories an hour (FM 21-18, p. 65); Kephart lists 3,400 a day for moderate work, 4,150 hard, 5,500 very hard (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 185), against everyday adult needs of 1,600–3,000 (Dietary Guidelines, p. 152). Plan 3,000–4,000 calories, about 2 lb of dry food, per person per walking day (arithmetic). - Calories per pound: fat about 4,080 and butter 3,410 (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 185); parched corn 1,915, cornmeal 1,655, bread 1,205 (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 159). Fresh food would be "five or six pounds a day" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 182). - Carry one extra day's food (TC 3-97.61, p. 74). Eat little and often: 25–75 g of carbohydrate an hour in four bits (ATP, p. 106). Parched corn (pinole), the lightest trail food in the library: 1. Parch dry corn "in clean hot ashes until it bursts", sift it, and pound it to meal (Parker, p. 118). 2. Stir it into water, "one tablespoonful to a pint" (same page). Two heaping tablespoons with raisins or chocolate made Kephart "a square meal" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 158). 3. Go easy: it swells. A handful (2 or 3 oz) was "even considered dangerous unless cooked" (Parker, p. 119). Make at home before you leave: jerky and pemmican ("Jerky and pemmican" in Preserving Food), hardtack ("Staples" in
food-on-the-move

or 3 oz) was "even considered dangerous unless cooked" (Parker, p. 119). Make at home before you leave: jerky and pemmican ("Jerky and pemmican" in Preserving Food), hardtack ("Staples" in Food From Scratch) and dried fruit. A fist-size piece of pemmican "would make a meal for two men" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 160). Eat lean jerky with fat and grain, not alone (rule of thumb). Little fuel: in fire season, plan no-fire meals or a legal stove (rule of thumb). A broad, shallow pot "boils water much sooner"; skip foods that need long boiling (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 106–107). Use a lid: only 10–40% of a fire's heat reaches the pot (Aprovecho, p. 7). In the wet season, burn "dry, dead hardwood no larger than a pencil" for "less smoke" (AFH, p. 563).
food-on-the-move

Choosing a campsite A good site has water; wood if fires are allowed; a level spot "well above any chance overflow" ("Observe the previous flood marks"); "Security against the spread of fire"; morning sun; shelter from winter wind; and privacy (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 213). Move on if the site is: - in a creek bottom, dry streambed or drainage (flash floods), under dead trees or dead limbs, in poison oak, or in a slide path, which shows as a strip of young growth down the slope (AFH, p. 195); - on the valley floor, where cold air pools (AFH, p. 194); camp "up the hillside above the valley floor", clear of rockfall (TC 3-97.61, p. 77); - beside brush, tall grass or boulders where snakes live (FM 3-05.70, p. 530), or on an animal trail (ODFW bears, p. 2).
choosing-a-campsite

Tarp and debris shelters - Tarp or poncho lean-to: back to the wind, a stick or line under the middle so rain can't pool (FM 3-05.70, pp. 69–70). Kephart tied one long side of a 7 × 9-ft cloth to a pole 4 ft up and staked the other out at 45° (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 104–105). More in "Emergency tarp and plastic shelters" in the Shelter guide. - Debris hut, warm with no fire (FM 3-05.70, pp. 82–83): 1. Rest one end of a long ridgepole on a stump, rock or two short stakes, about waist high. 2. Lean sticks along both sides as ribs, wide enough for your body and steep enough to shed rain; lay brush across. 3. Pile dry leaves, needles and grass at least 3 ft thick, "the thicker the better", with branches on top. 4. Put a 1-ft layer inside to lie on, and pull a heap of debris into the doorway behind you. - Off the cold ground: "Don't bed down on the cold, hard earth" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 105). Fir boughs are best, spruce prickly, pine thin (AFH, p. 222). Kephart's 1-lb "bed tick" is a cloth bag stuffed with dry leaves: "A 3-pound blanket on top of such a mattress is warmer than a 5-pound one without it" (p. 106). On snow, use a foam pad (TC 3-97.61, p. 73).
tarp-and-debris-shelters

Fire and fire season The law in 2026 (ODF closure, pp. 1–2), on forest land protected by ODF's Southwest Oregon District: - "Open fires are prohibited, including campfires, cooking fires and warming fires", except on private land with the owner's permission at low (GREEN) danger and at designated campgrounds. "Smoking is prohibited while traveling." - Camp stoves on bottled fuel are allowed in areas cleared "for 50 feet in all directions". While traveling, except on state highways, county roads and driveways, carry "one shovel and one gallon of water or one 2½ pound or larger fire extinguisher" (p. 2): on foot, a small shovel and a gallon among your bottles (rule of thumb). - The 2026 closure began May 15; ODF reissues it yearly. Treat June through October as no-fire months whether or not anyone says so (rule of thumb). Illegal outdoor burning can cost $12,000 a day (DEQ, p. 1). Where a fire is allowed (wet season or a legal fire ring): keep it small and off slopes; drown it, stir, and feel the ashes until "all steaming and sizzling stops"; "Never just bury a fire" (ODFW hunter manual, p. 34). Never burn poison oak: the smoke can put people in "intensive care" (OSU PNW 108, p. 4).
fire-and-fire-season

A quiet, hidden camp Kephart's "masked camp" is "invisible from trails, and from opposite ridges", screened by evergreens so smoke and firelight don't show, near a trail but not on it, with dead wood about so there's no noise of chopping, and with the way in and out hidden (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 237–238). Also BLISS: "Blend in", "Low silhouette", "Irregular shape", "Small", "Secluded location" (FM 3-05.70, p. 68). Toilet: a "cat hole" 6–8 inches deep, at least 200 ft from camp and water (NPS North Cascades, p. 1); more in the Sanitation guide.
a-quiet-hidden-camp

Food storage in bear country - Hang it: ODFW says "at least 10 feet high and 6 to 10 feet from a tree trunk" (ODFW bears, p. 2); BLM on the Rogue says twelve feet "between two trees and six feet from tree trunks" (BLM, p. 16). Use 10–12 ft up and 6 ft out, on a line between two trees, with food, pots, garbage and anything scented. Carry at least 50 ft of cord (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). - "Sleep at least 100 yards from cooking and eating areas"; no food, soap or lotion in the tent; "Do not bury garbage—bears will dig it up"; "Avoid berry patches"; "Don't hike after dark" (ODFW bears, p. 2).
food-storage-in-bear-country
