Poison oak, ticks and rattlesnakes - Poison oak is common in western Oregon in brush, woods, clearcuts, stream banks and canyons, as a shrub or vine, usually with three leaflets, red in fall (OSU PNW 108, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ photos, p. 3). The oil is in every part but the pollen, all year, bare winter stems too. It rides on clothes, packs, firewood and dogs: "Wash your skin with soap and water as soon as possible", wash clothes separately, wash the dog (p. 4). No water: wipe with dirt or sand, but not over blisters (FM 21-76, p. 132). - Ticks: check your whole body often (AFH, p. 70); pull a tick straight out with fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin, with no nail polish, petroleum jelly or heat (🖼️ CDC, p. 50). More in "Disease and safety" in the Hunting guide. - Rattlesnakes: no hands into crevices, heavy brush or hollow logs; "Don't step over a fallen tree. Step on the log and look" (FM 3-05.70, p. 531). Bites: "Rattlesnakes, spiders and stings" in Field Care (no cutting, sucking, ice or tourniquet).
poison-oak-ticks-and-rattlesnakes
🌊 River and creek crossings "The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated." Treat every stream as a danger and avoid it if you can (TC 3-97.61, p. 343).
river-and-creek-crossings

When not to cross - Knee-deep is the limit for one person, in "mild to moderate" current only. Swift water runs over 5 ft a second, about walking speed (arithmetic) (TC 3-97.61, p. 345). "Six inches of fast-moving water can knock you off" your feet (Spotter guide, p. 12). - Our rivers are cold all year. A fall in brings "involuntary gasping", and cold water "drains body heat 25 times faster than cold air" (OSMB, p. 17). In very cold water, "Wade across if you can get only your feet wet"; otherwise find another way (FM 3-05.70, p. 296). - Never cross above rapids, falls or a logjam. Logjams and fallen trees ("strainers", "sweepers") let water through but trap people (OSMB, p. 14; AFH, p. 496). - Wait for the water to drop. Snow-fed streams run lowest in early morning (TC 3-97.61, p. 343). After heavy winter rain, wait a day or more; a bridge is worth a long detour (rule of thumb). "Not every river or stream can be crossed safely. If it is possible, cross at a different time or place, use a different technique, or choose another route" (p. 351).
when-not-to-cross

Picking the spot and getting ready Look from high ground first. Cross where the river widens, usually shallower; avoid bends (the outside is deep and fast) and narrows; choose low banks (TC 3-97.61, pp. 343–344). Below the crossing you want a shallow bar to wash up on, not rapids (FM 3-05.70, p. 295). Riffles in a line mean rocks; a hump and drop behind a rock is a "hole" that sucks at your feet (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). Then (TC 3-97.61, p. 344 unless noted): 1. Sleeping bag, dry clothes and food in waterproof bags (trash bags work), dry clothes on top. 2. Socks and insoles off and stowed; boots back on for grip. 3. Pack high and snug, then unbuckle the waist and chest straps so you can get out of it if swept off your feet. "Unbuckle your pack straps ... Never tie yourself in while you cross" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). 4. The Army normally keeps clothes on, with dry ones packed. In our cold water, keep them on and change on the far bank (rule of thumb). 5. A stout pole about 3 in thick and 7–8 ft long (FM 3-05.70, p. 297). 6. A lookout 50–100 m upstream for floating logs, and someone downstream with a pole or rope to throw (TC 3-97.61, p. 351).
picking-the-spot-and-getting-ready

Crossing alone (TC 3-97.61, p. 345; 🖼️ Fig. 13-1 on the same page.) 1. Face slightly across the current; in strong current, turn more side-on and lean upstream. 2. Plant the pole upstream of you as a third leg, and probe with it. 3. Aim slightly downstream; going straight across fights the current. 4. Lead with the downstream foot in small steps; never move one foot until the other is set, and never cross your legs. 5. Step on the upstream side of rocks; the downstream side is scoured and the rock may roll. 6. On the far bank, drain your boots and put on dry socks (p. 344).
crossing-alone

Crossing as a group - Know who can't swim before you start (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). - Chain: side by side facing the far bank, arms linked, the biggest person upstream leaning into the current. Conga line: all face upstream, each holding the clothes or pack behind the shoulders of the person upstream. Wedge: the biggest at the upstream point, small people and the injured in the middle (pp. 346–347). One person calls each step. If someone loses control, don't cling so hard that the whole line goes down (p. 346). - Rope handline: stretched across at 30–45° downstream; cross on its downstream side, one at a time (p. 348; 🖼️ pp. 349–350). Taking the rope over first is the most dangerous job: the strongest swimmer, belayed, in a life jacket if you have one (pp. 347–348). Never tie directly into a rope in moving water; you must be able to let go (p. 348). - If you're swept away: shed the pack; face downstream, feet up in front to fend off rocks, and "work with the flow of water" toward the nearest bar; keep away from eddies. Get out and get warm fast: "Hypothermia will set in quickly in colder waters" (pp. 350–351).
crossing-as-a-group

❄️ Snow and the passes - Stay off the passes in storms and deep snow: snow can fall any month above 5,000 ft (FM 3-97.6, p. 15), and the back-road routes climb into country that holds snow into spring ("high passes can get snow", Start Here). In winter take the lower highway route or wait for a clear spell (rule of thumb). - Walking on snow: best is snow that holds you, next best calf-deep; avoid thigh-deep. Go early after a cold night, while the crust holds (AFH, p. 467). - Snowshoes: bend a sapling about 1 in thick and 5 ft long into a loop about 12 in wide and lace it with cord; in a pinch, lash pine boughs together at the cut ends and tie them on (AFH, pp. 255–256; 🖼️ TC 21-3, p. 52). Take them off when the snow holds you (AFH, p. 468). - Sunglasses against snow blindness (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). In fog or with snow over the trail, use the compass and pace count in the Navigation guide. Avalanche signs. Our danger is mostly on steep, open slopes and gullies high up after big storms (rule of thumb). - Most slides start on slopes of 30–45°; slab avalanches cause about 90% of deaths (AFH, p. 431). Watch winds of 15 mph or more, and the time during and just after storms (p.
snow-and-the-passes

on slopes of 30–45°; slab avalanches cause about 90% of deaths (AFH, p. 431). Watch winds of 15 mph or more, and the time during and just after storms (p. 433). - Slide paths: "Steep, open gullies and slopes, pushed over small trees, trees with limbs broken off, and tumbled rocks" (AFH, p. 434); "broken tree stumps at different heights" (TC 21-3, p. 46). - Danger now: "If the snow echoes or sounds hollow, conditions are dangerous. If the snow cracks and the cracks persist or run, the danger of a slab avalanche is imminent" (AFH, p. 434). - Crossing: one at a time, never tied together, each trailing a line about 100 ft long. If caught: drop the pack, "use swimming motions" toward the side, get an arm up, make a breathing space. Buried people have about a 50% chance after 30 minutes, so dig fast (p. 435).
snow-and-the-passes

🛡️ Safety on the road This is about avoiding trouble, calming it, and turning back. Fighting and patrolling are outside these guides. - Together, by day: "Don't travel or hunt alone" (NY hunter manual, p. 80); "Don't hike after dark" (ODFW bears, p. 2). - Low profile: a pack with "nothing exposed to advertise your mission" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 108); earth tones that "blend into your surroundings" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). Don't show food, tools or weapons; spread valuables among the packs (rule of thumb). - Most people are like you: in American disasters looting has been "very rare", though massive in some catastrophes abroad (Quarantelli, p. 12). - Meeting strangers (AFH, pp. 168–169): if you can, "wait until only one person is near and, if possible, let that person make the initial approach". "Displaying fear, displaying weapons, and making sudden or threatening movements" can "prompt a hostile response". Smile; "Approach them slowly and don't rush matters." Keep any promise; don't enter a house uninvited. What to say: "Don't be a target" in Home & Property Protection.
safety-on-the-road

Checkpoints and roadblocks No book on the drive covers these from the traveler's side; these steps are (rule of thumb): 1. Stop well short, in daylight and plain view. Never approach at night or try to slip around. 2. One person walks forward slowly, hands empty and visible; the rest wait. 3. Say who you are, where you're going and why, and ask to pass. Offer road news. 4. Keep your voice low and give them space ("Someone at the gate, strangers, or a break-in" in Home & Property Protection; De-escalation, p. 15). 5. Don't argue or force it. If refused, thank them and turn back or go another way. Pass towns by day; camp well away. Share freely (rule of thumb): bridges out, safe fords, fire and smoke, water, sickness on the road, weather. Keep to yourself: how many live at home, what you carry, where your cache is, when you'll be back, and whether you are armed. Oregon law on force is in Home & Property Protection.
checkpoints-and-roadblocks

📡 Staying in touch and trail signs - Radios: section 5, "FRS / GMRS / MURS", of the Radio guide. No radio: the Signals guide covers whistles, mirrors and "Runners, relays and written messages"; no signal fires June–October. Agree on whistle signals before you leave (stop, come here, help), as the Army settles its sound signals in advance (FM 21-18, p. 47). - Signs for people behind you: one stone set on another, a twig broken and left hanging, or a tuft of grass tied in a knot all mean "this is the trail" (Seton, p. 267; 🖼️ chart, p. 268). "All trails should be marked" (AFH, p. 429). - Notes at forks and camps: a dated note in a jar under a small cairn: names, date, which way, all well or not (rule of thumb). Write nothing you wouldn't want a stranger to read.

🆘 Getting lost Follow "Getting un-lost" in the Navigation guide: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Before leaving each place, "study their backtrail carefully" (AFH, p. 429). "If you get lost, the best thing you can do is stay put and wait", using a whistle, bright clothing or a mirror (NPS North Cascades, p. 1), but that works only if someone has your trip plan and will come. If no one will, walk a bearing to a big handrail such as US-199 or the Illinois River ("Terrain association" in the Navigation guide).

🚲 Bicycles, Carts & Hauling Without Fuel When the gas runs out, everything you move goes on your back, on wheels you push, or on a bicycle. This guide covers how much one person can move and how fast, travel times from Cave Junction, loading a bike, building a trailer (welded steel or no-weld pallets), hitches and trailer brakes, wheelbarrows and handcarts, hills, keeping a bike running with few tools, spares to stock, and local hazards. The books are in Bicycles-Carts\ (Bicycle-Repair and Trailers-Carts). Pack animals, wagons and harness are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ and the Horse guide; brazing and forge work are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ and the Blacksmithing guide. Know the limits of the books. The repair manuals date from 1896 to 1978. Their methods for tubes, tyres, spokes, cup-and-cone hubs, chains and steel frames still work. But the library has little on modern parts: hydraulic disc brakes, tubeless tyres, indexed ("click") shifting, suspension and e-bikes. Stock their spares (pads, bleed kit and fluid, sealant, cables) now. A plain steel bike with rim brakes is the easiest to keep running (rule of thumb). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - A loaded bike takes longer to stop (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike

p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike downhill (rule of thumb). - Don't wreck your body. A normal day load on your back is 10–20 kg (22–44 lb); 50 kg (110 lb) only for short distances (World Bank, p. 65). Put heavy loads on wheels. - Never ride a kinked frame tube or fork. A buckled tube is weakened and must be replaced (Burr, p. 73). Keep at least 2 in of seat post inside the frame (Henry, p. 54). - Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors, away from flames. - Fire season (June–October): don't drag metal. A chain or trailer part scraping on rock can start a wildfire. Haul in the cool early morning and carry water (rule of thumb). - Braze outdoors, and only steel frames. Brass gives off zinc fumes. Aluminium and carbon frames cannot be brazed.

🗺️ Travel times from Cave Junction Walking pace with a load (FM 21-18, p. 89): on roads 4.0 km/h (2.5 mph) by day, 3.2 km/h at night; cross-country 2.4 km/h by day, 1.6 km/h at night. A normal day is 20–32 km (12–20 mi), or 5–8 hours on the move. - Rest 15 minutes after the first 45 minutes, then 10 minutes in every hour (FM 21-18, p. 48). - At halts, lie down with your feet up. Carry spare socks; tape known hot spots before they blister (FM 21-18, p. 101; 🖼️ photo of friction blisters; Blister). In hills, plan by time, not miles. Add one-third to the map distance, then 1 hour for every 1,000 ft (300 m) of climb, or every 2,000 ft (600 m) of descent (FM 3-97.6, p. 72). 🎒 Loading a bicycle How to load it (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97): - Touring cyclists usually carry 30–50 lb, on the bike — a backpack makes balance harder. (Bicycle touring) - Put heavy items low in the panniers and split the load front and rear. Too much weight in front spoils the steering. - A loaded bike needs lower gears, sways more and takes longer to stop. Practise with the load before a real trip. Making a bike carry more (Practical Action, Bicycles): - Panniers can be sacks or baskets hung from wood across the carrier, or a light steel frame. Keep the sides balanced, and strengthen the carrier (p. 2; 🖼️ pannier frame drawing; Pannier). - The load is limited by the rear wheel and tyre; a stronger rear wheel helps (p. 3). - Longer carrier without cutting the frame: bolt on extra stays and move the rear wheel back about 250 mm (10 in). The chain and brake rods must be lengthened (p. 3; 🖼️ extension drawings). - A small 20-inch rear wheel is stronger, keeps the load low and makes pedalling easier, but handles potholes worse (p. 4; 🖼️ drawing). Pushing big loads: in Zambia, people pushed two 50 kg sacks of maize on one bicycle up to 30 km (19 mi) to town (Bicycle Trailers in Zambia, p. 1). Before a loaded trip (rule of

🛒 Bicycle trailers: welded steel or no-weld pallets A trailer lets a rider move about three times the bike's own load, roughly 200 kg (450 lb) (Practical Action, Bicycle Trailers, p. 1). But not always. In northern Ghana, trailers promoted in the 1990s failed: heavy to pull loaded, poor on footpaths, and twice the cost of a bicycle. A plain bike with a strong carrier was more flexible (World Bank, p. 39). Welded steel trailer (Bicycle Trailers, pp. 3–4; frame drawings: 🖼️ p. 2, 🖼️ p. 3): - Frame: 19 mm (3/4 in) mild-steel square tube, or round tube at least 22 × 1.5 mm (25 × 1.5 mm is better). Reinforce each joint with a piece of tube or bar inside it. - Ordinary bike wheels are fine for light loads on good roads, but not for heavy loads on rough tracks. Use strengthened wheels (p. 4). - A local welder in Zambia built these from the drawings for about $100 each (Zambia report, p. 1). No-weld pallet trailer — about one day and about 20 euros (Low-tech Lab). You need 2 pallets, 2 bicycle wheels, wood screws and 1 old inner tube; a crowbar, hammer, saw and screwdriver. 1. Decide what it must carry. Keep it no wider than 1 m (39 in) (p. 3). 2. Take the pallets apart with the crowbar and hammer (p. 3). 3.

1. Decide what it must carry. Keep it no wider than 1 m (39 in) (p. 3). 2. Take the pallets apart with the crowbar and hammer (p. 3). 3. Build the frame from the centre outward. The side boards must be as thick as the wheel so they frame it (p. 4; 🖼️ the numbered boards; Pallet). 4. Fix the wheels before the outer boards go on (p. 5). 5. Hitch it to the bike's rear rack with the inner tube (p. 6). Hitches (Bicycle Trailers, p. 4; 🖼️ hitch design; 🖼️ Poston's scrap-steel hitch): - Hitch above the rear wheel, to the carrier or the frame under the seat. It is simpler than an axle-level hitch, works on earth roads, and lets the trailer double as a handcart. - The recommended joint is a rubber ball in a steel socket. - Any hitch must hold the load, let the bike lean, come off easily, and take braking and pulling forces from every direction (Low-tech Lab, p. 6). Trailer brakes and carrying the injured (Bicycle Ambulance, pp. 2–3; 🖼️ frame diagram): a stretcher trailer carries two people, with a shock absorber and a ball-joint hitch so the bike can turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No

turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No trailer brake? 🛞 Wheelbarrows, handcarts, sledges and travois A better wheelbarrow (Wilson, The Wheelbarrow): - Use one large wheel with most of the load directly over it. Leave little weight on the handles, and take that with a shoulder strap. The traditional Chinese barrow built this way carried up to six people (p. 1). - A homemade barrow wheel can run on a standard bicycle axle and cone bearings, with a solid tyre of strips cut from old car tyres (p. 2; 🖼️ wheel drawing). - Choose air-filled tyres (adjust pressure for rough ground), keep the load low, and make several light trips rather than one heavy one (USFS Handtools for Trail Work, p. 42, with 🖼️ wheelbarrow drawings). Handcarts: - A balanced handcart, with most of the weight on the wheels, is easier than a one-wheel barrow (World Bank, p. 65). - A good load cart has a low centre of gravity, a wide wheelbase and big wheels. Pulled carts are easier to control on rough ground. A cart pulled from a hip belt finished a 3.2 km mixed course 54% faster than people carrying rucksacks. The carts were noisy in brush and rock, and gear caught in the wheels — so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones

so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones (Starkey, p. 85; 🖼️ big wheel vs small wheel in a rut; 🖼️ cart wheel, hub and bearing, labeled; Handcart). Sledges are cheap and narrow, and go where carts can't — too steep, muddy or narrow. But they pull harder, snag on stumps, and their ruts turn into gullies (Starkey, p. 83; 🖼️ simple wooden sledge; Sled). Travois (behind a horse or mule): two straight poles 14–20 ft long with a platform 2–3 ft wide behind the animal, and three people to handle it at ditches and streams (FM 25-7, p. 166; 🖼️ travois drawing). 📚 Go deeper: Wilson The Wheelbarrow — the big-wheel barrow and a homemade wheel; Wheelbarrow construction drawings — six dimensioned sheets for a steel barrow; Selvidge, p. 104 — replacing a wagon spoke, and p. 95 — shrinking on an iron tyre. ⛰️ Hills and grades The extra push on a slope is roughly the total weight times the grade (rule of thumb, simple physics). A 10% grade rises 10 ft for every 100 ft along the road (Grade)). | Grade | Extra push for a 220 lb (100 kg) load | | 5% | about 11 lb | | 10% | about 22 lb | | 15% | about 33 lb | That is on top of the push needed on the flat. (Rules of thumb:) - Pushing much over 25–30 lb for long is very tiring. - On grades over about 10%, use two people (one pulling with a rope or hip belt), or split the load. - A loaded bike on a steep Forest Service road is often faster walked and pushed than ridden. - Going down: a trailer with no brake shoves the bike. Slow down at the top, not halfway. Drag a foot or add a brake. On a handcart, put someone behind holding back on a rope. 📚 Go deeper: Knapik Load Carriage — terrain factors and energy cost; FM 3-97.6 — moving in steep country.

🩹 Flat tyres: patching tubes and booting tyres Patching a tube (Henry, pp. 61–65): 1. Before you take the tyre off, mark where it sits against the valve, or count spokes from the valve, so you can find the thorn later (p. 63). 2. Lever one side of the tyre off and pull the tube out. Careless levering tears the tube (p. 64; Tire lever, Inner tube). 3. Find the leak: pump the tube up a little and listen or feel near your face, or dunk it in water and watch for bubbles (p. 64). 4. Find the cause: feel inside the tyre at the matching spot for the thorn (p. 64). 5. Roughen around the hole with sandpaper (p. 65). 6. Coat tube and patch with rubber cement. Wait about 10 minutes until it is tacky (p. 65). 7. Press the patch on hard, dust with talc ("French chalk") and refit the tube dry (p. 65). Tips: old inner tubes make good patch rubber (p. 61). A patch kit more than a year old may have gone bad (p. 62). If a tyre goes soft with no hole, check the valve first (p. 62). Tyres lose 10–20 psi within a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch

a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch cut from an old tyre (Henry, p. 70). - Fill small tread cuts with leather dust (rasped from scrap leather) mixed into rubber cement (Henry, p. 69). - A modern road kit: two denim boots about 1 × 2 in, 6 patches, 2 tyre levers, a spare tube, talc and a pressure gauge (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). 📚 Go deeper: Henry Cycle Building and Repairing — tyres, tubes, valves and repairs; Adult Cycling Manual — the tool and tyre kit. 🔩 Wheels, hub bearings and chains Truing a wobbly wheel (Henry, pp. 44–46; 🖼️ truing a wheel in its own fork with chalk; Wheelbuilding): 1. Spin the wheel in the frame and hold chalk beside the rim so it marks the spots that stick out. 2. A spoke pulls the rim toward its own side of the hub. At each chalk mark, tighten the spokes that run to the other side of the hub, a little at a time, with a spoke (nipple) key. 3. Fix out-of-round the same way: tighten spokes at the high spots, loosen them at the low spots. 4. File off spoke ends that poke through the nipples, or they will puncture the tube. 5. Replace broken spokes one at a time, so you keep the lacing pattern (🖼️ lacing drawing; Spoke). Hub bearings (Henry, pp. 46–47; 🖼️ hub parts named; 🖼️ cup, cone, balls and locknut, with how to hold the spanners): - A clicking wheel usually has a broken ball or worn cones. Open the hub; clean cups, cones and axle in kerosene. - Throw away chipped balls. Take a sample ball when you look for new ones. - Grease the cups, put the balls back, screw the cone up tight, then back it off about half a turn. Twisted by its spokes, the wheel should spin freely with almost no side play. Chains:
wheels-hub-bearings-and-chains

balls back, screw the cone up tight, then back it off about half a turn. Twisted by its spokes, the wheel should spin freely with almost no side play. Chains: - Soak a filthy chain in kerosene for 2–3 days, hang it to drip, wipe it, then oil it (Henry, p. 52). - To shorten an old riveted chain, file off the burred pin heads and punch the pins out (Henry, p. 53; 🖼️ chain links drawn; 🖼️ putting a chain on). - Modern chains need a chain tool: push the pin almost out, leaving about 1/32 in in the side plate so it can go back in. A chain wears out in 1–2 years of average use, and a new chain may skip on a worn freewheel, so the two often need replacing together (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 104; Freewheel). 📚 Go deeper: Henry — lacing and truing wheels, hubs and chains; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 — chain cleaning, oiling and stiff links; Burr Bicycle Repairing — bearings, forks and shop-made tools. 🛑 Brakes, gears and field fixes Rim brakes (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 48; 🖼️ center-pull and side-pull brakes): released, the pads should sit about 1/16 in from the rim, and they should hit the rim before the lever reaches the handlebar. New cables stretch — tighten them again after about a week. Derailleur gears (p. 81; 🖼️ rear derailleur with its screws lettered): won't shift onto the largest cog? Back out its limit (stop) screw. Still short? Take up cable slack with the barrel adjuster. Shifts by itself? Tighten the thumbscrew holding the shift lever. Field fixes: - Bent crank: hold the bike steady and push the crank back with your foot — usually straight enough to finish the trip (Henry, p. 47). - Bent frame tube: a slight bend can be straightened, but a buckled (kinked) tube cannot. Replace it (Burr, p. 73; 🖼️ truing a frame; Bicycle frame). - Broken steel frame tube — braze it over a sleeve (Rowe, pp. 60–61; 🖼️ Burr's drawings of a tube mended over an inner sleeve; Lugged steel frame): 1. File the broken ends smooth and clean them bright, inside and out. 2. Fit a sleeve of light steel tube inside both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it
brakes-gears-and-field-fixes

both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it in a charcoal fire or a blacksmith's forge. At a low red heat, lay on brass spelter and let it flow into the joint. Don't overheat. 5. Work outdoors (zinc fumes). Steel only — aluminium frames (smooth welds, no lugs, often marked 6061 or 7005) and carbon frames cannot be brazed. 📦 Spares to stockpile (Rule of thumb, building on the kit list in the Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34.) - A good floor pump — above all (Bicycle pump) - Tubes and patch kits for every tyre size you own; spare tyres - Chains with spare links; brake pads; inner cables and housing - Spokes in the right lengths for each wheel - Loose bearing balls (3/16 in and 1/4 in are common), grease, chain oil, rim tape, valve cores - Tools: tyre levers, chain tool, spoke key, pressure gauge (Bicycle tools) Match tyres by the ISO number on the sidewall, not by "26 inch." A size like 37-622 means 37 mm wide on a 622 rim (rule of thumb). 🌲 Illinois Valley hazards (Rules of thumb for our area.) - Goatheads (puncturevine) grow in dry, disturbed ground — road edges, driveways, bare lots. Carry extra patches or thorn-resistant tubes. Learn the plant and pull it before it seeds (weed photo list, p. 53; Puncturevine). - Rocky and serpentine Forest Service roads cause pinch flats under load. Run tyres firmer when loaded, and walk the worst rock. (Serpentinite) - Fire season (June–October): keep chains and metal parts from dragging and throwing sparks. Haul in the early morning with plenty of water. - Wet winters wash the oil off chains and rust them. Wipe and re-oil after every rain ride. - Rim brakes stop much worse when wet. Brake earlier; drag them lightly first to wipe the rims. 📚 Go deeper: Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97 — riding a loaded bike safely; Knapik, p. 37 — carts on rough ground.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Homemade rubber cement from rubber dissolved in "benzine" (gasoline or naphtha) (Henry, p. 61). Very flammable, and benzene fumes are toxic. Use bought cement; if you must make it, mix it outdoors, far from any flame. - Boiling a chain in mutton tallow (Henry, p. 52). Hot fat is a fire hazard, and tallow holds grit. Soak in kerosene, wipe, and oil lightly. - Wrapping joints in asbestos cloth or wicking while brazing (Rowe, p. 61; p. 60). Asbestos causes cancer — use wet rags or a sheet-metal shield. Brass spelter gives off zinc fumes that cause "metal fume fever," so braze outdoors. - "Cleaning solvent from gasoline station" in the tool list (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors. - Obsolete parts: single-tube and beaded-edge tyres, cotter-pin cranks (Henry, p. 47) and 1890s frames. Skip those pages; the hub, wheel, patching, brazing and truing methods are still good. - Military load limits of 30–45% of body weight (Knapik, p. 20) are for fit young soldiers. Plan family loads on 10–20 kg. 📚 Go deeper: Henry, p. 46 — the sound old method: hubs cleaned in kerosene; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 — kerosene chain cleaning.

📐 Practical Math, Measuring & Geometry Homestead math with no stores: measuring with your body and a string, mixing by ratio, squaring a foundation, areas, tanks, woodpiles and loads, slopes and heights you can't reach, and the numbers behind water, power and medicine — each with a worked Illinois Valley example. The books are in Math-Measuring\Arithmetic-Geometry (Navy Mathematics courses), Math-Measuring\Measuring-Surveying (USDA surveying, quantities, timber measuring) and Math-Measuring\Units-Tables (NIST unit tables, Army Engineer Field Data); Ray's arithmetic is in Children-Learning\Arithmetic, and FM 5-426 Carpentry and FM 5-125 Rigging in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. The interactive 🔢 Unit converter & calculators page (Unit converter) does the arithmetic, the 🧮 Calculator (basic and scientific) handles any other sum, and this guide shows how to do it with a pencil. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst mistakes - Same units before you multiply. Turn everything into feet (or inches) first. Mixing inches and feet is the commonest error — off by 12, 144 or 1,728 times. - A British or Canadian "gallon" is about 20% bigger than a US gallon (NIST HB 44, p. 8). Check where a recipe or manual came from. - Medicine: only doses printed in the medical books, in mg and mL, never drops. A second person redoes the arithmetic before anyone swallows it. - Loads are heavier than they look. A cubic yard of damp packed earth weighs about 2,600 lb

never drops. A second person redoes the arithmetic before anyone swallows it. - Loads are heavier than they look. A cubic yard of damp packed earth weighs about 2,600 lb (FM 5-34, p. 292). Never stand under a lift. - Measure twice, check a second way, and round the safe way: more posts, a bigger pipe, a smaller dose.

📐 Right angles and layout The 3-4-5 triangle (Pythagorean theorem): from the corner, mark 3 ft along one string and 4 ft along the other; when the marks are exactly 5 ft apart, the corner is square (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 199). Multiples work — 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20 — and bigger is more accurate: never start under 6 ft; use 12-16-20 for a 50 × 100 ft layout (FM 5-426, p. 48). Check the diagonals: a rectangle is square only when both diagonals are equal (same page). For a 20 × 30 ft shed, √(400 + 900) = 36.06 ft (36 ft ⅝ in) each. Hang the lines on batter boards set back from the corners so they survive digging (FM 5-426, p. 46). With a string and stakes (a rope compass): - Bisect a line: swing equal arcs from each end; the line through the crossings halves it at a right angle (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 198). Bisect an angle the same way from its arms (🖼️ p. 199). - Center of a round thing (tank, millstone): bisect two chords; the lines cross at the center (🖼️ p. 200). - Circle: string on a center stake; 10 ft of string gives 62.8 ft around (C = 2πr). - Oval (ellipse) bed or pond, 20 × 12 ft (geometry): two stakes 16 ft apart on the long center

🌲 Heights and distances you can't reach Shadows (similar triangles)): height = your height × tree's shadow ÷ your shadow, at the same moment (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 207). You: 6 ft, 4½-ft shadow; the fir's shadow 48 ft → 6 × 48 ÷ 4.5 = 64 ft. Stick (45°) method (similar triangles): hold a stick upright at arm's length with as much above your fist as from your eye to your fist. Back up until the fist lines up with the base and the stick top with the treetop: your distance from the trunk ≈ the height. A cruiser's stick does the same with printed marks (🖼️ FB 1210, p. 14; Biltmore stick). Abney or clinometer (percent): height = level distance × (top % − base %) ÷ 100, base negative if below your eye. At 66 ft, top +110%, base −8%: 66 × 1.18 = 78 ft. Felling: see the Firewood guide. Width of a river: - Compass: at A, opposite tree B, read B's bearing; walk along the bank until it has changed by 45°. The distance walked = the width (🖼️ FM 5-34, p. 162). - No compass (geometry): from A pace 50 steps along the bank and plant a stick (C), 50 more to D; from D walk straight away from the river until C lines up with B. Those paces = the width.

Thumb jump (rule of thumb): thumb at arm's length, close one eye then the other; it "jumps" along the far hillside. Judge the jump from a known width (a 60-ft barn) and multiply by 10 — arm's length is about ten times the space between your eyes. Check yours on a paced distance. 🏋️ Levers, pulleys and loads Lever: push × your side of the pivot = load × load side. The mechanical advantage is how many times it multiplies your push — 10 lb lifting 100 lb is 10 (FM 5-125, p. 105). A 6-ft bar with the pivot 6 in from the load: 5½ ÷ ½ = 11, so a 100-lb push lifts about 1,100 lb. Block and tackle: count the rope lines holding the moving block — that's the advantage (FM 5-125, p. 110; 🖼️ p. 112). Each sheave adds friction of about 10% of the load (p. 114); pull = (load + friction) ÷ advantage (p. 115). A 600-lb engine on 4 lines over 4 sheaves: (600 + 240) ÷ 4 = 210 lb. A person pulls about 100 lb straight down, 60 lb along the ground (same page): put three on it. Ramps (physics; friction adds more): push ≈ weight × height ÷ ramp length: a 500-lb log up a 12-ft skid onto a 3-ft wagon bed takes 125 lb plus friction (Bicycles & Carts guide). Rope: safe load = breaking strength ÷ at least 4; knots, sharp bends and age cut strength up to 50%. Fiber rope rule: safe tons = diameter in inches squared — ½-in rope = ¼ ton (FM 5-125, p. 20). ⚡ Electricity by the numbers - Watts = volts × amps (NEETS 1, p. 120): a 12-V pump drawing 5 A uses 60 W. - Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms — cover the one you want on the circle (🖼️ NEETS 1, p. 116). A 12-ohm heater on 120 V draws 10 A = 1,200 W. - Watt-hours = watts × hours; 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh (p. 126). The pump 2 hours a day = 120 Wh. - Battery energy = volts × amp-hours. A 12-V, 100-Ah battery is 1,200 Wh on the label, but size a lead-acid bank on only 40% of that (IEA, p. 17): 480 Wh → the pump for 4 days. - Long wires waste power: volts lost = 2 × one-way feet × amps × ohms per 1,000 ft ÷ 1,000. Use the Off-Grid guide's wire table (Voltage drop). - 1 horsepower = 746 W (NIST SP 811, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 1, ch. 3 — Ohm's law, power and energy with practice questions; Off-Grid Power guide — load lists and battery sizing.

💧 Water flow and pressure - Flow by bucket and stopwatch: a 5-gallon bucket in 20 seconds = 5 ÷ 20 × 60 = 15 gpm; a 55-gallon drum in 40 seconds = 82.5 gpm (NCAT, p. 3). - Pressure from height (head): each foot of water = 0.433 psi (DOE, p. 113); each psi = 2.31 ft (NRCan, p. 41). A tank 40 ft above the house gives 17 psi before pipe friction; 60 psi on a gauge at the bottom of a full hose = 139 ft of drop (🖼️ DOE, p. 114). - Suction lift has a hard limit: 21.2 ft at 1,000 ft elevation, 20.4 ft at 2,000 ft (USDA FB 1448, p. 28). At our ~1,300 ft keep a suction pump within about 20 ft of the water; deeper, the pump goes down the well. A siphon has the same limit. - Creek power: watts ≈ gpm × feet of head ÷ 10, about what NCAT's table of typical outputs shows (NCAT, p. 9): 30 gpm falling 50 ft ≈ 150 W, day and night. 💊 Food, medicine and time math A year's food: people × calories a day × days, at 2,100 kcal per person a day and about 1,500 kcal per pound of dry grain (Food Security guide): 4 × 2,100 × 365 = 3,066,000 kcal ≈ 2,000 lb of grain-equivalent for a family of 4. Days of supply = stock ÷ daily use: 50 lb of flour at 1½ lb a day = 33 days. ### ⚠️ Medicine arithmetic — read this first - Use only doses printed in the medical books (Medical guide; WTND green pages). This is arithmetic only. - Write the unit on every number — mg, mL, kg. Mixing mg and mL, or lb and kg, kills. - A second person redoes it without seeing yours. If the answers differ, stop. - Never measure medicine in drops or with unchecked kitchen spoons. Dose by weight (mg/kg): kg = lb ÷ 2.2 (WTND ch. 8, p. 4); mg = mg per kg × kg. Made-up numbers, not a real dose for any medicine: 10 mg/kg for a 44-lb child: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg; 20 × 10 = 200 mg; from a liquid with 100 mg in 5 mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5

mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 Tbsp = 15 mL. Household spoons vary — mark one at exactly 5 mL of water from a syringe (🖼️ WTND ch. 8, p. 3). Drops are unreliable: two books here put 64 (USU, p. 20) and 75 (Henley's, p. 706) drops in a teaspoon, before the dropper or liquid changes. Time: "every 8 hours" = 3 times a day; "every 6 hours" = 4. 📚 Go deeper: WTND ch. 8 — grams, milligrams, spoons, child doses; Food and Nutrition Needs in Emergencies — adjusting calories; Field Care guide.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS — how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get — see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-or-death emergency, calling for help on whatever radio you have is generally accepted (the ham rules, 47 CFR §97.405, say nothing in them stops a station in distress from using any means it has). Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

3. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz–3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3–30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun. (🖼️ ground waves and sky waves; 🖼️ layers of the ionosphere; Ionosphere, Skywave) - Skip zone: HF can leave a zone of silence — a nearby station unheard while a far one is loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼️ skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼️ polarization drawing). Handhelds and car
3-how-radio-actually-works-the-60-second-version

loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼️ skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼️ polarization drawing). Handhelds and car whips are vertical — hold the radio upright. 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 10, p. 100 — the ionosphere by day and night; NEETS Module 12 — AM, FM and SSB.
3-how-radio-actually-works-the-60-second-version

4. CB Radio (Citizens Band) — no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1–15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 — traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 — highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1–40 — general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range — but both radios must use the same mode (Single-sideband modulation). - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup (🖼️ common whip antennas; Whip antenna). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — repairing a broken whip antenna (🖼️ repair drawing); Citizens band radio — channels, history and photos.
4-cb-radio-citizens-band-no-license-simple-vehicle-friendly
5. FRS / GMRS / MURS — the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.
5-frs-gmrs-murs-the-walkie-talkie-families

FRS (Family Radio Service) — no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies (Family Radio Service). 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5–2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5–2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.
frs-family-radio-service--no-license

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) — cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters — so range can reach 5–50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy (General Mobile Radio Service).
gmrs-general-mobile-radio-service--cheap-license-no-test

MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) — no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license (Multi-Use Radio Service). - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm. In hill country: use high ground, get clear of buildings and leafy trees (they soak up more signal than evergreens), and keep away from power lines (🖼️ good radio sites; 🖼️ poor radio sites). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 102 — choosing a good radio spot; Walkie-talkie — photos of handheld radios.
murs-multi-use-radio-service--no-license

6. Ham (Amateur) Radio — the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents (Amateur radio; Amateur radio emergency communications).
6-ham-amateur-radio-the-serious-emergency-option

Licensing (USA) — easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public — you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician — entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General — adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra — full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true life-or-death emergency, calling for help without a license is generally accepted (see 47 CFR §97.405) — but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.
licensing-usa--easier-than-you-think

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144–148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420–450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night — great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.
the-main-ham-bands-and-what-they-do

Repeaters — how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area (Repeater).
repeaters--how-hams-get-range-from-a-handheld

Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex — directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz. Wilderness protocol: back-country hams listen and call on 146.52 for 5 minutes at the top of the hour, every 3 hours from 7 AM to 7 PM, so someone beyond a repeater can be relayed (ARRL manual, p. 84).
simplex-radio-to-radio-no-repeater

HF from a valley: "NVIS" A wire dipole hung low — 1/10 to 1/4 of a wavelength up (roughly 25–60 ft on 80m, worked from the formula in section 8) sends its signal almost straight up; it comes back down like a fountain over a few hundred miles with no skip zone, and the hills matter much less (FM 24-18, p. 279; 🖼️ the "fountain" drawing; 🖼️ Army NVIS antennas; Near vertical incidence skywave).
hf-from-a-valley-nvis

Nets A net is a scheduled on-air meeting. In a directed net a net control station says who talks next. Listen first, check in when invited, keep a log, and tell net control if you leave (ARRL manual, p. 7, 18).
nets

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice (Winlink, FT8, APRS). 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 14 — ARES, traffic nets and RACES; FM 24-18, p. 278 — NVIS in full.
ham-digital--data-advanced-fyi

7. Shortwave (SWL) — hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8–30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away — because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400–162.550 MHz) — continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) — to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception (🖼️ long-wire antenna drawing). - NOAA Weather Radio: repeats every 4–6 minutes; a SAME radio set to your county code wakes up only for your county's alerts (NOAA brochure, p. 2; Specific Area Message Encoding). - No batteries at all: a crystal radio — wire, a homemade coil, a crystal detector and headphones — hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4; 🖼️ wiring diagram and
7-shortwave-swl-hearing-the-outside-world

coil, a crystal detector and headphones — hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4; 🖼️ wiring diagram and parts). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 120 — build a crystal set step by step; NBS Circular 121 — a sharper version.

8. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk. - EMP and solar storms: in government tests, most ham equipment wasn't damaged when its power cord was unplugged and the antenna coax disconnected (NCS TIB 85-10, p. 166) — more in the EMP Guide.
8-antennas-power-range-the-practical-stuff

Build a wire antenna (half-wave dipole) Total length in feet = 468 ÷ MHz (3–50 MHz; FM 24-18, p. 47), cut in two equal halves with the coax at the center. 3.980 MHz (Oregon Emergency Net): 117.6 ft · 7.2 MHz: 65 ft · 14.3 MHz: 32.7 ft. Look first: 🖼️ center-fed wire antenna between two supports, 🖼️ improvised half-wave doublet, 🖼️ how a dipole radiates. 1. Any wire works in an emergency; copper or aluminum is best. 2. Insulators at the ends and center — plastic or glass (plastic spoons, bottle necks) beat wood or rope. The wire must touch nothing else (FM 24-18, p. 55; 🖼️ improvised insulators; Insulator)). 3. Tie one end through a spring or strip of inner tube so swaying trees don't snap it. 4. Adjust length and height for the strongest signal from a distant station. ⚠️ Transmitter off before touching the antenna — it can cause serious injury (p. 56). For 2m/70cm, a J-pole from TV twin-lead is cheap (ARRL manual, p. 12; 🖼️ what twin-lead looks like; Twin-lead). Rocky mountain ground is a poor ground, so use a dipole, or a vertical with a counterpoise — wires spread just above the ground (FM 24-18, p. 144; 🖼️ wire counterpoise; 🖼️ ground-plane antenna). Set up high on a slope, not in a ravine, and away from your own generator and battery charger —
build-a-wire-antenna-half-wave-dipole

(FM 24-18, p. 144; 🖼️ wire counterpoise; 🖼️ ground-plane antenna). Set up high on a slope, not in a ravine, and away from your own generator and battery charger — they add noise (p. 102–103). Batteries: a car battery survives only about 20 deep discharges; deep-cycle batteries take 1,000 or more, and shallow use lasts far longer (about 800 cycles at 80% discharge vs 6,000 at 20%). Recharge stored sealed batteries about every 3 months. Charging batteries give off hydrogen — no sparks or flames (Practical Action, p. 5–6). Lightning: a lightning switch grounds the antenna whenever you're not using it — No. 14 or heavier copper wire to a water pipe or ground rod, never a gas pipe (NBS Circular 120, p. 8; Lightning arrester). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — field repair and expedient antennas; NEETS Module 10 — how antennas work.

9. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info (Mayday, Pan-pan). - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials — slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.
9-how-to-call-for-help-procedure

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero"). (NATO phonetic alphabet)
nato-phonetic-alphabet

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in. (Procedure word) 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 58 — procedure words, phonetic alphabet, signal reports; Pub 102, pp. 148–149 — the international voice distress procedure, with worked Mayday examples.
common-pro-words

10. Passing messages for others Much of radio's work after a disaster is carrying short messages for people with no radio. Send in this order (ARRL manual, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life and death — when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY (important, time-limited) → WELFARE ("Is my family OK?" / "All well here") → ROUTINE (last). - Write the message down first and count the words, so the receiver can check it (🖼️ a filled-in radiogram, part by part). - Ready-made welfare texts include "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." (🖼️ blank welfare message form) - Log the time, station, frequency and message. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 33–34 — welfare form, standard texts, how to write a radiogram; ICS 213 General Message form — the standard paper form emergency offices use.
10-passing-messages-for-others

11. When the radio can't reach: signals without one - Three of anything means distress: three fires in a triangle, three columns of smoke, three shots (FM 21-76, p. 238–243). In wildfire country keep signal fires small, cleared around and watched (rule of thumb). - A whistle is usually heard within about 200 yards (a few reports claim up to a mile — AFH 10-644, p. 509); a mirror is the best signal on a sunny day (🖼️ aiming a signal mirror). SOS: three short, three long, three short (SOS). - Ground-to-air symbols in a clearing: V = need help · X = need medical help · N = no · Y = yes · arrow = going this way. Make them at least 6 m (20 ft) long (the two Army manuals differ on width) (FM 3-05.70, p. 329; 🖼️ the symbols drawn). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-05.70, p. 318 — signaling devices and how to use them; Signals and Morse guide — mirrors, ground symbols, Morse by light and sound; AFH 10-644, p. 509 — the Air Force signaling chapter, with pictures.

A sensible emergency radio kit (shopping / checklist) - [ ] NOAA weather radio (hand-crank/solar + battery) — alerts & forecasts. - [ ] Shortwave receiver with SSB — hear news & ham traffic worldwide (RX only). - [ ] A pair+ of GMRS radios (and a GMRS license) — family/group, best bang for buck. FRS works with no license at shorter range. - [ ] A dual-band (2m/70cm) ham handheld (HT) — cheap; huge capability with a Technician license. Add a better antenna. - [ ] (Advanced) An HF ham radio + General license — true long distance. - [ ] CB if you travel by vehicle/convoy. - [ ] Power: spare batteries, 12V battery, solar panel, car charger (Solar panel). - [ ] Better antennas + coax; a roll of wire for an HF/long-wire antenna (Coaxial cable). - [ ] Printed frequency card (below), local repeater list, notebook & pencil. - [ ] Go-bag extras: earphone, mag-mount antenna, 50 ft of coax with barrel connectors, alkaline pack for the handheld. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 10–12 — basic and 72-hour go-kit checklists; Amateur Radio Emergency Service — how volunteer emergency hams are organized.

📡 Signals, Morse Code & Messages How to get a message across with no phones and no working radio: learning Morse by ear, sending it by lamp, whistle, flag or smoke, calling for help from the ground to an aircraft, mirrors and signal fires (and their danger in fire season), semaphore, alarm codes, runners, message forms, a neighborhood OK/HELP card plan, and what to listen to. Radios: the Radio guide and the Radio-Weather folder. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Three of anything means "help" — three fires, three blasts, three shots. Use threes for nothing else (FM 3-05.70, p. 318). - No signal fires or "tree torches" in fire season (roughly June–October). In our dry summers they can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling. Use a mirror, cloth panels, ground symbols and sound instead. - Learn only today's 5-symbol ground code: V = need help, X = need medical help (Pub 102, p. 144; 🖼️ the five symbols drawn). An old Army code in the library uses X for "unable to proceed". - Never hold a mirror flash on a pilot's cockpit for more than a few seconds — it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. few seconds — it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. The 1911 Scout handbook prints old American Morse, different for many letters. - Agree every alarm signal in advance, and use the alarm bell or horn for nothing else (FM 24-5, p. 129).

👂 Learning Morse by ear Morse is sounds, not dots on paper. Think of each letter as a sound ("di-dah" is A), never count dots and dashes, and practice by whistling or saying the sounds aloud (TM 11-459, pp. 3–5). Two proven methods (Pierpont, pp. 159–161; pp. 171–172): - Koch method: start with two letters sent fast (12 words per minute or more). Add one new letter at a time, and only when you copy 90% correctly. Don't look at a chart. - Farnsworth method: each letter is always sent at full speed (18–25 wpm), with wide gaps between letters that you close up as you improve. - Both avoid the "10 wpm plateau" of learning slowly (p. 161). - Short sessions work best: Koch recommended two half-hour sessions a day, spread apart; even 45 minutes gave less (p. 160). A 30-day plan (rule of thumb, built on Koch's rules). A partner sends from the table below by whistle or flashlight while you write what you hear. If you fall behind, stretch the plan — accuracy matters more than the calendar. | Days | What to do (two half-hour sessions a day) | | 1–2 | Two letters that sound very different, such as K and M, in random mixes, until you get 9 in 10. | | 3–20 | Add one letter each time you reach 90% on a

Keep mixing in all the letters. | | 26–28 | Procedure signals (AR, K, SK, BT, AS) and the calling routine below. Short real messages. | | 29–30 | Whole messages with your partner, by lamp and by whistle, across a field. | - Send each letter at full speed, even as a beginner — slow down only by leaving longer gaps between letters (TM 11-459, p. 4). - Look-alikes (S/H, U/V, and mirror pairs like B/V, D/U) cause most errors — give the ones you miss extra practice (Pierpont, p. 159). - Copy behind: at higher speeds, let a letter or two go by before writing (TM 11-459, p. 5). - After day 30, ten minutes a day keeps the skill (rule of thumb). 🔦 Morse without a radio: light, sound, flags and smoke - Light: flashlight, lantern or car headlights, with a hat or board as a shutter. Short flash = dot, longer flash = dash (Bluejackets, p. 442). Best at dusk and night. See Signal lamp; aiming a lamp's beam at a far station: 🖼️ FM 24-5 drawing. - Sound: whistle, horn or bugle (Whistle, Bugle) — short blast = dot, long blast = dash. On a drum, one tap = dot, two quick taps = dash. Sound works in fog and at night (Signal Book 1916, p. 34) but is slow and easily confused — keep to short, pre-agreed messages (Pub 102, p. 17). - Flags or arms: call with "AA AA AA" and end with AR (Pub 102, pp. 19–20). The Army rule: flag swung to your left for a dash, to your right for a dot (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - Smoke: spread a blanket over a smoky fire and lift it off to send short and long puffs (Seton, p. 270). Not in fire season — see the fire section below. See Smoke signal. - Knocking through a wall: Morse, or the 5×5-grid tap code (general practice). | If this goes wrong | Try this (rule of thumb) | | Dots and dashes blur together | Very short dots, long dashes, clear gaps | | They keep missing

🆘 Distress signals and talking to aircraft - Threes: three fires, three columns of smoke, three shots or three whistle blasts mean distress, because nature rarely makes things in threes (FM 3-05.70, p. 318; AFH 10-644, p. 509). - SOS by light, sound or flag: three short, three long, three short, sent as one sound and repeated (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - A flag flown upside down signals distress (Signal Book 1916, p. 41). Body signals to aircraft — stand in the open, move slowly and repeat until understood (FM 21-60, p. 59; 🖼️ the signals drawn): | Signal | Means | | Both arms straight up | "Pick us up" | | One arm up | "All OK, do not wait" — easy to confuse with the one above, so be deliberate | | Lying on your back, arms stretched overhead | "Need medical assistance" | | Arms waving, crossed overhead | "Do not land here" | | Cloth waved up and down / side to side | Yes / No | | Arms out to the sides, slowly raised and lowered again and again | Official distress signal (Pub 102, p. 140) | How a plane says "understood" (Pub 102, p. 144; AFH 10-644, p. 518): it rocks its wings by day, or flashes its landing or navigation lights twice at night (or flashes Morse T or R).

The Army manuals disagree (4 m × 6 m in FM 3-05.70, p. 329; 1 m × 6 m in FM 21-76, p. 243) — bigger is always better. 2. Straight lines and square corners — nature has none. 3. High, open ground seen from every side — a field, a river gravel bar, a logged ridge (local examples: rule of thumb). 6. 🪞 Signal mirrors The best daytime signal. A mirror flash has been seen up to 100 miles away and it works even on hazy or overcast days (AFH 10-644, p. 509). See Signal mirror. Aiming without a sighting hole (AFH 10-644, pp. 510–511): 1. Hold one arm out and make a V with two fingers, with the plane or distant hill in the V (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ FM 3-05.70 drawing). 2. Tilt the mirror so the bright spot of light lands on your fingers, then work it through the V onto the target. 3. Or line the target up with the top of a 4–5 ft stake, and sight along the mirror's top edge onto the stake top (🖼️ drawing). 4. Keep sweeping the horizon even when nothing is in sight — a pilot may see you first. - No mirror? A can lid, polished metal, foil or a shiny card will do (p. 510). The military mirror with a sighting hole, for comparison: 🖼️ the MK-3 signal mirror. - Don't flash rapidly, and don't hold the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds — it can blind the pilot (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Talking with mirrors: the old Army heliograph flashed Morse by mirror between hilltops; two people on sunny ridges can do the same (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 509–511 —

🔥 Signal fires and smoke — and the wildfire danger What the manuals teach (AFH 10-644, pp. 511–512): - Three fires in a triangle or a line. AFH 10-644 says about 100 ft apart; FM 3-05.70 says 25 m (83 ft) (p. 318). Bright flames at night, lots of smoke by day. - Smoke works best on calm, clear days and has been seen up to 50 miles away. - White smoke (green leaves, moss, wet plants) shows against dark forest. Black smoke (rubber, oily rags, plastic) shows against snow or sky — stay upwind of it (general practice). - Lay the fires before aircraft come, ready to light in seconds. ⚠️ Illinois Valley: June to October, do NOT build signal fires. - Only about 15% of our yearly rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25–30% (NRCS soil survey, p. 5). A tree torch or a spark can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling (Wildfire). - Clearing to bare earth under a tree torch, as the manuals say, is not enough in our brush and grass (AFH 10-644, p. 513; FM 3-05.70, p. 319). - A gasoline smoke pot can explode when lit (AFH 10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a

10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a pole, whistles and horns. - If you must burn (wet season, or truly no choice): a small fire on a cleared, wetted patch, with water, a shovel and a person watching it, put dead out afterward (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 511–514 — fire and smoke signals; Firewood guide — ashes and fire-season burning rules.

🚩 Flags, semaphore and signal stations Simple flag colors (FM 21-60, p. 37; 🖼️ Army flag signals drawn): red = danger; green = all clear / understood; yellow = disregard. At night use colored flashlights. Good for a gate or a lookout. Semaphore spells words with two flags (or bare arms) held at clock positions — by day and in sight only. Pictures: Bluejackets Manual, pp. 444–447 and Flag semaphore; full charts: 🖼️ Bluejackets alphabet, 🖼️ Signal Book 1916 hand-flag chart, 🖼️ FM 24-5 semaphore code. - Letters A to G use one arm stepping around a circle (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 234). - After the numeral sign, A–I mean 1–9 and K means 0. - Always face the receiving station. The receiver stops the sender by holding both arms straight out sideways (Signal Book 1916, pp. 22–23). Siting a flag or lamp station (Signal Book 1916, pp. 43–44): - Stand where the background behind you, as the other station sees it, is one plain color. Use a white flag against green or dark hillsides. - Record the compass bearing to each partner station and drive two aiming stakes in line with it (Compass). - How far you can see to a ground-level object: eye 10 ft up, about 4 miles; 30 ft, about 7; 100 ft, about 13. Ridges around the valley make good relay points (Horizon). 📚 Go

📣 Whistles, bells and alarm codes - Range: most whistle or shout contacts happen within 200 yards, a few at about a mile. A pole banged on a hollow log also carries (AFH 10-644, p. 509). - Rapid strokes of a bell, horn or whistle = "general alarm — act now", no answer needed (Signal Book 1916, p. 38). - Every alarm must be agreed in advance, known to everyone, and used only with good cause (same page). A bell, siren or air horn kept for alarms is never used for anything else (FM 24-5, p. 129; Air horn, Siren)). Visual signals get misunderstood — standardize and practice them (FM 21-60, p. 5). - The 1911 Scout whistle code is a good start: one long blast = "attention, look out for my next signal"; two short = "all right"; a string of short, sharp blasts = "rally, danger, alarm" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 236). 🏃 Runners, relays and written messages Briefing a runner (FM 24-5 (1939), pp. 68, 70) — tell them: - who the message is for and where to find them; - which route, and which danger spots to avoid; - how fast to go, and whether to wait for a reply; - where to report back, and what to do if it can't be delivered. Spoken messages must be short. The runner repeats it back to you and memorizes it (p. 70). Write it down whenever you can. Speeds and relays (FM 24-5, pp. 69, 71–72): a runner covers about 3 mph routine and 5 mph priority (urgent: as fast as they can and still arrive); a rider 6 and 8 mph. On dangerous routes send two runners in sight of each other, each with a copy, or use two routes. Mark routes with arrows at forks. For long, frequent runs, set up relay posts — say, a house halfway to O'Brien (rule of thumb). Use a standard form. The ICS 213 has To, From, Subject, Date, Time (24-hour clock), Message, Approved by, Reply and Replied by. The sender keeps a copy; the reply comes back on the bottom (ICS Forms Booklet, pp. 65–66; 🖼️ the blank form; Incident Command System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram"
runners-relays-and-written-messages

Booklet, pp. 65–66; 🖼️ the blank form; Incident Command System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram" works on paper too (ARRL manual, p. 34): number and precedence, address, text of 25 words or fewer (X for a period), and signature. The "check" is the word count, so the receiver knows nothing was lost (🖼️ a filled-in example, part by part). Precedence (ARRL, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life or death — when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY → WELFARE → ROUTINE. Short codes save time: - "ARL ONE" = "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." "ARL TWO" = "Coming home as soon as possible." (ARRL, p. 39). - One-letter signals you can flash or sound: V = I need assistance; W = I need medical assistance; K = I wish to communicate; N = no; C = yes (Pub 102, p. 26). Note: at sea W means medical help; on the ground the symbol is X. See International Code of Signals; the same letters as ship flags: International maritime signal flags. 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-5 (1939) — messengers, relay posts and a message center; ICS Forms Booklet — print blank 213 and 214 forms now; ARRL manual, pp. 33–39 — radiogram form and numbered texts.

🏘️ The neighborhood OK/HELP plan From the rural edition of Map Your Neighborhood (MYN Rural, pp. 1–2): 1. Pick a Neighborhood Communication Site everyone knows: a mailbox cluster, a crossroads, or a central home or barn. 2. After a disaster, each household takes its OK/HELP card there with name, date and time, plus the kind of help needed, and tapes it up. 3. Anyone who can help writes on the card what they'll do and when, then reports back. 4. Someone checks every home. Who to check first (MYN Discussion Guide, p. 8): HELP homes, then homes with no card — people there may be hurt. Then recheck the OK homes. Print the HELP/OK window card now (🖼️ what it looks like). Your household plan: a meeting place, a way to find each other if separated, and an out-of-area contact, posted at home (Oregon 2 Weeks Ready, p. 6; FEMA, p. 18). Add the neighborhood site, your signal card and a check-in time (rule of thumb). Locally: the county plan counts on door-to-door notice, broadcast stations and amateur radio, and the RVCOG Disaster Registry lists residents needing special help (County EOP, p. 71). Know who they are on your road. 📚 Go deeper: MYN Discussion Guide — the first meeting, 9 steps after a disaster, neighbor map; MYN Rural — rural sites, wells and propane.

📻 Listening when you can't transmit - NOAA Weather Radio repeats its message every 4–6 minutes; a SAME radio wakes up only for your county (NOAA brochure, p. 2; NOAA Weather Radio; Specific Area Message Encoding; Emergency Alert System). For Josephine County program SAME 041033 and try WXL85, 162.400 MHz (Medford). It officially covers eastern Josephine County, and mountain valleys may get poor reception — also try 162.475 and 162.550 and note which works at home (NOAA brochure, p. 3; Illinois Valley guide). - AM reaches farther at night: the layer of the sky that soaks up AM signals by day fades after dark (Navy Basic Electronics, p. 328; 🖼️ layers of the ionosphere; Skywave). Listen for outside news after sunset. - Keep every battery radio in the shelter. Small AM sets with built-in antennas are the most likely to survive an EMP (Nuclear War Survival Skills, p. 35). - Log what you hear (time, station, message) and post news at the Neighborhood Communication Site, so one radio serves the whole road (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NOAA Weather Radio brochure — how SAME alerts work; Radio guide — shortwave, crystal sets and local frequencies.

🧭 Navigation & Weather Without GPS or Forecasts How to find your way in the hills around the Illinois Valley with a paper map and compass — or with neither — and how to read the weather coming when there is no forecast: map reading, declination, pace count, terrain association, finding yourself when lost, the sun and stars, clouds and wind, our local weather from valley fog to east-wind fire days, lightning, and a home weather log. The books are in Navigation-Weather\Land-Navigation and Navigation-Weather\Weather; the local topo maps are in Maps\Topo-USGS and Maps\Forest-Service (see the Maps section of the Illinois Valley guide). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Set your compass to 14° East. Older maps print bigger numbers; always use the newest. Ignoring declination puts you about a quarter mile off for every mile you walk. - Leave a written trip plan with someone who stays home. With no search and rescue, nobody comes unless someone knows your route and your return time (NPS Trip Plan). - When you hear thunder, move: off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, and out of rock overhangs and cave mouths. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1–2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east

Lightning, pp. 1–2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east wind after a front in late summer or fall is extreme fire weather — the pattern behind the September 2020 fires. Be ready to leave. - Sun, watch, moon and moss methods are rough. Check any no-compass direction with a second method before you commit to a long walk.

🗺️ Reading a topo map Scale. The library's local quads (US Topo and FSTopo) are 1:24,000: 1 inch = 2,000 ft (🖼️ using the bar scale; Topographic map). On the 1:100,000 Forest Service sheet, 1 inch is about 1.6 miles. Map distance is "as the crow flies"; walking a steep slope is farther (USGS FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, p. 133). Contour lines (FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, pp. 41–42; Contour line; 🖼️ a contour map beside the land it shows; 🖼️ FM 3-25.26, p. 107): - Brown lines join points of equal height; the heavier, labeled ones are index contours. - Close together = steep. Far apart = gentle. Circles inside circles = a hilltop. - V-shaped bends point uphill and upstream — creeks and draws. - U-shaped bends point down a ridge — spurs and ridge ends. Name the land. 🧭 Compass and declination Use 14° East for the Illinois Valley. NOAA's model gives 13.9° E for Cave Junction in November 2026, shrinking about 0.1° a year. The FSTopo Cave Junction sheet prints 14°8′ (2024) and the US Topo sheet 14°18′ (2023). Older maps print larger numbers — use the newest value. See Magnetic declination. Which way to correct (FS 035-01, p. 2; PMS 475, p. 86): - Here the magnetic north (MN) arrow sits to the right (east) of true north (🖼️ north arrow on a quad; 🖼️ declination diagrams). - Map → compass: subtract 14°. A map bearing of 90° becomes 76° on an unadjusted compass. - Compass → map: add 14°. - Memory aid: "declination east, compass least." - Easiest: set the compass's declination screw to 14° E once and forget it. Why it matters: 1° of error puts you about 920 ft off in 10 miles (PMS 475, p. 86). Ignoring all 14° puts you about 1,300 ft off for every mile (general practice: worked out from the angle). Grid north on the Cave Junction quad is only about half a degree from true north — ignore it on foot. That's why the margin shows three norths (FM 3-25.26, p. 62; 🖼️ three norths). The way back (back azimuth): add 180° if the bearing is 180° or less; subtract 180° if more. A slip here can

norths (FM 3-25.26, p. 62; 🖼️ three norths). The way back (back azimuth): add 180° if the bearing is 180° or less; subtract 180° if more. A slip here can be disastrous — check it twice (FM 3-25.26, p. 58; 🖼️ direct and back bearing). Compass habits (PMS 475, p. 84; FM 3-25.26, p. 97; 🖼️ parts of a compass): - Hold it level at waist height (🖼️ centerhold), take every bearing twice, and walk where the direction-of-travel arrow points, not where your hunch says (🖼️ following a bearing). - Keep away from metal: 55 m (180 ft) from high-voltage lines, 18 m (60 ft) from a truck, 10 m (33 ft) from barbed wire or phone lines, half a meter from a rifle. Belt buckles and clipboards throw it off too. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Finding Your Way — taking a bearing off a topo map; PMS 475, pp. 82–86 — parts of a compass and setting declination.

👣 Pace count: measuring distance on foot (FM 3-25.26, pp. 52–53; PMS 475, pp. 133–134) 1. Measure a 100 m (328 ft) course on ground like where you'll travel — a road shoulder with a tape or a measured fence line works (rule of thumb). 2. Walk it naturally and count your steps. The Army's example is about 120 steps per 100 m. Walk it several times and average. 3. Expect more steps (🖼️ why the ground is longer than the map) uphill, into a headwind, in mud, sand, snow or brush, in rain, and in fog or darkness. 4. Keep a separate, shorter night count (p. 141). 5. Don't try to remember the count. Move a pebble from one pocket to the other, or tie a knot, every 100 m (pace count beads). ⚠️ The Forest Service (NWCG) counts a "pace" as two steps — every time the same foot lands. The Army counts every step. Pick one and never mix them. 📚 Go deeper: PMS 475, p. 133 — pacing worksheet; FM 3-25.26, p. 52 — pace count and other ways to measure distance.

🏞️ Terrain association: handrails, catching features, aiming off Match the map to the ground as you go (🖼️ drawing). It is far more forgiving than walking a compass line, because you keep comparing what you expected to see with what you do see. Pure compass walking piles up errors with every detour (FM 3-25.26, pp. 131, 139). Keep the map turned so its north matches the land (p. 140; 🖼️ by the land; 🖼️ by compass). Plan a route this way (FM 3-25.26, p. 140): - Handrail: a line you follow without careful compass work — a road, stream, ridge or power line. Ours include Hwy 199, the Illinois River and its East and West Forks, the Caves Highway (OR 46), and numbered Forest Service roads on the FSTopo sheets (local: rule of thumb). - Catching feature: something across your path that tells you you've gone too far. - Attack point: a sure landmark no more than about 500 m from the goal. From there, walk an exact bearing and pace count. Aim off on purpose (FM 3-25.26, p. 100; 🖼️ deliberate offset). Heading for a spot on a road or creek, aim about 10° to one side. When you hit the road, you know which way to turn. Each degree moves you about 18 m sideways per 1,000 m walked, so 10° is about 180 m. 📚 Go deeper:

📍 Finding yourself on the map (resection) Resection (FM 3-25.26, p. 68; Position resection; 🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ PMS 475, p. 131): 1. Orient the map. 2. Take compass bearings to two or three landmarks you can name on the map. 3. Turn each into a map bearing (add 14°, unless your compass is already set), then into its back azimuth (±180°). 4. Draw each line back from its landmark. Where they cross is you. Three lines make a small triangle — you are inside it. Local candidates are peaks on the FSTopo sheets such as Grayback Mountain, Kerby Peak and Eight Dollar Mountain — check on the sheet which you can really see from where you stand (rule of thumb). Modified resection (p. 70; 🖼️ drawing): if you know you're on a road, river or ridgeline, one bearing to one landmark is enough. You are where that line crosses your road or ridge. 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26, pp. 68–70 — intersection, resection and modified resection with drawings; PMS 475, p. 131 — finding your own position by triangulation; AFH 10-644, p. 406 — azimuth, biangulation and triangulation.
