🆘 Getting un-lost STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (Today's Hunter, p. 80): 1. Stop. Admit you're turned around. Sit down. 2. Think. Retrace your route in your head: the last place you were sure of, and what you've passed since. 3. Observe. Look for the five terrain features, a peak you can name, the sound of a road or the river. Try a resection. 4. Plan. Pick the nearest big handrail on the map (a road or river) and walk a bearing to it, aiming off so you know which way to turn when you reach it. - If you can't get back before dark, stop early and spend the effort on shelter, warmth and a signal (p. 80; Signals guide). - Staying put only works if someone will come. That page assumes searchers in "a few days." Now it works only if someone at home has your trip plan. - Never shelter under a rock overhang in a thunderstorm — lightning arcs across the gap. Trip plan before every trip into the hills (NPS Trip Plan, pp. 1–2): who is going, the route, start and return times, a backup plan, the vehicle and the gear. Leave it with someone who isn't going, check in when you're back, and agree that they act at the deadline. 📚 Go deeper: NPS Trip Plan form — print a stack; Today's Hunter, pp.

A thunderstorm cell lives about 30 minutes (🖼️ life cycle), but its gust front can set off new ones (AC 00-6B, pp. 167–168). Wind signs: - Roseburg (nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12–24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12

(nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12–24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12 hours (Garriott, p. 137). - Portland, Oregon: wind turning from northwest through northeast to southeast means rain; a shift to northwest means clearing (p. 131). - Cold front (🖼️ cold and warm fronts): wind from the south or southwest before it, then an abrupt shift to west, northwest or north (AH 360, p. 101). - Back to the wind, low pressure is on your left and a little ahead (AH 360, p. 84). - ⚠️ Valley winds are bent by the hills. Judge by cloud movement or ridgetop wind. Barometer: watch the trend, not the number. A drop of more than about 0.06 inch in 3 hours means change is coming; about 0.18 inch or more in 3 hours means a strong storm (general practice). The old Roseburg rule "rain after the barometer falls to 29.90" uses sea-level readings; at our ~1,300 ft an unadjusted barometer reads about 1.3–1.4 inches lower (general practice). Sayings that hold up (somewhat): "Evening red and morning gray…" (Red sky at morning; 🖼️ photo) has a basis, because weather mostly moves west to east (Garriott, p. 18). 🌦️ Illinois Valley weather through the year The baseline (NRCS soil survey, p. 5): winter averages 40°F at Cave Junction (record low −6°F, December 1972), with about 24 inches of snow a season in that older record (NOAA's 1991–2020 normal is only about 7 inches); summer averages 67°F, and Grants Pass has hit 108°F. Only about 15% of the rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25–30%. It cools 3–5°F for every 1,000 ft you climb, and above about 4,500 ft it can freeze in any month. Most winters bring one or two damaging windstorms; every few years a continental air mass from the east brings days well below freezing in winter, or a sweltering week in summer. Valley fog and inversions (AH 360, p. 35; AC 00-6B, p. 146; EPA Smoke Guide, p. 26; Inversion)): - On clear, calm nights cold air drains off the slopes (🖼️ drawing) and pools on the valley floor, deepening until about midnight. Fog forms if the air is moist (🖼️ radiation fog). - Fog is common the morning after rain then clearing, and usually burns off by noon unless cloud moves in above it. - In winter an inversion can trap fog and woodstove smoke for days (🖼️ smoke under an inversion). Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a
illinois-valley-weather-through-the-year

trap fog and woodstove smoke for days (🖼️ smoke under an inversion). Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a high or rising barometer, evening temperature at 40°F or below, clearing sky and light wind. Frost hits low spots first. The mid-slope "thermal belt" stays warmest at night — the best spot for tender crops, and also where wildfires stay active all night. Winter storms off the Pacific (NRCS, p. 5; Spotter Guide, p. 12): warm storms carrying a long plume of subtropical moisture (an atmospheric river) bring several inches of rain a day, high snow levels and fast-rising rivers (general practice). Cave Junction got 8.12 inches in one day on 22 December 1964. Stay off low crossings and out of creeks when they rise. Summer thunderstorms are most frequent over the mountains (NRCS, p. 5). In fire season, watch the ridges for smoke for a day or two after lightning (rule of thumb). Heat: in a hot spell, take regular breaks in shade and drink often; do heavy work in the cool morning (rule of thumb). Heat exhaustion — heavy sweat, pale clammy skin, dizziness, nausea — means shade, rest, water and cool wet cloths. Confusion or collapse is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency — cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188–189; Field care guide). East wind = fire

rest, water and cool wet cloths. Confusion or collapse is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency — cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188–189; Field care guide). East wind = fire weather (AH 360, p. 211; NWS Medford, pp. 14–15; Foehn wind): in late summer and fall, after a cold front, high pressure inland can send strong, dry north-to-east winds downslope, warming and drying as they come. On 7–9 September 2020, Medford's humidity fell to about 7% and Slater Butte (4,600 ft, near where the Slater Fire started south of Takilma and O'Brien) recorded gusts of 55–60 mph. Warning signs: very clear air, warm dry nights, and east wind on the ridges after a front. Pack the car and watch for smoke. Another nearby east-wind fire: the Chetco Bar Fire. Smoke: inversions hold smoke in the valley at night. With no air-quality reports, judge smoke by how far you can see (EPA Smoke Guide, pp. 95–96) — in daylight, not at sunrise or sunset, only when humidity is under 65%, looking at dark landmarks at known distances: | Farthest dark landmark you can see | Healthy adults | Children, elders, pregnant, heart or lung disease | | More than 10 miles | Watch for changes | Watch; shorten activity if you feel it | | 5–10 miles | Shorten and ease outdoor work | Minimize or avoid outdoor activity | |

⚡ Lightning safety (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1–2; NWS Lightning brochure, p. 2; Spotter Guide, p. 13) - If you can hear thunder, lightning is within about 10 miles. Start moving to shelter then. - Flash to bang: count the seconds and divide by 5 for miles. Don't stake your life on it. - Stay sheltered 30 minutes after the last thunder. People are struck going out too soon. - Ground current is the big danger, not a direct strike: about half of casualties come from current spreading through the ground; direct strikes cause only 3–5% of deaths. - Caught outside: get off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, out of overhangs and cave mouths (🖼️ safer and riskier terrain). Spread a group 20 ft apart, so one strike can't hurt everyone. Crouch with feet together (🖼️ the lightning position). - A struck person carries no charge. Start CPR or rescue breathing right away (Field care guide). - The US averages about 300 people struck and about 30 killed a year. - At home: unplug radios and ground antennas (Radio guide). 📚 Go deeper: Backcountry Lightning — picking terrain, group spacing, the lightning position; NWS brochure — family rules and first aid.

🤝 Community, Barter & Keeping Watch How neighbors look after each other when no government, police or stores are coming: forming a neighborhood group, running meetings and making fair decisions, knowing who has what skills and tools, sharing work, trading fairly and keeping records, keeping watch, calming angry people, settling disputes and theft without violence, and looking after people's minds through grief and long hard months. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ (Organizing-Neighbors, Barter-Trade, Watch-Conflict, Wellbeing); the Map Your Neighborhood plan and its OK/HELP card are in Southern-Oregon\Comms-Signals\Messaging-Plans. ### ⚠️ Rules that keep a group safe, fair and together - Rescuer safety comes first, and nobody goes alone — always teams of at least two. In the 1985 Mexico City earthquake untrained volunteers saved 700 lives, but about 100 of them died (CERT manual, pp. 2, 58). - Watchers watch and report. They don't confront, chase or carry weapons on patrol (Neighborhood Watch Manual, p. 20). - No punishment by force. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation slides, p. 4). Beatings and armed posses are crimes and start feuds that outlast the emergency (rule of thumb). - Help is voluntary. Pool work by agreement — never force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored

force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored (Watch Manual, p. 21). - Write it down — trades, stores and incidents (Braun, p. 19; De-escalation, p. 23).

🏘️ Forming a neighborhood group Keep it small. Map Your Neighborhood (MYN) uses 15–25 homes, ideally ones within sight of each other — any more can't all be checked in the "golden 60 minutes" after a disaster. In the country, include as many homes as you can check in an hour or two (MYN, pp. 3, 19). Invite people in person (a flyer on the porch doesn't bring them out), ask one or two neighbors to help, and meet in someone's home — attendance drops at a school or church (p. 19). 🗳️ Meetings and fair decisions Small group: "friendly, serious, courteous discussion is preferable to formal parliamentary procedure" (Braun 1933, p. 13). A bigger meeting (Robert's Rules, 1915, pp. 281–282, 291): - The organizers agree beforehand on the place, time, who calls the meeting to order and who will be nominated chair. - Elect the chair by majority voice vote, then a secretary to keep minutes. Simple rules of order (Robert's Rules, pp. 32, 286): 1. A member proposes something ("I move that…"). 2. Someone else seconds it — otherwise it isn't discussed. 3. The chair repeats it so everyone knows exactly what's being decided. 4. Discussion. One speaker at a time; everyone who wants to speak gets a turn before anyone speaks twice (rule of thumb). 5. The chair asks "Are you ready for the question?" and takes the vote. 6. The secretary writes down the decision. Before founding anything permanent, make sure a majority agrees with the plan — groups that skipped this "have found themselves in the minority" (p. 290). Choosing what to do first: list the problems and rank them, then rank again asking "Which can we do with our own resources?" and "Which will benefit the most people?" (Peace Corps PACA, p. 116). 🤲 Sharing the work - Give everyone a job. People are less frightened when they have responsible jobs. Set a daily routine, post the assignments, and rotate the unpleasant tasks (FEMA HS-4, p. 97). A useful job (sorting supplies) also calms a disruptive person (CERT, p. 152). - Pool teams and machines. Three small farms that work together can each finish haying in two or three days instead of the whole season, then help the big farm (USDA Circular 112, p. 7). Barn raising. - A labor committee lists everyone with farm (or other) experience who volunteers, and sends them where they're needed at rush times (p. 9). - People new to hard work should do light work, a few hours a day, for the first days (p. 10). - Credit the hours in the group's points ledger (next section), so work counts as much as goods. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Farm Labor Problem (1918) — pooling crews for planting and haying (use its methods, not its 1918 coercion); FEMA HS-4 — daily routine and duty rosters in a shelter.

🔄 Barter and fair trade What trades well (Barter): a good that many people need, that lasts, is cheap to store, divides into small amounts and is easy to carry (Menger 1892, pp. 30–31). Such goods naturally become money (p. 36; Commodity money). Plain barter fails when A wants what B has, B wants what C has, and C wants what A has (p. 21). Coincidence of wants. - Likely trade goods here: salt, sugar, coffee, soap, matches and lighters, seeds, canning lids, batteries, fuel, firewood — and skills: sewing, repair, medical care (general practice). - Don't trade prescription drugs casually (general practice) — fakes and wrong doses kill (see the Medical guide). Setting up a barter group (Braun 1933, pp. 13–15): a few people first survey what the community needs and has to trade; present it at a meeting; elect a steering committee; choose a trading place; write a membership agreement. Start small, "with people you know." Members meet weekly on practical trading business only — don't leave everything to one manager. The trader should be trustworthy, "a natural trader but not a sharp, hard bargain driver," and should arrange three-way trades: A has potatoes and wants oranges, B has oranges and wants beans, C has beans and wants potatoes (p. 15). 👀 Keeping watch Structure (Watch Manual, pp. 10–11): - One block captain per 10–15 houses. - A phone tree: call the next person, skip down if they're out, and the last person calls the captain to confirm. With phones down it becomes a runner chain (general practice). Practice it, and use it to stop rumors you've checked. - Daily check-in: OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or the radio check-ins on the Illinois Valley page. Patrol rules (p. 20): watch members "do not possess police powers and they shall not carry weapons or pursue." They "should never confront suspicious persons." Carry flashlights and radios that report to a staffed base. Walk in pairs, observe, report — don't intervene (general practice). Describing what you saw (p. 24): note what can't be changed — height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos. Clothes can change. Write it down at once, even on your hand. Never hesitate to say "I'm not sure." Night watch: keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule rather than switching shifts, and protect their daytime sleep — sentry duty is among the jobs most damaged by sleepiness (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). 🗣️ Calming an angry person From the Kentucky de-escalation slides (pp. 15–24): - Distance: slightly more than a leg's length, at an angle and off to the side (p. 17) — far enough that you can't be hit or kicked. Hands visible. Never touch a hostile person (p. 15). No face-to-face, toe-to-toe or finger-pointing (p. 16). - Voice: slow and calm (p. 19). Listen — really listen (p. 21). - Move onlookers away — they become "cheerleaders" or victims. Send one for help. Two calm people with one angry person lowers the chance of violence (same page). - Never say "I know how you feel," get into power struggles, raise your voice, threaten, or give ultimatums (p. 24). - Afterwards, write down every threatening incident (p. 23). 📚 Go deeper: Using Verbal De-Escalation — 25 plain slides on stance, voice and what not to say; CERT, p. 152 — giving a disruptive person a useful job; Conflict Resolution Education Guide, p. 31 — rules for fighting fair.

⚖️ Settling disputes and dealing with theft Where conflict comes from: limited resources, unmet needs, or different values. Values don't have to change — first admit each side sees it differently (Conflict Resolution Guide, pp. 22–23). Giving in ("soft") or threats ("hard") don't last; only "principled" responses tend to make agreements that hold (pp. 23–24). Four principles: separate the people from the problem; focus on interests, not positions; invent options that help both; use fair, outside standards. Six steps: set the stage, hear each side, find the interests, list options, judge the options, agree (pp. 24, 26). Fight fair: attack the problem, not the person; no put-downs; don't drag up the past (p. 31). Mediation (FAO, p. 27): a mediator helps both sides design their own solution; an arbitrator decides for them. To find interests, keep asking "Why is this important for you?" (p. 128). Turn insults into problems: "You are selfish, the whole community suffers" becomes "consider a solution that meets your family's interests and the community's" (p. 129). Water, firewood and fence-line disputes fit this well (general practice). Mediation. Protecting shared stores (general practice): don't advertise what you have; keep common stores in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing — a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts

written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing — a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts — what, when, who saw what. Not guesses or rumors. 2. Two calm people talk to the person privately. Listen first. 3. If it's still disputed, use a mediator; if both sides agree to it, three neutral members decide (arbitration). 4. Repair the harm: return it, replace it, or work it off in ledger points. 5. Repeated or serious harm: the group can vote, under its written agreement, to remove someone from the barter group or shared stores. Report crimes to the sheriff while there is one. 6. Never beatings, public humiliation, locking people up, or taking a family's own food. Remember that hungry people steal — fair food sharing prevents a lot of theft (see the Food Security guide). 📚 Go deeper: Conflict Resolution Education Guide — principled negotiation and mediation in plain English; FAO Negotiation and Mediation Techniques — disputes over land, water and wood.

💛 Grief, stress and psychological first aid Look, listen, link (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 25): look for safety, urgent needs and people in severe distress; listen and help them feel calm; link them to practical help, information and loved ones. - Don't pressure anyone to tell their story. Sit quietly, offer water, allow silence (p. 21). - Don't say "You should feel lucky you survived," don't make false promises, and don't take away their sense of being able to care for themselves (p. 22). - Someone who seems unreal or far away: feet on the floor, tap their hands on their lap, have them name what they see and hear, breathe slowly (p. 30). - Most people recover once basic needs are met and others support them. Don't leave a severely distressed person alone (p. 27). - Don't label normal reactions as disorders (PFA Field Guide, p. 12). Accept emotional injury as being as real as a sprained ankle (FM 4-25.11, p. 174). To the grieving, never say "It could be worse," "Everything happens for the best," or to a child, "You're the man of the house now" (PFA Field Guide, p. 41). Look after the helpers (🖼️ self-care toolkit): work in pairs (WHO, p. 50); watch for helpers taking on survivors' feelings and burning out — time away helps (CERT, p. 144); sleep, exercise, eat, and balance work,

Counter it with scheduled good activities, problem-solving and helpful thinking (Skills for Psychological Recovery, p. 49), deliberately rebuilding friendships (p. 65), and regular support-group meetings (Where Women Have No Doctor, p. 14). 👵 Children, elders and neighbors who need help - About 1 in 6 people has a disability that affects daily life (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 9). - Name one person to check on each older or disabled neighbor; keep wheelchairs and walkers in one fixed place; and ask neighbors now whether they're willing to help (Red Cross Seniors, pp. 8, 10, 15). - Older adults: speak clearly in a low pitch, and don't assume confusion is permanent (PFA Field Guide, p. 13). - Children: crouch to eye level and use simple feeling words — mad, sad, scared, not "terrified" (same page). Children cope the way their parents cope (FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 188). Schooling with no school: older children tutor younger ones (peer tutoring) (Peer Tutoring, pp. 17–21). Structured tutoring beats casual help; short focused stretches (up to 4 weeks) work best; math, then reading, show the biggest gains. Train tutors to be kind — untrained tutors drift into threats and put-downs (p. 21). The tutors gain skill and confidence too. For family talk and journaling, use the day-by-day prompts in the Oregon toolkit. One-room school. 📚 Go deeper: Red Cross Disaster Preparedness for Seniors by Seniors — written by elders after a two-week outage; NWREL Peer Tutoring — teaching mixed ages with few adults.

🛡️ Home & Property Protection (Defensive Only) How to keep your family, home, food, tools and animals from being easy targets when no deputy is coming: looking like a poor choice to thieves, hearing trouble early, slowing people down, getting everyone to safety, calling the neighbors, and staying within Oregon law. This guide is strictly defensive. On purpose, it has nothing on fighting, patrolling or building traps. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Home-Security\ (Home-Hardening, Safe-Room, Neighborhood-Watch, Rural-Property, Law), with the watch and de-escalation books in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ and guardian-dog books in Southern-Oregon\Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Never booby-trap anything: no spring guns, tripwires, spikes or rigged doors. Traps can't tell a thief from a child, a firefighter or a neighbor coming to help. In 2018 a man in Williams (here in Josephine County) rigged a house with shotgun traps. One went off into an FBI bomb technician's leg, and in 2023 he got 150 months in federal prison (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon, 2023). See the law. - Don't shoot at property, or at anyone who is not an immediate deadly threat to a person. Oregon never allows deadly force just to stop theft or vandalism (ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone running

(ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone running from a fire. - Keep firearms locked away from children and thieves. It's Oregon law (ORS 166.395). - A person's life is worth more than any property. Let things go. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation, p. 4). - Avoid confrontation and call the neighbors. Watchers "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20).

🧅 Layers: deter, detect, delay, respond Think of protection as layers. Each one makes a thief more likely to give up or be seen, and buys your family time. The Watch Manual compares it to sports: "the more defenses a team has... the less likely the opponent will be to score" (Watch Manual, p. 32). | Layer | What it means | On a Valley lot (examples) | | Deter | Make your place look like a poor choice | Someone home, a dog, no supplies on show, a locked gate | | Detect | Know early that someone is coming | Dog, geese, gate bell, gravel, motion light, radio check-ins | | Delay | Slow them down | Strong doors and strike plates, locked outbuildings, pinned windows | | Respond | Protect people, not things | Safe room or escape, whistle alarm, neighbors on the radio | Why layers matter more out here: - Secluded houses are attractive targets: set back on large lots, they "reduce the chance that neighbors or passersby will see or hear a burglar" (COPS Burglary, p. 22; 🖼️ photo). - Devices work best together. Burglars get in less often when a house has two or more (window locks, deadbolts, lights, alarms), and the devices "slow them down, making them more vulnerable to being seen" (p. 25). - Help is far away. 🤫 Don't be a target Look lived-in. "Most burglars do not target occupied houses, taking great care to avoid them"; some ring the doorbell first to check (COPS Burglary, p. 20). So: - Someone home most of the time, no set times when everyone leaves, and be seen around the property often (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - Never announce who is away (Watch Manual, p. 21). - No spare key under the mat or in the car. Leave one with a trusted neighbor (Seattle Police, Outside the Home, p. 2). Don't advertise supplies. Burglars read a house's contents from what they can see outside (COPS Burglary, p. 25). After a collapse the "signs of wealth" change (rule of thumb): | Gives you away | Quieter way (rule of thumb) | | Bright windows when every other house is dark | Curtains or blankets over lit rooms (cover windows people can see into: Seattle Police) | | A generator roaring every evening | Run it in daylight, only as needed, outdoors and away from windows (carbon monoxide). See the Off-Grid Power guide | | Cooking smoke and smells at all hours | Cook at the same times as the neighbors | | Empty food boxes and fuel cans by the road | Burn, compost or bury packaging well back from the road | | Talking about your stores at trades

Give through the group or a welcome point (below), so no one house becomes "the place with food" (rule of thumb). What to say to strangers (rule of thumb): friendly and short. 🚪 Doors, frames, locks and windows Doors get kicked, not picked. "The most common way used to force entry through a door with a wooden jamb is to kick it open." The weak point is "almost always the strike plate," which is held only by short screws into thin trim (Seattle Police, Door Security; 🖼️ how a strike plate sits in the jamb). The cheapest big fix (Seattle, Door Security): 1. Take out the short screws in every exterior door's strike plates and hinges. 2. Put in 3- to 4-inch wood screws that bite into the wall stud. "This one step alone will deter or prevent most through-the-door forced entries." 3. Better still, fit a four-screw heavy-duty strike plate, plus at least one long screw in each hinge. 4. Against pry bars, add a latch guard over the gap where the bolt meets the frame (🖼️ photo). Doors and locks (Watch Manual, pp. 32–33): - Exterior doors metal or solid wood. Hollow-core or poorly fitting doors "can mean trouble" (🖼️ door types; 🖼️ door and frame cross-section). - A deadbolt with a bolt that sticks out at least 1 inch, on every outside door and the door from the garage into the house. - Hinges on the inside, or pins that can't be pulled. Exterior doors carry 3 hinges (USDA AH 73, p. 146; 🖼️ hinge drawing). - Change the

🌳 Fences, gates, lighting and sightlines The three CPTED ideas (Crime prevention through environmental design; COPS CPTED, pp. 15, 17–19): 1. Control access. "Fences, tree lines, hedges, or berms define the boundaries"; drives and paths guide people; "gates and doors limit points of entry." 2. See and be seen. Lighting, windows that look out on the approaches, and plants chosen and trimmed so views are kept open (p. 18). 3. Show ownership. Gardens and upkeep "show that someone cares and is paying attention" (p. 19). Sightlines and brush, with fire safety first. Dense shrubs and privacy fences near doors and windows give a burglar cover (COPS Burglary, p. 21). Seattle Police use a 3/6 rule: shrubs under 3 ft, tree limbs above 6 ft (Outside the Home, p. 1; 🖼️ pictures). Here the stricter fire rules win: - Limbs on mature trees at least 10 ft up, none over the roof (OSU EM 9184, p. 8). - Nothing that burns within 5 ft of the house (Ready Set Go, p. 4; 🖼️ the zones). Seattle suggests thorny Oregon grape under windows; here, plant only beyond 5 ft, and pick fire-resistant shrubs (OSU PNW 590). - Clear brush that hides the driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property
fences-gates-lighting-and-sightlines

driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property owner's primary line of defense." Make gates strong, mounted securely, and locked with heavy chain and padlock; use ditches, large rocks or locking posts to close side gaps (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - A solid privacy fence hides a burglar. See-through fencing such as chain-link keeps the view open (Seattle, Outside the Home, p. 2). - Make sure helpers can get in. Neighbors and the fire crew must be able to open or cut the gate fast (rule of thumb). Skip razor wire or spikes where children or firefighters might climb. Lighting (security lighting): enough to see about 100 ft at the entry, with motion lights on side and back yards (Seattle, p. 1). On a secluded lot a motion-activated light works as an alert, while steady light only helps if someone is there to see (COPS Burglary, p. 22). With no grid, aim solar lights along the approaches (Off-Grid Power guide). Signs and address: "No Trespassing" signs define the boundary (WSDA, p. 1), but signs "are only good if you can back them up" (Seattle, p. 2). Keep a reflective address sign visible from both directions, day and night, so neighbors and responders find you (OSU EM 9184,

🧱 Fortifying the property: barriers that delay without harming The aim is to make getting in, and carrying things out, slow, noisy and easy to see, so a thief gives up or gets noticed. Full-height fences with locked gates "hinder a burglar in carrying away stolen goods" (COPS Burglary, p. 47). Nothing here may hurt anyone who touches, climbs or runs into it in the dark, block a way out of the house, or keep out a fire engine (see the rules at the top and the limits at the end).

One way in: the driveway and vehicle barriers One entrance you can watch. The U.K. "Secured by Design" scheme cut burglary partly by "creating greater oversight around a single road entry" (COPS Burglary, p. 46). On a rural lot that means one driveway gate, with every other gap closed to vehicles by boulders, which don't burn (PNW 590, p. 8); posts or bollards of steel, concrete or heavy timber (Alberta Farm Fuel Storage, p. 22); or earth berms and ditches (COPS CPTED, p. 17; WSDA, p. 1). Keep every barrier easy to see by day and night (white paint, reflectors), and never dig a ditch or pit across a path or drive (rule of thumb). Keep it open to a fire engine (FEMA P-737, pp. 75–76; 🖼️ drawings): - Set the gate about 50 ft back from the public road, so a fire engine or a visitor waiting at it is out of the traffic lane. - Driveway at least 12 ft wide, strong enough for 40,000 lb, no steeper than 16%, with gate openings "wide enough" (Ready Set Go, p. 7). A drive longer than 150 ft needs a turnaround (inside radius 30 ft, or a "T" 60 ft across). - 13.6 ft clear overhead. Other books say 13.5 ft (OSU EM 9184, p. 8) or 15 ft (Firewise, p. 2); use FEMA's figure as the least, and the

Stronger windows and glass doors - Stronger glass, ground-floor windows first (Seattle, Window Security, p. 1): "double-pane, storm or divided light windows, or laminated glass that is forced-entry resistant" (COPS Burglary, p. 40). For glass doors: double- or triple-pane laminated glass, or film and metal grilles (Seattle, p. 2). - In fire country (FEMA P-737, pp. 48–49): laminated glass comes apart when its plastic core gets hot, so shutter it or pair it with tempered glass in a double-pane unit, which lasts about 10 minutes in a wildfire, twice as long as single-pane. No plastic glazing (acrylic, polycarbonate): it "can melt during a wildfire". - Shutters: solid metal. They "are unlikely to ignite or melt and are therefore recommended over wooden or plastic shutters" (p. 49). Closed, they also stop a quick smash-and-grab (rule of thumb). - Bars and grilles only with an inside quick-release. They "may violate building codes and pose a safety threat by blocking fire exits" (COPS, p. 40). Use them on "particularly vulnerable" windows such as secluded basement ones, with interior release latches on any fire-exit window; in bedrooms they must come off "easily from the inside" (Seattle, p. 2). Never bar the only way out of a room. - Glass block meets Oregon's wildfire window rule (Oregon BCD, p. 8) but can't be opened: use it only where nobody needs to climb out, like a

of a room. - Glass block meets Oregon's wildfire window rule (Oregon BCD, p. 8) but can't be opened: use it only where nobody needs to climb out, like a bathroom (rule of thumb). - In an emergency: planks or small tree trunks across windows, clear sticky tape on the glass "to prevent flying glass", and heavy curtains (ICRC First Aid in Armed Conflicts, p. 256). Living fences: thorny hedges that don't feed a fire Thorny shrubs "deter perimeter access" where you can't keep a view (COPS Burglary, p. 47). Here are the thorny ones on OSU's fire-resistant hedge list for Jackson and Josephine counties (OSU Privacy Screens, p. 8), plus two natives: | Plant | Grows to | Notes | | Pyracantha | 12 ft tall, 12 ft wide | Evergreen; sun or part shade; little water (p. 11) | | Thorny silverberry (Elaeagnus ebbingei) | 12 ft tall, 12 ft wide | Evergreen; sun; little water. Not E. umbellata, which is invasive (p. 11) | | Flowering quince | 12–15 ft tall, 10–12 ft wide | Many trunks; sun; little water (p. 9) | | Black hawthorn, native | 15–20 ft tall, 10–15 ft wide | A small tree (PNW 590, p. 48) | | Native roses: Wood's, Nootka, bald-hip | Wood's rose 3–6 ft each way | Spreads. Blackberry thickets are also "flammable" and burn "well in winter"; get rid of them (OSU EM 9184, p. 20). Fire spacing comes first: - Nothing within 5 ft of the house. From 5 to 30 ft, groups 10 ft or more

rid of them (OSU EM 9184, p. 20). Fire spacing comes first: - Nothing within 5 ft of the house. From 5 to 30 ft, groups 10 ft or more apart, and "avoid planting in rows" (PNW 590, p. 7). Farther out, shrubs at least 2–3 times their height apart (EM 9184, p. 16), or a dense screening clump with 5–10 ft cleared around it (p. 5). - A hedge touching a fence or shed is a wick that can carry fire to a wooden building, "possibly your home" (OSU Privacy Screens, p. 4). - So plant staggered clumps of mixed kinds, not a solid row (pp. 6–7), in the gaps where people would push through (rule of thumb). A wall against stray bullets: protecting people A thick wall keeps a stray shot from reaching the family: along a safe room's outside wall, or on the side of the house that faces the road. It is never a place to shoot from. "Protection from view (e.g. a bush) is not necessarily protection from fire" (ICRC, p. 254). Thickness that stops an ordinary rifle bullet (the Army's 7.62 mm; 🖼️ FM 5-34, Table 4-1, p. 127): | Concrete | Gravel, small rocks, brick or rubble | Soil or sand | Solid timber | | 12 in | 20 in | 42 in (3½ ft) | 36 in (3 ft) | A sandbag wall (FM 5-34, p. 139, with a drawing): 1. Use fill that isn't serpentine (limits below). Build on the ground, clear of the house. 2. Fill bags three-quarters full (for a lasting wall, 1 part cement to 10 parts earth). Set the bottom row about 6 in below ground, then lay rows alternately end-on and side-on, like brickwork. Against a bank, lean the wall into it, about 1 ft in for every 4 ft up. 3. Earth-filled bags count as soil, so make the wall about 3½ ft thick (rule of thumb, from the table). Earth-filled boxes, baskets or oil drums work too (ICRC, p. 256). Earth is heavy: about 90 lb per sq ft for each foot

thick (rule of thumb, from the table). Earth-filled boxes, baskets or oil drums work too (ICRC, p. 256). Earth is heavy: about 90 lb per sq ft for each foot of depth, so a sandbag wall 6 ft high presses about 540 lb on each square foot under it (arithmetic). To carry earth on a wooden floor, Kearny adds a beam of three 2x6s under the joists, on posts about 4½ ft apart (Nuclear War Survival Skills, p. 55). Keep soil off wood: "there should be no wood-soil contact of any kind". Use metal flashing or a covered 2–3 in air gap, and never bank earth against siding or sills (USDA FB 1993, p. 13). A FEMA safe room is tested against flying debris (a 15-lb 2x4 at 100 mph), not bullets (P-320, p. 26). With no wall, lie down away from windows, in the middle of the building, with "at least two walls between you and the direction from which the sound of shooting is coming" (ICRC, p. 255). After the firing stops, wait 10–20 minutes more (p. 254).

Outbuildings, fuel and the well - Fuel-theft checklist (Alberta Farm Fuel Storage, p. 14): tanks in a well-lit spot, out of sight of the road but in sight of the house; valves and caps locked; pump power off at a switch in a locked building; hoses with cam-lock (quick-coupler) fittings, taken off and locked away; and a log of fuel bought and used, so a loss shows. - Distances from a tank (p. 21): 3 ft from another fuel tank, 10 ft from any building, 20 ft from flames, propane, grass and weeds, 100 ft from forest or water, 165 ft from a well (Alberta's metric figures, rounded (arithmetic)). Ring the tank with boulders or posts against vehicles (p. 22). - Keep fuel, fertilizer and pesticides out of the well house: spills reach the water "through the top of the casing". Keep the well capped, its sanitary seal unbroken and vent screens in place (OSU EM 8651, p. 3). - Barn doors: an old fastening slides two bars into slots above and below double doors and "may be also worked from the inside"; a simple latch goes inside the door that closes first (Handy Farm Devices, p. 195; 🖼️ p. 194). Any building with people or animals in it needs a door that opens from inside (rule of thumb). - Buried valuables: "During the Civil War, people buried their valuables

Gravel and noisy birds: sources for two old tricks - A gravel strip at least 5 ft wide around the house is a fire rule: a "noncombustible area" of "gravel, rock mulches, or hard surfaces" (OSU EM 9184, p. 5). The crunch underfoot is a bonus (rule of thumb). - Geese are "large, hardy, aggressive, noisy birds", sometimes kept to "act as watch dogs", and may live 30 years. Guinea fowl "are valued for watch dog services on some farms" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124).

Fire and legal limits on any barrier 1. Two ways out of every room (Firewise, p. 2). Anything over an escape window opens from inside, without a key or tool. 2. Burnable fence parts at least 10 ft from the house (FEMA P-737, p. 64), and the first 5 ft of fence must not burn: use a metal gate or panel (OSFM, p. 11). A wooden gate on a garage "ignited and led the fire to the home" (🖼️ FEMA P-737, p. 63). 3. Open the gate when you evacuate if the fence by the house can burn, "to break up the wick to your home" (OSFM, p. 11). Leave the driveway gate unlocked for the fire crew (rule of thumb). 4. Don't dig serpentine soil for berms or bags: common in the valley (Start Here), it can carry natural asbestos (UC ANR 8400, p. 1). Use boulders, or fill from other ground (rule of thumb). 5. Barriers stay on your own land: never block a public road (ORS 166.025). And no traps, spikes or hidden pits, ever (the law). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-737, Fact Sheets 10, 14 and 17 — windows and shutters, fences, and driveways in fire country; Alberta Farm Fuel Storage and Handling — theft, siting and barriers for fuel tanks; OSU Fire-Resistant Shrubs and Trees for Privacy — a screen that won't spread fire.

🔔 Early warning with no grid Dogs. "A dog's presence is a close substitute for human occupancy, and most burglars avoid houses with dogs." Small dogs bark and draw attention (COPS Burglary, pp. 20–21). "A good watch dog in the house and yard area is one of the best security measures" (WSDA, p. 1; Guard dog). Livestock guardian dogs guard stock, not people. Common breeds are the Great Pyrenees, Anatolian Shepherd, Maremma and Akbash (Texas A&M, p. 5; Livestock guardian dog; Great Pyrenees; Anatolian Shepherd; Maremma; 🖼️ photo). Socialize them with people: unsocialized dogs may "harm employees" (same page). Known problems include dogs "overly aggressive to people" and dogs that roam onto neighbors' land (USDA AIB 588, p. 28). See the predator sections of the Rabbits & Chickens and Goats, Dairy & Bees guides. Other alarm animals. "Donkeys, llamas and cattle will sometimes protect sheep that graze with them" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 133; 🖼️ guard llama). Geese honk loudly at strangers and are an old farm alarm (general practice). Simple noise alarms (rule of thumb): - A bell on every gate and door that rings when it opens. - Cans with pebbles tied to fence wire, where people don't walk. - Gravel on paths and under windows crunches underfoot. - Never string a line across a path, driveway or doorway. It trips children, elders and firefighters in the dark,

🏠 A safe room and a household plan A safe room is a place to wait behind a strong door while help comes. It is not a place to fight from. FEMA's full version. Taking Shelter from the Storm (FEMA P-320) has plans for reinforced tornado rooms, which also make a strong hardened room: - Where: a basement, a bathroom, closet or laundry room, or a separate room within 150 ft (p. 41; 🖼️ floor plans). - Size: at least 3 sq ft per person for a short stay, 7 for a long one, 10 for a wheelchair user (p. 37). - Door: ordinary steel house doors fail FEMA's tests; a real safe room needs a tested, labeled door (p. 53; 🖼️ label). - Cost: about $9,400–$25,500 new, plus the door, and more in an existing house (p. 56; 🖼️ construction drawings). The everyday version (rule of thumb, built from the door advice above): - An inside room with a solid-wood or metal door, a deadbolt, and the strike plate and hinges screwed into the studs with 3-inch screws. - A second way out (a window that opens from inside), a smoke alarm and a fire extinguisher (🖼️ how to use one). A locked room in a burning house is a death trap. If there is smoke, get out. - Kept stocked (P-320, p. 69): 1 gallon of water per

use one). A locked room in a burning house is a death trap. If there is smoke, get out. - Kept stocked (P-320, p. 69): 1 gallon of water per person per day, food, first-aid kit and medicines, a flashlight for every 4 people, a battery radio, a portable toilet, a crowbar to open a jammed door, plus a whistle or air horn and an FRS radio. The household plan (rule of thumb; fill it in on the Oregon My Pocket Plan): | Decide now | Example | | Who goes where | Kids and grandma to the back bedroom; one adult with the radio | | Who calls for help, and how | Air horn, then FRS channel 3 to the neighbors | | Two ways out | Front door; back bedroom window | | Outside meeting spot | The neighbor's barn | | Code words | "Safe room now," "all clear," and one that secretly means "I'm being forced, stay hidden" | Practice it, once at night too, until the children know it (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-320 — sizing, locations and full building plans; FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 62 — preparing a safe room.

🥫 Protecting food, water, fuel, tools and livestock Food and water: - Shared stores go in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log, and it takes two people to open them (Community guide). - Don't keep everything in one place. Split stores between the house, the cellar and an outbuilding, so a thief or a fire takes only part (rule of thumb). - A hidden cache (rule of thumb): sealed, rodent-proof containers of foods that keep (Food Security guide). Tell one other adult where. - Lock the pump house (rule of thumb; Wells guide). Fuel (WSDA, pp. 1–2): - Lockable caps on fuel outlets; fuel tanks, pumps and electric-fence units secured and locked. - Place fuel tanks where they can be seen from the house. Keep stored fuel, chemicals and fertilizer "to a minimum" and locked up. Storage and safety: Fuel guide. Tools, machinery and valuables: - Mark everything in at least two places, one easy to see and one hidden (WSDA, p. 2). - Operation ID (Watch Manual, p. 34): engrave your Oregon driver's license number starting with "OR" and ending with "DL". Never your Social Security number. Marked items are hard to sell, so burglars avoid them. - Keep a property list with serial numbers and marks, plus photos, stored away from the things themselves (p. 34). - Machinery: take the keys out; remove the distributor cap,

- Keep a property list with serial numbers and marks, plus photos, stored away from the things themselves (p. 34). - Machinery: take the keys out; remove the distributor cap, rotor or battery; chain it up; park it where a neighbor can see it (WSDA, p. 1). - Firearms are a top target. Burglars steal "cash and goods they can easily carry and sell," weapons included (COPS Burglary, p. 25). Lock them up (the law). 👥 Neighborhood watch after the collapse How to set up a watch, block captains, the phone or runner tree, describing people and the night shift table are all in the Community guide: Keeping watch. The key rules: - Watchers watch and report. They "shall not carry weapons or pursue" and "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20; Neighborhood watch). - What counts as suspicious (p. 24): someone peering into cars or windows, people at homes at unusual hours, tampering with gas, power or water, signs of forced entry, and "anything that feels uncomfortable or looks out of place." A roster that doesn't wear people out (rule of thumb, from the Community guide): - 2-hour shifts in pairs, the same nights each week, with a written handover. Protect watchers' daytime sleep (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Nobody stands watch two nights running. Spread it across every capable adult; give elders, parents of babies and the sick lighter daytime jobs. - In fire season the watch is also the fire lookout. Daily check-in: post OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or follow the Signals guide's OK/HELP plan. Checkpoints: a welcome point, not a roadblock (rule of thumb): - Never block a public road. Obstructing "vehicular or pedestrian traffic on a public way" is disorderly conduct under Oregon law (ORS 166.025). Gates on your own driveway

Gates on your own driveway are fine. - Put a table at a crossroads turnout, on private land with permission, with two calm, unarmed neighbors, a radio, water and a news board. - Everyone may pass. Nobody is stopped or searched. The table offers news and help, and quietly notes descriptions and vehicles (Watch Manual, p. 24). 🚧 Someone at the gate, strangers, or a break-in Before you open anything: 1. Find out who it is: through the viewer, a window, or by calling out. 2. Talk through the closed door or gate. Don't open it. Let them know someone is home; most burglars avoid occupied houses (COPS Burglary, p. 20). 3. Point them to help that isn't your house, such as the welcome point (rule of thumb). If they're upset, use the Community guide's Calming an angry person: a slow, calm voice, hands visible, never threats or ultimatums (De-escalation, pp. 15–24; De-escalation). If someone is trying to get in, or is already inside (rule of thumb): 1. Sound the alarm: air horn or whistle, a string of short blasts. 2. Everyone goes to the safe room, or out the escape route to the meeting spot. Take the kids and elders first. 3. Call the neighbors on the radio: who you are, where, what's happening. 4. Stay put. Don't go looking for the intruder. Let them take things. Property can be replaced. People can't. Remember what you saw (Watch Manual, p. 24): what can't be changed (height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos) and the vehicle's make, type and plate. Write it down at once. "Never hesitate to say, 'I'm not sure.'" Afterwards (WSDA, p. 2): - Check everyone first, then give first aid (Injuries guide).

⚖️ Oregon law on force in defense of people and property This is not legal advice. It quotes the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition, from oregonlegislature.gov) in plain words. Laws change, and courts decide each case on its facts. The key test in every section is what you "reasonably believe," and other people judge that afterwards. | Situation | What the law says | In plain words | | Defending yourself or another person (ORS 161.209) | You may use physical force against "what the person reasonably believes to be the use or imminent use of unlawful physical force," and only "a degree of force which the person reasonably believes to be necessary" | Only against a real, present attack, and only as much force as needed | | If you started it (ORS 161.215) | No justification if you provoked it or were "the initial aggressor," unless you withdraw and make that clear | Starting a fight takes away your defense | | Deadly force (ORS 161.219) | Only if you reasonably believe the other person is committing or attempting a felony that uses or threatens force against a person, or a burglary in a dwelling, or is using or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical
oregon-law-on-force-in-defense-of-people-and-property

or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical force to stop a criminal trespass when you reasonably believe it necessary. Deadly force only to defend a person (as above), or to prevent arson or "a felony by force and violence by the trespasser" | Trespassing alone never justifies deadly force | | Your things (ORS 161.229) | "Physical force, other than deadly physical force," to stop theft or criminal mischief | Never deadly force over property | | Pointing a gun (ORS 166.190) | Purposely pointing a loaded or empty firearm at someone "except in self-defense" is a crime | Don't wave guns at people at the gate | | Threatening (ORS 163.190) | Menacing: trying "to place another person in fear of imminent serious physical injury" by word or conduct | Threats are a crime too | "Deadly physical force" means force that "is readily capable of causing death or serious physical injury" (ORS 161.015). Booby traps and spring guns. No Oregon law allows them. A trap can't "reasonably believe" anything; it hits whoever comes: a child, a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting a loaded spring gun, set gun or any device rigged to fire when someone touches a wire or string is a crime
oregon-law-on-force-in-defense-of-people-and-property

a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting a loaded spring gun, set gun or any device rigged to fire when someone touches a wire or string is a crime in itself (ORS 166.320). Any trap also creates "a substantial risk of serious physical injury to another person," which is recklessly endangering (ORS 163.195), and if someone is hurt or killed the charges grow. Courts have long made trap-setters pay even when the person hurt was a trespasser (Katko v. Briney; Spring-gun; Booby trap). Then there's the Williams case in the warning box at the top. Firearm storage: the Cindy Yuille and Steve Forsyth Act (SB 554 as passed): - Whenever a firearm is not carried by or under the control of its owner or an authorized person, it must be secured with an engaged trigger or cable lock, in a locked container, or in a locked gun room (ORS 166.395; trigger locks, gun safe). - It is not secured if the key or combination is "readily available" to someone not authorized. - The fine is higher if a minor gets an unsecured gun. If an unsecured gun is used to hurt someone within two years, the owner is treated as negligent in a lawsuit (with narrow exceptions). - Report loss or theft within 72 hours (ORS 166.397). Directly supervise any minor you hand a firearm to, with some hunting

as negligent in a lawsuit (with narrow exceptions). - Report loss or theft within 72 hours (ORS 166.397). Directly supervise any minor you hand a firearm to, with some hunting and target-range exceptions (ORS 166.403). Training: if you keep firearms, get real training from a qualified instructor. This guide doesn't teach firearm use. Why it still matters when the courts are closed: courts reopen, and in Oregon a prosecution for murder or "any degree of manslaughter may be commenced at any time" (ORS 131.125). Neighbors remember, too: a shooting over a chainsaw can start a feud that outlasts the emergency (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Oregon SB 554 (2021), enrolled — the full storage, theft-reporting and transfer law, with the legislature's reasons; ORS chapter 161 (sections 161.195–161.275) is quoted above from oregonlegislature.gov.

🔥 Fire as a threat to your home A fire, whether set on purpose or blown in from the hills, can take everything at once. The defenses are those in the Illinois Valley wildfire section: - First 5 ft: nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; Defensible space)). - Within 100 ft: grass short, trees spaced, and no ladder fuels (🖼️ drawing). - Vents covered with 1/8-inch metal mesh (🖼️ how embers get in). Water and tools ready (rule of thumb): full buckets or barrels, a charged hose if you have pressure, shovels and rakes by the door, and a fire extinguisher you know how to use (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep: 🖼️ CERT, pp. 171–172). At night: the watch looks for smoke and glow as well as people (Community guide). If the house is on fire, everyone gets out. Never stay in a safe room in a burning building. 📚 Go deeper: OSFM Defensible Space Homeowner Guide — the zones, step by step; FEMA P-737 — hardening the house itself; OSU EM 9184 — year-round checklists. 🔥 No fire department coming? 😴 Stress, fatigue and judgment The worst outcomes come from tired, frightened people deciding fast in the dark (rule of thumb). - Sleep is protection. Keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Check rumors before acting. Use the phone or runner tree to confirm facts (Community guide). - Don't escalate. Two calm people with one angry person is safer than one (De-escalation, p. 21). Swap out anyone losing their temper (rule of thumb). - Look after the helpers. Watchers and helpers burn out; time away helps (CERT, pp. 144–146). - After a scare, use psychological first aid: look, listen, link (Community guide; Psychological first aid). - Despair and guns don't mix. Oregon's legislature found that "a proven barrier to the impulse to commit suicide is securing firearms with a lock or storing firearms in locked containers" (SB 554, p. 1). In hard months, let a trusted person hold the key for anyone who is struggling (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Psychological First Aid — a short field guide; CERT, p. 144 — stress in helpers.

⏳ What to Expect: Disaster Scenarios & Timelines What really happens, hour by hour and month by month, in the disasters most likely to hit the Illinois Valley, and what to do at each stage. The timelines come from official plans and after-action reports: the Oregon Resilience Plan, the Josephine County hazard plan, the state's review of the 2020 Labor Day fires, federal and state power-outage and fuel plans, and fifty years of disaster research. The books are in Disaster-Scenarios\ (Cascadia-Earthquake, Local-Hazards, Fire-Heat-Drought, Grid-Supply-Pandemic, How-People-Respond), with more in Wildfire\, Earthquake-Tsunami\, Nuclear-Radiation\ and EMP-Solar-Storms\. ### ⚠️ Five rules that hold in every scenario 1. Plan to be on your own for at least two weeks. The state's own Cascadia exercise said so (Cascadia Rising, p. 12). At the end of one highway, plan longer. 2. Leave early. Alerts fail when cell towers burn or lose power (2020 fire review, p. 9). A Level 2 "Be Set" notice may be the only warning you get. 3. Check on people who live alone. Most who died in the 2021 heat dome lived alone (heat report, p. 10). 4. Generators, grills and camp stoves stay outdoors. Carbon monoxide kills in every outage (CPSC). 5. Expect neighbors to help, and be one. Panic and looting are rare; survivors do most of the rescuing (Quarantelli, p. 16).

❄️ 2. Winter storm, ice, flood and landslides What it is and how likely here. The county rates winter storms #2 of all hazards: high probability, high vulnerability. Recent ones: in February 2019 fallen trees closed US-199 at the California line and 2,500 customers lost power around Grants Pass, Cave Junction and O'Brien; in January 2021 snow left 45,000 customers in the area without power (county plan, p. 64). The valley is "one way in, one way out": a storm on US-199 can strand Cave Junction and cut the whole valley's power "for an extended period" (p. 140). Floods are rated high probability, moderate damage. The benchmark is the Christmas flood of 1964: 10 inches of rain in six days, the Rogue and Illinois Valleys cut off and I-5 closed (p. 45). In 2015, water covered US-199 near Selma and closed roads near O'Brien (p. 46). 🌡️ 3. Extreme heat and drought What it is and how likely here. The county rates heat waves high probability, moderate damage. Days with a heat index over 90 °F are expected to rise from about 13 a year to about 40 by the 2050s (county plan, p. 57). In the June 2021 heat dome Josephine County saw 92–108 °F, with two more heat waves later that summer (p. 58). In Portland it killed 72 people; in a normal year, none. Most were 60 or older and lived alone, and half had only a fan (heat report, pp. 2, 8–12). Drought is also rated high probability: extreme drought years 1924, 1977 and 2001, severe ones as recently as 2014 and 2020 (p. 33). 🦠 5. Pandemic What it is and how likely here. A new germ spreads around the world, usually "within several weeks or months." The last century had flu pandemics in 1918, 1957, 1968 and 2009 (WHO, pp. 51–52), and then COVID-19 — so expect one or two in a lifetime (estimate). A pandemic comes in waves of several weeks to a few months, and a later wave can be worse: the mild spring wave of 1918 came before the deadly autumn one (p. 52; Spanish flu). ⛽ 6. Economic crisis, fuel and supply-chain breakdown What it is and how likely here. Oregon has no refineries; more than 90% of its fuel comes from four refineries near Seattle, mostly through one pipeline to the Portland fuel hub (fuel plan, p. 9). Gas stations hold about two to three days of fuel (p. 11). Groceries hold more shelf-stable food than most people think; the real problem in a catastrophe is delivery, not supply (CNA, p. 9). In the 1970s oil shortages states used odd-even days to cut gas lines (NASEO, p. 45; 1973 oil crisis). In the Great Depression people formed barter associations to trade work and goods (Braun 1933, p. 5). 🌎 7. Cascadia M9 earthquake (and the coast tsunami) What it is and how likely here. The Cascadia subduction zone last broke on January 26, 1700 (1700 Cascadia earthquake). About half of past quakes were centered off the southern Oregon coast; the odds of one hitting southern Oregon in the next 50 years are about 37% (Resilience Plan, p. 31). 🚨 8. Riots and law and order breaking down What it is and how likely here. Fifty years of disaster research found panic flight so rare that fire researchers stopped using the idea, and looting "unusual in the typical natural and technological disasters" of countries like ours (Quarantelli, pp. 6–7, 11–12). Mass looting did happen after Hurricane Hugo on St. Croix and after Hurricane Katrina, where three things came together: many poor people living beside obvious wealth, organized youth gangs, and a police force that was ineffective or corrupt (pp. 13–14). Even there, help between people "swamped" the theft, and after the first emergency days reported crime usually drops (p. 14). The EMP Commission warns that disorder becomes more likely when shortages cause conflict and police are absent for a long time (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). 🤝 What every scenario has in common The first 72 hours. No outside help, so neighbors are the first responders. In the first half hour after a disaster, about a third of survivors search for missing people and about one in ten actively rescue them (Quarantelli, p. 16). Your jobs: injuries, fires, water, a toilet, warmth or cooling, and checking the people next door. The 2-week mark. Oregon tells everyone to be ready for at least two weeks (Be 2 Weeks Ready, p. 2). The old 2004 FEMA book's "at least three days" (p. 33) is too short for here. Two weeks is also about when most big storm outages have ended, and the longest disruption most businesses can stand (Resilience Plan, p. 22). When things usually improve. Most storm, fire and heat emergencies ease within days to weeks. A Cascadia quake, EMP or national crisis takes months to years (see the tables). Plan for the long tail, not just the first days. Why most neighbors help. After disasters, help and sharing far outweigh theft, even in the worst cases (Quarantelli, p. 14); citizen groups spring up to clear debris, move supplies and pass messages (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). Plan on cooperating, and organize early. Rumor control. Rumors make things worse. Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with

Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with the time and who said it (rule of thumb); help correct misinformation (Psychological First Aid, p. 35). Mental health. Feeling overwhelmed, confused, afraid or numb is a normal reaction (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 9). Keep routines, give everyone a job, keep children close and talking, and watch for anyone who stops eating or caring for themselves (rule of thumb). 🔥 Wildfire: Defending Your Place With No Grid How a household in the Illinois Valley can get its people, house, animals and land through a wildfire when no engine, air tanker, alert or phone is coming: reading the danger, hardening and clearing with hand tools, water without the grid, hand line, deciding ahead whether to stay or go, the fire's arrival, and the years after. The basics (5-ft and 30-ft rules, vent mesh, evacuation levels, a cleaner-air room) are in the Illinois Valley guide ("Wildfire"), Home Defense ("Fire as a threat to your home") and the Shelter guide ("Earthquake and wildfire hardening"). Most books are in Southern-Oregon\Wildfire: the federal firefighters' Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG), fire-behavior guide (PMS 437) and tactics guide (PMS 465); the Australian Country Fire Authority's (CFA) plan for staying to defend a house, adapted here because it assumes phone apps and daily ratings; Cohen's Forest Service research on how homes ignite; the State Fire Marshal (OSFM); and OSU Extension. FEMA P-737 is in Southern-Oregon\Shelter-Building\Wildfire-Quake-Hardening, Fire Weather (AH 360) in Southern-Oregon\Navigation-Weather\Weather, and the thinning and slash bulletins in Southern-Oregon\Firewood\Woodlot. ### The short version - Leaving early beats staying late. Deaths "can occur because people wait too long to leave" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 2); leaving early "does not mean waiting to see or smell smoke" (CFA, p. 11). Decide before fire season, not on the day. -

East wind: the night is not safe "East wind in fire control means an exceptionally dry wind from an easterly quadrant that may blow continuously for 24 to 48 hours or longer. East wind often reaches maximum strength during night and early morning hours. Surface wind of 60 mph is not uncommon", with humidity "extremely low around the clock" (PMS 465, p. 227; Foehn wind). 🏠 How houses catch fire Three ways: embers land on something that burns; a surface fire creeps to the walls or roof; or radiant heat from burning plants or buildings nearby. "Most commonly, homes are lost in wildfires when they come into contact with embers or low-intensity surface fires — not from a giant wall of flames" (OSU EM 9247, p. 2). - Embers cause up to 90% of house fires (OSFM, p. 5), get in "through vents, windows, and other openings" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 3), and pile up where snow drifts on the roof and deck (p. 5). - Flames have to be close. By Cohen's calculations even crown fires won't light wood walls more than 40 m (130 ft) away (Cohen, p. 2): there a wall needs over 10 minutes of heat, but crown-fire flames last about 1 minute in one spot (p. 3). Test walls 10 m (33 ft) from crown fires didn't ignite, and homes with nonflammable roofs and 10–18 m (33–60 ft) of clearance survived 95% of the time (pp. 3–4). - The house can be the fuel: homes with flammable roofs "ignite and burn without the surrounding vegetation also burning" (Cohen, p. 4). The roof "is the most vulnerable component" (EM 9247, p. 3). - Late burning comes from "residual spot fires or creeping ground fire" (IRPG, p. 31). Single-pane glass can fail

🔨 Hardening the house with what you have Vents, gutters and woodpiles are in the Shelter guide; windows, fences, gates and the driveway in Home Defense. The order: 1. Roof first. Clean it and the gutters spring and fall, and in summer under madrones, which drop leaves then (EM 9184, p. 9); debris gathers in valleys and where roof meets wall (P-737, p. 25). Untreated wood shakes are unrated and "not desirable" (BCD, p. 3): keep hand-split shakes for sheds, and salvage metal roofing from buildings you won't defend (rule of thumb). 2. Vents: 1/8-inch metal mesh over the old 1/4–1/2 in screen, which "may be plastic" (OSFM, p. 8). This follows current Oregon advice over FEMA's 2008 "maximum opening of 1/4 inch" (P-737, p. 40). 1/16 in clogs, and clogged debris can make embers; keep cardboard away from vents (BCD, p. 5). 3. Vent covers. Ready, Set, Go! says cover attic and ground vents with "pre-cut plywood" (p. 9); FEMA advises against it because people fall (P-737, p. 42). So cut and label covers now; always fit the ground and crawlspace vents; gable vents only from a tied-off ladder with time to spare (rule of thumb). 4. Gaps and gutters. Caulk gaps; open eaves trap heat (BCD, p. 6). Seal pipe and wire holes with mortar (P-737, p. 72; lime mortar: Masonry & Roads). Vinyl gutters "can fail under

🪓 Clearing around the house with hand tools Work from the house outward (rule of thumb). The books differ on trees; this guide uses: - Spacing: at least 10 ft between crowns within 100 ft (OSFM, p. 14), 15–20 ft within 30 ft of the house and more on slopes (EM 9247, p. 5); branches 15 ft from the house (PNW 590, p. 7), 10 ft from a chimney (OSFM, p. 15). - Limbing: 6 ft up, or a third of the height on trees under 18 ft (OSFM, p. 14); mature trees 10 ft, taking no more than a third of the live branches at once; conifers in fall and winter, hardwoods in spring (EM 9184, p. 7). - Keep some: deciduous trees "block embers" (OSFM, p. 15); mature ponderosa pine and bigleaf maple "catch and filter embers" (EM 9247, p. 5). Brush and ladder fuels. Small trees and brush under big ones are "ladder" fuels that carry a ground fire into the crowns (EC 1573, p. 2). Space shrubs 2–3 times their height apart (EM 9184, p. 16), none over one metre (about 3 ft) by a window (CFA, p. 4). Worst burners: Scotch broom, gorse, blackberry, juniper, many manzanitas and ceanothus (EM 9184, p. 15). - Oak, madrone and tanoak resprout, and the sprouts "can quickly become new ladder fuels"; sometimes don't cut (EM 9184, pp. 15–17).

Brush the driveway back 10 ft: "If firefighters can't see down your driveway, they will not enter" (p. 7).

💧 Water with no power "Loss of power will prevent ... electric pumps from working" (CFA, p. 8), so plan water that needs no grid. And "Never rely on water for firefighter safety" (IRPG, p. 31): water is not your escape plan. | What | How much | Source | | To defend a house | 10,000 litres (about 2,640 gal) or more, with gear that works if the power goes out | CFA, p. 3 | | Reserve you never touch | 100 gal | IRPG, p. 31 | | Filling 100 ft of hose | ¾-in 2 gal; 1-in 4 gal | IRPG, p. 104 | | Forestry nozzle, 3/16-in tip | 7 gal a minute at 50 psi | IRPG, p. 104 | | A fire hose | 50–125 gal a minute | P-737, p. 67 | | Water extinguisher | 2.5 gal, reaching 30–40 ft | CERT, p. 170 | At 7 gal a minute, 2,640 gallons lasts about 6 hours; a fire hose empties it in 20–50 minutes (arithmetic). Use small nozzles, short bursts and dirt, and save water for embers. Storing it - Tanks of "steel, concrete, or ferrocement"; fiberglass "may be placed underground" (P-737, p. 77). Clear 10 ft around a plastic tank and bury its pipe (rule of thumb). A tank up the hill: Storing Energy ("Gravity that works"); each 2 ft
