(P-737, p. 77). Clear 10 ft around a plastic tank and bury its pipe (rule of thumb). A tank up the hill: Storing Energy ("Gravity that works"); each 2 ft of height gives about 1 psi (IRPG, p. 104). - Ponds, pools and creeks. A "dry hydrant" (fixed suction pipe) needs water at least 2 ft deep (P-737, p. 78). Oregon needs no water right for "emergency firefighting" (OWRD, p. 2). Keep a hard road within 10 ft (PNW 783, p. 7). Inside, fill the bath and buckets (CFA, p. 7). Getting it there - A gas fire pump lifts at most 22 ft at sea level, minus 1 ft per 1,000 ft of elevation (IRPG, p. 104): about 20 ft on the valley floor (arithmetic). Pumping uphill, fit a check-and-bleeder valve (same page). Keep "sufficient fuel which is clean" (CFA, p. 6); run it each spring and time how long a gallon lasts (rule of thumb). The well: Water Wells ("Running the well pump without the grid"). - Backpack pumps, buckets, mops. "A few squirts from a backpack pump can easily cool down hot embers" (PMS 465, p. 85); most hold about 5 gal (rule of thumb). CFA adds "mops, metal buckets, ladders and rakes" (p. 5). - Hoses to reach every side of the house (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 7), but "Long hose lays are not recommended"; "Charge
water-with-no-power

"mops, metal buckets, ladders and rakes" (p. 5). - Hoses to reach every side of the house (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 7), but "Long hose lays are not recommended"; "Charge garden hoses" (fill them) beforehand (IRPG, p. 31). Plastic melts: bring plastic fittings and hoses in before the front (CFA, p. 9); use brass (rule of thumb). - Sprinklers on the ridge or under the eaves, fed by a tank (P-737, pp. 68–69), though "High winds ... can significantly degrade" them (p. 70). Ready, Set, Go!'s "Don't leave sprinklers on" (p. 9) is about town pressure; with a tank, turn them on "When embers start to appear", and "Block downpipes and fill gutters with water" (CFA, p. 8). - Dirt is water too. "Water can be used very sparingly but effectively when hand tools are used to expose burning fuels and mix soil with fire" (PMS 465, p. 85). "Let no person use water alone, but always with another person with a hand tool" (p. 52); "If a pump should fail, enough hand tools should be available to extinguish the fire with mineral soil" (p. 91).
water-with-no-power

⛏️ Hand tools and firebreaks Pulaski): ax plus grub hoe, "about 5½ pounds"; short, shallow swings, the hoe landing on its corner; goggles; "Never sharpen the top of the hoe" (MTDC, p. 25). McLeod): rake plus hoe, "inefficient in rocky or unusually brushy areas" (p. 26). Fire shovel: scrapes "down to mineral soil" (p. 29). Carry tools "at your side and downhill, with blades forward"; "Never throw a tool" (p. 11). Saws in fire season: Firewood guide ("Bucking and limbing").
hand-tools-and-firebreaks

Building a hand line A hand line (fireline) is a strip cleared of fuel and scraped to bare mineral soil (Firebreak). 1. Anchor it to something that won't burn: road, creek, rock, plowed field or burned ground (IRPG, p. 23). Building "without safe anchor point" is one of the 18 Watch Out Situations (p. 140). 2. Width: "one and one half times as wide as the dominate fuel is high", 1–3 ft of it scraped to mineral soil, on the side away from the fire; in timber, 20–30 ft cleared with a 3–4 ft scrape (PMS 465, p. 42). Brush 6 ft tall needs a 9-ft line (arithmetic). 3. Down to mineral soil, or fire creeps through roots; unburned material goes outside the line, burning material into the burn (p. 37). Limb the trees on both sides: heat crosses a narrow line without flames touching (pp. 40–41). 4. Below a fire on a slope, dig a "cup trench" to catch rolling logs and cones (p. 38); above it, the steeper the slope, the wider the line (p. 17). 5. Short and straight, tied to roads, rock and creeks; on a ridge, on top or just over (IRPG, p. 101). Never build line downhill toward a fire, mid-slope above it, or with unburned fuel between you and it (p. 20). The burning edge itself is the "Safest place to work; firefighters
building-a-hand-line

build line downhill toward a fire, mid-slope above it, or with unburned fuel between you and it (p. 20). The burning edge itself is the "Safest place to work; firefighters can usually escape into the burned area" (IRPG, p. 99). "Most firelines will be unsuccessful in stopping a crown fire" (PMS 465, p. 42).
building-a-hand-line

How fast can you build line? | Fuel | 20-person crew, chains an hour (SDTDC, p. 10) | Per person, feet an hour (arithmetic) | | Short grass | 9.5 | about 30 | | Chaparral, brush, timber litter | 6.8–7 | about 22 | Those are trained crews, measured over a whole shift. The older PMS 465 gives 1–2 chains (66–132 ft) per person-hour in our forests (p. 228); plan on the measured rates. Three adults might build 70 ft an hour in brush (arithmetic), while fire there spreads 2–10 chains (130–660 ft) an hour (same page). You can't out-dig a fire on the day: build breaks in the wet season, and on the day use tools on spot fires, the 5-ft strip and the burned edge (rule of thumb).
how-fast-can-you-build-line

Small fires, spot fires and wet sacks - "Don't overestimate your ability" (ODFW, p. 34). "Do not ever try to fight a fire alone"; "Always have two ways to exit"; "If you feel the heat, you are too close" (CERT, p. 173). - Dirt first: throw mineral soil, scrape a line around, stir hot embers into dirt (PMS 465, pp. 52, 91). - In grass: let it burn to a barrier, "cold-trail" the dead edge (feel along it, line any live spot), or use a "gunnysack or swatter" (PMS 465, pp. 30, 59; Fire flapper). Soak a burlap sack, work from the burned side, press or drag it on the base of the flames instead of flapping, and re-wet it often (rule of thumb). - "Getting frequent spot fires across line" is a Watch Out: time to go (IRPG, p. 140).
small-fires-spot-fires-and-wet-sacks

Burning out: mostly don't Burning out is "setting fire inside the fireline to consume fuel between the fireline and the edge of the fire", so crews "keep one foot in the black"; backfiring sets fire well ahead of the main fire, a riskier method (PMS 465, pp. 112–113). Firing needs lookouts, escape routes, anchor points and "Adequate resources ... for both firing and holding" (IRPG, p. 26). Household rule (rule of thumb): never backfire. Burn out only a narrow strip of grass or litter off a finished, anchored line, with the wind carrying it away from the line, someone holding the line with water and tools, and a lookout. If unsure, don't.
burning-out-mostly-dont

🚪 Stay or go: decide before fire season "Do not wait to be advised to leave" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 10). Alerts failed in 2020 (What to Expect guide); now there are none. Stay only if every answer is yes (CFA, p. 3): - [ ] At least two fit adults "physically and mentally prepared to work long and hard" - [ ] About 2,600 gal of water, and pumps and hoses that run with the power out, tested this season - [ ] Protective clothing for each, and the house hardened and cleared to 100 ft - [ ] A safety zone at the house: "Do not commit to stay and protect a structure unless a safety zone ... has been identified" (IRPG, p. 27) - [ ] Not a worst-weather day; children, elders and the sick already gone (CFA, p. 3), and the animals - [ ] Everyone knows "staying to defend may involve trauma, injury or possibly death" (CFA, p. 5) Places you can't defend: "narrow canyon bottoms, mid-slope with fire below, and narrow ridges near chimneys and saddles" (IRPG, p. 28). Worst-weather days: "Do not plan to defend on CATASTROPHIC days" (CFA, p. 3). With no ratings, call it catastrophic when an east wind breaks twigs from trees and humidity is under 15%, or leaves crumble to dust (rule of thumb, from CFA, p. 2 and
stay-or-go-decide-before-fire-season

ratings, call it catastrophic when an east wind breaks twigs from trees and humidity is under 15%, or leaves crumble to dust (rule of thumb, from CFA, p. 2 and IRPG, pp. 59–65); then leave "The night before" or "Early in the morning" (CFA, p. 11).
stay-or-go-decide-before-fire-season

Triggers: write them down A trigger is something you can see that means "go now". Leaving early "does not mean waiting for a warning or a siren" (CFA, p. 11); firefighters "Set trigger point for safe retreat" (IRPG, p. 30). Examples (rule of thumb): a worst-weather day; a smoke column building over a named ridge upwind; ash or embers falling; fire crossing a named road or creek (time your escape against its spread, IRPG, p. 21); any one adult saying "go".
triggers-write-them-down

LCES for a household Firefighters' LCES "must be established and known to ALL firefighters BEFORE it is needed" (IRPG, p. 21): | | Firefighters' rule (same page) | At home (rule of thumb) | | Lookouts | "good vantage points"; "Knowledge of trigger points" | Someone on a high point with binoculars, day and night on east-wind days, taking turns | | Communications | "Sound alarm early, not late" | Whistle and bell codes (Signals guide); walkie-talkies (Radio guide) | | Escape routes | "More than one"; "Avoid steep, uphill escape routes"; "Timed considering slowest person"; "Marked for day or night" | Two roads out, driven at night; a printed map (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 8); car facing out (CFA, p. 7) | | Safety zones | "Back into clean burn"; rock, water, meadows, roads; bigger if upslope, downwind or near heavy fuel | A plowed or grazed-down field, irrigated pasture, gravel lot or big pond, sized below |
lces-for-a-household

Safety zones: how big "Separation distance between the firefighter and the flames should be at least four times the maximum continuous flame height" (IRPG, p. 22): | Flame height | Distance to the flames | Area | | 10 ft | 40 ft | 1/10 acre | | 20 ft | 80 ft | ½ acre | | 50 ft | 200 ft | 3 acres | | 100 ft | 400 ft | 12 acres | That counts radiant heat only, on flat ground with no wind, for a three-person crew, and is "Not intended for structure protection" (same page). With wind over 10 mph or slope over 20%, it may need "more than double" (p. 21).
safety-zones-how-big

Getting out and last resort - Keep "old shoes and a flashlight handy in case of a sudden evacuation at night" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 8). Lock up (CFA, p. 11); open any wood gate joined to the house to break the "wick" (OSFM, p. 11). Don't leave "the key in the ignition" (FEMA 2004, p. 127): keep it on a hook by the door (rule of thumb). - Caught outside (IRPG, p. 46): "Escape if you can." In light fuels "you may be able to move through the flames into the black"; on a flank, "try to get below the fire"; "Use bodies of water" and "heat barriers such as large rocks"; "Structures and vehicles may be an option for temporary refuge". Expect "Extremely heavy ember showers" and a "Superheated air blast" before the flames; lie face down, protect your airway, and "WHEN IN DOUBT, WAIT IT OUT" (p. 47). You have no fire shelter: a pond or plowed ground is your last refuge (rule of thumb).
getting-out-and-last-resort

Hours before the front 1. Protective clothing on: "always first thing to do" (CFA, p. 8). Anyone not defending leaves now. 2. Fill the bath, buckets and tanks; roll out hoses; set up and test pumps and backpack sprayers (CFA, p. 7). 3. Clear the walls: furniture, doormats and BBQ cylinders away; inside, furniture away from windows (same page); cloth curtains down unless the blinds are metal (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). 4. Close up: windows, doors, vent covers; gas off at the tank (same page); fans off so they can't draw embers in (P-737, pp. 42–43); wet wool blankets or cotton towels around the inside of windows and doors (CFA, p. 8); a ladder under the attic hatch and a flashlight in the attic (p. 7). 5. Wet the house: fill the gutters, "Hose down the side of the house facing the fire", sprinklers on when embers appear; "Patrol for embers ... You may need to do this for several hours"; "Drink lots of cool water" (CFA, p. 8).
hours-before-the-front

As the front passes: shelter inside "As the fire front approaches it will become extremely hot outside. You will be unable to survive out in the open" (CFA, p. 9). Bring plastic hoses and fittings in, and go inside when "The skin on your ears and hands will alert you" (same page). Then: - Stay where you can see the fire. "Most bathrooms are unsuitable to shelter in": one door. Every shelter room needs two ways out; a window counts. Check the roof space for embers; drink water. - If the house catches fire: shut the door on the burning room, close doors as you move to the far end, then go out to burned ground. "Do not return to the house for any reason if it's on fire." "If it's hot inside the house, it is four to five times hotter outside" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). The flames pass quickly: about a minute in one spot for a crown fire (Cohen, p. 3).
as-the-front-passes-shelter-inside

Right after: ember patrol "Exercise extreme caution before deciding to go outside", then "Actively patrol your property for embers for hours after the fire has passed" (CFA, p. 10): roof lines and gutters, garden beds and mulch, outdoor furniture, woodpiles, doormats, decks, sheds, window ledges and door sills, under the house, inside the roof and under the floorboards (same page), and the attic (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). "Water down the outside of the house, including the roof" (CFA, p. 10); stay clear of "the structural collapse zone" (IRPG, p. 31). Duff, stumps and log piles smolder for days: patrol day and night for at least 3 days, then daily for 2 weeks and after every dry, windy day (rule of thumb).
right-after-ember-patrol

😷 Smoke, heat and people Protective clothing (CFA, p. 7): a wide-brimmed hat, smoke goggles, a P2 (N95-type) mask, a long-sleeved collared shirt and long pants of cotton or another natural fibre, "Tough leather garden gloves – not rubber or synthetic", sturdy boots, wool or cotton socks. Many synthetics "can melt or catch fire" (AFH 10-644, p. 177). If your clothes catch fire, "do not run ... Lie down and roll" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 284). A bandana is not a mask. "Cloth face coverings, bandanas (damp or dry), handkerchiefs ... should not be relied on" (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 78). CFA lists a cotton scarf as an option (p. 7); this guide follows the EPA: cotton shields skin from embers, not lungs. Use an N95 or P100 marked "NIOSH", two head straps, no ear loops; a beard breaks the seal; replace it when breathing gets hard; it raises heat-illness risk (EPA Protect Your Lungs, pp. 1–2). For ages 2 to 7 an N95 rarely fits (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 77): children leave early. Smoke and carbon monoxide bring "headaches and visual impairment, then impaired decision-making, and possible death"; rotate people out, and don't sleep where "smoke can concentrate at night" (IRPG, p. 44). With no power for a filter fan, open windows at night to cool off even if some smoke comes in, then close them and the curtains
smoke-heat-and-people

night" (IRPG, p. 44). With no power for a filter fan, open windows at night to cool off even if some smoke comes in, then close them and the curtains by day (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 49); night inversions can hold smoke here, so look first. Heat and burns. Drink "lots of cool water often even if you don't feel thirsty" (CFA, p. 9). Care: Field Care ("Heat and cold in the Valley"; "Burns"); exhaustion: Home Defense ("Stress, fatigue and judgment").
smoke-heat-and-people

🐐 Animals and livestock Leave early, in daylight, to places agreed ahead (PNW 783, pp. 7–8). "Never leave pets behind"; keep them "indoors or leashed" (ODA, p. 2). Horses: Horse guide ("Local dangers"); poultry and rabbits: Rabbits & Chickens. If they must stay (PNW 783, p. 8): a pasture "light on fuel", such as one "heavily grazed", or a ploughed paddock (CFA, p. 4); "remove rugs and halters" (p. 7); "Leave gates open"; feed and water for "seven to 10 days"; irrigation on; electricity and propane off; "disked, plowed or scraped ground" around the barn; dry bedding wetted or removed. A burning barn (4-H Horse, p. 61): "Never lock stall doors". Blindfold a horse that won't lead with a wet cloth. "Do not turn a horse loose, because it might run back into the barn." "Do not risk your own life". After: burned animals may hide pain; badly burned ones may need to be put down (PNW 783, pp. 8–9). Burns "may worsen for up to six (6) weeks"; froth from nose or mouth means fluid in the lungs (ODA, pp. 1–2).
animals-and-livestock

Hot ground, stump holes and mop-up - Stump holes: roots burn underground under hot ash; "Minor burns are often experienced due to burning stump holes" (PMS 465, p. 262). Probe ash with a tool before stepping, and mark holes (rule of thumb). - Mop-up "is normally a slow, tedious job": "break up and scatter burning fuels, then cool them down with water. Dig, scrape, and scatter." Water alone "can actually insulate hot spots" (PMS 465, p. 85). "dig out burning roots" and stir embers into dirt (p. 52). Crews mop up a set distance, "100 feet, 500 feet" (p. 51); do at least 100 ft around buildings (rule of thumb). - Mix ash and dirt "until all steaming and sizzling stops"; "Never just bury a fire" (ODFW, p. 34). A smoldering log can "break out afresh with a rising wind" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 186).
hot-ground-stump-holes-and-mop-up

Burned trees - Warning signs: "Trees burning for any period of time"; "Dead, broken, or burning tops"; "Absence of needles, bark, or limbs"; "Leaning or hung-up trees"; "Potential for trees to domino" (IRPG, p. 36). Mark "No Work Zones" (p. 37). - Fall zone: a circle as wide as the tree is tall, up to 1.5 times, and farther downhill on a slope (FS-1273, p. 36). Trees with recent fire damage fail more (p. 56); near the house, take dead trees down the year they die (p. 84). Felling: Firewood guide ("Felling trees safely").
burned-trees

Ash, ruins and wells - Ash from burned buildings can hold arsenic, lead, asbestos and caustic chemicals; dust masks don't stop asbestos or carbon monoxide. A burned lithium battery that pops, hisses or smokes: move "upwind at least ... (330 feet)" (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 120). - Ash from CCA-treated decks and fences "may contain lethal amounts of arsenic". Mist, don't dry-sweep; wash garden produce; children, pregnant women and elders stay out of cleanup (p. 121). - Fence any new sinkhole, "as it may be a dug well" (OWRD, p. 1). Don't use a propane cylinder with "fire damage" (propane safety, p. 8). - Water: see Water Purification ("After a wildfire") and Water Wells ("Keeping well water clean").
ash-ruins-and-wells

Debris flows and erosion A debris flow is a fast mudflow of soil, rock, trees and ash. On burned land one can start "after only a few minutes of heavy rainfall—about half an inch an hour or more", "days to years after a fire", travel many miles, and hit places "that were neither burned nor received any rain" (USGS, p. 1; Debris flow). USGS (same page): "LEAVE BEFORE A STORM ARRIVES. IF YOU WAIT, YOU ARE TOO LATE"; if you can't, "GET TO HIGH GROUND" (upstairs, the roof, uphill, a tree); listen for "cracking, breaking, roaring, or a fast-moving freight train". With no forecast, people below a burned slope go when the first hard rain of the season starts (rule of thumb). Slowing erosion by hand. Severe heat can make the top few inches of soil shed water ("hydrophobic"); treat first where "streams, roads or buildings are directly downslope" (OSU EM 9562, p. 2). - Contour logs need no fuel: burned trees 6–10 in thick, 10–30 ft long, laid across the slope "in full contact" with the ground so soil settles behind them (EM 9562, p. 3). - Straw mulch at 1–2 tons an acre (p. 2); straw-bale check dams last only "the first few storm events" (p. 3). Don't sow non-native grass: it does little the first year and can "increase fire hazard as they cure" (p. 2).
debris-flows-and-erosion

Replanting - Grasses, shrubs and hardwoods return on their own. For conifers, "Most seed falls within one or two tree lengths" of a seed tree, and bare mineral soil is a good seedbed for most (OSU EM 9561, p. 1). Thick-barked black and Oregon white oaks resist heat; tanoak and canyon live oak "re-sprout after being top-killed" (KBO oak guide, p. 45). - Use seed from "parent trees adapted to local conditions"; plantings fail from poor site preparation, competing plants and animal damage (EM 9561, p. 3). With no nursery, gather cones and seedlings from surviving local trees (rule of thumb). Near the house, plant fire-resistant kinds (PNW 590, p. 7; OSU privacy plants).
replanting

🤝 Neighbors: lookouts, signals and shared breaks "In rural areas, your neighbor can be at your home faster than any emergency response" (EM 9247, p. 2); now they are the only response. "Your Home Ignition Zone overlaps onto adjacent properties" (p. 5), and "your trees may pose a greater risk to your neighbor's home than to your own" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 4). - Lookouts on worst-weather days, in turns, day and night, who know the triggers and sound the alarm "early, not late" (IRPG, p. 21; the rota (rule of thumb)). - Signals: agree an alarm ahead (Signals guide: "Whistles, bells and alarm codes", "The neighborhood OK/HELP plan"; Radio guide). Give a fire's "exact location" (ODFW, p. 34). No signal fires in fire season. - A meeting place such as a mailbox cluster, crossroads or central barn (MYN Rural, p. 1), and a road map of water, gates, fuel breaks, hazards and livestock (PNW 783, p. 7). - A road crew clears brush along the shared road out and keeps shared water signed and clear (P-737, p. 77). Mow or slash a 3 m (10 ft) break around each property (CFA, p. 4), joined along the lines; small owners can pool work (EC 1575, p. 3). - A new smoke is the best chance to stop a fire and also where firefighters die (IRPG, p. 19): go with tools
neighbors-lookouts-signals-and-shared-breaks

can pool work (EC 1575, p. 3). - A new smoke is the best chance to stop a fire and also where firefighters die (IRPG, p. 19): go with tools and water, LCES first (rule of thumb). Organizing: Community & Barter ("Forming a neighborhood group"; "Keeping watch").
neighbors-lookouts-signals-and-shared-breaks

🍂 Burning on purpose: wet season only The books put the fire season at June through September (AH 360, p. 211), but east winds peak in September and fall can stay dry. This library's rule: no open burning June–October, until real rain (rule of thumb). Oregon allowed burning only outside fire season, on burn days, with fines "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1), a permit from ODF and the fire district (EC 1574, p. 4), and liability "if the fire escapes" (p. 3). What not to burn, and the burn barrel: Sanitation ("Burning trash and brush, and ash"). Slash piles (EC 1574, pp. 3–4): 1. In the open, 10 ft from trees, snags and brush, 100 ft from streams, away from buildings, propane and power lines. 2. Twigs under ½ in at the bottom, limbs parallel, at least 4 ft wide and 4 ft high; cover it when about 80% built so it will light in the rain. 3. Burn "during daylight, and when it's wet or rainy with little or no wind", with "a shovel and water nearby". 4. Check it after: piles "may smolder for days or even weeks, roaring back to life in windy, warm weather, even during dry winter conditions" (p. 3). Stir and drown the last of it; look again after the next dry, windy day (rule of thumb). "Many wildfires start from
burning-on-purpose-wet-season-only

weather, even during dry winter conditions" (p. 3). Stir and drown the last of it; look again after the next dry, windy day (rule of thumb). "Many wildfires start from escaped burn piles", and broadcast burning around homes is "very risky" (EM 9184, p. 14). Never burn poison oak (p. 25). Fire in the oak woods. The region's low-elevation oak woodlands are "fire adapted", kept by "Relatively frequent low- to mixed-severity fire"; prescribed burns there go "prior to leaf out in the spring or after leaf fall in the autumn" (KBO oak guide, p. 45). Cultural burning, the way the valley's first peoples tended the land with fire, is covered in "Tending the land with fire" in Skills of the Valley's First Peoples (Cultural burning).
burning-on-purpose-wet-season-only

☢️ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals — shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides — are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast — 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it — the flash can blind you even when you are too far away for the blast to hurt you (FEMA H-20, p. 14). The blast wave can arrive many seconds later — stay down until it passes. Being outdoors in the first minute can mean burns, cuts from flying glass and broken bones (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 76). What happens in those seconds: 🖼️ flash, heat and blast drawing; Effects of nuclear explosions, Flash blindness. - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15–30 minutes; 100–200 miles downwind, often 5–10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20, p. 7; 🖼️ how fallout comes down; Nuclear fallout) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed., p. 54) - Know the sirens. A 3–5 minute steady blast means "turn on the radio." A 3–5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning — go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12; what they look like: Civil defense siren) First-hour

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). See the 🖼️ FEMA drawing of protection inside different buildings and Fallout shelter. Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own (Planning Guidance, p. 76). Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A — see the 🖼️ Door-Covered Trench Shelter and 🖼️ Pole-Covered Trench Shelter drawings). Permanent backyard plans: 🖼️ FEMA H-12-1 outside concrete shelter, 🖼️ FEMA H-12-2 aboveground shelter. - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go; 🖼️ CDC picture: best places inside a building) - No need to tape windows or hang plastic sheeting — fallout shelters don't have to be airtight. A building with minor damage still works if it is structurally sound. (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 31;

⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). (FEMA H-20, p. 8; see the 🖼️ seven-ten rule chart and the 🖼️ decay curve for the first two days) | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12–24 hours unless officials say otherwise or fire, collapse or a medical emergency forces you out (FEMA Planning Guidance, pp. 53, 76). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20, p. 9). USDA adds that where fallout is light or moderate you might be able to come out for part of each day after 2–3 days (PA-515, p. 6). - Late fallout decays more slowly where you are — if it arrives 8 hours after the blast, it takes about two days to fall to one-tenth (KFM report ORNL-5040, p. 69). - Gritty dust on ledges, cars or walks after an attack = assume fallout (H-20, p. 33). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below.

🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC Decontamination; EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 32; pictures: 🖼️ CDC step-by-step sheet, 🖼️ FEMA self-decontamination steps, Radioactive contamination) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can, and do it gently so dust doesn't shake loose. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo — no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. Keep suds out of your mouth and don't swallow the water. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. No clean clothes? Take off the outer layer, shake or brush it off, put it back on, then rewash your hands and face. - A cut or wound with fallout in it: flush with plenty of clean water or saline, or keep it covered (EPA Q&A, p. 33). - Visitors: have them strip the outer layer, bag it, and wash before coming in — then they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing

they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, keep your cuts (and theirs) covered, rinse completely, then wash yourself (EPA Q&A, p. 44). - Fallout looks like sand, ash or grit (🖼️ photos of real fallout particles). Brush or hose it off roofs and away from the house after levels drop; wear a dust mask, gloves and a hat, and wash afterward. 💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to — or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). Iodine dietary supplements aren't either — use only FDA-approved KI. (CDC How KI Works; FDA, p. 12; 🖼️ CDC picture sheet: how KI fills the thyroid; where the gland is: Thyroid) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3–4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Making liquid KI for children — the two FDA sheets give the same recipe for one 130 mg tablet or two 65 mg tablets (FDA, one 130 mg tablet; FDA, two 65 mg tablets): 1. Put the tablet(s) in a small bowl with 4 teaspoons of water. Soak 1 minute. 2. Crush with the back of a spoon until there are no large pieces. 3. 🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 29; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside — bag the wiping cloths. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear — then wash and peel it. Leafy vegetables: strip the outer leaves of cabbage and lettuce and wash the rest thoroughly. Roots and tubers: normal washing and peeling is enough. Fruit: wash before eating. (FB 2107, p. 14; PA-515, p. 7) - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine — the radioactive iodine (Iodine-131) decays away (it loses half its strength every 8 days — USDA Ag Handbook 234, p. 9; USDA puts the wait at 30–60 days — PA-515, p. 8). If you have a baby, keep canned or dry milk in a protected place. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay

and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water — or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. Then disinfect as usual. - Cover rain barrels, tanks and well heads ahead of time. (Rain barrel) Water sources, safest first (NWSS 1979, pp. 76–77): deep wells and covered tanks → covered shallow wells → deep lakes → shallow ponds → streams (worst after the first heavy rains) → roof runoff → melted snow. With the power off, a well can still be used with a homemade bail-can on a rope (🖼️ bail-can drawing; Well). Settling method (NWSS 1979, pp. 78–79): 1. Fill a bucket three-quarters full of the doubtful water. 2. Dig clay or clayey soil from at least 4 inches below the surface (fallout stays near the top). 3. Stir in about 1 inch of dry clay for every 4 inches of water until it's all suspended. 4. Let it settle at least 6 hours. The clay carries the fallout down. 5. Dip or siphon off the clear water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let

5. Dip or siphon off the clear water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let it settle — PA-515, p. 8.) Earth filter (NWSS 1979, pp. 77–78; 🖼️ cut-away drawing of the filter can): 1. Punch about a dozen nail holes, from the bottom upward, within 2 inches of the center of the bottom of a 5-gallon can or bucket. 2. Put in 1½ inches of washed pebbles, then one layer of towel or burlap cut a bit bigger than the can. 3. Add 6–7 inches of crumbled soil with some clay in it, dug from 4+ inches deep, pressed down in layers. Not pure clay (too tight) or sand (too loose). 4. Cover with one layer of towel held by a few stones. Set the can on sticks over a pan. 5. Pour in (settled) water. Expect about 6 quarts an hour at first, 2 quarts an hour later. If it runs faster than a quart in 10 minutes, repack the soil. Replace the soil after about 50 quarts. Disinfect the filtered water. Disinfecting afterward: boil, or use plain unscented bleach — 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon, double if cloudy or very cold, wait 30 minutes (EPA Emergency Disinfection, pp. 1–2). 📚 Go deeper: Nuclear War

🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, pp. 8–14, PA-516; Oregon ODOE, p. 2) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed — hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins (🖼️ USDA plan: dairy barn with a built-in family fallout shelter; Silage). - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. Fallout on soil decays and is diluted by digging it in. More from USDA FB 2107 (pp. 8–14): - Animals are as sensitive to radiation as people. Crowd them into the barn — they shield each other; ventilation, not floor space, is the limit. Dairy animals first (Dairy cattle) — milk them before fallout arrives if you can, and turn calves in with the cows (pp. 9–11). - Feed: fallout only coats the outside of a haystack or stack of feed bags. Peel off the outer layer and feed the inside; a tarp over a field stack ahead of time is enough (p. 10). - Tanks and ponds: use what's already in a covered tank first. Pond water usually clears in a few days — keep stock off it a few

enough (p. 10). - Tanks and ponds: use what's already in a covered tank first. 📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions — when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale — check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. See it first: 🖼️ photos of a finished KFM, 🖼️ full-scale cut-away drawing. It is a kind of electroscope. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people (Geiger counter). Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation. What a KFM is made of (ORNL-5040, pp. 33, 39): an 8-ounce can (or a cut-down soup can), 2 square feet of aluminum foil, clean thread, clear plastic, doorbell wire. A drying agent goes in the bottom — gypsum from heated drywall, or silica gel, not calcium chloride or salt. Charge it by rubbing a plastic ruler on dry paper (🖼️ the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69–73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the
measuring-radiation

on dry paper (🖼️ the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69–73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the paper scale. 2. Hold it on a stick about 3 feet above the ground for a set time — 1 minute if you have no idea of the level — then read again. The table on the meter turns the drop into a dose rate. 3. Dose = dose rate × time. At 1,200 R/hr, a 30-second dash outside is 10 R. 4. Keep a daily dose record for every person, and use the meter indoors to find the lowest-dose spot in your shelter, then add shielding there. 📍 Our area - The region's only operating nuclear power plant is the Columbia Generating Station at Hanford, Washington — roughly 350 miles from the Illinois Valley, far outside its planning zones. (Oregon ODOE, p. 1; Columbia Generating Station, Hanford Site) Its zones are a 10-mile plume zone (Oregon is not in it) and a 50-mile ingestion zone that reaches parts of northern Oregon (ODOE, p. 2). - The more realistic threats here are fallout drifting from detonations elsewhere and fallout carried across the Pacific on west winds. After Chernobyl (Chernobyl disaster), radioactive iodine showed up in milk in northwest Oregon. (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1987) Even in the 1960s, Chinese test fallout put measurable radioactive iodine in American milk (NWSS 1979, pp. 117–118). Winds across the U.S. run mostly west to east, but change day to day (FEMA H-20, p. 7). - OISM, publisher of Nuclear War Survival Skills, is in Cave Junction — the printed edition (with accurate KFM patterns) may be easy to get locally (Nuclear War Survival Skills). - Stay tuned locally: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts on seven frequencies, 162.400–162.550 MHz (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 167; NOAA Weather Radio). ⚡ EMP, Solar Storms & Faraday Cages What a nuclear electromagnetic pulse (EMP) or a severe solar storm would really do, how to protect radios, solar gear and this library, how to build and test a Faraday container, what to do when a solar-storm warning comes, and how to check and repair equipment afterward. It's based on what government tests actually measured, not internet stories. The reports are in EMP-Solar-Storms\ (Effects-and-Threat, Protection-Shielding, Grounding-Surge, Recovery). ### The short version - The danger comes in through long wires — power lines, antennas, long cables. Small gear that isn't plugged into anything mostly survives. - Unplugged, switched-off cars and trucks were not affected in tests; a few running ones stalled and restarted. - A solar storm threatens the power grid, not your phone. You'd likely get 18–72 hours' warning. - The real long-term problem is the grid going down for months. Plan for that (see the off-grid power section of the Illinois Valley guide). - Keep spares and a second copy of this library in a metal container, sealed at the seams.

⚡ Two different threats | | Nuclear EMP (a bomb exploded high above the U.S.) | Solar storm (geomagnetic storm, like 1859, 1921, 1989, May 2024) | | Warning | None | 18–72 hours after the Sun erupts; 20–45 min final warning (CISA, p. 21) | | Parts | E1: a pulse rising in billionths of a second — hits electronics through wires and antennas. E2: like lightning over a huge area. E3: slow, seconds to minutes — like a solar storm (EMP Commission 2004, p. 13; 🖼️ the three parts drawn) | Like a weak, hours-long E3 only — no fast pulse (Geomagnetically induced current) | | What it hits | Electronics connected to wires/antennas; computers and control systems; the power grid | Very long conductors: power lines, big transformers, pipelines, long phone cables. Also GPS and HF radio | | What it doesn't | People (a high-altitude burst puts no radiation on the ground) | Unplugged phones, laptops, radios, cars, solar panels | Why only long wires matter in a solar storm: the storm induces a few volts per kilometer — measured worst cases are about 7–20 V/km, and under 1.1 V/km in Colorado during the May 2024 storm (Meta-R-319; LANL 2024 storm study). A 6-ft cord sees hundredths of a volt; a 100-mile power line sees hundreds to thousands (rule of thumb arithmetic). In 1989 that was

In 1989 that was enough to collapse Quebec's grid in 90 seconds and destroy a large transformer in New Jersey — and big transformers take about a year to replace (Meta-R-319, p. 149; 🖼️ photo of transformer damage from the 1989 storm; 🖼️ map of how far the 1989 storm reached; March 1989 geomagnetic storm, Transformer). E1 isn't the same strength everywhere: it's strongest south of the point under the burst, and averages only about a tenth of the peak over the affected area (Meta-R-320, p. 38; 🖼️ the "smile" map of E1 strength; 🖼️ how one high burst covers a continent). 🔬 What the tests actually found | Claim | What testing showed | | "Every car will die." | 37 cars and 18 trucks were tested up to about 50 kV/m. Vehicles that were off: no effects. Of running cars, 3 stalled (at 30 kV/m or more) and needed a restart; one had dashboard electronics damaged; most just had blinking lights. Of running trucks, 3 stalled — 2 restarted at once, 1 needed towing (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). | | "All electronics fry." | Handheld and vehicle radios — stored, idle or operating — had no damage up to 50 kV/m; some locked up and worked after switching off and on (EMP Commission 2008, p. 169). Plugged-in household gear: at 6.7 kV/m 20% were upset (fixed by power-cycling); at 16.6 kV/m about 6% were damaged — mostly items on antenna cables (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). | | "Pocket radios are useless after." | Small battery radios weren't damaged unless near cables carrying huge currents (DCPA 1975). | | "Solar panels get destroyed." | Panels hit with up to 100 kV/m showed only very minor change (Sandia, p. 39; 🖼️ panels in the test chamber); rooftop microinverters survived 20–60 kV pulses (Sandia microinverter tests). The surge travels down the panel wires toward the charge controller/inverter — that's the part to keep a spare of. | | "A surge strip

🔌 Rule one: unplug and disconnect Wires are the antennas. Even a few feet of cable can pick up thousands of volts from E1; long power and antenna lines pick up far more (Low Cost EMP Protection (Navy 1982)). (CISA guidelines, p. 44; 🖼️ drawing: E1 reaches a radio the way a broadcast or lightning does) - Unplug at the device — power, data and antenna cables — not just at the wall. Coil any cable you can't remove. - Pull battery packs from small electronics in storage; turn phones and radios off and take them off chargers. - Disconnect outdoor antennas and coax (Coaxial cable) from radios when not in use. - Unplug everything or nothing: pulling only a TV's power cord while it stays on cable or phone lines removes its ground path (NIST Surges Happen, p. 11; 🖼️ NIST drawing of a surge crossing between two connections). - Backup generators: don't leave one connected to the grid through an automatic transfer switch without strong surge protection — the utility line can carry the pulse in (CISA, p. 45; Transfer switch). A generator stored disconnected is far better off. - Surge protectors still help with lightning and the surge when power comes back — just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses (Surge protector). 📚 Go deeper: CISA EMP Protection and Resilience Guidelines —

🗑️ Faraday containers: building one that works How it works: a closed metal shell keeps the pulse on the outside. It only works if the shell is continuous — the leaks are at seams, lid edges and holes, and a long narrow slot leaks far more than a round hole. Seams must be bare metal touching bare metal (no paint) (MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1, p. 275; 🖼️ how fields leak through an opening; 🖼️ a badly joined seam, warped between rivets; Electromagnetic shielding). A plain metal box is not automatically a Faraday cage — ordinary cabinets gave little protection until their seams were taped and gasketed (Navy 1982). Options, best to simplest (CISA, pp. 45, 86): 1. Metal can with a tight metal lid (galvanized trash can, paint can, cookie tin, steel ammo can — Waste container, Ammunition box): - Wrap each item in a plastic or paper bag or cardboard so it doesn't touch the metal. - Seal the lid seam with conductive tape (aluminum or copper foil tape — the kind with conductive glue) all the way around. Trash cans leak at the lid, handles and base unless sealed. - Ammo cans: the rubber gasket breaks metal contact — scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼️

scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼️ right and wrong ways through a shield). 2. Foil wrap: item in a plastic bag, then 2 or more layers of heavy-duty foil, every seam folded and overlapped, any cables inside the wrap (Aluminium foil; folded-over joint: 🖼️ overlap seam). 3. Nesting adds protection: a foil-wrapped item inside a sealed metal can is better than either alone. 4. Microwave oven (unplugged, never switched on; Microwave oven): an expedient shield for small items — test it first. Weak or useless: Mylar food bags (little protection); refrigerators (plastic liner and rubber gasket); many cheap "Faraday bags" (the closure leaks). Does it need a ground wire? No — a closed storage container doesn't need to be grounded (rule of thumb). How good is good enough? For stored spare electronics, CISA considers 20 dB of shielding adequate (CISA appendix, p. 126); critical military gear uses 80 dB (DHS 2022). See the difference: 🖼️ modeled damage with 0, 10, 20 and 30 dB of protection; what "dB" means: Decibel. Testing yours (and what it doesn't prove): - Put a phone inside and call it, and a battery AM/FM radio tuned to a station. If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell
faraday-containers-building-one-that-works

prove): - Put a phone inside and call it, and a battery AM/FM radio tuned to a station. If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell has no big leaks at those frequencies. - This is a rough check, not a measurement — silence just means the signal dropped below what the radio can hear. The AM test matters most (low frequencies are hardest to block). Close the lid the same way every time (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: CISA guidelines — foil and container methods, pp. 45 & 86; MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1 — seams and slots, p. 275; Wikipedia: Faraday cage.

📦 What to keep in it From CISA's list plus practical extras (rule of thumb where not cited): - A second copy of this library on a USB drive or small SSD — and a cheap laptop or tablet with its charger to read it. Or build the Ammo-Can Library Computer: a Raspberry Pi that lives in a sealed can and shares the library and AI to phones when you open it. - Battery AM/FM/NOAA weather radio, and a handheld ham or GMRS radio with a spare antenna (CISA, p. 44). - Spare solar charge controller and a small inverter — the parts of a solar system most at risk (Charge controller, Power inverter). - Multimeter (Multimeter), LED flashlights/headlamps, rechargeable batteries and a small USB solar charger. - Spare fuses (vehicle, equipment, solar), spare surge protectors and MOVs (Fuse), Varistor). - Small spare electronics you depend on (a phone, a radio's spare power supply). - For older vehicles, a spare ignition module or electronic part if you can get one. Handheld gear with no long wires attached is fairly tough anyway; the container is cheap insurance (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: ORNL — radio communications and spare-equipment procedures; CISA — Level 1 steps for small equipment, p. 44; Radio guide.

☀️ When a solar-storm warning comes Pictures of where a storm starts: 🖼️ the May 2024 sunspot group; 🖼️ computer model of its eruptions heading for Earth; Coronal mass ejection, Sunspot. NOAA rates geomagnetic storms G1 to G5 (NOAA Space Weather Scales): | Level | How often (per 11-year cycle) | What happens | | G3 strong | ~200 | Grid voltage corrections; GPS and HF radio come and go; auroras as far south as Oregon (Aurora) | | G4 severe | ~100 | Widespread grid voltage problems; some protection systems trip; GPS degraded for hours | | G5 extreme | ~4 | Grid collapse and transformer damage possible; HF radio out 1–2 days; GPS degraded for days | For a G4–G5 warning (rule of thumb): 1. Charge batteries, power banks, radios and laptops; fill water containers; get fuel. 2. Unplug sensitive electronics from the wall — the risk is outages and surges when power returns. 3. Disconnect long outdoor antennas and feedlines. 4. Expect GPS and HF radio to be unreliable; have paper maps (Maps\) and use VHF/UHF locally. 5. Solar panels don't need protecting from a solar storm — their wiring is far too short. (S5 "solar panel damage" on NOAA's scale means satellites.) 6. Have the generator ready, connected only through a transfer switch or interlock — never backfeed. 📚 Go deeper: NOAA scales, p. 1; LANL

🔧 After an event: check and repair 1. Power-cycle anything that's locked up — in tests most "upsets" cleared this way (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). 2. Vehicles: restart. If one won't run, disconnect the battery for several minutes to reset the electronics, then check fuses (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). 3. Fuses and breakers (Circuit breaker): a surge protector firing can blow the equipment's fuse — check and replace. Breakers are likely fine; reset them (ORNL radio study; Sandia breakers). 4. Surge protectors fail one of two ways: no power, or power with no protection left. Replace any that took a hit (NIST Surges Happen, p. 7). 5. Look and sniff: burnt smell, scorch marks, swollen or leaking capacitors. Discharge big capacitors before touching (inverters, microwaves, power supplies). What to look for: 🖼️ scorch marks where a capacitor blew off a board; 🖼️ a resistor exploding under a test pulse; swollen capacitors: Capacitor plague. 6. Radios: if dead, suspect the antenna input stage and power supply first — those took the damage in tests (ORNL radio study). 7. Solar: panels are probably fine; test the charge controller and inverter; swap in shielded spares. 8. Generators: check the output breaker, brushes and voltage regulator — see the Engines guide. 9. Expect the grid to stay down a long time — the EMP Commission expected months to years for recovery (Executive

Hypothermia Prevention Monitoring and Management CPG 23 (Joint Trauma System 2023). Keeping injured, bleeding and burned people warm: insulation from the ground, wet clothing, vapor barriers, safe use of heat packs. Public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Trauma-Bleeding.

Prolonged Casualty Care Guidelines CPG 91 (Joint Trauma System 2021). What to do hour by hour when evacuation is delayed or impossible: re-checking and converting tourniquets, shock, oral fluids, infection, monitoring. US government, public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Trauma-Bleeding.

WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care - Approach to the Acutely Ill and Injured (WHO 2018). ABCDE check of any sick or hurt person, trauma, breathing trouble, shock, confusion, burns chart, recovery position, splinting, spine care. CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. In Medical / Field-Care / Trauma-Bleeding.

Acute Traumatic Wound Management in Prolonged Field Care CPG 62 (Joint Trauma System 2017). Burn Wound Management in Prolonged Field Care CPG 57 (Joint Trauma System 2017). Sizing burns, drinking-based fluid replacement when there is no IV, urine targets, blisters, daily dressing care, pain control. Public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Wounds-Burns-Fractures.

Sepsis Management in Prolonged Field Care CPG 83 (Joint Trauma System 2020). Spotting an infection that has spread to the whole body (fever, fast pulse and breathing, confusion) before blood pressure falls, and what to do. Public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Wounds-Burns-Fractures.

Snakebite Envenomation CPG 81 (Joint Trauma System 2026). Current snakebite care incl. North American rattlesnakes: what to do, and the outdated first aid (bands, cutting, suction, ice) that must not be done. Public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Wounds-Burns-Fractures.

Spider and Scorpion Envenomation CPG 84 (Joint Trauma System 2026). Black widow and recluse-type bites: signs, pain control, wound care, what not to do. Public domain. In Medical / Field-Care / Wounds-Burns-Fractures.

Surgical Care at the District Hospital (WHO 2003). WHO all rights reserved, free download. In Medical / Field-Care / Wounds-Burns-Fractures.

War Surgery - Working with Limited Resources Vol 1 (ICRC 2010). Special Forces Medical Handbook ST 31-91B 1982. US Army ST 31-91B Special Forces Medical Handbook (1 March 1982), searchable scan; austere diagnosis and treatment; its drug information is now outdated (public domain). In Medical / Manuals-PDF.

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL PATTERN FOR SURVIVAL Develop a survival pattern that lets you beat the enemies of survival. This survival pattern must include food, water, shelter, fire, first aid, and signals placed in order of importance. For example, in a cold environment, you would need a fire to get warm; a shelter to protect you from the cold, wind, and rain or snow; traps or snares to get food; a means to signal friendly aircraft; and first aid to maintain health. If injured, first aid has top priority no matter what climate you are in. Change your survival pattern to meet your immediate physical needs as the environment changes. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 2 - PSYCHOLOGY OF SURVIVAL It takes much more than the knowledge and skills to build shelters, get food, make fires, and travel without the aid of standard navigational devices to live successfully through a survival situation. Some people with little or no survival training have managed to survive life-threatening circumstances. Some people with survival training have not used their skills and died. A key ingredient in any survival situation is the mental attitude of the individual(s) involved. Having survival skills is important; having the will to survive is essential. Without a desk to survive, acquired skills serve little purpose and invaluable knowledge goes to waste. There is a psychology to survival. The soldier in a survival environment faces many stresses that ultimately impact on his mind. These stresses can produce thoughts and emotions that, if poorly understood, can transform a confident, well-trained soldier into an indecisive, ineffective individual with questionable ability to survive. Thus, every soldier must be aware of and be able to recognize those stresses commonly associated with survival. Additionally, it is imperative that soldiers be aware of their reactions to the wide variety of stresses associated with survival. This

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL Any event can lead to stress and, as everyone has experienced, events don't always come one at a time. Often, stressful events occur simultaneously. These events are not stress, but they produce it and are called "stressors." Stressors are the obvious cause while stress is the response. Once the body recognizes the presence of a stressor, it then begins to act to protect itself. In response to a stressor, the body prepares either to "fight or flee." This preparation involves an internal SOS sent throughout the body. As the body responds to this SOS, several actions take place. The body releases stored fuels (sugar and fats) to provide quick energy; breathing rate increases to supply more oxygen to the blood; muscle tension increases to prepare for action; blood clotting mechanisms are activated to reduce bleeding from cuts; senses become more acute (hearing becomes more sensitive, eyes become big, smell becomes sharper) so that you are more aware of your surrounding and heart rate and blood pressure rise to provide more blood to the muscles. Stressors are not courteous; one stressor does not leave because another one arrives. Stressors add up. Anger and Frustration Frustration arises when a person is continually thwarted in his attempts to reach a goal. The goal of survival is to stay alive until you can reach help or until help can reach you. To achieve this goal, the soldier must complete some tasks with minimal resources. It is inevitable, in trying to do these tasks, that something will go wrong; that something will happen beyond the soldier's control; and that with one's life at stake, every mistake is magnified in terms of its importance. Thus, sooner or later, soldiers will have to cope with frustration when a few of their plans run into trouble. One outgrowth of this frustration is anger. There are many events in a survival situation that can frustrate or anger a soldier. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 5 - SHELTERS A shelter can protect you from the sun, insects, wind, rain, snow, hot or cold temperatures, and enemy observation. It can give you a feeling of well-being. It can help you maintain your will to survive. In some areas, your need for shelter may take precedence over your need for food and possibly even your need for water. For example, prolonged exposure to cold can cause excessive fatigue and weakness (exhaustion). An exhausted person may develop a "passive" outlook, thereby losing the will to survive. The most common error in making a shelter is to make it too large. A shelter must be large enough to protect you. It must also be small enough to contain your body heat, especially in cold climates. Natural Shelters Do not overlook natural formations that provide shelter. Examples are caves, rocky crevices, clumps of bushes, small depressions, large rocks on leeward sides of hills, large trees with low-hanging limbs, and fallen trees with thick branches.
